title: 2D and 3D cell cultures – a comparison of different types of cancer cell cultures
abstract: Cell culture is a widely used in vitro tool for improving our understanding of cell biology, tissue morphology, and mechanisms of diseases, drug action, protein production and the development of tissue engineering. Most research regarding cancer biology is based on experiments using two-dimensional (2D) cell cultures in vitro. However, 2D cultures have many limitations, such as the disturbance of interactions between the cellular and extracellular environments, changes in cell morphology, polarity, and method of division. These disadvantages led to the creation of models which are more closely able to mimic conditions in vivo. One such method is three-dimensional culture (3D). Optimisation of the culture conditions may allow for a better understanding of cancer biology and facilitate the study of biomarkers and targeting therapies. In this review, we compare 2D and 3D cultures in vitro as well as different versions of 3D cultures.

title: 2D and 3D cell cultures – a comparison of different types of cancer cell cultures
abstract: This state-of-the-art review examines the differences between two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) cancer cell culture systems, highlighting their respective advantages and limitations in modeling tumor biology. While 2D cultures are widely used due to their simplicity and cost-effectiveness, they fail to accurately replicate the complex cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions, morphology, and microenvironment found in vivo, leading to altered gene expression and cellular behavior. In contrast, 3D culture models—including suspension cultures, gel-based systems, and scaffold-based approaches—better mimic the architecture and physiological conditions of tumors, preserving cellular polarity, morphology, and heterogeneity. These models facilitate more accurate studies of cancer-initiating cells, invasion, metastasis, drug response, and biomarker discovery. The review underscores the importance of selecting appropriate culture systems for cancer research to enhance the relevance of experimental findings and support the development of effective therapeutic strategies.

title: Astrocytes: biology and pathology
abstract: Astrocytes are specialized glial cells that outnumber neurons by over fivefold. They contiguously tile the entire central nervous system (CNS) and exert many essential complex functions in the healthy CNS. Astrocytes respond to all forms of CNS insults through a process referred to as reactive astrogliosis, which has become a pathological hallmark of CNS structural lesions. Substantial progress has been made recently in determining functions and mechanisms of reactive astrogliosis and in identifying roles of astrocytes in CNS disorders and pathologies. A vast molecular arsenal at the disposal of reactive astrocytes is being defined. Transgenic mouse models are dissecting specific aspects of reactive astrocytosis and glial scar formation in vivo. Astrocyte involvement in specific clinicopathological entities is being defined. It is now clear that reactive astrogliosis is not a simple all-or-none phenomenon but is a finely gradated continuum of changes that occur in context-dependent manners regulated by specific signaling events. These changes range from reversible alterations in gene expression and cell hypertrophy with preservation of cellular domains and tissue structure, to long-lasting scar formation with rearrangement of tissue structure. Increasing evidence points towards the potential of reactive astrogliosis to play either primary or contributing roles in CNS disorders via loss of normal astrocyte functions or gain of abnormal effects. This article reviews (1) astrocyte functions in healthy CNS, (2) mechanisms and functions of reactive astrogliosis and glial scar formation, and (3) ways in which reactive astrocytes may cause or contribute to specific CNS disorders and lesions.

title: Astrocytes: biology and pathology
abstract: Astrocytes, the most abundant glial cell type in the central nervous system (CNS), play critical roles in maintaining CNS homeostasis, supporting neuronal function, and modulating synaptic activity. Traditionally viewed as passive support cells, astrocytes are now recognized for their active participation in information processing and neural circuit regulation. In response to CNS injury or disease, astrocytes undergo reactive astrogliosis, a highly regulated and context-dependent process characterized by a spectrum of molecular and structural changes ranging from reversible gene expression alterations to permanent glial scar formation. Advances in molecular profiling and transgenic mouse models have elucidated the diverse mechanisms underlying reactive astrogliosis and highlighted its dual potential to be either protective or detrimental, depending on the context. Loss of normal astrocyte functions or gain of abnormal effects through reactive changes can contribute to the pathogenesis of various CNS disorders. This review synthesizes recent progress in understanding astrocyte biology in healthy tissue, the mechanisms and consequences of reactive astrogliosis and glial scar formation, and the emerging evidence for astrocyte involvement in specific neuropathological conditions.

title: A decade of systems biology.
abstract: Systems biology provides a framework for assembling models of biological systems from systematic measurements. Since the field was first introduced a decade ago, considerable progress has been made in technologies for global cell measurement and in computational analyses of these data to map and model cell function. It has also greatly expanded into the translational sciences, with approaches pioneered in yeast now being applied to elucidate human development and disease. Here, we review the state of the field with a focus on four emerging applications of systems biology that are likely to be of particular importance during the decade to follow: (a) pathway-based biomarkers, (b) global genetic interaction maps, (c) systems approaches to identify disease genes, and (d) stem cell systems biology. We also cover recent advances in software tools that allow biologists to explore system-wide models and to formulate new hypotheses. The applications and methods covered in this review provide a set of prime exemplars useful to cell and developmental biologists wishing to apply systems approaches to areas of interest.
venue: Annual Review of Cell and Developmental Biology

title: A decade of systems biology.
abstract: Over the past decade, systems biology has emerged as a transformative approach for modeling and understanding complex biological systems through the integration of systematic, genome-scale measurements and computational analyses. This review traces the evolution of the field, highlighting technological advances in high-throughput data generation and the development of analytical frameworks that enable predictive, hypothesis-driven research. Systems biology has expanded from its origins in model organisms to address fundamental questions in human development and disease, influencing areas such as molecular diagnostics, genetic interaction mapping, disease gene identification, and stem cell biology. We discuss the challenges posed by exponential data growth, cellular and genetic heterogeneity, and the need for integrative models that encompass both physical and functional system properties. The review also examines emerging applications—such as pathway-based biomarkers and global genetic interaction maps—and recent progress in software tools that facilitate interactive exploration of system-wide models. Collectively, these advances underscore the increasing relevance of systems approaches for cell and developmental biologists seeking to apply network-based methods to diverse biomedical problems.
venue: Annual Review of Cell and Developmental Biology

title: A Holistic Approach to Marine Eco-Systems Biology
abstract: The structure, robustness, and dynamics of ocean plankton ecosystems remain poorly understood due to sampling, analysis, and computational limitations. The Tara Oceans consortium organizes expeditions to help fill this gap at the global level.

title: A Holistic Approach to Marine Eco-Systems Biology
abstract: Marine ecosystems play a critical role in regulating Earth’s biogeochemical cycles and climate, yet their complexity and dynamics remain insufficiently understood. This paper presents the Tara Oceans project, a global, multidisciplinary initiative that integrates optical and genomic methods to systematically sample and analyze viruses, bacteria, archaea, protists, and metazoans across diverse oceanic environments and depths. By combining traditional and innovative sampling techniques with high-throughput sequencing, quantitative imaging, and advanced bioinformatics, the project generates comprehensive open-access datasets linking organismal diversity to physico-chemical parameters. This holistic approach enables unprecedented insights into the morphological, genetic, and functional biodiversity of planktonic communities, their ecological interactions, and their roles in global biogeochemical processes. The Tara Oceans consortium’s coordinated efforts aim to inform ecosystem modeling, improve predictions of climate impacts and fish stock distributions, and uncover novel bioactive compounds, ultimately advancing our understanding and stewardship of marine ecosystems.

title: A review of imaging techniques for systems biology
abstract: This paper presents a review of imaging techniques and of their utility in system biology. During the last decade systems biology has matured into a distinct field and imaging has been increasingly used to enable the interplay of experimental and theoretical biology. In this review, we describe and compare the roles of microscopy, ultrasound, CT (Computed Tomography), MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging), PET (Positron Emission Tomography), and molecular probes such as quantum dots and nanoshells in systems biology. As a unified application area among these different imaging techniques, examples in cancer targeting are highlighted.

title: A review of imaging techniques for systems biology
abstract: This review examines the diverse imaging techniques that have become integral to systems biology, a field focused on modeling the dynamics and structure of complete biological systems through interdisciplinary approaches. The paper discusses the roles, principles, and applications of microscopy, ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), and molecular probes such as quantum dots and nanoshells. Emphasis is placed on how these modalities enable visualization and quantification of biological processes across multiple spatial and temporal scales, facilitating both experimental investigation and mathematical modeling. The review highlights the iterative interplay between imaging data and computational models, which is central to systems biology’s methodology, and underscores the importance of digital image processing techniques like segmentation and registration for model creation and validation. Cancer research is presented as a key application area, where advances in molecular imaging are accelerating understanding of complex signaling pathways and informing targeted therapeutic strategies. The paper concludes that ongoing improvements in imaging resolution, acquisition speed, and molecular specificity will further enhance the predictive power of systems biology models and drive progress in biomedical research.

title: A systems biology approach for pathway level analysis.
abstract: A common challenge in the analysis of genomics data is trying to understand the underlying phenomenon in the context of all complex interactions taking place on various signaling pathways. A statistical approach using various models is universally used to identify the most relevant pathways in a given experiment. Here, we show that the existing pathway analysis methods fail to take into consideration important biological aspects and may provide incorrect results in certain situations. By using a systems biology approach, we developed an impact analysis that includes the classical statistics but also considers other crucial factors such as the magnitude of each gene's expression change, their type and position in the given pathways, their interactions, etc. The impact analysis is an attempt to a deeper level of statistical analysis, informed by more pathway-specific biology than the existing techniques. On several illustrative data sets, the classical analysis produces both false positives and false negatives, while the impact analysis provides biologically meaningful results. This analysis method has been implemented as a Web-based tool, Pathway-Express, freely available as part of the Onto-Tools (http://vortex.cs.wayne.edu).

title: A systems biology approach for pathway level analysis.
abstract: High-throughput genomics technologies generate extensive lists of differentially expressed genes, yet translating these data into meaningful biological insights remains challenging due to the complexity of signaling pathways and gene interactions. Existing pathway analysis methods, such as over-representation analysis (ORA) and functional class scoring (FCS), assess pathways independently and fail to account for pathway topology, gene roles, and the magnitude of expression changes, often resulting in biologically irrelevant or misleading findings. We present a systems biology-based impact analysis approach that integrates classical statistical significance with critical biological factors, including gene expression magnitude, gene type and position within pathways, and pathway topology. This method calculates an impact factor for each pathway, capturing both the statistical over-representation of differentially expressed genes and their functional influence within the network. Application to multiple datasets demonstrates that impact analysis reduces false positives and negatives compared to traditional methods, yielding results that more accurately reflect underlying biological processes. The approach is implemented in Pathway-Express, a freely available web-based tool, providing researchers with a robust framework for pathway-level interpretation of genomics data.

title: Bioconductor: open software development for computational biology and bioinformatics
abstract: The Bioconductor project is an initiative for the collaborative creation of extensible software for computational biology and bioinformatics. The goals of the project include: fostering collaborative development and widespread use of innovative software, reducing barriers to entry into interdisciplinary scientific research, and promoting the achievement of remote reproducibility of research results. We describe details of our aims and methods, identify current challenges, compare Bioconductor to other open bioinformatics projects, and provide working examples.

title: Bioconductor: open software development for computational biology and bioinformatics
abstract: The Bioconductor project is a collaborative, open-source initiative aimed at developing extensible software tools for computational biology and bioinformatics. Motivated by the increasing computational demands of high-throughput biological data and the need for transparent, reproducible research, Bioconductor provides a flexible environment that lowers barriers to interdisciplinary collaboration and facilitates the adoption of advanced statistical methods by biologists. The project emphasizes open development practices, modular design, comprehensive documentation, and community engagement to ensure efficient software evolution and widespread usability. This paper details the project's organizational strategies, technical infrastructure, and development methodologies, compares Bioconductor to other open bioinformatics platforms, discusses ongoing challenges such as data integration and scalability, and illustrates its utility through practical examples in genomic data analysis.

title: Biology and biotechnology of Trichoderma
abstract: Fungi of the genus Trichoderma are soilborne, green-spored ascomycetes that can be found all over the world. They have been studied with respect to various characteristics and applications and are known as successful colonizers of their habitats, efficiently fighting their competitors. Once established, they launch their potent degradative machinery for decomposition of the often heterogeneous substrate at hand. Therefore, distribution and phylogeny, defense mechanisms, beneficial as well as deleterious interaction with hosts, enzyme production and secretion, sexual development, and response to environmental conditions such as nutrients and light have been studied in great detail with many species of this genus, thus rendering Trichoderma one of the best studied fungi with the genome of three species currently available. Efficient biocontrol strains of the genus are being developed as promising biological fungicides, and their weaponry for this function also includes secondary metabolites with potential applications as novel antibiotics. The cellulases produced by Trichoderma reesei, the biotechnological workhorse of the genus, are important industrial products, especially with respect to production of second generation biofuels from cellulosic waste. Genetic engineering not only led to significant improvements in industrial processes but also to intriguing insights into the biology of these fungi and is now complemented by the availability of a sexual cycle in T. reesei/Hypocrea jecorina, which significantly facilitates both industrial and basic research. This review aims to give a broad overview on the qualities and versatility of the best studied Trichoderma species and to highlight intriguing findings as well as promising applications.

title: Biology and biotechnology of Trichoderma
abstract: Trichoderma species are globally distributed soilborne ascomycetes renowned for their ecological versatility, efficient substrate colonization, and potent degradative enzyme systems. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the biodiversity, phylogeny, and distinguishing characteristics of Trichoderma, highlighting advances in molecular identification and genome sequencing that have clarified species boundaries and evolutionary relationships. The genus exhibits diverse interactions with plant hosts, ranging from beneficial biocontrol to occasional pathogenicity, underpinned by sophisticated defense mechanisms and secondary metabolite production. Trichoderma reesei, in particular, is a cornerstone of industrial biotechnology due to its prolific cellulase production for biofuel generation, with genetic engineering and the recent discovery of a sexual cycle further enhancing its utility in research and industry. The availability of genomic resources for multiple Trichoderma species has facilitated functional studies on environmental response, enzyme regulation, and metabolic adaptation. Collectively, these insights underscore the genus’s significance as both a model organism in fungal biology and a valuable resource for sustainable agricultural and biotechnological applications.

title: Biology and pathogenesis of Acanthamoeba
abstract: Acanthamoeba is a free-living protist pathogen, capable of causing a blinding keratitis and fatal granulomatous encephalitis. The factors that contribute to Acanthamoeba infections include parasite biology, genetic diversity, environmental spread and host susceptibility, and are highlighted together with potential therapeutic and preventative measures. The use of Acanthamoeba in the study of cellular differentiation mechanisms, motility and phagocytosis, bacterial pathogenesis and evolutionary processes makes it an attractive model organism. There is a significant emphasis on Acanthamoeba as a Trojan horse of other microbes including viral, bacterial, protists and yeast pathogens.

title: Biology and pathogenesis of Acanthamoeba
abstract: Acanthamoeba is a ubiquitous free-living protist with a complex biology and significant pathogenic potential, notably causing keratitis and granulomatous encephalitis in humans and animals. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the organism’s life cycle, cellular structure, genetic diversity, and environmental distribution, highlighting its adaptability and resilience through trophozoite and cyst stages. Acanthamoeba’s role as both a direct pathogen and a reservoir for other microorganisms underscores its clinical relevance, particularly among immunocompromised individuals and contact lens users. The organism’s unique cellular features, including actin-based motility and specialized membrane composition, make it a valuable model for studying eukaryotic cell biology, differentiation, and host-pathogen interactions. Understanding the factors influencing Acanthamoeba infections informs the development of targeted therapeutic and preventive strategies, while its ecological versatility raises concerns about emerging risks in both medical and veterinary contexts.

title: Biology in bloom: implementing Bloom's Taxonomy to enhance student learning in biology.
abstract: We developed the Blooming Biology Tool (BBT), an assessment tool based on Bloom's Taxonomy, to assist science faculty in better aligning their assessments with their teaching activities and to help students enhance their study skills and metacognition. The work presented here shows how assessment tools, such as the BBT, can be used to guide and enhance teaching and student learning in a discipline-specific manner in postsecondary education. The BBT was first designed and extensively tested for a study in which we ranked almost 600 science questions from college life science exams and standardized tests. The BBT was then implemented in three different collegiate settings. Implementation of the BBT helped us to adjust our teaching to better enhance our students' current mastery of the material, design questions at higher cognitive skills levels, and assist students in studying for college-level exams and in writing study questions at higher levels of Bloom's Taxonomy. From this work we also created a suite of complementary tools that can assist biology faculty in creating classroom materials and exams at the appropriate level of Bloom's Taxonomy and students to successfully develop and answer questions that require higher-order cognitive skills.

title: Biology in bloom: implementing Bloom's Taxonomy to enhance student learning in biology.
abstract: This study presents the development and implementation of the Blooming Biology Tool (BBT), an assessment instrument grounded in Bloom’s Taxonomy, designed to enhance alignment between biology instruction and assessment in postsecondary education. By categorizing and analyzing nearly 600 biology exam questions from diverse sources, the BBT enables faculty to evaluate the cognitive demands of their assessments and adjust teaching strategies accordingly. The tool was implemented across multiple collegiate settings, facilitating the creation of exam questions and learning activities that target higher-order cognitive skills. Results indicate that the BBT supports both instructors in diagnosing student learning and designing more effective assessments, and students in developing metacognitive awareness and advanced study strategies. The paper also introduces complementary resources to further assist biology educators in fostering critical thinking and deeper conceptual understanding through discipline-specific application of Bloom’s Taxonomy.

title: Biology of breast cancer in young women
abstract: Breast cancer arising at a young age is relatively uncommon, particularly in the developed world. Several studies have demonstrated that younger patients often experience a more aggressive disease course and have poorer outcome compared to older women. Expression of key biomarkers, including endocrine receptors, HER2 and proliferation markers, appears to be different in younger patients and young women are more likely to harbor a genetic predisposition. Despite these differences, little research to date has focused on the biology of these tumors to refine prognosis, and potentially direct treatment strategies, which remain similar to those offered to older patients. Accumulating evidence suggests the differences in breast stroma in younger patients and changes that occur with pregnancy and breastfeeding likely contribute to the different biology of these tumors. Reproductive behaviors appear to impact the biology of tumors developing later in life. In addition, tumors arising during or shortly following pregnancy appear to exhibit unique biological features. In this review, we discuss our emerging understanding of the biology of breast cancer arising at a young age at both the pathologic and the genomic level. We elucidate the potential role of genomic signatures, the impact of pregnancy and breastfeeding on breast cancer biology, and how even current knowledge might advance the clinical management of young breast cancer patients.

title: Biology of breast cancer in young women
abstract: Breast cancer in young women, though relatively rare, is characterized by more aggressive pathological features and poorer outcomes compared to older patients. Young women are more likely to present with larger, higher-grade, node-positive, and endocrine receptor-negative tumors, as well as higher rates of HER2 positivity and basal-like subtypes. Distinct molecular and genomic profiles, including increased PI3K and Myc pathway deregulation, further differentiate these tumors from those in older women. Genetic predisposition is more common in this population, and reproductive factors such as pregnancy and breastfeeding may influence tumor biology and subtype distribution. Despite these differences, treatment strategies for young women largely mirror those for older patients, highlighting a need for research focused on the unique biology of breast cancer in this group to inform prognosis and guide tailored therapies. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the pathological and molecular characteristics of breast cancer in young women, explores the impact of reproductive behaviors, and discusses implications for clinical management.

title: Biology of RANK, RANKL, and osteoprotegerin
abstract: The discovery of the receptor activator of nuclear factor-κB ligand (RANKL)/RANK/osteoprotegerin (OPG) system and its role in the regulation of bone resorption exemplifies how both serendipity and a logic-based approach can identify factors that regulate cell function. Before this discovery in the mid to late 1990s, it had long been recognized that osteoclast formation was regulated by factors expressed by osteoblast/stromal cells, but it had not been anticipated that members of the tumor necrosis factor superfamily of ligands and receptors would be involved or that the factors involved would have extensive functions beyond bone remodeling. RANKL/RANK signaling regulates the formation of multinucleated osteoclasts from their precursors as well as their activation and survival in normal bone remodeling and in a variety of pathologic conditions. OPG protects the skeleton from excessive bone resorption by binding to RANKL and preventing it from binding to its receptor, RANK. Thus, RANKL/OPG ratio is an important determinant of bone mass and skeletal integrity. Genetic studies in mice indicate that RANKL/RANK signaling is also required for lymph node formation and mammary gland lactational hyperplasia, and that OPG also protects arteries from medial calcification. Thus, these tumor necrosis factor superfamily members have important functions outside bone. Although our understanding of the mechanisms whereby they regulate osteoclast formation has advanced rapidly during the past 10 years, many questions remain about their roles in health and disease. Here we review our current understanding of the role of the RANKL/RANK/OPG system in bone and other tissues.

title: Biology of RANK, RANKL, and osteoprotegerin
abstract: The RANK/RANKL/osteoprotegerin (OPG) system, discovered in the late 1990s, is central to the regulation of bone resorption and has expanded our understanding of bone biology and immunology. RANKL, a member of the tumor necrosis factor superfamily, expressed by osteoblasts and stromal cells, binds to its receptor RANK on osteoclast precursors to drive their differentiation, activation, and survival, processes essential for normal bone remodeling and implicated in pathological conditions such as osteoporosis and rheumatoid arthritis. OPG acts as a decoy receptor for RANKL, inhibiting its interaction with RANK and thereby protecting against excessive bone loss; thus, the RANKL/OPG ratio is a key determinant of skeletal integrity. Genetic studies have revealed that this signaling axis also plays roles beyond bone, including lymph node development, mammary gland function, and vascular calcification prevention. The identification of these molecules has provided significant insights into osteoclast biology, the interplay between bone and immune systems, and potential therapeutic targets for skeletal and systemic diseases. This review summarizes current knowledge of the RANK/RANKL/OPG system in bone remodeling and highlights emerging evidence of its broader physiological functions.

title: Biology of the TAM receptors.
abstract: The TAM receptors--Tyro3, Axl, and Mer--comprise a unique family of receptor tyrosine kinases, in that as a group they play no essential role in embryonic development. Instead, they function as homeostatic regulators in adult tissues and organ systems that are subject to continuous challenge and renewal throughout life. Their regulatory roles are prominent in the mature immune, reproductive, hematopoietic, vascular, and nervous systems. The TAMs and their ligands--Gas6 and Protein S--are essential for the efficient phagocytosis of apoptotic cells and membranes in these tissues; and in the immune system, they act as pleiotropic inhibitors of the innate inflammatory response to pathogens. Deficiencies in TAM signaling are thought to contribute to chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease in humans, and aberrantly elevated TAM signaling is strongly associated with cancer progression, metastasis, and resistance to targeted therapies.
venue: Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology

title: Biology of the TAM receptors.
abstract: The TAM receptor family, comprising Tyro3, Axl, and Mer, represents a distinct class of receptor tyrosine kinases that are dispensable for embryonic development but serve critical homeostatic functions in adult tissues. These receptors and their ligands, Gas6 and Protein S, are widely expressed in the immune, reproductive, hematopoietic, vascular, and nervous systems, where they mediate efficient phagocytosis of apoptotic cells and act as pleiotropic inhibitors of innate immune responses. Structural features unique to TAM receptors and their ligands underlie their activation mechanisms and downstream signaling, which predominantly involve the PI3K/AKT pathway but also intersect with cytokine receptor pathways such as JAK/STAT in immune cells. Genetic ablation studies in mice reveal that loss of TAM signaling leads to degenerative phenotypes in adult tissues subject to continuous renewal, highlighting their essential roles in tissue maintenance and immune regulation. Dysregulation of TAM signaling is implicated in chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases as well as cancer progression and therapeutic resistance. This review synthesizes current understanding of TAM receptor biology, emphasizing their structural characteristics, signaling pathways, evolutionary emergence, and significance in health and disease.
venue: Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology

title: Biopython: freely available Python tools for computational molecular biology and bioinformatics
abstract: The Biopython project is a mature open source international collaboration of volunteer developers, providing Python libraries for a wide range of bioinformatics problems. Biopython includes modules for reading and writing different sequence file formats and multiple sequence alignments, dealing with 3D macro molecular structures, interacting with common tools such as BLAST, ClustalW and EMBOSS, accessing key online databases, as well as providing numerical methods for statistical learning. Availability: Biopython is freely available, with documentation and source code at www.biopython.org under the Biopython license. Contact: All queries should be directed to the Biopython mailing lists, see www.biopython.org/wiki/_Mailing_listspeter.cock@scri.ac.uk.

title: Biopython: freely available Python tools for computational molecular biology and bioinformatics
abstract: Biopython is a comprehensive open-source collection of Python libraries designed to facilitate computational molecular biology and bioinformatics. Developed through international collaboration, Biopython provides modules for reading and writing a wide range of sequence and alignment file formats, manipulating biological sequences and annotations, parsing macromolecular structures, and interfacing with widely used tools such as BLAST, ClustalW, and EMBOSS. The toolkit also supports access to key online databases, statistical learning methods, population genetics analyses, and graphical visualization of genomic data. With its extensible object-oriented framework and integration with other open bioinformatics projects, Biopython serves both as an application programming interface for software development and as a resource for routine bioinformatics scripting tasks. Freely available under an open license, Biopython is supported by extensive documentation and an active user community.

title: Bright ideas for chemical biology.
abstract: Small-molecule fluorescent probes embody an essential facet of chemical biology. Although numerous compounds are known, the ensemble of fluorescent probes is based on a modest collection of modular 'core' dyes. The elaboration of these dyes with diverse chemical moieties is enabling the precise interrogation of biochemical and biological systems. The importance of fluorescence-based technologies in chemical biology elicits a necessity to understand the major classes of small-molecule fluorophores. Here, we examine the chemical and photophysical properties of oft-used fluorophores and highlight classic and contemporary examples in which utility has been built upon these scaffolds.

title: Bright ideas for chemical biology.
abstract: Small-molecule fluorescent probes are fundamental tools in chemical biology, enabling the visualization and interrogation of diverse biochemical and biological processes. Despite the vast number of available probes, most are derived from a limited set of modular core fluorophores that can be chemically tailored for specific applications. This review surveys the major classes of small-molecule fluorophores, examining their chemical structures, photophysical properties, and practical considerations for probe selection and design. Historical developments, including the origins of fluorescence and the evolution of synthetic dyes, are discussed alongside contemporary advances such as quantum dots and fluorescent proteins. The review highlights how understanding the strengths, limitations, and optimal uses of each dye class empowers researchers to leverage fluorescence-based technologies for innovative studies in chemical biology.

title: Cation-π interactions in structural biology
abstract: Cation-pi interactions in protein structures are identified and evaluated by using an energy-based criterion for selecting significant sidechain pairs. Cation-pi interactions are found to be common among structures in the Protein Data Bank, and it is clearly demonstrated that, when a cationic sidechain (Lys or Arg) is near an aromatic sidechain (Phe, Tyr, or Trp), the geometry is biased toward one that would experience a favorable cation-pi interaction. The sidechain of Arg is more likely than that of Lys to be in a cation-pi interaction. Among the aromatics, a strong bias toward Trp is clear, such that over one-fourth of all tryptophans in the data bank experience an energetically significant cation-pi interaction.

title: Cation-π interactions in structural biology
abstract: Cation-π interactions, noncovalent forces between cationic and aromatic sidechains, are increasingly recognized as important contributors to protein structure and stability. In this study, we present a comprehensive analysis of cation-π interactions in proteins using an energy-based criterion derived from a modified OPLS force field, focusing on the electrostatic component to identify energetically significant pairs. Applying this protocol to a large dataset of high-resolution protein structures from the Protein Data Bank, we find that cation-π interactions are common, with arginine more frequently involved than lysine and tryptophan showing the strongest aromatic preference. Our results reveal that over one-fourth of all tryptophans participate in significant cation-π interactions and that these contacts are biased toward geometries favorable for such interactions. The study establishes a robust, generalizable method for identifying cation-π interactions and underscores their prevalence and potential structural roles in proteins.

title: CellProfiler 3.0: Next-generation image processing for biology
abstract: CellProfiler has enabled the scientific research community to create flexible, modular image analysis pipelines since its release in 2005. Here, we describe CellProfiler 3.0, a new version of the software supporting both whole-volume and plane-wise analysis of three-dimensional (3D) image stacks, increasingly common in biomedical research. CellProfiler’s infrastructure is greatly improved, and we provide a protocol for cloud-based, large-scale image processing. New plugins enable running pretrained deep learning models on images. Designed by and for biologists, CellProfiler equips researchers with powerful computational tools via a well-documented user interface, empowering biologists in all fields to create quantitative, reproducible image analysis workflows.

title: CellProfiler 3.0: Next-generation image processing for biology
abstract: CellProfiler 3.0 is a major update to the open-source image analysis software designed for biological research, introducing support for three-dimensional (3D) image stack analysis, enhanced infrastructure for large-scale and cloud-based processing, and integration with deep learning models through new plugins. The software maintains its modular, user-friendly interface tailored for biologists, enabling flexible and reproducible quantitative workflows without requiring programming expertise. Improvements in performance, installation, and documentation further lower barriers to adoption, while expanded capabilities for 3D object identification and measurement address the growing prevalence of multidimensional imaging in biomedical research. CellProfiler 3.0 thus empowers researchers to efficiently analyze complex image datasets and fosters reproducibility and collaboration within the scientific community.

title: Coronavirus biology and replication: implications for SARS-CoV-2
abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic and its unprecedented global societal and economic disruptive impact has marked the third zoonotic introduction of a highly pathogenic coronavirus into the human population. Although the previous coronavirus SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV epidemics raised awareness of the need for clinically available therapeutic or preventive interventions, to date, no treatments with proven efficacy are available. The development of effective intervention strategies relies on the knowledge of molecular and cellular mechanisms of coronavirus infections, which highlights the significance of studying virus–host interactions at the molecular level to identify targets for antiviral intervention and to elucidate critical viral and host determinants that are decisive for the development of severe disease. In this Review, we summarize the first discoveries that shape our current understanding of SARS-CoV-2 infection throughout the intracellular viral life cycle and relate that to our knowledge of coronavirus biology. The elucidation of similarities and differences between SARS-CoV-2 and other coronaviruses will support future preparedness and strategies to combat coronavirus infections. In this Review, Thiel and colleagues discuss the key aspects of coronavirus biology and their implications for SARS-CoV-2 infections as well as for treatment and prevention strategies.

title: Coronavirus biology and replication: implications for SARS-CoV-2
abstract: Coronaviruses are a diverse family of enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses that infect a broad range of hosts, posing significant public health, veterinary, and economic challenges. While several human coronaviruses cause mild respiratory illnesses, zoonotic emergence of highly pathogenic strains such as SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in severe respiratory diseases with high morbidity and mortality. The coronavirus life cycle is characterized by specific spike protein-mediated entry via host receptors such as ACE2, complex replication involving large RNA genomes with unique structural and accessory proteins, and the formation of specialized replication organelles. Despite advances in understanding coronavirus biology—particularly following recent outbreaks—effective antiviral therapies or vaccines remain limited. This review synthesizes current knowledge on coronavirus molecular biology and replication, emphasizing the mechanisms of SARS-CoV-2 infection and pathogenesis. Understanding virus-host interactions at the molecular level is crucial for identifying therapeutic targets and informing strategies to prevent and control future coronavirus outbreaks.

title: Diffusion of synthetic biology: a challenge to biosafety
abstract: One of the main aims of synthetic biology is to make biology easier to engineer. Major efforts in synthetic biology are made to develop a toolbox to design biological systems without having to go through a massive research and technology process. With this “de-skilling” agenda, synthetic biology might finally unleash the full potential of biotechnology and spark a wave of innovation, as more and more people have the necessary skills to engineer biology. But this ultimate domestication of biology could easily lead to unprecedented safety challenges that need to be addressed: more and more people outside the traditional biotechnology community will create self-replicating machines (life) for civil and defence applications, “biohackers” will engineer new life forms at their kitchen table; and illicit substances will be produced synthetically and much cheaper. Such a scenario is a messy and dangerous one, and we need to think about appropriate safety standards now.
venue: Journal of Systems and Synthetic Biology

title: Diffusion of synthetic biology: a challenge to biosafety
abstract: Synthetic biology aims to simplify the engineering of biological systems, enabling broader participation and accelerating innovation. However, this democratization and “de-skilling” of biotechnology pose significant biosafety challenges, as individuals outside traditional scientific disciplines gain access to powerful tools for creating self-replicating organisms. The rise of interdisciplinary practitioners and “biohackers,” often lacking formal biosafety training or regulatory oversight, increases the risk of accidental or deliberate misuse, including home-based genetic engineering and the potential for illicit production of drugs and other substances. Existing strategies such as biosafety education, specialized manuals, and expanded institutional oversight may mitigate risks within professional settings but are insufficient for unregulated environments. As synthetic biology continues to diffuse, urgent development and implementation of robust safety standards are essential to address the unprecedented risks to public health, the environment, and security.
venue: Journal of Systems and Synthetic Biology

title: Ecological Stoichiometry: The Biology of Elements from Molecules to the Biosphere
abstract: Different areas in biology are often criticized for being either too myopic and not asking questions about how their results fit into a larger framework or for being too broad and ignoring important details. A few research programs are now attempting to make general claims derived from simple, micro-level phenomena. This is great progress for biology, resolving some of the tensions between different approaches. A merging of these fields may lead to even greater advances. One of the most exciting of these new programs is ecological stoichiometry (ES), which has been spearheaded by Sterner and Elser. Their recent book provides an overview of this developing field. With clear exposition they explain how analysis at the level of molecules can have broad implications for many macro-level ecological phenomena. Moreover, they keep their theory closely tied to available data and to the design of new experiments, thereby bridging the gap between two dividing perspectives in biology. As such, Ecological Stoichiometry contains a much needed overview of this research program as well as a good example of future directions in biology. Sterner and Elser use the first part of their book to develop the essential ideas behind ES. The foremost assumption is that an entire organism can be treated as a single, extremely large molecule. title: Ecological Stoichiometry: The Biology of Elements from Molecules to the Biosphere
abstract: Ecological stoichiometry is a rapidly expanding field that examines the balance of energy and multiple chemical elements in ecological interactions, integrating perspectives from molecular biology to ecosystem and biosphere scales. Initially rooted in studies of freshwater plankton, the approach now encompasses diverse ecosystems including streams, soils, grasslands, and forests. This paper synthesizes foundational theories, such as the Growth Rate Hypothesis and Threshold Elemental Ratio, and highlights the integration of stoichiometric principles into physiological ecology, community ecology, biogeochemistry, and evolutionary biology. Key reviews and meta-analyses are discussed, demonstrating how stoichiometric imbalances influence nutrient cycling, species coexistence, and ecosystem functioning. The historical development of ecological stoichiometry is traced from Liebig’s Law of the Minimum through Redfield’s pioneering work to contemporary mathematical models linking elemental composition with population dynamics. The review underscores the dynamic nature of the field and identifies future research directions involving new elements, trophic levels, and analytical techniques, emphasizing ecological stoichiometry’s central role in understanding biological processes across scales.

title: Effects of abiotic stress on plants: a systems biology perspective
abstract: The natural environment for plants is composed of a complex set of abiotic stresses and biotic stresses. Plant responses to these stresses are equally complex. Systems biology approaches facilitate a multi-targeted approach by allowing one to identify regulatory hubs in complex networks. Systems biology takes the molecular parts (transcripts, proteins and metabolites) of an organism and attempts to fit them into functional networks or models designed to describe and predict the dynamic activities of that organism in different environments. In this review, research progress in plant responses to abiotic stresses is summarized from the physiological level to the molecular level. New insights obtained from the integration of omics datasets are highlighted. Gaps in our knowledge are identified, providing additional focus areas for crop improvement research in the future.

title: Effects of abiotic stress on plants: a systems biology perspective
abstract: Abiotic stresses such as drought, salinity, temperature extremes, and nutrient deficiencies significantly constrain plant growth and crop productivity worldwide. Plant responses to these stresses are highly complex, involving dynamic interactions at physiological, cellular, and molecular levels. Systems biology approaches, which integrate high-throughput omics data including transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, have enabled the identification of key regulatory networks and molecular hubs underlying stress responses. This review summarizes recent advances in understanding plant adaptation to abiotic stress from a systems biology perspective, highlighting the roles of central regulators such as reactive oxygen species, hormones like abscisic acid and ethylene, and the intricate signaling pathways they control. The integration of multi-omics datasets has provided new insights into genotype-to-phenotype relationships and revealed knowledge gaps that represent opportunities for future research and crop improvement. By leveraging systems-level analyses, researchers can better predict plant behavior under stress and design strategies to enhance resilience in agricultural systems facing environmental challenges.

title: Electrostatic correlations: from plasma to biology
abstract: Electrostatic correlations play an important role in physics, chemistry and biology. In plasmas they result in thermodynamic instability similar to the liquid–gas phase transition of simple molecular fluids. For charged colloidal suspensions the electrostatic correlations are responsible for screening and colloidal charge renormalization. In aqueous solutions containing multivalent counterions they can lead to charge inversion and flocculation. In biological systems the correlations account for the organization of cytoskeleton and the compaction of genetic material. In spite of their ubiquity, the true importance of electrostatic correlations has come to be fully appreciated only quite recently. In this paper, we will review the thermodynamic consequences of electrostatic correlations in a variety of systems ranging from classical plasmas to molecular biology.

title: Electrostatic correlations: from plasma to biology
abstract: Electrostatic correlations are fundamental to the behavior of a wide range of systems, from classical plasmas and polar fluids to charged colloidal suspensions and biological macromolecules. This paper reviews the thermodynamic consequences of electrostatic correlations, emphasizing their role in phenomena such as phase transitions, charge renormalization, screening, charge inversion, and like-charge attraction. Through the analysis of simple models—including the Debye-Hückel theory and extensions—the review demonstrates how electrostatic correlations drive complex behaviors that are not captured by mean-field or perturbative approaches, especially in systems with strong coupling or asymmetry. The discussion encompasses electrolyte solutions, two-dimensional plasmas, colloidal systems, polyelectrolyte solutions with multivalent counterions, and biological assemblies such as DNA and cytoskeletal structures. By highlighting both the successes and limitations of various theoretical frameworks, the paper underscores the necessity of accounting for electrostatic correlations to accurately describe the structure, stability, and phase behavior of soft matter and biological systems.

title: Evolutionary Biology for the 21st Century
abstract: New theoretical and conceptual frameworks are required for evolutionary biology to capitalize on the wealth of data now becoming available from the study of genomes, phenotypes, and organisms - including humans - in their natural environments.

title: Evolutionary Biology for the 21st Century
abstract: This essay examines the transformative role of evolutionary biology in addressing the scientific and societal challenges of the 21st century, highlighting how advances in technology and data accessibility have expanded the field’s reach across disciplines. Evolutionary principles underpin critical applications in medicine, agriculture, conservation, computation, and justice, providing frameworks for understanding disease, improving food security, sustaining biodiversity, informing engineering design, and supporting forensic science. The integration of large-scale genomic, phenotypic, and environmental data enables novel research directions and enhances predictive capabilities for issues such as pathogen resistance, crop resilience, and species adaptation to climate change. The authors emphasize the necessity of evolutionary thinking for solving pressing global problems and advocate for continued investment in interdisciplinary collaboration, infrastructure development, and training to realize the full potential of evolutionary biology in shaping a sustainable future.

title: Fluorine in medicinal chemistry and chemical biology
abstract: The extraordinary potential of fluorine-containing molecules in medicinal chemistry and chemical biology has been recognized by researchers outside of the traditional fluorine chemistry field, and thus a new wave of fluorine chemistry is rapidly expanding its biomedical frontiers. With several of the best selling drugs in the world crucially containing fluorine atoms, the incorporation of fluorine to drug leads has become an essential practice in biomedical research, especially for drug design and discovery as well as development. Focusing on the unique and significant roles that fluorine plays in medicinal chemistry and chemical biology, this book reviews recent advances and future prospects in this rapidly developing field. Topics covered include: Discovery and development of fluorine containing drugs and drug candidates. New and efficient synthetic methods for medicinal chemistry and the optimisation of fluorine-containing drug candidates. Structural and chemical biology of fluorinated amino acids and peptides. Fluorine labels as probes in metabolic study, protein engineering and clinical diagnosis. Applications of 19F NMR spectroscopy in biomedical research. An appendix presents an invaluable index of all fluorine-containing drugs that have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration, including information on structure and pharmaceutical action. Fluorine in Medicinal Chemistry and Chemical Biology will serve as an excellent reference source for graduate students as well as academic and industrial researchers who want to take advantage of fluorine in biomedical research.

title: Fluorine in medicinal chemistry and chemical biology
abstract: This comprehensive volume explores the multifaceted roles of fluorine in medicinal chemistry and chemical biology, highlighting its unique physicochemical properties and their impact on drug discovery and development. The book presents a detailed overview of fluorine’s influence on molecular stability, bioactivity, and pharmacokinetics, illustrated through case studies of fluorinated pharmaceuticals such as tafluprost, fluoroartemisinins, and fluoro-taxoids. It examines advances in the synthesis of fluorinated nucleosides, amino acids, and heteroaromatic scaffolds, as well as innovative strategies for incorporating fluorine into biologically active molecules. Applications in protein design, membrane-active peptides, and metabolic studies using advanced spectroscopic techniques are discussed, emphasizing the expanding utility of fluorinated compounds in both therapeutic and diagnostic contexts. An appendix catalogs FDA-approved fluorine-containing drugs for human and veterinary use, underscoring the clinical relevance of this element. Collectively, the contributions provide a state-of-the-art resource for researchers seeking to harness the distinctive attributes of fluorine in chemical biology and drug development.
