title: Freshwater crayfish :: biology, management and exploitation
abstract: This comprehensive volume provides an in-depth examination of freshwater crayfish, encompassing their biology, management, and exploitation. The book is organized into two main sections: general biology and species of economic importance. The first section addresses key aspects of crayfish morphology, distribution, evolution, growth, reproduction, ecology, feeding habits, disease, and immune mechanisms. The second section focuses on economically significant genera and species across North America, Europe, and Australia, detailing their production methods, distribution patterns, and associated challenges. Contributions from leading experts offer insights into adaptive radiation, interspecies interactions, and the impact of introduced species on native populations. By integrating fundamental biological knowledge with practical management strategies, this work serves as a valuable resource for researchers, aquaculturists, and policymakers involved in the conservation and sustainable use of freshwater crayfish.

title: Genetics and biology of prostate cancer
abstract: Here, Wang et al. review available prostate cancer model systems, the prostate cancer genome atlas, cellular and functional heterogeneity in the tumor microenvironment, tumor-intrinsic and tumor-extrinsic mechanisms underlying therapeutic resistance, and technological advances focused on disease detection and management

title: Genetics and biology of prostate cancer
abstract: Prostate cancer is the most common noncutaneous malignancy in men and remains a significant clinical challenge, particularly in its metastatic form, which is largely incurable due to profound genetic and cellular heterogeneity. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the genetics and biology of prostate cancer, highlighting advances in model systems, genomic profiling, and the characterization of tumor microenvironmental heterogeneity. The progression from prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia to localized and metastatic disease involves complex interactions between diverse epithelial cell types and stromal components, with androgen receptor signaling playing a central role in tumor development and therapeutic resistance. Emerging aggressive variants, including androgen receptor-low and neuroendocrine phenotypes, underscore the adaptive capacity of prostate tumors under therapeutic pressure. Mechanisms of metastasis, particularly to bone, involve epithelial–mesenchymal transition, circulating tumor cells, and specific molecular mediators such as CXCL12/CXCR4 and integrins. Advances in disease detection, biomarker development, artificial intelligence-driven decision support, and adaptive clinical trials are poised to refine patient management and accelerate the development of more effective therapies. A deeper understanding of tumor–host interactions and resistance mechanisms is essential for designing durable treatment strategies and ultimately improving outcomes for patients with advanced prostate cancer.

title: Genome Sequence of the Pea Aphid Acyrthosiphon pisum
abstract: The genome of the pea aphid shows remarkable levels of gene duplication and equally remarkable gene absences that shed light on aspects of aphid biology, most especially its symbiosis with Buchnera.

title: Genome Sequence of the Pea Aphid Acyrthosiphon pisum
abstract: The draft genome sequence of the pea aphid Acyrthosiphon pisum, a model organism for studies of insect-plant interactions, symbiosis, and phenotypic plasticity, is presented as the first published whole genome of a basal hemimetabolous insect. The 464 Mb assembly reveals extensive gene duplication in over 2000 gene families and notable losses of evolutionarily conserved genes, including those involved in the IMD immune pathway, selenoprotein utilization, purine salvage, and the urea cycle. Gene family expansions are observed in chromatin modification, miRNA synthesis, and sugar transport, while only a limited number of genes appear to have been acquired from bacterial symbionts. The metabolic gene inventory suggests extensive metabolite exchange between the aphid and its obligate symbiont Buchnera aphidicola, particularly in amino acid biosynthesis. These genomic features provide insights into the unique biology of aphids, including their reproductive strategies and symbiotic relationships, and establish a foundation for future research on fundamental biological processes and agricultural pest management.

title: Graph theory and networks in Biology.
abstract: A survey of the use of graph theoretical techniques in Biology is presented. In particular, recent work on identifying and modelling the structure of bio-molecular networks is discussed, as well as the application of centrality measures to interaction networks and research on the hierarchical structure of such networks and network motifs. Work on the link between structural network properties and dynamics is also described, with emphasis on synchronisation and disease propagation.

title: Graph theory and networks in Biology.
abstract: This paper surveys the application of graph theory and network analysis in biology, focusing on recent advances in modeling and understanding the structure of biomolecular networks such as metabolic, protein-protein interaction, and transcriptional regulatory networks. The authors review mathematical foundations including directed and undirected graphs, node degree, adjacency matrices, and centrality measures. Key topics include the identification of network motifs and hierarchical organization, the relationship between network structure and dynamics—particularly synchronization phenomena relevant to neurological disorders—and the impact of network topology on disease propagation in populations. The survey highlights both the progress made in extracting biological insights from complex network data and the ongoing challenges in integrating structural and dynamic perspectives to address fundamental questions in biology and medicine.

title: Handbook of freshwater fishery biology
abstract: These volumes have, for over 30 years, been the most readily available source listing the scattered articles, theses, bulletins, and research on freshwater fish in the United States and Canada. 'The Handbook of Freshwater Fishery Biology' summarizes the available data on age, growth, length weight, fecundity, reproductive behavior feeding habits, and necessary environment for each freshwater species. The comparison of species is presented in a manner easily used by fishery mangers and biologists.

title: Handbook of freshwater fishery biology
abstract: This handbook provides a comprehensive compilation of tabular data on the growth, length-weight relationships, condition indices, fecundity, and life histories of freshwater fish species found in the United States and Canada. Designed as a reference source for conservationists, biologists, and researchers, it consolidates widely scattered fishery information from both published and unpublished sources to facilitate comparative studies and bibliographical research. The handbook includes detailed instructions for interpreting tables, addresses methodological variations in fish measurement, and highlights the importance of sample size and statistical analysis in evaluating population data. By systematically organizing species-specific data and offering conversion tables and bibliographic codes, this work aims to support efficient access to essential fishery biology information while encouraging further publication of unpublished data and careful application of summarized findings across diverse aquatic environments.

title: Helicobacter pylori persistence: biology and disease.
abstract: Helicobacter pylori are bacteria that have coevolved with humans to be transmitted from person to person and to persistently colonize the stomach. Their population structure is a model for the ecology of the indigenous microbiota. A well-choreographed equilibrium between bacterial effectors and host responses permits microbial persistence and health of the host but confers risk of serious diseases, including peptic ulceration and gastric neoplasia.

title: Helicobacter pylori persistence: biology and disease.
abstract: Helicobacter pylori is a human-adapted bacterium that persistently colonizes the stomach, establishing a dynamic equilibrium with its host through complex interactions shaped by coevolution. This review explores the biological mechanisms underlying H. pylori persistence, emphasizing the bacterium’s remarkable genetic diversity generated by high mutation and recombination rates, which enable adaptation to host-specific selective pressures. The resulting population structure resembles a quasispecies, with closely related variants occupying distinct gastric microniches and responding to local environmental cues. Host-microbial cross-signaling mediates both microbial persistence and host responses, balancing health and disease risk. While H. pylori colonization increases susceptibility to peptic ulceration and gastric cancer, emerging evidence suggests protective roles against certain esophageal diseases and broader impacts on human physiology. The principles governing H. pylori’s long-term colonization provide a paradigm for understanding persistent host-microbe relationships, with implications for chronic inflammation, oncogenesis, and modern metabolic disorders.

title: Integrated Management of Insects in Stored Products
abstract: Identification and biology: coleoptera Identification and biology: lepidoptera and pscoptera. Ecology. Sampling to detect or estimate insect populations. Physical control. Chemical control. Biological control. Pesticide resistance management. Integrated pest management.

title: Integrated Management of Insects in Stored Products
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the integrated management of insect pests in stored products, focusing on key pest groups including Coleoptera, Lepidoptera, and Psocoptera. It examines the identification and biological characteristics of these insects, their ecological interactions within storage environments, and effective sampling methods for population detection and estimation. The study evaluates a range of control strategies, encompassing physical, chemical, and biological approaches, while addressing the challenges posed by pesticide resistance. Emphasis is placed on the principles and implementation of integrated pest management (IPM) as a sustainable framework that combines multiple tactics to minimize insect damage and preserve product quality in storage systems.

title: Longevity, senescence, and the genome
abstract: Featuring extensive references, updated for this paperback edition, 'Longevity, Senescence, and the Genome' constitutes a contribution to biomedicine and the evolutionary biology of ageing. To enhance gerontology's focus on human age-related dysfunctions, Caleb E. Finch provides a comparative review of all the phyla of organisms, broadening gerontology to intersect with behavioral, developmental, evolutionary, and molecular biology. By comparing species that have different developmental and life spans, Finch proposes a typology of senescence from rapid to gradual to negligible, and he provides the first multiphyletic calculations of mortality rate constants.

title: Longevity, senescence, and the genome
abstract: This comprehensive volume by Caleb E. Finch offers an in-depth exploration of the biological and genetic mechanisms underlying longevity and senescence across a wide range of plant and animal species. Integrating advances in molecular genetics with comparative biology, the book examines fundamental questions regarding the measurement, onset, and variability of senescence, as well as the influence of genes at multiple organizational levels. Finch critically evaluates the roles of selective versus random changes in gene expression, the impact of developmental and environmental factors, and the universality of age-related degeneration. The analysis highlights that genetic mechanisms affecting lifespan and certain aspects of senescence are identifiable in specific organisms, suggesting that senescence may be modifiable through genetic interventions. While evolutionary perspectives and broad taxonomic coverage occasionally overshadow human-specific pathology, the work stands as a masterful synthesis that provides essential insights for researchers and students in the rapidly expanding field of aging biology.

title: Malignant astrocytic glioma: genetics, biology, and paths to treatment.
abstract: Malignant astrocytic gliomas such as glioblastoma are the most common and lethal intracranial tumors. These cancers exhibit a relentless malignant progression characterized by widespread invasion throughout the brain, resistance to traditional and newer targeted therapeutic approaches, destruction of normal brain tissue, and certain death. The recent confluence of advances in stem cell biology, cell signaling, genome and computational science and genetic model systems have revolutionized our understanding of the mechanisms underlying the genetics, biology and clinical behavior of glioblastoma. This progress is fueling new opportunities for understanding the fundamental basis for development of this devastating disease and also novel therapies that, for the first time, portend meaningful clinical responses.

title: Malignant astrocytic glioma: genetics, biology, and paths to treatment.
abstract: Malignant astrocytic gliomas, particularly glioblastoma (GBM), represent the most common and aggressive primary brain tumors, characterized by rapid progression, extensive invasion, resistance to conventional and targeted therapies, and poor prognosis. Recent advances in stem cell biology, genomics, and molecular modeling have significantly enhanced our understanding of the genetic and biological mechanisms underlying GBM pathogenesis, revealing substantial intratumoral heterogeneity and distinct molecular subtypes with unique genetic alterations. Classification of gliomas now integrates histopathological, immunohistochemical, and molecular features, with markers such as GFAP, OLIG2, and emerging stem cell-associated proteins aiding in diagnosis and prognostication. The identification of cancer stem cell populations and key genetic lesions driving hallmark features of malignancy has informed the development of refined model systems and novel therapeutic strategies targeting critical pathways. Although challenges remain in overcoming therapeutic resistance and disease recurrence, these scientific advances provide a foundation for more precise classification, improved understanding of disease origins, and the rational design of targeted treatments that hold promise for meaningful clinical benefit in this otherwise intractable disease.

title: Mathematical models in biology
abstract: Mathematical Models in Biology is an introductory book for readers interested in biological applications of mathematics and modeling in biology. A favorite in the mathematical biology community, it shows how relatively simple mathematics can be applied to a variety of models to draw interesting conclusions. Connections are made between diverse biological examples linked by common mathematical themes. A variety of discrete and continuous ordinary and partial differential equation models are explored. Although great advances have taken place in many of the topics covered, the simple lessons contained in Mathematical Models in Biology are still important and informative.  Shortly after the publication of Mathematical Models in Biology, the genomics revolution turned Mathematical Biology into a prominent area of interdisciplinary research. With this new millennium, biologists have discovered that mathematics is not only useful, but indispensable! As a result, there has been much resurgent interest in, and a huge expansion of, the fields collectively called mathematical biology. This book serves as a basic introduction to concepts in deterministic biological modeling.

title: Mathematical models in biology
abstract: This dissertation explores the development and analysis of mathematical models to describe key biological processes, focusing on aerotaxis in bacteria, growth cone guidance in neurons, and endothelial cell deformation. For aerotaxis, the work presents a detailed comparison between conventional chemotaxis and oxygen-driven movement in Azospirillum brasilense, including experimental observations and the derivation of new mathematical models that incorporate turning frequencies and non-dimensional scaling. Numerical simulations and analytical results are used to investigate band formation and steady-state distributions. In the context of neuronal growth cone guidance, the dissertation reviews biological mechanisms of gradient sensing and constructs theoretical models, such as the cAMP-adenylate cyclase switch and adaptation-diffusion frameworks, to elucidate signal transduction pathways and cellular responses to external cues. The study further extends to modeling the viscoelastic properties of endothelial cells using networks of Kelvin bodies arranged in series and parallel, with parameter sensitivity analyses and network simulations revealing how mechanical forces influence cellular deformation under various flow conditions. Together, these investigations demonstrate the power of mathematical modeling in providing quantitative insights into complex biological phenomena and highlight directions for future research at the interface of mathematics and biology.

title: Mathematics Is Biology's Next Microscope, Only Better; Biology Is Mathematics' Next Physics, Only Better
abstract: Joel Cohen offers a historical and prospective analysis of the relationship between mathematics and biology.

title: Mathematics Is Biology's Next Microscope, Only Better; Biology Is Mathematics' Next Physics, Only Better
abstract: This paper explores the evolving and reciprocal relationship between mathematics and biology, arguing that mathematics serves as biology’s next microscope by enabling the discovery and interpretation of complex biological phenomena beyond the reach of traditional observation, while biology is poised to become mathematics’ next physics by inspiring fundamentally new mathematical concepts and methods. Drawing on historical milestones such as Harvey’s quantification of blood circulation and Mendel’s genetic laws, the paper illustrates how mathematical reasoning has been integral to major advances in biology. It highlights the unique challenges posed by biological heterogeneity and diversity, which surpass those found in non-living systems and demand novel mathematical frameworks. The discussion traces the mutual enrichment of both fields over centuries, emphasizing that future progress in understanding life’s complexity will require deeper integration of mathematical innovation driven by biological questions, ultimately transforming both disciplines.

title: Metalloproteinases in biology and pathology of the nervous system
abstract: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) have been implicated in several diseases of the nervous system. Here we review the evidence that supports this idea and discuss the possible mechanisms of MMP action. We then consider some of the beneficial functions of MMPs during neural development and speculate on their roles in repair after brain injury. We also introduce a family of proteins known as ADAMs (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase), as some of the properties previously ascribed to MMPs are possibly the result of ADAM activity.

title: Metalloproteinases in biology and pathology of the nervous system
abstract: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and related metalloproteinases, including the ADAM family, are critical regulators of cellular function in the nervous system, extending beyond their classical roles in extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the structure, regulation, and diverse functions of MMPs and ADAMs, highlighting their involvement in both physiological processes such as neural development, repair, and signaling, as well as in pathological conditions including multiple sclerosis, malignant gliomas, stroke, Alzheimer’s disease, and viral infections of the central nervous system. The paper details the mechanisms governing metalloproteinase activity at transcriptional and post-translational levels and discusses the interplay between MMPs, their endogenous inhibitors (TIMPs), and cell-surface localization. Additionally, it explores the unique structural features and dual adhesive-proteolytic activities of ADAMs, underscoring their emerging significance in CNS pathophysiology. By integrating evidence from recent studies, this review emphasizes the complex and context-dependent roles of metalloproteinases in nervous system health and disease.

title: Molecular biology of microbial hydrogenases.
abstract: Hydrogenases (H2ases) are metalloproteins. The great majority of them contain iron-sulfur clusters and two metal atoms at their active center, either a Ni and an Fe atom, the [NiFe]-H2ases, or two Fe atoms, the [FeFe]-H2ases. Enzymes of these two classes catalyze the reversible oxidation of hydrogen gas (H2 <--> 2 H+ + 2 e-) and play a central role in microbial energy metabolism; in addition to their role in fermentation and H2 respiration, H2ases may interact with membrane-bound electron transport systems in order to maintain redox poise, particularly in some photosynthetic microorganisms such as cyanobacteria. Recent work has revealed that some H2ases, by acting as H2-sensors, participate in the regulation of gene expression and that H2-evolving H2ases, thought to be involved in purely fermentative processes, play a role in membrane-linked energy conservation through the generation of a protonmotive force. The Hmd hydrogenases of some methanogenic archaea constitute a third class of H2ases, characterized by the absence of Fe-S cluster and the presence of an iron-containing cofactor with catalytic properties different from those of [NiFe]- and [FeFe]-H2ases. In this review, we emphasise recent advances that have greatly increased our knowledge of microbial H2ases, their diversity, the structure of their active site, how the metallocenters are synthesized and assembled, how they function, how the synthesis of these enzymes is controlled by external signals, and their potential use in biological H2 production.

title: Molecular biology of microbial hydrogenases.
abstract: Microbial hydrogenases are diverse metalloproteins that catalyze the reversible oxidation of molecular hydrogen, playing essential roles in microbial energy metabolism, including fermentation, respiration, and redox balancing. The major classes—[NiFe]-hydrogenases, [FeFe]-hydrogenases, and iron-sulfur cluster-free Hmd hydrogenases—differ in active site composition, structure, and phylogeny. Advances in molecular biology, X-ray crystallography, and spectroscopy have elucidated the structure and function of these enzymes, revealing mechanisms of metallocenter assembly and regulation by environmental signals. Some hydrogenases also function as H2 sensors, influencing gene expression and energy conservation via protonmotive force generation. Understanding the molecular biology and diversity of microbial hydrogenases not only provides insights into microbial physiology but also underpins efforts to harness these enzymes for sustainable biological hydrogen production.

title: Molecular Biology of the Cell
abstract: Much of the research in the Pringle laboratory exploits the power of yeast as an experimentally tractable model eukaryote to investigate fundamental problems in cell and developmental biology such as the mechanisms of cell polarization and cytokinesis. In regards to cell polarization, the major current foci are the roles of cortical marker proteins and of a GTPase-based signal-transduction cascade in the selection of the polarization axes (as defined by the bud sites). Interestingly, the marker proteins appear to be delivered to polarized sites in the cell surface by an unconventional arm of the secretory pathway. In regards to cytokinesis, the major current foci are the roles of the septin proteins and the interactions among the actomyosin contractile ring, the enzymes of extracellular-matrix (cell-wall) synthesis, and proteins that appear to be involved in plasma-membrane reorganization. Our working hypothesis is that the conserved core mechanism is the rearrangements of the membrane during cleavage-furrow formation and that the actomyosin ring and extracellular matrix play accessory roles. In a departure from our many years of yeast work, a major new project involves developing the small sea anemone Aiptasia pallida as a model system for study of the molecular and cellular biology of the dinoflagellate-cnidarian symbiosis, which is critical for the survival of most reef-building corals but still very poorly understood. Processes to be investigated include the recognition and signaling events involved in symbiosis establishment, the temporal and spatial coordination of symbiont and host cell cycles during symbiosis maintenance, and the signaling and cellular processes involved in symbiosis breakdown under stress. Currently much of our effort is directed at genomic analysis and method development that will underpin later studies.

title: Molecular Biology of the Cell
abstract: Molecular Biology of the Cell, 2nd edition, provides a comprehensive and lucid overview of contemporary cell and molecular biology, reflecting the rapid advancements in the field since its first edition. The text is organized into three main sections covering cellular biochemistry, molecular organization, and the transition from single cells to multicellular organisms, with clear explanations and extensively revised illustrations. Topics include genetic mechanisms, membrane and cytoplasmic organization, cell signaling, growth control, cell adhesion, development, immune and nervous systems, plant cell organization, and cancer biology. The book is notable for its clarity, up-to-date content with references through late 1988, and practical approach that integrates clinical relevance. It serves as an essential resource for pathologists and biologists seeking to remain current with modern cellular biology and is highly recommended for both trainees and established professionals.

title: Nanoparticles and their applications in cell and molecular biology.
abstract: Nanoparticles can be engineered with distinctive composition, size, shape, and surface chemistry to enable novel techniques in a wide range of biological applications. The unique properties of nanoparticles and their behavior in biological milieu also enable exciting and integrative approaches to studying fundamental biological questions. This review will provide an overview of various types of nanoparticles and concepts of targeting nanoparticles. We will also discuss the advantages and recent applications of using nanoparticles as tools for drug delivery, imaging, sensing, and for the understanding of basic biological processes.

title: Nanoparticles and their applications in cell and molecular biology.
abstract: Nanoparticles, with their tunable compositions, sizes, shapes, and surface chemistries, offer unique physical and chemical properties that have revolutionized cell and molecular biology research. This review provides an overview of the major classes of nanoparticles—including liposomes, albumin-bound nanoparticles, polymeric nanoparticles, dendrimers, iron oxide nanoparticles, quantum dots, and gold nanoparticles—highlighting their structural features and functionalities relevant to biological applications. The paper discusses how these platforms enable advancements in drug delivery, imaging, biosensing, and the elucidation of fundamental biological processes. Special emphasis is placed on strategies for nanoparticle targeting, including both passive and active approaches, which enhance specificity and efficacy in biomedical applications. The integration of nanoparticles into cell and molecular biology has not only improved the sensitivity and precision of experimental techniques but has also facilitated the development of novel therapeutics and diagnostics. Collectively, these advances underscore the transformative potential of nanotechnology in addressing complex biological questions and improving human health.

title: Oligodendrocytes: biology and pathology
abstract: Oligodendrocytes are the myelinating cells of the central nervous system (CNS). They are the end product of a cell lineage which has to undergo a complex and precisely timed program of proliferation, migration, differentiation, and myelination to finally produce the insulating sheath of axons. Due to this complex differentiation program, and due to their unique metabolism/physiology, oligodendrocytes count among the most vulnerable cells of the CNS. In this review, we first describe the different steps eventually culminating in the formation of mature oligodendrocytes and myelin sheaths, as they were revealed by studies in rodents. We will then show differences and similarities of human oligodendrocyte development. Finally, we will lay out the different pathways leading to oligodendrocyte and myelin loss in human CNS diseases, and we will reveal the different principles leading to the restoration of myelin sheaths or to a failure to do so.

title: Oligodendrocytes: biology and pathology
abstract: Oligodendrocytes, the central nervous system’s myelinating cells, arise from a complex lineage involving tightly regulated proliferation, migration, and differentiation processes. This review synthesizes current knowledge, primarily from rodent studies, on the developmental origins and competitive dynamics of oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), highlighting the functional redundancy and regulatory mechanisms guiding their migration and maturation. The spatial and temporal orchestration of OPC differentiation and myelination is discussed, including the roles of signaling pathways such as Notch and NRG1/ErbB, and the influence of neuronal activity on myelin formation. Comparative insights into human oligodendrocyte development are provided, alongside an examination of pathological mechanisms leading to oligodendrocyte and myelin loss in CNS diseases. The review concludes by addressing principles underlying remyelination and the factors contributing to its success or failure in disease contexts.

title: On the Economics and Biology of Trust
abstract: In recent years, many social scientists have claimed that trust plays an important role in economic and social transactions. Despite its proposed importance, the measurement and the definition of trust seem to be not fully settled, and the identification of the exact role of trust in economic interactions has proven to be elusive. It is still not clear whether trust is just an epiphenomenon of good institutions or whether it plays an independent causal role capable of shaping important aggregate economic outcomes. In this paper, I rely on a behavioral definition of trust that enables us to relate it to economic primitives such as preferences and beliefs. I review strong biological and behavioral evidence indicating that trusting is not just a special case of risk-taking, but based on important forms of social preferences such as betrayal aversion. Behaviorally defined trust also opens the door for understanding national and ethnic trust differences in terms of differences in preferences and beliefs, and it suggests ways to examine and interpret a causal role of trust.

title: On the Economics and Biology of Trust
abstract: This paper examines the multifaceted nature of trust by integrating insights from economics and biology, focusing on its definition, measurement, and causal role in economic outcomes. Employing a behavioral definition rooted in preferences and beliefs, the study reviews experimental, neurobiological, and genetic evidence to demonstrate that trust is not merely a function of risk-taking or beliefs about others’ trustworthiness, but is also shaped by social preferences such as betrayal aversion. The analysis highlights that both survey and behavioral measures of trust are influenced by individual risk attitudes and social preferences, and that differences in national and ethnic trust can be traced to variations in these underlying factors. The paper also addresses the endogeneity of trust beliefs and critically evaluates existing empirical approaches to establishing the causal impact of trust on aggregate economic variables. Despite substantial progress in understanding the determinants and correlates of trust, the paper concludes that robust evidence for its independent causal effect on economic performance remains elusive, underscoring the need for further research using more rigorous identification strategies.

title: PEtab—Interoperable specification of parameter estimation problems in systems biology
abstract: Reproducibility and reusability of the results of data-based modeling studies are essential. Yet, there has been—so far—no broadly supported format for the specification of parameter estimation problems in systems biology. Here, we introduce PEtab, a format which facilitates the specification of parameter estimation problems using Systems Biology Markup Language (SBML) models and a set of tab-separated value files describing the observation model and experimental data as well as parameters to be estimated. We already implemented PEtab support into eight well-established model simulation and parameter estimation toolboxes with hundreds of users in total. We provide a Python library for validation and modification of a PEtab problem and currently 20 example parameter estimation problems based on recent studies.

title: PEtab—Interoperable specification of parameter estimation problems in systems biology
abstract: Parameter estimation is a critical task in systems biology, requiring the integration of experimental data with mathematical models to infer unknown parameters. However, the diversity of modeling tools and formats has led to challenges in reproducibility, interoperability, and transparency of parameter estimation workflows. Here, we present PEtab, a standardized and interoperable specification for parameter estimation problems in systems biology. PEtab defines a set of tabular and YAML-based formats to describe models, experimental conditions, measurements, observables, and parameter constraints in a tool-agnostic manner. By providing a clear and extensible structure, PEtab enables seamless exchange of parameter estimation problems between different software tools and facilitates reproducible research. We demonstrate the utility of PEtab through integration with multiple modeling environments and showcase its application to a range of published models. Our results highlight that PEtab fosters transparency, comparability, and reusability in parameter estimation tasks, thereby accelerating model-driven discovery in systems biology.

title: Random walk models in biology
abstract: Mathematical modelling of the movement of animals, micro-organisms and cells is of great relevance in the fields of biology, ecology and medicine. Movement models can take many different forms, but the most widely used are based on the extensions of simple random walk processes. In this review paper, our aim is twofold: to introduce the mathematics behind random walks in a straightforward manner and to explain how such models can be used to aid our understanding of biological processes. We introduce the mathematical theory behind the simple random walk and explain how this relates to Brownian motion and diffusive processes in general. We demonstrate how these simple models can be extended to include drift and waiting times or be used to calculate first passage times. We discuss biased random walks and show how hyperbolic models can be used to generate correlated random walks. We cover two main applications of the random walk model. Firstly, we review models and results relating to the movement, dispersal and population redistribution of animals and micro-organisms. This includes direct calculation of mean squared displacement, mean dispersal distance, tortuosity measures, as well as possible limitations of these model approaches. Secondly, oriented movement and chemotaxis models are reviewed. General hyperbolic models based on the linear transport equation are introduced and we show how a reinforced random walk can be used to model movement where the individual changes its environment. We discuss the applications of these models in the context of cell migration leading to blood vessel growth (angiogenesis). Finally, we discuss how the various random walk models and approaches are related and the connections that underpin many of the key processes involved.
venue: Journal of the Royal Society Interface

title: Random walk models in biology
abstract: Random walk models provide a fundamental mathematical framework for understanding the movement of animals, micro-organisms, and cells in biological systems. This review introduces the core concepts and mathematical underpinnings of random walks, including simple isotropic random walks, correlated random walks, and biased random walks, and explains their relationships to diffusion processes such as Brownian motion. The paper details how these models are extended to incorporate drift, persistence, waiting times, and first passage times, and discusses their application to key biological phenomena such as animal dispersal, population redistribution, navigation, and chemotaxis. Special attention is given to the use of hyperbolic models for correlated movement and reinforced random walks for scenarios where individuals modify their environment. The review also addresses the benefits and limitations of various model approaches, highlights the connections between different modelling frameworks used in ecology and cell biology, and provides a comprehensive reference linking theoretical developments with practical applications in fields ranging from animal movement ecology to cell migration and angiogenesis.
venue: Journal of the Royal Society Interface
