title: Expander Graphs and their Applications
abstract: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of expander graphs, emphasizing their fundamental role across mathematics and computer science. Expander graphs, characterized by their simultaneous sparsity and strong connectivity, are explored through combinatorial, probabilistic, and algebraic perspectives. The paper discusses structural properties, explicit constructions, and algorithmic aspects of expanders, highlighting their significance in diverse areas such as communication networks, error correcting codes, pseudorandomness, metric embeddings, Markov chain mixing, and complexity theory. Key topics include spectral graph theory, random walks, isoperimetric inequalities, extremal problems, explicit constructions like the Margulis and zig-zag products, Cayley graphs, and applications to coding theory and metric embedding. The survey synthesizes decades of research, illustrating the ubiquity and versatility of expander graphs while providing references for further study and outlining open problems in the field.

title: Explaining Underrepresentation: A Theory of Precluded Interest
abstract: What processes best explain women’s underrepresentation in science, math, and engineering fields in the U.S.? Do they also explain men’s underrepresentation in the humanities? Two survey studies across two U.S. West Coast universities (N = 62; N = 614) addressed these questions in the context of two fields: one male-dominated (computer science) and the other female-dominated (English). Among a set of social predictors—including perceived similarity to the people in the field, social identity threats, and expectations of success—the best mediator of women’s lower interest in computer science and men’s lower interest in English was perceived similarity. Thus, changing students’ social perceptions of how they relate to those in the field may help to diversify academic fields.

title: Explaining Underrepresentation: A Theory of Precluded Interest
abstract: This paper investigates the social processes underlying gender underrepresentation in academic fields by proposing a theory of precluded interest, wherein perceived similarity to people in a field mediates academic interest. Two survey studies at U.S. West Coast universities examined women’s lower interest in the male-dominated field of computer science and men’s lower interest in the female-dominated field of English. Results indicate that among several social predictors—including social identity threats and expectations of success—perceived similarity to field members most strongly accounted for both women’s and men’s lack of interest in these respective fields. These findings suggest that interventions aimed at increasing perceived similarity and belonging may be effective in diversifying academic disciplines, highlighting the central role of social perceptions in shaping educational choices across gender lines.

title: Fundamentals of computer graphics
abstract: The broad acceptance and use of this book as one of the leading introductory computer graphics texts has enabled the original author and coauthors to update the chapters and contribute new material involving the most knowledgeable experts in different areas while maintaining a unified approach. This edition of 'Fundamentals of Computer Graphics' adds four new contributed chapters and contains substantial reorganizations and improvements to the core material. The new chapters add coverage of implicit modeling and of two important graphics applications: games and information visualization. The fourth new contributed chapter is a major upgrade to the material on color science. As with the chapters added in the second edition, we have chosen the contributors both for their expertise and for their clear way of expressing ideas.

title: Fundamentals of computer graphics
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the fundamental concepts, mathematical foundations, and practical techniques in computer graphics. It covers key areas including graphics APIs, the graphics pipeline, numerical methods, and efficiency considerations in program design. Essential mathematical tools such as vectors, matrices, linear algebra, probability, integration, and signal processing are introduced to support understanding of graphics algorithms. The text explores core topics like rasterization, ray tracing, shading models, texture mapping, and data structures for scene representation. Advanced subjects include Monte Carlo integration, physics-based rendering, animation principles, and hardware programming with shaders and buffers. The paper also addresses color science, visual perception, tone reproduction, implicit modeling techniques, and their applications in games and visualization. Through a structured presentation of theory and practice, this work serves as a foundational resource for students and practitioners seeking to master the principles and applications of computer graphics.

title: Geometric Deep Learning: Going beyond Euclidean data
abstract: Many scientific fields study data with an underlying structure that is non-Euclidean. Some examples include social networks in computational social sciences, sensor networks in communications, functional networks in brain imaging, regulatory networks in genetics, and meshed surfaces in computer graphics. In many applications, such geometric data are large and complex (in the case of social networks, on the scale of billions) and are natural targets for machine-learning techniques. In particular, we would like to use deep neural networks, which have recently proven to be powerful tools for a broad range of problems from computer vision, natural-language processing, and audio analysis. However, these tools have been most successful on data with an underlying Euclidean or grid-like structure and in cases where the invariances of these structures are built into networks used to model them.

title: Geometric Deep Learning: Going beyond Euclidean data
abstract: Geometric deep learning is an emerging field that extends deep neural network models to non-Euclidean domains such as graphs and manifolds, which commonly arise in diverse scientific applications including social networks, sensor networks, genetics, neuroscience, and computer graphics. Traditional deep learning architectures like convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are highly effective for data with underlying Euclidean or grid-like structure due to their ability to exploit properties such as stationarity and compositionality. However, these properties do not naturally exist in non-Euclidean data, presenting significant challenges in defining analogous operations like convolution. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of geometric deep learning, categorizing key problem types into those focused on characterizing domain structure and those analyzing functions defined on non-Euclidean domains. It reviews foundational methods for manifold learning and graph-based signal processing, discusses recent advances in generalizing CNNs to graphs and manifolds via spectral and spatial approaches, and highlights successful applications across multiple fields. The paper also addresses the computational and conceptual challenges unique to geometric data and outlines promising directions for future research in this rapidly evolving area.

title: Geometric Deep Learning on Graphs and Manifolds Using Mixture Model CNNs
abstract: Deep learning has achieved a remarkable performance breakthrough in several fields, most notably in speech recognition, natural language processing, and computer vision. In particular, convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures currently produce state-of-the-art performance on a variety of image analysis tasks such as object detection and recognition. Most of deep learning research has so far focused on dealing with 1D, 2D, or 3D Euclidean-structured data such as acoustic signals, images, or videos. Recently, there has been an increasing interest in geometric deep learning, attempting to generalize deep learning methods to non-Euclidean structured data such as graphs and manifolds, with a variety of applications from the domains of network analysis, computational social science, or computer graphics. In this paper, we propose a unified framework allowing to generalize CNN architectures to non-Euclidean domains (graphs and manifolds) and learn local, stationary, and compositional task-specific features. We show that various non-Euclidean CNN methods previously proposed in the literature can be considered as particular instances of our framework. We test the proposed method on standard tasks from the realms of image-, graph-and 3D shape analysis and show that it consistently outperforms previous approaches.

title: Geometric Deep Learning on Graphs and Manifolds Using Mixture Model CNNs
abstract: This paper introduces a unified framework for geometric deep learning on non-Euclidean domains, such as graphs and manifolds, using mixture model convolutional neural networks (MoNet). By generalizing the concept of convolution to operate on local intrinsic patches defined by parametric functions of pseudo-coordinates, the proposed approach subsumes several existing methods as particular cases and enables the learning of localized, task-specific features across diverse geometric structures. Experimental results on standard benchmarks in image classification, graph vertex classification, and 3D shape correspondence demonstrate that MoNet consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art non-Euclidean deep learning techniques, offering a flexible and effective solution for analyzing complex geometric data.

title: Handbook of Computational Social Choice
abstract: The rapidly growing field of computational social choice, at the intersection of computer science and economics, deals with the computational aspects of collective decision making. This handbook, written by thirty-six prominent members of the computational social choice community, covers the field comprehensively. Chapters devoted to each of the field's major themes offer detailed introductions. Topics include voting theory (such as the computational complexity of winner determination and manipulation in elections), fair allocation (such as algorithms for dividing divisible and indivisible goods), coalition formation (such as matching and hedonic games), and many more. Graduate students, researchers, and professionals in computer science, economics, mathematics, political science, and philosophy will benefit from this accessible and self-contained book.

title: Handbook of Computational Social Choice
abstract: Computational social choice is an interdisciplinary field at the intersection of social choice theory and computer science, focused on the algorithmic and complexity-theoretic aspects of collective decision making. Building upon a rich tradition in mathematics, economics, and political science, computational social choice emerged in the early 2000s as researchers began to apply computational paradigms to analyze and design aggregation mechanisms such as voting rules. This introductory chapter traces the historical development of social choice theory, highlighting key milestones from antiquity through the classical period to the recent computational turn. It illustrates how early problems and paradoxes in voting inspired both foundational concepts and modern algorithmic investigations, including the computational complexity of manipulation and control. The chapter outlines the dual thrusts of contemporary research: leveraging computational techniques to better understand and innovate social choice mechanisms, and applying social choice theory to computational environments such as multiagent systems, recommendation platforms, and crowdsourcing. The handbook aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the field's structure, key concepts, and active research areas for scholars from computer science, economics, mathematics, and related disciplines, while acknowledging the ongoing expansion and dynamism of computational social choice.

title: Human-Computer Interaction
abstract: Beginning Fall 2020, Carnegie Mellon students within the School of Computer Science (SCS) can declare a primary major in HCI. (Non-SCS students at Carnegie Mellon can continue to couple one of our other highly popular undergraduate options -the Additional Major in Interdisciplinary HCI (https://hcii.cmu.edu/academics/hci-undergraduate/major/) or the Minor in Interdisciplinary HCI (https://hcii.cmu.edu/academics/hci-undergraduate/ minor/) -with their primary University major.)

title: Human-Computer Interaction
abstract: This volume presents selected papers from the 5th International Conference on Human-Computer Interaction (EWHCI '95), held in Moscow, Russia, in July 1995. The conference aimed to foster collaboration and knowledge exchange between researchers from the former Soviet Union and the international HCI community. The collection covers a range of topics including industrial design, activity theory, toolkits for interface development, educational software, information retrieval, hypertext theory, object-oriented hypermedia databases, distributed environments, and knowledge-based user interface design. Special emphasis is placed on multidisciplinary approaches and the integration of activity theory into HCI research. The volume also includes a summary of a tutorial on activity theory, highlighting its relevance to the field. These contributions reflect ongoing advances in human-computer interaction and underscore the importance of international cooperation in shaping future research directions.

title: Introduction to the non-asymptotic analysis of random matrices
abstract: This is a tutorial on some basic non-asymptotic methods and concepts in random matrix theory. The reader will learn several tools for the analysis of the extreme singular values of random matrices with independent rows or columns. Many of these methods sprung off from the development of geometric functional analysis since the 1970's. They have applications in several fields, most notably in theoretical computer science, statistics and signal processing. A few basic applications are covered in this text, particularly for the problem of estimating covariance matrices in statistics and for validating probabilistic constructions of measurement matrices in compressed sensing. These notes are written particularly for graduate students and beginning researchers in different areas, including functional analysts, probabilists, theoretical statisticians, electrical engineers, and theoretical computer scientists.

title: Introduction to the non-asymptotic analysis of random matrices
abstract: This tutorial introduces the non-asymptotic analysis of random matrices, focusing on methods and concepts for understanding the behavior of extreme singular values in matrices with independent rows or columns. Unlike classical asymptotic random matrix theory, which describes limiting spectral properties as dimensions grow, the non-asymptotic approach provides quantitative probabilistic guarantees valid for fixed dimensions, making it particularly relevant for applications in statistics, geometric functional analysis, and compressed sensing. The text develops tools from high-dimensional probability and geometric functional analysis, including properties of sub-gaussian and sub-exponential random variables, isotropic vectors, large deviation inequalities, and covering arguments. Four main models are considered: matrices with independent sub-gaussian or heavy-tailed rows or columns. Applications discussed include covariance matrix estimation from high-dimensional data and the construction of measurement matrices with restricted isometry properties for compressed sensing. The exposition is tailored for graduate students and researchers across mathematics, statistics, engineering, and computer science, emphasizing foundational techniques over exhaustive coverage of results.

title: Julia: A Fresh Approach to Numerical Computing
abstract: Bridging cultures that have often been distant, Julia combines expertise from the diverse fields of computer science and computational science to create a new approach to numerical computing. Julia is designed to be easy and fast and questions notions generally held to be “laws of nature' by practitioners of numerical computing: \beginlist \item High-level dynamic programs have to be slow. \item One must prototype in one language and then rewrite in another language for speed or deployment. \item There are parts of a system appropriate for the programmer, and other parts that are best left untouched as they have been built by the experts. \endlist We introduce the Julia programming language and its design---a dance between specialization and abstraction. Specialization allows for custom treatment. Multiple dispatch, a technique from computer science, picks the right algorithm for the right circumstance. Abstraction, which is what good computation is really about, recognizes what remains the same after dif...

title: Julia: A Fresh Approach to Numerical Computing
abstract: Julia is a high-level, dynamic programming language designed to address the longstanding trade-off between productivity and performance in numerical computing. By integrating concepts from computer science and computational science, Julia challenges the conventional separation between user-friendly high-level languages and fast low-level languages. Its core innovations include multiple dispatch, an expressive type system, and generic programming, enabling both abstraction and specialization. This design allows users to write code that is both easy to read and capable of generating efficient machine code, eliminating the need for rewriting prototypes in lower-level languages for performance. Julia’s architecture supports the development of high-performance libraries entirely in the language itself, overcoming limitations of retrofitting existing dynamic languages. Through illustrative examples and case studies, the paper demonstrates how Julia delivers on the promise of combining ease of use with computational speed, offering a unified platform that advances both productivity and performance in scientific computing.

title: Modularity and community structure in networks.
abstract: Many networks of interest in the sciences, including social networks, computer networks, and metabolic and regulatory networks, are found to divide naturally into communities or modules. The problem of detecting and characterizing this community structure is one of the outstanding issues in the study of networked systems. One highly effective approach is the optimization of the quality function known as 'modularity' over the possible divisions of a network. Here I show that the modularity can be expressed in terms of the eigenvectors of a characteristic matrix for the network, which I call the modularity matrix, and that this expression leads to a spectral algorithm for community detection that returns results of demonstrably higher quality than competing methods in shorter running times. I illustrate the method with applications to several published network data sets.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Modularity and community structure in networks.
abstract: Many real-world networks, such as social, biological, and technological systems, exhibit community structure, where nodes cluster into groups with dense internal connections and sparser links between groups. Detecting and characterizing these communities is a central challenge in network science. This paper introduces a spectral method for community detection based on the optimization of modularity, a quality function that measures the strength of division of a network into modules by comparing the observed edge density within groups to that expected in a random network. The modularity is reformulated in terms of the eigenvectors of a newly defined modularity matrix, enabling the development of an efficient spectral algorithm for community detection. This approach yields higher-quality partitions and faster computation than existing methods, as demonstrated through applications to several empirical network data sets. The results highlight the effectiveness of modularity maximization and spectral techniques for uncovering meaningful structure in complex networks.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Multimodal Emotion Recognition using Deep Learning
abstract: New research into human-computer interaction seeks to consider the consumer's emotional status to provide a seamless human-computer interface. This would make it possible for people to survive and be used in widespread fields, including education and medicine. Multiple techniques can be defined through human feelings, including expressions, facial images, physiological signs, and neuroimaging strategies. This paper presents a review of emotional recognition of multimodal signals using deep learning and comparing their applications based on current studies. Multimodal affective computing systems are studied alongside unimodal solutions as they offer higher accuracy of classification. Accuracy varies according to the number of emotions observed, features extracted, classification system and database consistency. Numerous theories on the methodology of emotional detection and recent emotional science address the following topics. This would encourage studies to understand better physiological signals of the current state of the science and its emotional awareness problems.
venue: Journal of Applied Science and Technology Trends

title: Multimodal Emotion Recognition using Deep Learning
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive review of recent advancements in multimodal emotion recognition using deep learning techniques, emphasizing the integration of facial expressions, speech, and physiological signals to enhance the accuracy and robustness of emotion detection systems. The study discusses the limitations of unimodal approaches and highlights the superiority of multimodal systems in capturing the complexity of human emotions. Various deep learning architectures, including convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and hybrid fusion models, are examined for their effectiveness in feature extraction and classification across different modalities. The paper also surveys recent research on combining audio, text, and visual data, detailing innovative fusion strategies such as attention mechanisms and self-supervised learning frameworks. Comparative analyses demonstrate that multimodal deep learning approaches achieve higher precision in emotion classification, with performance influenced by factors such as the number of emotion categories, feature selection methods, and dataset consistency. The review concludes by identifying current challenges and suggesting directions for future research to further improve real-time emotion recognition systems in diverse applications ranging from healthcare to human-computer interaction.
venue: Journal of Applied Science and Technology Trends

title: Noise stability of functions with low influences: Invariance and optimality
abstract: In this paper, we study functions with low influences on product probability spaces. The analysis of Boolean functions f {-1, 1}/sup n/ /spl rarr/ {-1, 1} with low influences has become a central problem in discrete Fourier analysis. It is motivated by fundamental questions arising from the construction of probabilistically checkable proofs in theoretical computer science and from problems in the theory of social choice in economics. We prove an invariance principle for multilinear polynomials with low influences and bounded degree; it shows that under mild conditions the distribution of such polynomials is essentially invariant for all product spaces. Ours is one of the very few known non-linear invariance principles. It has the advantage that its proof is simple and that the error bounds are explicit. We also show that the assumption of bounded degree can be eliminated if the polynomials are slightly 'smoothed'; this extension is essential for our applications to 'noise stability '-type problems. In particular; as applications of the invariance principle we prove two conjectures: the 'Majority Is Stablest' conjecture [29] from theoretical computer science, which was the original motivation for this work, and the 'It Ain't Over Till It's Over' conjecture [27] from social choice theory. The 'Majority Is Stablest' conjecture and its generalizations proven here, in conjunction with the 'Unique Games Conjecture' and its variants, imply a number of (optimal) inapproximability results for graph problems.
venue: IEEE Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science

title: Noise stability of functions with low influences: Invariance and optimality
abstract: This paper investigates the noise stability of functions with low influences on product probability spaces, a topic central to discrete Fourier analysis and motivated by questions in theoretical computer science and social choice theory. The authors establish a new invariance principle for multilinear polynomials of bounded degree with low influences, demonstrating that their distributions are essentially invariant across all product spaces under mild conditions. This principle, notable for its simplicity and explicit error bounds, is further extended to unbounded degree polynomials via smoothing techniques, enabling applications to noise stability problems. Leveraging this framework, the paper resolves two longstanding conjectures: the “Majority Is Stablest” conjecture in hardness of approximation and the “It Ain’t Over Till It’s Over” conjecture in social choice. These results highlight the extremal role of the Majority function among low-influence functions and provide powerful new tools for analyzing optimization problems and voting schemes.
venue: IEEE Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science

title: On the Computational Complexity of Algorithms
abstract: This paper introduces a systematic framework for classifying algorithms and sequences based on their computational complexity, measured by the time required for multitape Turing machines to compute sequence terms. The authors define complexity classes ST, where a sequence is T-computable if it can be generated within a computable time bound T(n), and establish that each class is recursively enumerable but no single class contains all computable sequences, yielding a hierarchy of complexity. Key results include a speed-up theorem showing invariance under constant scaling of time bounds, containment and noncontainment conditions between classes, and the unsolvability of the general containment problem. The study examines the impact of varying machine models, such as the relationship between one-tape and multitape machines, and extends the classification to numbers, functions, and recognition problems, including explicit examples of languages not recognizable in real time. The findings support the view that numbers and functions possess intrinsic computational complexity and highlight open questions for further research in this foundational area.

title: Organizational Analysis in Computer Science
abstract: This paper argues that the discipline of computer science must broaden its theoretical and practical foundations to include organizational analysis, in order to address the growing demand for computing applications that effectively support high-performance human organizations. Drawing on recent policy reports and trends in computing, the paper highlights the limitations of traditional mathematical models in addressing issues of usability and organizational impact. It contends that computer scientists and graduates increasingly require skills in analyzing human organizations to develop systems that are both technically robust and socially valuable. The integration of organizational informatics into computer science research and education is presented as essential for understanding the complex socio-technical contexts in which computing systems are designed, implemented, and used. By embracing organizational analysis, the field can better justify large-scale research investments and produce graduates equipped to meet the challenges of contemporary computing in diverse application domains.

title: Outlier Detection in High Dimensional Data
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the science that allows computers to replicate human intelligence in areas such as decision-making, text processing, visual perception. Artificial Intelligence is the broader field that contains several subfields such as machine learning, robotics, and computer vision. Machine Learning is a branch of Artificial Intelligence that allows a machine to learn and improve at a task over time. Deep Learning is a subset of machine learning that makes use of deep artificial neural networks for training. The paper proposed on outlier detection for multivariate high dimensional data for Autoencoder unsupervised model.

title: Outlier Detection in High Dimensional Data
abstract: This paper presents an approach for outlier detection in high dimensional multivariate data using an autoencoder-based unsupervised model. Outlier detection is essential for identifying data points that deviate significantly from normal patterns, which is critical in applications such as fraud detection, network intrusion, and healthcare analysis. The study reviews various outlier detection methods, including statistical, proximity-based, and clustering techniques, and highlights the challenges associated with high dimensional data. The proposed methodology employs a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) autoencoder neural network that learns to reconstruct input data and identifies anomalies based on reconstruction error exceeding a defined threshold. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the autoencoder model in distinguishing outliers from normal instances in time series datasets, with performance evaluated using training and validation loss metrics. The findings suggest that autoencoder-based unsupervised learning offers a robust solution for detecting anomalies in complex, high dimensional datasets.

title: Philosophy of Computer Science: An Introductory Course
abstract: There are many branches of philosophy called 'the philosophy of X,' where X = disciplines ranging from history to physics. The philosophy of artificial intelligence has a long history, and there are many courses and texts with that title. Surprisingly, the philosophy of computer science is not nearly as well-developed. This article proposes topics that might constitute the philosophy of computer science and describes a course covering those topics, along with suggested readings and assignments.

title: Philosophy of Computer Science: An Introductory Course
abstract: This paper addresses the underdeveloped field of the philosophy of computer science by outlining the structure, content, and rationale of an introductory university course on the subject. Distinguishing the philosophy of computer science from the more established philosophy of artificial intelligence, the course explores foundational metaphysical, epistemological, and ethical questions unique to computer science, such as the nature of computation, algorithms, programs, and their relation to science and engineering. The syllabus is organized around key philosophical questions and incorporates critical thinking and argument analysis tailored for computer science students. The article surveys relevant literature, suggests readings, discusses assignments, and reflects on student engagement and learning outcomes. By presenting this course model, the paper advocates for broader inclusion of philosophical inquiry in computer science education to enhance analytical skills and interdisciplinary understanding.

title: Quantum computational advantage using photons
abstract: A light approach to quantum advantage Quantum computational advantage or supremacy is a long-anticipated milestone toward practical quantum computers. Recent work claimed to have reached this point, but subsequent work managed to speed up the classical simulation and pointed toward a sample size–dependent loophole. Quantum computational advantage, rather than being a one-shot experimental proof, will be the result of a long-term competition between quantum devices and classical simulation. Zhong et al. sent 50 indistinguishable single-mode squeezed states into a 100-mode ultralow-loss interferometer and sampled the output using 100 high-efficiency single-photon detectors. By obtaining up to 76-photon coincidence, yielding a state space dimension of about 1030, they measured a sampling rate that is about 1014-fold faster than using state-of-the-art classical simulation strategies and supercomputers. Science, this issue p. 1460 Quantum computational advantage is demonstrated using boson sampling with photons. Quantum computers promise to perform certain tasks that are believed to be intractable to classical computers. Boson sampling is such a task and is considered a strong candidate to demonstrate the quantum computational advantage. We performed Gaussian boson sampling by sending 50 indistinguishable single-mode squeezed states into a 100-mode ultralow-loss interferometer with full connectivity and random matrix—the whole optical setup is phase-locked—and sampling the output using 100 high-efficiency single-photon detectors. The obtained samples were validated against plausible hypotheses exploiting thermal states, distinguishable photons, and uniform distribution. The photonic quantum computer, Jiuzhang, generates up to 76 output photon clicks, which yields an output state-space dimension of 1030 and a sampling rate that is faster than using the state-of-the-art simulation strategy and supercomputers by a factor of ~1014.

title: Quantum computational advantage using photons
abstract: We report the experimental demonstration of quantum computational advantage using Gaussian boson sampling with photons. By generating 50 high-purity, highly indistinguishable single-mode squeezed states and injecting them into a 100-mode ultralow-loss, fully connected interferometer, we achieve sampling with up to 76 detected photon clicks. The system is phase-locked to maintain coherence across all photon number superpositions and utilizes 100 high-efficiency single-photon detectors. The resulting output state space reaches a dimension of approximately 10^30, and the sampling rate exceeds that of the best known classical simulation strategies and supercomputers by a factor of about 10^14. Rigorous validation against alternative hypotheses—including thermal states, distinguishable photons, and uniform distributions—confirms the quantum nature of the sampling process. Our results establish a clear quantum computational advantage in photonic systems and provide strong evidence against the Extended Church-Turing thesis by demonstrating a task intractable for classical computation with current technology.

title: Quantum Hamiltonian Complexity
abstract: Constraint satisfaction problems are a central pillar of modern computational complexity theory. This survey provides an introduction to the rapidly growing field of Quantum Hamiltonian Complexity, which includes the study of quantum constraint satisfaction problems. Over the past decade and a half, this field has witnessed fundamental breakthroughs, ranging from the establishment of a 'Quantum Cook-Levin Theorem' to deep insights into the structure of 1D low-temperature quantum systems via so-called area laws. Our aim here is to provide a computer science-oriented introduction to the subject in order to help bridge the language barrier between computer scientists and physicists in the field. As such, we include the following in this survey: 1 The motivations and history of the field, 2 a glossary of condensed matter physics terms explained in computer-science friendly language, 3 overviews of central ideas from condensed matter physics, such as indistinguishable particles, mean field theory, tensor networks, and area laws, and 4 brief expositions of selected computer science-based results in the area. For example, as part of the latter, we provide a novel information theoretic presentation of Bravyi's polynomial time algorithm for Quantum 2-SAT.
venue: Foundations and Trends® in Theoretical Computer Science

title: Quantum Hamiltonian Complexity
abstract: Quantum Hamiltonian Complexity (QHC) is an interdisciplinary field at the intersection of quantum physics, computer science, and mathematics, focused on the computational study of quantum constraint satisfaction problems through the lens of local Hamiltonians. This survey provides a comprehensive introduction to QHC, tracing its historical development from both computer science and physics perspectives, and highlighting key breakthroughs such as the quantum analogue of the Cook-Levin Theorem and area laws for one-dimensional quantum systems. It aims to bridge disciplinary gaps by offering accessible explanations of foundational concepts in quantum information, a glossary of condensed matter physics terminology, and overviews of central techniques including mean-field theory, tensor networks, and renormalization methods. The survey also reviews pivotal results in the field, such as the QMA-completeness of k-local Hamiltonian problems and efficient algorithms for special cases like Quantum 2-SAT, presented with novel information-theoretic insights. By synthesizing motivations, methods, and results, this work serves as a foundational resource for researchers seeking to understand the computational complexity inherent in quantum many-body systems.
venue: Foundations and Trends® in Theoretical Computer Science

title: Real-time computing: a new discipline of computer science and engineering
abstract: This paper surveys the state of the art in real-time computing. It introduces basic concepts and identifies key issues in the design of real-time systems. Solutions proposed in literature for tackling these issues are also briefly discussed. >

title: Real-time computing: a new discipline of computer science and engineering
abstract: This paper surveys the emerging discipline of real-time computing within computer science and engineering, emphasizing its foundational concepts, key challenges, and current solutions. Real-time systems are distinguished by their stringent timing constraints, where the correctness of operations depends not only on logical outcomes but also on the timeliness of task completion. The paper classifies real-time tasks based on their periodicity and deadline criticality—hard, firm, or soft—and discusses the implications of these classifications for system design. Predictability is highlighted as a central requirement, necessitating guarantees that system timing constraints will be met under specified assumptions. The survey addresses additional constraints such as resource availability, task precedence, and dependability, and explores how system architecture, operating systems, and programming languages must support timing guarantees at multiple abstraction levels. By reviewing state-of-the-art scheduling techniques and identifying unresolved issues, the paper establishes real-time computing as a distinct and vital area warranting further research and development.

title: Sisvar: a computer statistical analysis system
abstract: Sisvar is a statistical analysis system, first released in 1996 although its development began in 1994. The first version was done in the programming language Pascal and compiled with Borland Turbo Pascal 3. Sisvar was developed to achieve some specific goals. The first objective was to obtain software that could be used directly on the statistical experimental course of the Department of Exact Science at the Federal University of Lavras. The second objective was to initiate the development of a genuinely Brazilian free software program that met the demands and peculiarities of research conducted in the country. The third goal was to present statistical analysis software for the Brazilian scientific community that would allow research results to be analyzed efficiently and reliably. All of the initial goals were achieved. Sisvar gained acceptance by the scientific community because it provides reliable, accurate, precise, simple and robust results, and allows users a greater degree of interactivity.

title: Sisvar: a computer statistical analysis system
abstract: Sisvar is a free, user-friendly statistical analysis software developed to address the specific needs of Brazilian researchers and educators, particularly in experimental statistics. Initially created in Pascal and later updated for Windows, Sisvar offers robust modules for analysis of variance (ANOVA), multiple comparisons, regression, and hypothesis testing, with a focus on balanced data and fixed Gauss-Markov linear models. Its interactive interface and detailed output have contributed to its widespread adoption in academic and research institutions across Brazil. Key advantages include the ability to efficiently slice interaction effects in linear models and perform advanced procedures such as the Scott-Knott test, which are not available in most competing software. While Sisvar is limited to balanced designs and fixed effects, its reliability, accessibility, and tailored features make it a valuable tool for statistical analysis in the Brazilian scientific community. Ongoing development aims to further expand its capabilities with a new Java-based version.

title: Six Degrees: The Science of a Connected Age
abstract: 'Six degrees of separation' is a cliche, as is 'it's a small world', both cliches of the language and cliches of everyone's experience. We all live in tightly bonded social networks, yet linked to vast numbers of other people more closely than we sometimes think. Only in recent years, however, have scientists begun to apply insights from the theoretical study of networks to understand forms of network as superficially different as social networks and electrical networks, computer networks and economic networks, and to show how common principles underlie them all. Duncan Watts explores the science of networks and its implications, ranging from the Dutch tulipmania of the 17th century to the success of Harry Potter, from the impact of September 11 on Manhattan to the brain of the sea-slug, from the processes that lead to stockmarket crashes to the structure of the world wide web. As stimulating and life-changing as James Gleick's Chaos, Six Degrees is a ground-breaking and important book.

title: Six Degrees: The Science of a Connected Age
abstract: This paper reviews the development of network science, focusing on the emergence of random graph theory and its application to real-world networks as explored in Duncan J. Watts’s Six Degrees: The Science of a Connected Age and Albert-László Barabási’s Linked. It traces the origins of the field from the foundational work of Erdős and Rényi on random graphs, through Milgram’s small-world experiments, to the formulation of the Watts-Strogatz small-world model and Barabási-Albert preferential attachment model. The review highlights how these models explain key properties observed in diverse networks, such as short average path lengths, high clustering, and power-law degree distributions. It also discusses the limitations and misinterpretations of these models when applied to empirical data, emphasizing that while preferential attachment produces power laws, not all power laws arise from this mechanism. The paper concludes by noting the profound impact of network science on understanding complex systems in social, biological, and technological domains, while cautioning against overgeneralization of its results.

title: Soft Computing
abstract: Soft Computing is dedicated to system solutions based on soft computing techniques. It provides rapid dissemination of important results in soft computing technologies, a fusion of research in evolutionary algorithms and genetic programming, neural science and neural net systems, fuzzy set theory and fuzzy systems, and chaos theory and chaotic systems. Soft Computing encourages the integration of soft computing techniques and tools into both everyday and advanced applications. By linking the ideas and techniques of soft computing with other disciplines, the journal serves as a unifying platform that fosters comparisons, extensions, and new applications. As a result, the journal is an international forum for all scientists and engineers engaged in research and development in this fast growing field. title: Soft Computing
abstract: Soft computing is a computational paradigm inspired by the human ability to make approximate decisions and solve problems under imprecise or uncertain conditions, without requiring high precision or accuracy. Unlike traditional AI approaches that rely on symbolic processing and precise reasoning, soft computing aims to develop methodologies that tolerate imprecision and uncertainty, enabling simpler and more effective inference and problem-solving in real-world scenarios. Key technologies supporting soft computing include fuzzy theory, neural networks, probabilistic reasoning, genetic algorithms, chaos theory, and knowledge engineering. The concept of toll sets, introduced by Dubois and Prade, extends fuzzy set theory by associating a cost or penalty with membership, providing a new perspective for modeling uncertainty. Ongoing research, such as the Berkeley Initiative for Soft Computing (BISC), continues to advance the field by fostering collaboration and innovation in these methodologies.

title: The Book of Why: The New Science of Cause and Effect†
abstract: Judea Pearl is on a mission to change the way we interpret data. An eminent professor of computer science, Pearl has documented his research and opinions in scholarly books and papers. Now, he has ...

title: The Book of Why: The New Science of Cause and Effect†
abstract: This review critically examines The Book of Why: The New Science of Cause and Effect by Judea Pearl and Dana Mackenzie, highlighting its accessible synthesis of the historical and conceptual evolution of causal inference. Pearl’s central argument challenges the traditional reliance on association in observational studies, advocating for a structured approach to causality through his Ladder of Causation, which distinguishes between association, intervention, and counterfactual reasoning. The review explores the limitations of model-free statistical methods and underscores the transformative potential of graphical models and the do-operator in extracting causal relationships from data. Through historical examples such as the smoking-lung cancer debate and contemporary controversies like social network studies on obesity, the review illustrates the practical implications and ongoing debates in causal analysis. Pearl’s framework is presented as a significant advancement that clarifies the assumptions underlying empirical research and enhances our ability to answer “why” questions in science, with broad applications ranging from public health to artificial intelligence.

title: The Computer Revolution in Philosophy: Philosophy, Science, and Models of Mind
abstract: The book presented deep important connections between Artificial Intelligence and Philosophy, based partly on an argument that both philosophy and science are primarily concerned with identifying and explaining possibilities contrary to a common view that science is primarily concerned with laws. The book attempted to show in principle how the construction, testing and debugging of complex computational models, explaining possibilities in a new way, can illuminate a collection of deep philosophical problems, e.g. about the nature of mind, the nature of representation, the nature of mathematical discovery. However it did not claim that this could be done easily or that the problems would be solved soon. 40 years later many of them have still not been solved, including explaining how biological brains made possible the deep mathematical discoveries made millennia ago, long before the development of modern logic, often wrongly assumed to provide foundations for all of mathematics. Later work on these ideas includes the author's Meta-Morphogenesis project, inspired by Alan Turing's work: http://www.cs.bham.ac.uk/research/projects/cogaff/misc/meta-morphogenesis.html Originally published in 1978 by Harvester Press, this went out of print. An electronic version was created from a scanned in copy and then extensively edited with corrections, addtional text, and notes, available online as html or pdf, intermittently updated. This pdf version was created on 2019/07/09.

title: The Computer Revolution in Philosophy: Philosophy, Science, and Models of Mind
abstract: This work explores the transformative impact of computational concepts and artificial intelligence on philosophy, science, and our understanding of the mind. Challenging traditional boundaries between disciplines, it argues that both science and philosophy fundamentally seek to explain possibilities—how various kinds of entities, states, and processes can exist—rather than merely cataloguing laws or empirical regularities. The book develops the notion of virtual machinery as a central explanatory tool for biological and psychological phenomena, emphasizing the significance of compositionality and generative explanation in understanding intelligence. It provides a critical analysis of conceptual analysis, intuition, analogical reasoning, learning, perception, and the ethical implications of intelligent machines. Through detailed case studies and theoretical models, it demonstrates how computational approaches reshape longstanding philosophical debates about mind, knowledge, and explanation, offering new frameworks for interdisciplinary research in cognitive science, artificial intelligence, neuroscience, and philosophy.

title: The Deluge of Spurious Correlations in Big Data
abstract: Very large databases are a major opportunity for science and data analytics is a remarkable new field of investigation in computer science. The effectiveness of these tools is used to support a “philosophy” against the scientific method as developed throughout history. According to this view, computer-discovered correlations should replace understanding and guide prediction and action. Consequently, there will be no need to give scientific meaning to phenomena, by proposing, say, causal relations, since regularities in very large databases are enough: “with enough data, the numbers speak for themselves”. The “end of science” is proclaimed. Using classical results from ergodic theory, Ramsey theory and algorithmic information theory, we show that this “philosophy” is wrong. For example, we prove that very large databases have to contain arbitrary correlations. These correlations appear only due to the size, not the nature, of data. They can be found in “randomly” generated, large enough databases, which—as we will prove—implies that most correlations are spurious. Too much information tends to behave like very little information. The scientific method can be enriched by computer mining in immense databases, but not replaced by it.

title: The Deluge of Spurious Correlations in Big Data
abstract: The rapid expansion of big data has fueled claims that data-driven correlations can supplant traditional scientific methods, suggesting that with sufficient data, statistical associations alone are sufficient for prediction and decision-making, rendering causal understanding and theoretical models obsolete. This paper challenges such assertions by drawing on results from ergodic theory, Ramsey theory, and algorithmic information theory to demonstrate that very large datasets inevitably contain numerous arbitrary correlations that arise purely due to their size rather than any underlying causal structure. These spurious correlations, which can be found even in randomly generated large datasets, undermine the reliability of conclusions drawn solely from data mining without scientific interpretation. The analysis shows that an overabundance of information can paradoxically mimic the effects of having too little, leading to misleading patterns and false insights. The authors argue that while computational tools and large-scale data analysis can enrich scientific inquiry, they cannot replace the need for hypothesis-driven research, critical thinking, and the search for meaning through causal explanation.

title: The structure of scientific collaboration networks.
abstract: The structure of scientific collaboration networks is investigated. Two scientists are considered connected if they have authored a paper together and explicit networks of such connections are constructed by using data drawn from a number of databases, including MEDLINE (biomedical research), the Los Alamos e-Print Archive (physics), and NCSTRL (computer science). I show that these collaboration networks form 'small worlds,' in which randomly chosen pairs of scientists are typically separated by only a short path of intermediate acquaintances. I further give results for mean and distribution of numbers of collaborators of authors, demonstrate the presence of clustering in the networks, and highlight a number of apparent differences in the patterns of collaboration between the fields studied.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: The structure of scientific collaboration networks.
abstract: This study analyzes the structure of scientific collaboration networks by constructing explicit graphs in which nodes represent scientists and edges indicate coauthorship, using data from large-scale databases across biomedical research, physics, and computer science. The results reveal that these networks exhibit small-world properties, with most scientists connected by short paths of intermediate collaborators. The analysis quantifies the mean and distribution of collaborators per author, demonstrates significant clustering indicative of tightly knit research communities, and identifies notable differences in collaboration patterns across disciplines. These findings provide insight into the social organization of science and have implications for understanding information flow and innovation within scientific communities.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Topic Modeling in Management Research: Rendering New Theory from Textual Data
abstract: Increasingly, management researchers are using topic modeling, a new method borrowed from computer science, to reveal phenomenon-based constructs and grounded conceptual relationships in textual da...

title: Topic Modeling in Management Research: Rendering New Theory from Textual Data
abstract: This paper reviews the emergence and application of topic modeling as a methodological innovation in management research, highlighting its capacity to generate new theoretical constructs and conceptual relationships from large-scale textual data. By positioning topic modeling as a rendering process that bridges qualitative and quantitative approaches, the authors distinguish it from related techniques such as content analysis, grounded theorizing, and general natural language processing. The review outlines the steps involved in rendering with topic modeling and analyzes its contributions to five key areas of management theory: detecting novelty and emergence, developing inductive classification systems, understanding online audiences and products, analyzing frames and social movements, and exploring cultural dynamics. The authors further discuss recent trends in topic modeling and emphasize the continued importance of researcher interpretation alongside computational analysis. Ultimately, the paper demonstrates how topic modeling can advance theory building in management by enabling scholars to systematically extract meaning from complex textual corpora while maintaining interpretive rigor.

title: Arbitrage Theory in Continuous Time
abstract: The fourth edition of this textbook on pricing and hedging of financial derivatives, now also including dynamic equilibrium theory, continues to combine sound mathematical principles with economic applications. Concentrating on the probabilistic theory of continuous time arbitrage pricing of financial derivatives, including stochastic optimal control theory and optimal stopping theory, the book is designed for graduate students in economics and mathematics, and combines the necessary mathematical background with a solid economic focus. It includes a solved example for every new technique presented, contains numerous exercises, and suggests further reading in each chapter. All concepts and ideas are discussed, not only from a mathematics point of view, but the mathematical theory is also always supplemented with lots of intuitive economic arguments. In the substantially extended fourth edition Tomas Björk has added completely new chapters on incomplete markets, treating such topics as the Esscher transform, the minimal martingale measure, f-divergences, optimal investment theory for incomplete markets, and good deal bounds. There is also an entirely new part of the book presenting dynamic equilibrium theory. This includes several chapters on unit net supply endowments models, and the Cox–Ingersoll–Ross equilibrium factor model (including the CIR equilibrium interest rate model). Providing two full treatments of arbitrage theory—the classical delta hedging approach and the modern martingale approach—the book is written in such a way that these approaches can be studied independently of each other, thus providing the less mathematically oriented reader with a self-contained introduction to arbitrage theory and equilibrium theory, while at the same time allowing the more advanced student to see the full theory in action.

title: Arbitrage Theory in Continuous Time
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive and rigorous treatment of arbitrage theory in continuous time, bridging foundational discrete-time models with advanced stochastic calculus and martingale techniques. Beginning with the binomial and general one-period frameworks, the exposition develops key concepts such as arbitrage, risk-neutral valuation, and market completeness. The mathematical underpinnings are established through stochastic integrals, differential equations, and the Itô calculus, enabling the transition to continuous-time portfolio dynamics and pricing. Central results include the derivation of the Black-Scholes equation, martingale pricing methods, and the characterization of hedging strategies in both complete and incomplete markets. Extensions cover a wide range of financial instruments—including forwards, futures, options with dividends, currency derivatives, and interest rate products—employing tools such as change of numeraire, Girsanov's theorem, and stochastic discount factors. The work further explores optimal investment and consumption via stochastic control and martingale approaches, addresses utility-based pricing in incomplete markets, and introduces equilibrium models such as Cox-Ingersoll-Ross. Through its unified framework, the paper elucidates the interplay between probability theory, partial differential equations, and financial economics in modern arbitrage pricing.

title: Asymmetric Price Transmission: A Survey
abstract: Asymmetric price transmission has been the subject of considerable attention in agricultural economics. It is not only important because it may point to gaps in economic theory, but also because its presence is often considered for policy purposes to be evidence of market failure. In this paper we survey the literature on asymmetric price transmission. A wide variety of often conflicting theories of, and empirical tests for, asymmetry co‐exist in this literature. We classify the different types and causes of asymmetric price transmission and describe the econometric techniques used to quantify it. We also briefly review the results of empirical applications. Outstanding methodological problems and suggestions for future research are discussed. Our main conclusion is that the existing literature is far from being unified or conclusive, and that it has often been largely method‐driven, with little attention devoted to theoretical underpinnings and the plausible interpretation of results. Hence, much interesting theoretical and empirical work remains to be done.

title: Asymmetric Price Transmission: A Survey
abstract: This paper surveys the literature on asymmetric price transmission, a phenomenon where price adjustments in response to shocks differ in speed or magnitude depending on the direction of the initial change. The survey classifies types of asymmetry, distinguishing between magnitude and speed effects, and considers both vertical and spatial dimensions. It reviews theoretical explanations, with particular attention to market power, adjustment costs, political intervention, asymmetric information, and inventory management. The paper also examines econometric methods used to detect and quantify asymmetry, highlighting methodological challenges such as the risk of excessive rejection of symmetry due to standard testing procedures. The review finds that existing theories and empirical evidence are often conflicting and inconclusive, with current tests unable to discriminate effectively among competing explanations. The authors conclude that despite decades of research, significant gaps remain in understanding asymmetric price transmission, cautioning against drawing strong policy or theoretical conclusions from the current literature and emphasizing the need for further methodological and empirical work.

title: Auctions: Theory and Practice
abstract: This book is a non-technical introduction to auction theory; its practical application in auction design (including many examples); and its uses in other parts of economics. It can be used for a graduate course on auction theory, or – by picking selectively – an advanced undergraduate or MBA course on auctions and auction design. Part A introduces the basic theory. Part B shows how modern auction-theoretic tools illuminate a range of mainstream economic questions that are superficially unconnected with auctions. Part C discusses practical auction design. Part D describes the one-hundred-billion dollar 3G mobile-phone license auctions. None of the writing is technical, except in the Appendices. The material was presented as the inaugural (2003) Toulouse Lectures in Economics and is forthcoming at Princeton University Press. This document contains the Contents, Preface and Introduction to the book. A draft of the FULL BOOK is available at http://www.paulklemperer.org.

title: Auctions: Theory and Practice
abstract: This book provides a comprehensive, non-technical introduction to auction theory, its practical applications in auction design, and its broader relevance across economics. It is structured to serve as a resource for graduate, advanced undergraduate, or MBA courses, as well as for general readers. The text begins by outlining fundamental auction theory and surveying key literature, then demonstrates how auction-theoretic tools can illuminate diverse economic phenomena beyond traditional auction settings. Subsequent sections focus on practical aspects of auction design, highlighting the importance of addressing issues such as collusion and entry deterrence, and drawing lessons from real-world examples. The book culminates in an in-depth case study of the record-setting 3G mobile-phone license auctions, analyzing their design, execution, bidder strategies, and outcomes. Throughout, the material emphasizes the critical role of thoughtful auction design in achieving successful outcomes and illustrates how insights from auction theory can inform both policy and practice in economics.

title: Behavioral economics: reunifying psychology and economics.
abstract: 'Behavioral economics' improves the realism of the psychological assumptions underlying economic theory, promising to reunify psychology and economics in the process. Reunification should lead to better predictions about economic behavior and better policy prescriptions.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Behavioral economics: reunifying psychology and economics.
abstract: Behavioral economics seeks to reunify psychology and economics by integrating more realistic psychological assumptions into economic theory, thereby improving predictions of economic behavior and informing policy. Historically, the disciplines diverged due to differing scientific approaches—economists favoring mathematical formalism and psychologists emphasizing experimental methods—and the adoption of rationality assumptions that ignored psychological evidence. Recent advances in behavioral economics incorporate psychological insights into core economic principles, offering alternatives to traditional models such as prospect theory for risky decision-making, hyperbolic discounting for intertemporal choice, social utility models for altruism and fairness, and empirically grounded learning rules for equilibrium processes. These developments demonstrate that psychologically informed models can be mathematically tractable, parsimonious, and predictive, supporting a productive reunification of the two fields and promising richer understanding and application of economic behavior.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Benefit and Distance Functions
abstract: Abstract We explore the relationship between R. W. Shephard's input distance function (“Cost and Production Functions,” Princeton Univ. Press, Princeton, 1953) and D. G. Luenberger's benefit function ( J. Math. Econ. 21 (1992a), 461–481). We point out that the latter can be recognized in a production context as a directional input distance function which can exhaustively characterize technologies in both price and input space. D. McFadden's (Cost, revenue, and profit functions, in “Production Economics: A Dual Approach to Theory and Applications, “North-Holland/Elsevier, New York, 1978) composition rules for input sets and input distance functions are then extended to the directional input distance function. Journal of Economic Literature Classification Numbers : D21, D24, D29.

title: Benefit and Distance Functions
abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between Shephard’s input distance function and Luenberger’s benefit function, demonstrating that the latter can be interpreted as a directional input distance function within a production framework. The analysis shows that, under appropriate assumptions regarding input disposability, the directional input distance function provides a complete characterization of production technologies. The paper extends McFadden’s composition rules for input sets and input distance functions to the directional case, establishing equivalences between primal and dual representations of technology. Duality theorems are discussed, linking cost functions and distance functions, and variations of Shephard’s Lemma are derived for both the standard and directional distance functions. The results highlight the theoretical and empirical utility of benefit and distance functions in representing production technologies and their dual relationships with cost structures.

title: Beyond the Lecture: Case Teaching and the Learning of Economic Theory
abstract: The use of the case method in a liberal arts college and a research university is discussed. The students' reactions a re reported as overwhelmingly positive. They felt that the cases were more useful than texts and lectures in learning about institutional arrangements, how to use economic data, and how to use economics to solve real problems.

title: Beyond the Lecture: Case Teaching and the Learning of Economic Theory
abstract: This paper investigates the effectiveness of case teaching as an alternative to traditional lecture-based instruction in the learning of economic theory. Drawing on classroom experiments and comparative analysis, the study examines how case-based pedagogy influences students’ comprehension, retention, and application of core economic concepts. The authors present evidence that case teaching fosters greater student engagement, critical thinking, and real-world problem-solving skills by situating theoretical material within practical contexts. The findings suggest that integrating case methods into economics curricula enhances both conceptual understanding and the ability to apply theory to complex situations, offering a compelling complement or substitute to conventional lecture formats in economics education.

title: Capabilities and Governance: The Rebirth of Production in the Theory of Economic Organization
abstract: We argue that since Coase’s seminal 1937 paper on “The Nature of the Firm,” there has been an odd and unjustified separation between price theory and the economics of organization. For example, matters of production has been the domain of the former exclusively. However, a new approach to economic organization, here called “the capabilities approach,” that places production center-stage in the explanation of economic organization, is now emerging. We discuss the sources of this approach and its relation to the mainstream economics of organization.

title: Capabilities and Governance: The Rebirth of Production in the Theory of Economic Organization
abstract: This paper critiques the longstanding division between price theory and the economics of organization that has characterized post-Coasean literature, arguing that production has been unduly relegated to the former while the latter has focused almost exclusively on transaction costs and governance structures. The authors document the historical roots and intellectual consequences of this separation, highlighting how modern theories have tended to overlook the role of productive knowledge, capabilities, and coordination within firms. They introduce and elaborate on the emerging “capabilities approach,” which places production and organizational learning at the center of the theory of economic organization. By integrating insights from evolutionary economics and knowledge-based perspectives, this approach challenges the prevailing transaction cost paradigm and suggests that firms’ internal capabilities are crucial to understanding their boundaries, structures, and performance. The paper concludes that a renewed focus on production enriches the analysis of economic organization and opens new avenues for research on firm behavior and industrial dynamics.

title: Complexity Thinking and Evolutionary Economic Geography
abstract: Thus far, most of the work towards the construction of an evolutionary economic geography has drawn upon a particular version of evolutionary economics, namely the Nelson-Winter framework, which blends Darwinian concepts and metaphors (especially variety, selection, novelty and inheritance) and elements of a behavioural theory of the firm. Much less attention has been directed to an alternative conception based on complexity theory, yet in recent years complexity theory has increasingly been concerned with the general attributes of evolutionary natural and social systems. In this article we explore the idea of the economic landscape as a complex adaptive system. We identify several key notions of what is being called the new ‘complexity economics’, and examine whether and in what ways these can be used to help inform an evolutionary perspective for understanding the uneven development and adaptive transformation of the economic landscape.

title: Complexity Thinking and Evolutionary Economic Geography
abstract: This paper examines the potential of complexity thinking as a foundation for evolutionary economic geography, contrasting it with the dominant neo-Darwinian Nelson-Winter framework that emphasizes variety, selection, novelty, and inheritance. While evolutionary economic geography has traditionally borrowed concepts from evolutionary biology, there is ongoing debate about the appropriateness and limits of such analogies. The authors argue that complexity theory, which conceptualizes economic landscapes as complex adaptive systems, offers alternative insights into the uneven development and adaptive transformation of regions. Drawing on developments in the science of complexity—including notions of self-organization, non-linearity, and emergent behavior—the paper explores how these ideas have influenced economics and other social sciences but have only recently begun to impact human geography. The discussion highlights the challenges of defining complexity theory due to its holistic and often elusive nature, yet points to its promise in providing a more dynamic and process-oriented understanding of spatial economic evolution. The authors conclude that while complexity thinking does not offer a unified theory, it enriches evolutionary perspectives in economic geography by emphasizing adaptive processes, path dependence, and the interplay between order and instability in shaping economic landscapes.

title: Discrete convex analysis: A tool for economics and game theory
abstract: This paper presents discrete convex analysis as a tool for use in economics and game theory. Discrete convex analysis is a new framework of discrete mathematics and optimization, developed during the last two decades. Recently, it has been recognized as a powerful tool for analyzing economic or game models with indivisibilities. The main feature of discrete convex analysis is the distinction of two convexity concepts, M-convexity and L-convexity, for functions in integer or binary variables, together with their conjugacy relationship. The crucial fact is that M-concavity in its variant is equivalent to the gross substitutes property in economics. Fundamental theorems in discrete convex analysis such as the M-L conjugacy theorems, discrete separation theorems and discrete fixed point theorems yield structural results in economics such as the existence of equilibria and the lattice structure of equilibrium price vectors. Algorithms in discrete convex analysis provide iterative auction algorithms for finding equilibria.

title: Discrete convex analysis: A tool for economics and game theory
abstract: This paper introduces discrete convex analysis as a foundational framework for addressing economic and game-theoretic models characterized by indivisibilities. Discrete convex analysis extends classical convex analysis to discrete settings, distinguishing between M-convexity and L-convexity for functions on integer or binary domains and elucidating their conjugacy relationship. A central insight is the equivalence between M-concavity and the gross substitutes property, which underpins key results in market equilibrium theory. The paper surveys fundamental theorems such as discrete separation and fixed point theorems, demonstrating their implications for equilibrium existence and the lattice structure of price vectors. Additionally, it highlights algorithmic developments, including iterative auction mechanisms derived from discrete convex analysis, and explores applications to matching markets, assignment problems, and submodular flows. By providing rigorous definitions, structural results, and computational tools, this work establishes discrete convex analysis as a versatile and powerful tool for economic theory and combinatorial optimization in environments with discrete choices.

title: Economics of Crime
abstract: This paper starts with a review the economics of criminal behavior. Then, the authors discuss the theory of public enforcement. The economic analysis of criminal behavior and criminal law has been a hugely successful enterprise. As an academic enterprise, it has achieved the goal of research—it has generated a large and growing literature. More important than academic success, however, has been the influence of this branch of learning on actual practice. The understanding of deterrence effects and rational responses by criminals has substantially changed the purpose and functioning of the criminal justice system.

title: Economics of Crime
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the economics of crime, focusing on the application of rational choice models to criminal behavior and the economic analysis of public law enforcement. Beginning with Becker’s foundational work, the authors review theoretical frameworks in which individuals weigh the costs and benefits of legal versus illegal activities, considering factors such as the probability and severity of sanctions. Empirical studies are examined to assess the deterrent effects of punishment and the influence of socio-economic variables like unemployment. The paper also addresses methodological challenges, including issues of rationality assumptions, statistical identification, and measurement errors. The analysis extends to topics such as capital punishment, gun control, and abortion, while highlighting the impact of economic research on criminal justice policy. The study concludes that economic approaches have significantly advanced both academic understanding and practical policy in crime prevention and law enforcement.

title: Economic Theory and Experimental Economics
abstract: This paper explores the questions of how economic theory can be used to design and interpret experiments and how experimental results can be used to construct and interpret economic theories. The relationship between economic theory and experiments is modeled and illustrated with examples from both theoretical and experimental work. The emphasis is on combing theory and experiment to the benefit of both.

title: Economic Theory and Experimental Economics
abstract: This paper examines the evolving relationship between economic theory and experimental economics, focusing on how these two approaches can be constructively integrated to enhance our understanding of economic behavior. Using the ultimatum game as a central example, the paper highlights the divergence between theoretical predictions and experimental outcomes, particularly regarding subgame-perfect equilibrium. It discusses issues of external and internal validity in experimental design, the robustness of experimental findings across various contexts, and the implications for refining economic models. The analysis explores how experiments can test the accuracy and precision of theories, while theory can inform the interpretation and design of experiments. The paper concludes that a careful, iterative dialogue between theory and experiment is essential for advancing both fields, emphasizing the need for nuanced standards in evaluating when experimental results support or challenge existing theories.

title: ETHICS AND ECONOMIC INTERPRETATION
