abstract: Bearing on problem of scope and method, 454. — Both economics and ethics deal with value, 454. — Economics as a pure science has given too little attention to separation of constants from variables, 455. — Sense in which wants can be considered as data, 455. — Economic interpretation as a theory of conduct, 459. — Are human motives predominantly economic, 460. — Are they predominantly instinctive, 466. The adaptation theory, 469. — The pleasure theory, 469. — Economics as a study of the adaptation of means to ends, 472. — What becomes of ethics, 476. — Three kinds of treatment of conduct, 481.

title: ETHICS AND ECONOMIC INTERPRETATION
abstract: This paper examines the complex relationship between ethics and economic interpretation, focusing on the methodological and conceptual challenges that arise from their shared engagement with values. It critiques the traditional economic assumption of treating human desires as static data, arguing that such desires are inherently dynamic and shaped by cultural, social, and economic processes. The analysis highlights the limitations of viewing economics as a purely value-neutral science and questions whether ethical considerations can be meaningfully separated from economic reasoning. By exploring the evolving nature of human motivations and the interplay between individual conduct and societal norms, the paper contends that a rigid distinction between economics and ethics is untenable. Instead, it suggests that both disciplines are interdependent, with ethical reflection necessary for a fuller understanding of economic behavior and policy. The discussion ultimately calls for a more nuanced approach to economic theory—one that recognizes the fluidity of human values and the essential role of ethical critique in interpreting economic phenomena.

title: Evolutionary Game Theory: A Renaissance
abstract: Economic agents are not always rational or farsighted and can make decisions according to simple behavioral rules that vary according to situation and can be studied using the tools of evolutionary game theory. Furthermore, such behavioral rules are themselves subject to evolutionary forces. Paying particular attention to the work of young researchers, this essay surveys the progress made over the last decade towards understanding these phenomena, and discusses open research topics of importance to economics and the broader social sciences.

title: Evolutionary Game Theory: A Renaissance
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of recent advances in evolutionary game theory, emphasizing its resurgence and expanding relevance within the social sciences. By moving beyond the traditional focus on Nash equilibrium, the review highlights how evolutionary models capture the adaptive, context-dependent behaviors of agents who may not be fully rational or farsighted. The survey organizes progress around key themes: the evolution and structure of agency, assortativity in interactions, the development of behavioral traits and cultural conventions, and applications to economic phenomena such as market selection and macroeconomic dynamics. It further examines methodological innovations in dynamic modeling, including reinforcement learning and imitation, as well as empirical studies testing evolutionary predictions. Special attention is given to contributions from emerging scholars and to open research questions that point toward future directions. The paper argues that evolutionary game theory offers a more realistic and empirically grounded framework for understanding complex social and economic systems, where simple individual rules can give rise to intricate collective outcomes.

title: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
abstract: An innovator in contemporary thought on economic and political development looks here at decline rather than growth. Albert O. Hirschman makes a basic distinction between alternative ways of reacting to deterioration in business firms and, in general, to dissatisfaction with organizations: one, “exit,” is for the member to quit the organization or for the customer to switch to the competing product, and the other, “voice,” is for members or customers to agitate and exert influence for change “from within.” The efficiency of the competitive mechanism, with its total reliance on exit, is questioned for certain important situations. As exit often undercuts voice while being unable to counteract decline, loyalty is seen in the function of retarding exit and of permitting voice to play its proper role.  The interplay of the three concepts turns out to illuminate a wide range of economic, social, and political phenomena. As the author states in the preface, “having found my own unifying way of looking at issues as diverse as competition and the two-party system, divorce and the American character, black power and the failure of ‘unhappy’ top officials to resign over Vietnam, I decided to let myself go a little.”

title: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
abstract: This paper explores the interplay between exit, voice, and loyalty as mechanisms through which individuals and groups respond to decline in firms, organizations, and states. By introducing the concepts of exit (the act of leaving or withdrawing) and voice (the act of expressing dissatisfaction), the study examines how these responses reflect economic and political dynamics. The analysis considers the latitude for deterioration within organizations, highlighting how slack can persist due to insufficient feedback mechanisms. The paper investigates the limitations of exit as a corrective tool, especially in contexts where competition is imperfect or collusive, and discusses how voice emerges as a crucial alternative or complement to exit. Special attention is given to the challenges of combining exit and voice, particularly under monopoly conditions or in spatial duopolies such as two-party political systems. The role of loyalty is theorized as a moderating factor that influences the choice between exit and voice, shaping organizational resilience and adaptability. Overall, the study provides a framework for understanding how economic and political actors navigate decline and change through their available options.

title: Fat-Tailed Uncertainty in the Economics of Catastrophic Climate Change
abstract: In this article, I revisit some basic issues concerning structural uncertainty and catastrophic climate change. My target audience here are general economists, so this article could also be viewed as a somewhat less technical exposition that supplements my previous work. Using empirical examples, I argue that it is implausible that low-probability, high-negative impact events would not much influence an economic analysis of climate change. I then try to integrate the empirical examples and the theory together into a unified package with a unified message that the possibility of catastrophic climate change needs to be taken seriously.
venue: Review of Environmental Economics and Policy

title: Fat-Tailed Uncertainty in the Economics of Catastrophic Climate Change
abstract: This paper examines the profound implications of fat-tailed uncertainty for the economics of catastrophic climate change, arguing that deep structural uncertainty and the potential for extreme, low-probability, high-impact events fundamentally challenge standard benefit-cost analyses. Through intuitive empirical examples and theoretical discussion, the paper demonstrates that conventional economic models often underestimate or inadequately represent the risks associated with unprecedented increases in greenhouse gases and uncertain climate sensitivity. The analysis highlights how standard approaches may fail to capture the full scope of potential damages, particularly in the tails of probability distributions where catastrophic outcomes reside. The author contends that these uncertainties necessitate a more robust integration of fat-tailed risk into climate policy analysis, as ignoring them can lead to dangerously incomplete or misleading conclusions about optimal climate action.
venue: Review of Environmental Economics and Policy

title: Instruments of Development: Randomization in the Tropics, and the Search for the Elusive Keys to Economic Development
abstract: There is currently much debate about the effectiveness of foreign aid and about what kind of projects can engender economic development. There is skepticism about the ability of econometric analysis to resolve these issues, or of development agencies to learn from their own experience. In response, there is movement in development economics towards the use of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to accumulate credible knowledge of what works, without over-reliance on questionable theory or statistical methods. When RCTs are not possible, this movement advocates quasi-randomization through instrumental variable (IV) techniques or natural experiments. I argue that many of these applications are unlikely to recover quantities that are useful for policy or understanding: two key issues are the misunderstanding of exogeneity, and the handling of heterogeneity. I illustrate from the literature on aid and growth. Actual randomization faces similar problems as quasi-randomization, notwithstanding rhetoric to the contrary. I argue that experiments have no special ability to produce more credible knowledge than other methods, and that actual experiments are frequently subject to practical problems that undermine any claims to statistical or epistemic superiority. I illustrate using prominent experiments in development. As with IV methods, RCT-based evaluation of projects is unlikely to lead to scientific progress in the understanding of economic development. I welcome recent trends in development experimentation away from the evaluation of projects and towards the evaluation of theoretical mechanisms.

title: Instruments of Development: Randomization in the Tropics, and the Search for the Elusive Keys to Economic Development
abstract: This paper critically examines the increasing reliance on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and instrumental variable (IV) methods in development economics as tools for identifying effective policies and projects in low-income countries. While these approaches are often promoted as providing more credible or scientific evidence than traditional econometric analyses, the paper argues that both RCTs and IV strategies are subject to significant limitations, including misunderstandings about exogeneity, inadequate handling of heterogeneity, and practical challenges in implementation. Drawing on examples from the literature on aid effectiveness and project evaluation, the paper contends that neither randomization nor quasi-randomization guarantees policy-relevant or generalizable knowledge about economic development. Instead, it suggests that a narrow focus on project-level impacts is unlikely to yield cumulative scientific progress or uncover the fundamental mechanisms driving development. The author advocates for a shift in emphasis toward understanding the theoretical mechanisms underlying interventions and their contextual applicability, arguing that this approach holds greater promise for advancing knowledge and informing policy in development economics.

title: Introducing Procedural Utility: Not Only What, But Also How Matters
abstract: People not only care about outcomes, they also value the procedures which lead to the outcomes. Procedural utility is a potentially important source of human well-being. This paper aims at introducing the concept of procedural utility into economics, and argues that it should be incorporated more widely into economic theory and empirical research. Three building blocks of a concept of procedural utility are outlined and it is suggested how procedural utility can be fruitfully integrated. Evidence from a broad range of social sciences is reviewed in order to show that procedural utility is a relevant concept for economics.

title: Introducing Procedural Utility: Not Only What, But Also How Matters
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of procedural utility, arguing that individuals derive well-being not only from outcomes but also from the processes and institutions that lead to those outcomes. In contrast to the traditional economic focus on outcome utility, procedural utility encompasses the non-instrumental value people place on how they are treated and the fairness, autonomy, and respect inherent in decision-making procedures. The authors outline three building blocks of procedural utility—hedonic content, self-relatedness, and non-instrumental process value—and review evidence from psychology, law, organizational behavior, and political science to demonstrate its empirical relevance. The paper discusses the theoretical relationship between procedural and outcome utility, explores contexts in which procedural concerns are particularly salient, and highlights the policy implications of incorporating procedural utility into economic analysis. The findings suggest that recognizing procedural utility enriches our understanding of human well-being and calls for its integration into economic theory and policy design.

title: Lab Experiments Are a Major Source of Knowledge in the Social Sciences
abstract: Experimental Economics The disciplines of social science, with the notable exception of psychology, have traditionally steered clear of laboratory. The field of economics, and in particular econometrics, has amassed an imposing arsenal of quantitative and statistical methods for analyzing observational data in assessing economic theory and in making causal inferences. More recently, laboratory experiments carried out under controlled conditions and randomized field experiments carried out under natural conditions have gained some currency as complementary approaches. Falk and Heckman (p. 535) review the strengths and shortfalls of these recent developments. Laboratory experiments are a widely used methodology for advancing causal knowledge in the physical and life sciences. With the exception of psychology, the adoption of laboratory experiments has been much slower in the social sciences, although during the past two decades the use of lab experiments has accelerated. Nonetheless, there remains considerable resistance among social scientists who argue that lab experiments lack “realism” and generalizability. In this article, we discuss the advantages and limitations of laboratory social science experiments by comparing them to research based on nonexperimental data and to field experiments. We argue that many recent objections against lab experiments are misguided and that even more lab experiments should be conducted.

title: Lab Experiments Are a Major Source of Knowledge in the Social Sciences
abstract: Laboratory experiments have become an increasingly important methodology in the social sciences for generating causal knowledge, yet their adoption has lagged behind that of the natural sciences due to concerns about realism and generalizability. This paper examines the historical growth of lab experiments in fields such as economics and political science, addresses common criticisms regarding subject pools and ecological validity, and argues that many objections are based on misunderstandings of the scientific method. By enabling controlled variation and precise manipulation of decision environments, lab experiments allow researchers to isolate causal effects that are difficult to identify in field or observational studies. The paper demonstrates how laboratory methods have challenged traditional assumptions about human behavior, such as universal self-interest, and have contributed to practical solutions in market design and policy evaluation. Rather than viewing laboratory and field approaches as mutually exclusive, the authors advocate for a complementary perspective that recognizes the unique strengths of laboratory experimentation in advancing social science knowledge.

title: Lecture Notes in Economics and Mathematical Systems
abstract: This series reports on new developments in mathematical economics, economic theory, econometrics, operations research and mathematical systems. The series welcomes proposals for: 1. Research monographs 2. Lectures on a new field or presentations of a new angle in a classical field 3. Seminars on topics of current research 4. Reports of meetings provided they are of exceptional interest and devoted to a single topic. In the case of a research monograph, or of seminar notes, the timeliness of a manuscript may be more important than its form, which may be preliminary or tentative. Manuscripts should be no less than 150 and preferably no more than 500 pages in length. The series and the volumes published in it are indexed by Scopus and ISI (selected volumes).

title: Lecture Notes in Economics and Mathematical Systems
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive overview of the book proposal process for the Lecture Notes in Economics and Mathematical Systems series, detailing the required information and guidelines for prospective authors and editors. It outlines the essential components of a successful submission, including author biographies, book descriptions, originality statements, estimated length and figures, table of contents, keywords, unique selling points, and audience analysis. The proposal form emphasizes the importance of search engine optimization (SEO) to maximize discoverability and provides instructions for open access options and competing title analysis. By systematically guiding applicants through each step, this resource aims to streamline the evaluation process for both authors and publishers while ensuring high-quality, targeted academic content for the economics and mathematical systems community.

title: Modelling Asymmetric Exchange Rate Dependence
abstract: We test for asymmetry in a model of the dependence between the Deutsche mark and the yen, in the sense that a different degree of correlation is exhibited during joint appreciations against the U.S. dollar versus during joint depreciations. We consider an extension of the theory of copulas to allow for conditioning variables, and employ it to construct flexible models of the conditional dependence structure of these exchange rates. We find evidence that the mark-dollar and yen-dollar exchange rates are more correlated when they are depreciating against the dollar than when they are appreciating. Copyright 2006 by the Economics Department Of The University Of Pennsylvania And Osaka University Institute Of Social And Economic Research Association.

title: Modelling Asymmetric Exchange Rate Dependence
abstract: This paper investigates the presence of asymmetric dependence between the Deutsche mark–U.S. dollar and Japanese yen–U.S. dollar exchange rates, focusing on whether their correlation differs during joint appreciations versus joint depreciations against the U.S. dollar. Extending copula theory to incorporate conditioning variables, the study develops flexible models for the conditional dependence structure of these exchange rates using daily data from 1991 to 2001. The results reveal that the mark–dollar and yen–dollar rates are more strongly correlated during joint depreciations than appreciations, consistent with theories of asymmetric central bank intervention and portfolio rebalancing. The analysis also identifies a significant structural break in dependence following the introduction of the euro in 1999, with a notable decline in correlation and a reversal in asymmetry. The paper demonstrates that conditional copulas provide a powerful framework for modeling time-varying, asymmetric dependence in exchange rates, offering important implications for risk management and financial modeling.

title: Organizing Entrepreneurial Judgment
abstract: Entrepreneurship, long neglected by economists and management scholars, has made a dramatic comeback in the last two decades, not only among academic economists and management scholars, but also among policymakers, educators and practitioners. Likewise, the economic theory of the firm, building on Ronald Coase's (1937) seminal analysis, has become an increasingly important field in economics and management. Despite this resurgence, there is still little connection between the entrepreneurship literature and the literature on the firm, both in academia and in management practice. This book fills this gap by proposing and developing an entrepreneurial theory of the firm that focuses on the connections between entrepreneurship and management. Drawing on insights from Austrian economics, it describes entrepreneurship as judgmental decision made under uncertainty, showing how judgment is the driving force of the market economy and the key to understanding firm performance and organization.

title: Organizing Entrepreneurial Judgment
abstract: This paper critically examines the evolution of entrepreneurship research, highlighting the limitations of mainstream economics and management theories in accounting for the entrepreneurial function. Drawing on Austrian economics and Frank Knight’s concept of entrepreneurial judgment, the authors argue that current opportunity discovery literature inadequately distinguishes between opportunity identification and exploitation, often misinterpreting its theoretical origins. The paper surveys key approaches in economics and management, emphasizing the need to re-center entrepreneurship research on judgment under uncertainty rather than treating it as a stylized or passive role within firms. By clarifying these conceptual distinctions, the paper advances a more robust theoretical foundation for understanding the organization of entrepreneurial judgment and its centrality to firm strategy and value creation.

title: Path Dependence, its Critics, and the Quest for ‘Historical Economics’
abstract: It is now widely acknowledged that institutions are a crucial factor in economic performance. Major developments have been made in our understanding of the nature and evolution of economic institutions in the last few years. This book brings together some key contributions in this area by leading internationally renowned scholars including Paul A. David, Christopher Freeman, Alan P. Kirman, Jan Kregel, Brian J. Loasby, J. Stanley Metcalfe, Bart Nooteboom and Ugo Pagano. This essential reader covers topics such as the relationship between institutions and individuals, institutions and economic development, the nature and role of markets, and the theory of institutional evolution. The book not only outlines cutting-edge developments in the field but also indicates key directions of future research for institutional and evolutionary economics.

title: Path Dependence, its Critics, and the Quest for ‘Historical Economics’
abstract: This paper examines the concept of path dependence as a defining feature of evolutionary processes in economics, clarifying its meaning through precise definitions linked to non-ergodicity in stochastic systems. Addressing widespread confusion and misinterpretation, the analysis distinguishes path dependence from general claims that ‘history matters’ and explores its relationship to market failure and the phenomenon of ‘lock-in’. The discussion highlights the challenges of evaluating the economic significance of path dependence, emphasizing the importance of counterfactual analysis and dynamic welfare assessment over static end-state comparisons. The paper argues that policy implications drawn from path dependence are more nuanced than critics suggest, often contradicting conventional laissez-faire concerns. Finally, it applies the notion reflexively to economics itself, proposing that resistance to historical approaches reflects a form of cognitive lock-in driven by intellectual sunk costs, and advocates for greater theoretical investment to advance historical economics.

title: Perspectives on Mechanism Design in Economic Theory
abstract: Roger B. Myerson delivered his Prize Lecture on 8 December 2007 at Aula Magna, Stockholm University. He was introduced by Professor Jorgen Weibull, Chairman of the Economics Prize Committee.

title: Perspectives on Mechanism Design in Economic Theory
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of mechanism design within economic theory, tracing its historical evolution from early concerns with resource allocation to the modern focus on incentives and information. The analysis highlights how classical economics emphasized allocative efficiency under resource constraints, but the limitations of price theory in addressing institutional differences necessitated new frameworks. Building on foundational contributions from game theory and the recognition of information asymmetries, the paper discusses the pivotal role of incentive compatibility and the revelation principle in characterizing feasible social coordination mechanisms. By formalizing incentive constraints alongside resource constraints, mechanism design theory enables rigorous analysis of adverse selection and moral hazard, offering new tools for evaluating and designing institutions that effectively communicate information and align individual incentives with social objectives. This perspective expands the analytical reach of economic theory, providing a unified approach to understanding and improving the performance of diverse economic institutions.

title: Property rights theory, transaction costs theory, and agency theory: an organizational economics approach to strategic management
abstract: Property rights theory has common antecedents with contractual theories of the firm such as transaction costs and agency theories, and is yet distinct from these theories. We illustrate fundamental theoretical principles derived from these three theories by analyzing the business case of oil field unitization. Theoretical principles and application of theory to oil field unitization are each summarized. From this, it is possible to see how property rights theory is well suited to explain business situations where inefficient economic outcomes persist. Additionally, property rights theory forges new theoretical connections with other branches of organizational economics, in particular, resource-based theory. Copyright © 2005 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.

title: Property rights theory, transaction costs theory, and agency theory: an organizational economics approach to strategic management
abstract: This paper examines the foundational roles of property rights theory, transaction costs theory, and agency theory within the organizational economics approach to strategic management. While these theories share intellectual origins and a common focus on the limitations of neoclassical economics in explaining firm behavior, property rights theory remains underutilized in strategic management research. The paper provides an overview of both classical and modern streams of property rights theory, tracing their development from Coase’s seminal contributions to more recent formal models. By analyzing the case of oil field unitization, the authors illustrate how property rights theory complements transaction costs and agency theories in explaining persistent inefficiencies and complex ownership structures in business settings. The analysis highlights property rights theory’s unique capacity to address issues such as shared ownership, institutional change, and the interface between law, economics, and organization theory. The paper concludes that integrating property rights theory with established organizational economics frameworks can enhance understanding of firm boundaries, governance structures, and strategic decision-making, offering new directions for research in strategic management.

title: Reported Subjective Well-Being: A Challenge for Economic Theory and Economic Policy
abstract: Over the past few years, there has been a steadily increasing interest from economists in happiness research. This paper argues that reported subjective well-being is a satisfactory empirical approximation to individual utility and endeavors to provide an impression of this new, and challenging, development. We study data from the German Socio-Economic Panel to understand (i) the role of aspirations in the relationship between income and happiness better and (ii) the effect of unemployment on people’s satisfaction with life. We discuss some of the consequences for economic policy and for economic theory.
venue: Journal of Contextual Economics – Schmollers Jahrbuch

title: Reported Subjective Well-Being: A Challenge for Economic Theory and Economic Policy
abstract: This paper examines the growing integration of subjective well-being measures into economic research, arguing that self-reported life satisfaction provides a credible empirical proxy for individual utility. Utilizing data from the German Socio-Economic Panel, the study investigates two key areas: the influence of income aspirations on the relationship between income and happiness, and the significant negative impact of unemployment on life satisfaction, independent of income effects. The findings challenge traditional economic assumptions that rely solely on observable choices and objective utility, highlighting the value of incorporating subjective well-being data to better understand individual welfare. The paper discusses the implications of these insights for both economic theory and policy, suggesting that a focus on reported well-being can inform more effective and human-centered economic policies.
venue: Journal of Contextual Economics – Schmollers Jahrbuch

title: Seeking the Roots of Entrepreneurship: Insights from Behavioral Economics
abstract: There is a growing body of evidence that many entrepreneurs seem to enter and persist in entrepreneurship despite earning low risk-adjusted returns. This has lead to attempts to provide explanations—using both standard economic theory and behavioral economics—for why certain individuals may be attracted to such an apparently unprofitable activity. Drawing on research in behavioral economics, in the sections that follow, we review three sets of possible interpretations for understanding the empirical facts related to the entry into, and persistence in, entrepreneurship. Differences in risk aversion provide a plausible and intuitive interpretation of entrepreneurial activity. In addition, a growing literature has begun to highlight the potential importance of overconfidence in driving entrepreneurial outcomes. Such a mechanism may appear at face value to work like a lower level of risk aversion, but there are clear conceptual differences—in particular, overconfidence likely arises from behavioral biases and misperceptions of probability distributions. Finally, nonpecuniary taste-based factors may be important in motivating both the decisions to enter into and to persist in entrepreneurship.

title: Seeking the Roots of Entrepreneurship: Insights from Behavioral Economics
abstract: This paper investigates the persistent puzzle of why individuals choose to enter and remain in entrepreneurship despite empirical evidence showing low average, risk-adjusted returns and high rates of failure. Drawing on Frank Knight’s distinction between risk and uncertainty, the authors review research on the individual determinants of entrepreneurial activity, focusing on how standard economic models based on expected utility fall short in explaining observed entrepreneurial behavior. The paper critically evaluates three main behavioral economic explanations—differences in risk aversion, overconfidence, and nonpecuniary motivations—and finds that while each offers some explanatory power, none fully accounts for the empirical patterns. The authors argue that a comprehensive understanding of entrepreneurship likely requires integrating multiple perspectives and highlight the importance of distinguishing between behavioral biases and preferences for informing effective entrepreneurship policy. The paper concludes by outlining promising directions for future research aimed at unraveling the complex roots of entrepreneurial decision-making.

title: Social limits to economic theory
abstract: This dissertation effects a complete re-orientation of economic theory. It shows how the economic cannot be analysed separately from the political and the social, and lays the foundation for an integrated political economy. The work examines the philosophical difficulties faced by economists, and re-draws the history of economic thought as a response to methodological dilemmas. The traditional History of Economics textbooks re-write the history in terms of the contemporary paradigm. This dissertation, by contrast, shows how the philosophical debates have shaped the trajectory of economics, and how the orientations of the schools undergo major changes so as to attempt to deal with the fundamental dilemmas of a 'policy science’. It brings out the 'hidden history’ of economics, and shows both how laissez-faire can only be defended by dropping any notion of economic 'science', and how economic theory has an implied political theory. It then considers the debate over political economic theory and the consequences for economic organisation and for environmental disruption.

title: Social limits to economic theory
abstract: This dissertation critically examines the foundational assumptions of economic theory, arguing that economics cannot be meaningfully separated from its social and political context. Through a historical and methodological analysis, it demonstrates how the evolution of economic thought has been shaped by persistent philosophical dilemmas, particularly the tension between aspirations to scientific objectivity and the inherently normative nature of policy questions. The study reveals that attempts to construct a value-neutral, positive economics are fundamentally flawed, as all economic theories and policies embed implicit social and political value judgments. By tracing debates from utilitarianism through market socialism and institutionalism to contemporary approaches, the thesis exposes the limitations of orthodox economics and advocates for an integrated political economy that explicitly incorporates social norms and political structures. The work concludes by outlining the necessity and possible contours of such a normative theory, contending that only through this integration can economic analysis adequately address real-world issues such as poverty and environmental disruption.

title: Some Simple Economics of Crowdfunding
abstract: It is not surprising that the financing of early-stage creative projects and ventures is typically geographically localized since these types of funding decisions are usually predicated on personal relationships and due diligence requiring face-to-face interactions in response to high levels of risk, uncertainty, and information asymmetry. So, to economists, the recent rise of crowdfunding—raising capital from many people through an online platform—which offers little opportunity for careful due diligence and involves not only friends and family but also many strangers from near and far, is initially startling. On the eve of launching equity-based crowdfunding, a new market for early-stage finance in the United States, we provide a preliminary exploration of its underlying economics. We highlight the extent to which economic theory, in particular transaction costs, reputation, and market design, can explain the rise of nonequity crowdfunding and offer a framework for speculating on how equity-based crowdfunding may unfold. We conclude by articulating open questions related to how crowdfunding may affect social welfare and the rate and direction of innovation.

title: Some Simple Economics of Crowdfunding
abstract: This paper explores the economic foundations of crowdfunding, a novel mechanism for financing early-stage creative projects and ventures through online platforms. Traditionally, such funding has been geographically localized and reliant on personal relationships due to high risk and information asymmetry. The emergence of crowdfunding, which enables capital-raising from a dispersed pool of strangers with limited due diligence, challenges these conventions. Drawing on economic theory, the authors examine how transaction costs, reputation mechanisms, and platform design have facilitated the growth of non-equity crowdfunding. Empirical findings reveal that crowdfunding transcends geographic constraints, exhibits highly skewed funding distributions, is influenced by herding behavior and early contributions from friends and family, and tends to reinforce existing regional agglomerations of innovation. The paper also discusses the potential for crowdfunding to substitute for traditional financing sources and highlights the overoptimism of both creators and funders regarding project outcomes. Finally, the authors outline open questions about the implications of equity-based crowdfunding for social welfare and innovation, providing a framework for future research as regulatory changes expand crowdfunding’s scope in early-stage finance.

title: Theory and methods of economic evaluation of health care.
abstract: Most economic evaluations of health care programmes at the moment are cost­ effectiveness and cost-utility analyses. The problem with these methods is that their theoretical foundations are unclear. This has led to confusion about how to define the costs and health effects and how to interpret the results of these studies. In the environmental and traffic safety fields it is instead common to carry out traditional cost-bene:fit analyses of health improving programmes. This striking difference in how health programmes are assessed in different fields was the original motivation for writing this book. The aim of the book is to tty and provide a coherent framework within cost-bene:fit analysis and welfare economics for the different methods of economic evaluation in the health care field. The book is written in an easily accessible manner and several examples of applications of the different methods are provided. It is my hope that it will be useful both for teaching purposes and as a guide for practitioners in the field. Glenn C. Blomquist, John D. Graham, Rich O'Conor and four anonymous referees provided helpful comments on previous versions of the manuscript. I would also like to express my gratitude to the following persons for helping me to prepare the manuscript: Carl-Magnus Berglund, Carin Blanksvard, Ann Brown, and Ziad Obeid.
venue: Developments in health economics and public policy

title: Theory and methods of economic evaluation of health care.
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive examination of the theoretical foundations and methodological approaches to the economic evaluation of health care interventions. It begins with an exploration of welfare economics principles, including the Pareto principle, market failure, and social welfare functions, as they relate to health care resource allocation. The analysis then addresses methods for valuing health changes, such as willingness-to-pay measures and both revealed and expressed preference techniques. Detailed attention is given to the estimation of costs, encompassing program, morbidity, and mortality costs, as well as issues like discounting and tax treatment in cost-benefit analysis. The paper further distinguishes between cost-benefit, cost-effectiveness, and cost-utility analyses, discussing their respective applications, effectiveness measures, and methodological challenges such as discounting and choice of outcome metrics like QALYs. Finally, the implications of economic evaluation for health policy are considered, including its role in treatment guidelines, organizational decision-making, technology assessment, reimbursement, and pricing. The work concludes by highlighting the critical importance of rigorous economic evaluation methods for informed policy-making in health care.
venue: Developments in health economics and public policy

title: Theory, General Equilibrium and Political Economy in Development Economics
abstract: I discuss the role of economic theory in empirical work in development economics with special emphasis on general equilibrium and political economy considerations. I argue that economic theory plays (should play) a central role in formulating models, estimates of which can be used for counterfactual and policy analysis. I discuss why counterfactual analysis based on microdata that ignores general equilibrium and political economy issues may lead to misleading conclusions. I illustrate the main arguments using examples from recent work in development economics and political economy.

title: Theory, General Equilibrium and Political Economy in Development Economics
abstract: This paper examines the essential role of economic theory, particularly general equilibrium and political economy considerations, in the empirical analysis of development economics. It argues that theory is crucial for ensuring the external validity of econometric estimates and for guiding counterfactual and policy analysis. The paper highlights how analyses that ignore general equilibrium effects—such as changes in factor prices or technology resulting from large-scale interventions—and political economy constraints—such as the influence of interest groups and institutional responses—can lead to misleading conclusions about policy impacts. Through illustrative examples, the paper demonstrates that partial equilibrium approaches may fail to capture important systemic responses, and stresses that robust development policy evaluation requires integrating theoretical frameworks capable of addressing these broader interactions. The discussion underscores the need for structural parameters that provide meaningful guidance beyond specific samples or contexts, and advocates for a central role for theory in both empirical estimation and policy design within development economics.

title: The Antitrust Analysis of Multi-Sided Platform Businesses
abstract: This Chapter provides a survey of the economics literature on multi-sided platforms with particular focus on competition policy issues, including market definition, mergers, monopolization, and coordinated behavior. It provides a survey of the general industrial organization theory of multi-sided platforms and then considers various issues concerning the application of antitrust analysis to multi-sided platform businesses. It shows that it is not possible to know whether standard economic models, often relied on for antitrust analysis, apply to multi-sided platforms without explicitly considering the existence of multiple customer groups with interdependent demand. It summarizes many theoretical and empirical papers that demonstrate that a number of results for single-sided firms, which are the focus of much of the applied antitrust economics literature, do not apply directly to multi-sided platforms.

title: The Antitrust Analysis of Multi-Sided Platform Businesses
abstract: This paper surveys the economics literature on multi-sided platform businesses with a focus on competition policy issues such as market definition, mergers, monopolization, and coordinated behavior. It reviews the industrial organization theory underlying multi-sided platforms and examines how antitrust analysis must be adapted to account for the presence of multiple interdependent customer groups. The paper demonstrates that standard economic models used in antitrust analysis for single-sided firms often do not apply directly to multi-sided platforms, highlighting the need for explicit consideration of cross-group interactions and indirect network effects. The survey synthesizes theoretical and empirical findings, showing that multi-sided platforms require distinct analytical approaches in antitrust contexts due to their unique economic characteristics, and discusses the implications for competition authorities and policy makers as these platforms play increasingly significant roles in modern industries.

title: The Economics and Politics of Women's Rights
abstract: Women’s rights and economic development are highly correlated. Today, the discrepancy between the legal rights of women and men is much larger in developing compared to developed countries. Historically, even in countries that are now rich women had few rights before economic development took off. Is development the cause of expanding women’s rights, or conversely, do women’s rights facilitate development? We argue that there is truth to both hypotheses. The literature on the economic consequences of women’s rights documents that more rights for women lead to more spending on health and children, which should benefit development. The politicaleconomy literature on the evolution of women’s rights finds that technological change increased the costs of patriarchy for men, and thus contributed to expanding women’s rights. Combining these perspectives, we discuss the theory of Doepke and Tertilt (2009), where an increase in the return to human capital induces men to vote for women’s rights, which in turn promotes growth in human capital and income per capita.

title: The Economics and Politics of Women's Rights
abstract: This paper surveys the relationship between women’s legal rights, economic development, and political change, emphasizing both historical and contemporary perspectives. The authors document a strong correlation between women’s rights and economic development across countries, noting that legal gender equality lags in developing nations. They review evidence showing that expanded rights for women—particularly in property ownership, political participation, and bodily autonomy—lead to increased investments in health, education, and children’s welfare, which in turn foster economic growth. The paper also examines the political economy of women’s rights, highlighting how technological change and shifts in the demand for human capital have altered men’s incentives to support gender equality. Theoretical models suggest a feedback loop wherein economic development and the expansion of women’s rights mutually reinforce each other. The analysis concludes that causality runs in both directions: development can promote gender equality, while women’s rights can accelerate development.

title: The Economics Approach to Cities
abstract: The economic approach to cities relies on a spatial equilibrium for workers, employers and builders. The worker's equilibrium implies that positive attributes in one location, like access to downtown or high wages, are offset by negative attributes, like high housing prices. The employer's equilibrium requires that high wages be offset by a high level of productivity, perhaps due to easy access to customers or suppliers. The search for the sources of productivity differences that can justify high wages is the basis for the study of agglomeration economies which has been a significant branch of urban economics in the past 20 years. The builder's equilibrium condition pushes us to understand the causes of supply differences across space that can explain why some places have abundant construction and low prices while others have little construction and high prices. Since the economic theory of cities emphasizes a search for exogenous causes of endogenous outcomes like local wages, housing prices and city growth, it is unsurprising that the economic empirics on cities have increasingly focused on the quest for exogenous sources of variation. The economic approach to urban policy emphasizes the need to focus on people, rather than places, as the ultimate objects of policy concern and the need for policy to anticipate the mobility of people and firms.

title: The Economics Approach to Cities
abstract: This paper outlines the economic approach to understanding cities, emphasizing the centrality of spatial equilibrium among workers, firms, and builders. It explains how positive attributes in one location, such as higher wages or better amenities, are typically offset by negatives like higher housing costs or disamenities, resulting in a no-arbitrage condition across space. The analysis highlights the importance of agglomeration economies in explaining productivity differences that justify wage disparities between cities, and investigates how variations in construction costs and regulatory environments shape housing supply and prices. The paper also discusses empirical methods in urban economics, focusing on the search for exogenous variation to identify causal relationships. Finally, it argues that urban policy should prioritize improving individual welfare over place-based interventions, taking into account the mobility of people and firms and the incentives created by policy choices.

title: The Search for R&D Spillovers
abstract: R&D spillovers are, potentially, a major source of endogenous growth in various recent 'new growth theory' models. This paper reviews the basic model of R&D spillovers and then focuses on the empirical evidence for their existence and magnitude. It surveys the older empirical literature with special attention to the economic difficulties of actually coming up with convincing evidence on this topic. Taken individually, many of the studies are flawed and subject to a variety of reservations, but the overall impression remains that R&D spillovers are both prevalent and important. Copyright 1992 by The editors of the Scandinavian Journal of Economics.

title: The Search for R&D Spillovers
abstract: This paper examines the concept and empirical evidence of research and development (R&D) spillovers, a key mechanism underlying endogenous growth in new growth theory. It reviews the theoretical foundations of R&D spillovers and surveys the empirical literature, highlighting both case studies and regression-based approaches to estimating social returns to R&D investments. The analysis addresses the challenges of measuring spillovers, including issues of attribution, data limitations, and econometric identification. While individual studies often face methodological shortcomings and data constraints, the cumulative evidence suggests that R&D spillovers are widespread and play a significant role in driving productivity growth. The paper concludes that despite measurement difficulties, the existence and importance of R&D spillovers are well supported by the literature, underscoring their relevance for innovation policy and economic growth.

title: Variety of Methodological Approach in Economics
abstract: It has been argued by some that the distinction between orthodox economics and heterodox economics does not fit the growing variety in economic theory, unified by a common methodological approach. On the other hand, it remains a central characteristic of heterodox economics that it does not share this methodological approach, but rather represents a range of alternative methodological approaches. The paper explores the evidence, and arguments, for variety in economics at different levels, and a range of issues which arise. This requires in turn a discussion of the meaning of variety in economics at the different levels of reality, methodology, method and theory. It is concluded that there is scope for more, rather than less, variety in economic methodologies, as well as within methodologies. Further, if variety is not to take the form of 'anything goes', then critical discussion by economists of different approaches to economics, and of variety itself, is required. Copyright 2007 The Author Journal compilation © 2007 Blackwell Publishing Ltd.

title: Variety of Methodological Approach in Economics
abstract: This paper examines the increasing methodological variety within economics, challenging the traditional binary distinction between orthodox and heterodox approaches. Drawing on recent literature and historical developments, it explores how economic theory has become more pluralistic, with fragmentation and specialization both within and across schools of thought. The analysis distinguishes between variety at different levels—reality, methodology, method, and theory—and considers the implications of pluralism for the discipline’s coherence and progress. While the expansion of methodological approaches offers opportunities for richer analysis and cross-disciplinary engagement, the paper cautions against unstructured eclecticism that undermines critical standards. It concludes that greater openness to methodological diversity, coupled with constructive critique, is essential for advancing economic knowledge and improving communication across specializations. The concepts of orthodoxy and heterodoxy remain relevant as meta-methodological categories for understanding this evolving landscape.

title: Where is the Economics in Spatial Econometrics?
abstract: Spatial econometrics has been criticized by some economists because some model specifications have been driven by data-analytic considerations rather than having a firm foundation in economic theory. In particular this applies to the so-called W matrix, which is integral to the structure of endogenous and exogenous spatial lags, and to spatial error processes, and which are almost the sine qua non of spatial econometrics. Moreover it has been suggested that the significance of a spatially lagged dependent variable involving W may be misleading, since it may be simply picking up the effects of omitted spatially dependent variables, incorrectly suggesting the existence of a spillover mechanism. In this paper we review the theoretical and empirical rationale for network dependence and spatial externalities as embodied in spatially lagged variables, arguing that failing to acknowledge their presence at least leads to biased inference, can be a cause of inconsistent estimation, and leads to an incorrect understanding of true causal processes.

title: Where is the Economics in Spatial Econometrics?
abstract: This paper addresses the critique that spatial econometric models often lack a solid grounding in economic theory, particularly regarding the specification of the spatial weights matrix (W), which underpins endogenous and exogenous spatial lags and spatial error processes. We review the theoretical and empirical justifications for incorporating network dependence and spatial externalities within spatial econometric frameworks, emphasizing that neglecting these factors can result in biased inference, inconsistent estimation, and misinterpretation of causal mechanisms. The paper highlights concerns that significant spatially lagged dependent variables may reflect omitted spatially dependent regressors rather than genuine spillover effects. We argue that while some applications of spatial econometrics have been overly data-driven, there are numerous examples where economic theory robustly informs model specification, especially in contexts such as neoclassical growth, urban economics, and new economic geography. Furthermore, we explore how hierarchical (multilevel) modeling can complement spatial econometric approaches by capturing nested sources of variation and interdependence across different spatial scales. By integrating spatial effects into both single-equation and panel data models, we demonstrate the importance of theoretically motivated model design for accurate identification of endogenous and exogenous group effects. The paper concludes that a closer alignment between economic theory and spatial econometric practice is essential for advancing understanding of spatial processes in economics.

title: Analysing teacher knowledge for technology education in primary schools
abstract: Teacher knowledge guides a teacher’s behaviour in the classroom. Teacher knowledge for technology education is generally assumed to play an important role in affecting pupils’ learning in technology. There are an abundant number of teacher knowledge models that visualise different domains of teacher knowledge, but clear empirical evidence on how these domains interact is lacking. Insights into the interaction of teacher knowledge domains could be useful for teacher training. In this study, the hypothesised relations between different domains of teacher knowledge for technology education in primary schools were empirically investigated. Subject matter knowledge, pedagogical content knowledge, attitude, and self-efficacy were measured with tests and questionnaires. Results from a path analysis showed that subject matter knowledge is an important prerequisite for both pedagogical content knowledge and self-efficacy. Subsequently, teachers’ self-efficacy was found to have a strong influence on teachers’ attitude towards technology. Based on the findings in this study, it is recommended that teacher training should first of all focus on the development of teachers’ subject matter knowledge and pedagogical content knowledge. This knowledge will positively affect teachers’ confidence in teaching and, in turn, their attitude towards the subject. More confidence in technology teaching and a more positive attitude are expected to increase the frequency of technology education, which consequently increases teaching experience and thereby stimulates the development of teachers’ pedagogical content knowledge. This circle of positive reinforcement will eventually contribute to the quality of technology education in primary schools.
venue: International Journal of Technology and Design Education

title: Analysing teacher knowledge for technology education in primary schools
abstract: This study investigates the interrelationships among primary school teachers’ subject matter knowledge (SMK), pedagogical content knowledge (PCK), attitude, and self-efficacy in the context of technology education. Recognizing that teacher knowledge significantly influences classroom practice and pupil learning, the research addresses a gap in empirical evidence regarding how these domains interact. Using tests and questionnaires administered to Dutch primary school teachers, the study employs path analysis to examine hypothesized relationships between knowledge domains. Results indicate that SMK is a crucial foundation for both PCK and self-efficacy, while self-efficacy strongly shapes teachers’ attitudes toward technology. The findings suggest that teacher training should prioritize the development of SMK and PCK, as these enhance confidence and foster more positive attitudes toward technology teaching. This positive cycle is expected to increase the frequency and quality of technology instruction, thereby supporting ongoing professional growth and improved technology education in primary schools.
venue: International Journal of Technology and Design Education

title: Applying educational theory to develop a framework to support the delivery of experiential entrepreneurship education
abstract: Experiential approaches have become increasingly common in entrepreneurship education in response to calls for different approaches to the traditional didactic process-driven approach. Experiential approaches offer the potential to develop the skills and mindset that are required in entrepreneurship. Research has highlighted the critical importance of educator pedagogical competence in the delivery and quality of teaching and learning in further and higher education. Nevertheless, educator narratives and practices are often based on foundations that suggest a lack in the depth of knowledge and understanding of the underlying pedagogic learning theories and practice. This paper brings educational theory and pedagogic practice together in a three-stage framework of the experiential entrepreneurship learning process to support entrepreneurship educators within further and higher education.,This paper reviews and brings together the seminal educational theories and philosophies of constructivism, objectivism, Kolb's (1984) theory of experiential learning, Schon's (1983) reflection-in-action and Mezirow's (1997) theory of transformative learning, to develop a framework which underpins the experiential entrepreneurship learning process.,This paper develops a three-stage framework which informs the roles of an educator and a learner in experiential entrepreneurship education within further and higher education, based on educational theories and philosophies that inform the learning process.,The developed framework supports the pedagogic competence of educators in the delivery of experiential entrepreneurship education through a deeper understanding of the supporting theory that informs the pedagogic practice. This will provide consolidation to enable educators to maximise the effectiveness of their educational practice (Kaynardag, 2019) and can increase the legitimacy of entrepreneurship education (Foliard et al., 2018).,This paper meets calls in the literature to provide a closer engagement between educational theory and pedagogic practice to afford guidance as to how educators can navigate some of the different educational theories and philosophies to consolidate the effective delivery of quality experiential entrepreneurship education. Applying seminal educational theories and philosophies to ensure the quality of experiential education can support the legitimacy of experiential entrepreneurship education.

title: Applying educational theory to develop a framework to support the delivery of experiential entrepreneurship education
abstract: This paper addresses the need for a stronger theoretical foundation in experiential entrepreneurship education by developing a framework that integrates key educational theories and philosophies. Drawing on constructivism, objectivism, Kolb’s experiential learning theory, Schön’s reflection-in-action, and Mezirow’s transformative learning, the authors propose a three-stage framework to guide educators in further and higher education. The framework clarifies the roles of both educators and learners within experiential entrepreneurship education, supporting pedagogical competence and enhancing the quality and legitimacy of educational practice. By bridging the gap between educational theory and pedagogic practice, this research offers practical guidance for educators seeking to maximize the effectiveness of experiential approaches and responds to calls in the literature for closer engagement with foundational educational theory in entrepreneurship education.

title: As tendências pedagógicas e a prática educativa nas ciências da saúde
abstract: Educational practices are widely used in the health field, both in continuing education for health professionals and health education for the general population. These two fields intersect through the development of educational knowledge oriented by a set of target representations of man and society. Such representations are demonstrated by teaching/learning processes in the four main pedagogical trends in Brazil: traditional, renewed, conditioning-based, and liberating (or the Paulo Freire approach). Based on their respective principles, methods, and individual and social consequences, we contend that liberating pedagogy can produce better results than the others by allowing the student's active participation in the learning process, thus fostering continuous development of human skills in both the health services clientele and health workers.

title: As tendências pedagógicas e a prática educativa nas ciências da saúde
abstract: This paper examines the main pedagogical trends influencing educational practices in the health sciences, focusing on both continuing education for health professionals and health education for the general population. By analyzing traditional, renewed, conditioning-based, and liberating pedagogical approaches within the Brazilian context, the study explores how each model shapes teaching-learning processes and reflects underlying conceptions of individuals and society. The discussion highlights the limitations of transmissive and authoritarian models, which often fail to connect educational content with learners’ realities or foster critical engagement. In contrast, liberating pedagogy, inspired by Paulo Freire, is identified as particularly effective for promoting active participation, critical reflection, and the continuous development of human skills among both health workers and service users. The paper concludes that adopting liberating educational practices can better support the goals of comprehensive health promotion and professional development by aligning educational strategies with principles of social transformation and empowerment.

title: A hybrid learning pedagogy for surmounting the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic in the performing arts education
abstract: For performing arts education, Sage on the stage and Learn from the Masters were halted by the COVID-19 pandemic, and so did everything else. All lectures, tutorials and other face-to-face skill-based training sections were cancelled and were replaced by the online model. Such a model was only seen as one of the supplementary components for performing arts education in the past. From January 2020, this online pedagogy was inevitably placed to surmount the challenges caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. The social distancing measures demanded the blended pedagogy into a new online approach, in which the traditional face-to-face teaching to be replaced by synchronous online learning (facilitated by technologies such as Zoom, Cisco Webex, Google Class, Panopto etc.). Meanwhile, to offer opportunities for cognitive participation which allows students to process the learning and be reflective, webinar and innovative performance projects were launched from the concept of ‘flipped classroom and outcome-based education.’ This mixed approach (blended learning, flipped classroom, and outcome-based education) is described as ‘hybrid learning’ in this study. The ‘hybrid learning’ pedagogy is implemented at the Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts (HKAPA) for all teaching activities in the 2nd semester 2020/2021 to overcome the challenges caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. A questionnaire survey about how it affected the performing arts education, and how the new pedagogy was implemented took place in July 2020. The survey results from both the teachers (76) and students (163) share lessons, insights, and new understandings on teaching and learning online. Hybrid learning has been widely investigated and researched, yet study on hybrid learning in performing arts such as creative art, theatre art and music, remains insufficient. This study fills the research gap.
venue: Education and Information Technologies : Official Journal of the IFIP technical committee on Education

title: A hybrid learning pedagogy for surmounting the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic in the performing arts education
abstract: This study examines the implementation of a hybrid learning pedagogy at the Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts (HKAPA) as a response to the unprecedented challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic. With traditional face-to-face instruction suspended, performing arts education rapidly transitioned to a mixed model integrating synchronous online learning, flipped classroom strategies, and outcome-based education. A questionnaire survey conducted with 163 students and 76 teachers assessed the effectiveness of this hybrid approach in maintaining educational quality and engagement during campus closure. Results indicate that hybrid learning facilitated continued skill development, cognitive participation, and reflective practice despite social distancing constraints. The findings highlight both the successes and challenges of adapting performing arts pedagogy to an online environment, addressing a significant research gap in the field. This study offers insights for educators seeking resilient instructional models in the performing arts and contributes to the broader discourse on technology-enhanced education during global crises.
venue: Education and Information Technologies : Official Journal of the IFIP technical committee on Education

title: A research framework of smart education
abstract: The development of new technologies enables learners to learn more effectively, efficiently, flexibly and comfortably. Learners utilize smart devices to access digital resources through wireless network and to immerse in both personalized and seamless learning. Smart education, a concept that describes learning in digital age, has gained increased attention. This paper discusses the definition of smart education and presents a conceptual framework. A four-tier framework of smart pedagogies and ten key features of smart learning environments are proposed for foster smart learners who need master knowledge and skills of the 21st century learning. The smart pedagogy framework includes class-based differentiated instruction, group-based collaborative learning, individual-based personalized learning and mass-based generative learning. Furthermore, a technological architecture of smart education, which emphasizes the role of smart computing, is proposed. The tri-tier architecture and key functions are all presented. Finally, challenges of smart education are discussed.

title: A research framework of smart education
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive research framework for smart education, addressing the integration of advanced technologies and pedagogical strategies to enhance learning in the digital age. The authors define smart education as a learner-centered paradigm that leverages smart devices, wireless networks, and intelligent technologies to facilitate personalized, seamless, and context-aware learning experiences. A four-tier framework of smart pedagogies—class-based differentiated instruction, group-based collaborative learning, individual-based personalized learning, and mass-based generative learning—is proposed alongside ten key features of smart learning environments aimed at cultivating 21st-century skills. The paper also introduces a tri-tier technological architecture emphasizing the role of smart computing in supporting adaptive and efficient educational processes. Global initiatives and developments in smart education are reviewed to contextualize the framework. Finally, the paper discusses challenges and future directions for researchers and practitioners seeking to design and implement effective smart education systems.

title: Balancing Technology, Pedagogy and the New Normal: Post-pandemic Challenges for Higher Education
abstract: The Covid-19 pandemic has presented an opportunity for rethinking assumptions about education in general and higher education in particular. In the light of the general crisis the pandemic caused, especially when it comes to the so-called emergency remote teaching (ERT), educators from all grades and contexts experienced the necessity of rethinking their roles, the ways of supporting the students’ learning tasks and the image of students as self-organising learners, active citizens and autonomous social agents. In our first Postdigital Science and Education paper, we sought to distil and share some expert advice for campus-based university teachers to adapt to online teaching and learning. In this sequel paper, we ask ourselves: Now that campus-based university teachers have experienced the unplanned and forced version of Online Learning and Teaching (OLT), how can this experience help bridge the gap between online and in-person teaching in the following years? The four experts, also co-authors of this paper, interviewed aligning towards an emphasis on pedagogisation rather than digitalisation of higher education, with strategic decision-making being in the heart of post-pandemic practices. Our literature review of papers published in the last year and analysis of the expert answers reveal that the ‘forced’ experience of teaching with digital technologies as part of ERT can gradually give place to a harmonious integration of physical and digital tools and methods for the sake of more active, flexible and meaningful learning.

title: Balancing Technology, Pedagogy and the New Normal: Post-pandemic Challenges for Higher Education
abstract: This paper examines the post-pandemic challenges facing higher education as institutions seek to balance technology integration and pedagogical innovation within the emerging “new normal.” Drawing on recent literature and expert interviews, the study explores how the forced adoption of emergency remote teaching (ERT) during Covid-19 has prompted educators to reconsider their roles, support for student learning, and perceptions of students as autonomous agents. The analysis distinguishes between ERT and well-designed online learning and teaching (OLT), highlighting the limitations of crisis-driven digitalization and the underdevelopment of pedagogical strategies prior to the pandemic. Findings suggest that while the shift to ERT was often disruptive, it has also fostered openness to blended and flexible learning models. The authors argue that future higher education practices should prioritize pedagogical decision-making over mere digitalization, leveraging lessons from the pandemic to achieve a more harmonious integration of physical and digital tools. Ultimately, the paper advocates for a strategic approach that foregrounds active, meaningful learning and supports both teachers’ and students’ evolving needs in a post-Covid landscape.

title: Beyond Linguistic Purism in Language-in-education Policy and Practice: Exploring Bilingual Pedagogies in a Hong Kong Science Classroom
abstract: This paper proposes to overcome the traditional essentialist and dichotomous ways of conceptualising language and language pedagogies, i.e. to go beyond linguistic purist perspectives. Analysing bilingual teaching practices in a science lesson, the paper proposes that practical bilingual pedagogies can be developed to help students in bilingual education programmes to access dominant linguistic resources and discourses by capitalising on their indigenous linguistic and cultural resources.

title: Beyond Linguistic Purism in Language-in-education Policy and Practice: Exploring Bilingual Pedagogies in a Hong Kong Science Classroom
abstract: This paper challenges traditional linguistic purism in language-in-education policy by analyzing bilingual pedagogies in a Hong Kong science classroom. Drawing on sociolinguistic theory and classroom data, it argues that essentialist and dichotomous views of language—such as strict separations between English and mother tongues—fail to reflect the complex, hybrid linguistic realities of postcolonial societies like Hong Kong. The study demonstrates how students and teachers fluidly draw on both Cantonese and English, leveraging indigenous linguistic and cultural resources to access dominant scientific discourses. By situating bilingual practices within broader debates on globalization, identity, and educational equity, the paper advocates for practical bilingual pedagogies that democratize access to powerful knowledge without marginalizing local languages. It concludes that moving beyond purist models enables more inclusive, context-sensitive approaches to language policy and pedagogy, supporting both academic achievement and the affirmation of hybrid identities.

title: Boundary crossing pedagogy in STEM education
abstract: This commentary aims to discuss an overarching boundary crossing framework under which integrated STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics) pedagogy can be conceptualized. Four potential learning dialogical processes for boundary crossing are presented and used as the main theoretical construct for the discussion. A proposal of an interactive pedagogical framework is put forward accompanied by a provisional statement to relate the connective factors that are critical in the formation of a boundary crossing STEM pedagogy. These factors are situated learning, communities of practices, problem solving, learning dialogical processes, and boundary objects. A Hong Kong school STEM case is employed to illustrate the applicability of this framework. The commentary ends with a reflective remark on boundary crossing STEM pedagogy.

title: Boundary crossing pedagogy in STEM education
abstract: This commentary explores a boundary crossing framework for conceptualizing integrated STEM pedagogy, emphasizing the need to address epistemic and pedagogical boundaries between STEM disciplines. The paper identifies four dialogical learning processes as central to boundary crossing and proposes an interactive pedagogical framework that highlights situated learning, communities of practice, problem solving, dialogical processes, and boundary objects as key connective factors. Drawing on theoretical perspectives and a Hong Kong school case study, the commentary illustrates how boundary crossing can facilitate authentic integration of disciplinary knowledge while maintaining disciplinary rigor. The discussion underscores the importance of designing learning environments that support dynamic interactions among STEM domains and concludes with reflective insights on advancing boundary crossing pedagogy in STEM education.

title: Constructivism: reflections on twenty five years teaching the constructivist approach in medical education
abstract: There is no single overarching theoretical framework that accounts for how we learn in all situations. There are many theories of how we learn from our experiences and there are many theories of what experiences are. We know that we do learn and that we have knowledge but there is no consensus on the relationship between the mechanism by which our brains learn and the optimal way in which we should be taught. In other words there is no necessary connection between epistemology and pedagogy. We seem capable of learning from a wide variety of pedagogical processes and although there is empirical evidence that some ways of learning are more effective than others in specific situations no one pedagogical method dominates. However, reflecting on twenty five years as a medical educationalist I have come to the conclusion that there is one framework that makes more connections between different epistemological and pedagogical theories than others and that could have support from neuroscience. I wish to explore the connections between a variety of educational, communication and psychotherapeutic processes and try to show that constructivism holds the promise of providing some unity to the practice of education and learning. The constructivist model The constructivist theory of learning, whose philosophical origins are frequently ascribed to Kant and whose educational origins to Piaget, is based on the premise that the act of learning is based on a process which connects new knowledge to pre-existing knowledge. I do not intend to go into all the arguments surrounding this theory and to describe the variety of constructivist models that have been created. The reader is referred to the extensive literature on the subject.1-6 For the purposes of my argument it is simply necessary to acknowledge some basic assumptions underpinning the theory from which important connections to other educational theories can be made as well as to therapeutic practices, neuroscience and even the nature of scientific knowledge.
