These materials enable electrical stimulation of cells, which can enhance cellular activities such as adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation, making them particularly valuable for engineering electrically responsive tissues including nerve, muscle, cardiac, and bone. However, the inherent brittleness and limited processability of pure conducting polymers have prompted the development of composite biomaterials that integrate conducting polymers with biodegradable natural or synthetic polymers to improve mechanical properties and processability. This review summarizes the fabrication methods and properties of various conductive biomaterials—including films, nanofibers, hydrogels, and scaffolds—produced through techniques such as electrospinning, in situ polymerization, and surface coating. The applications of these materials in tissue engineering are discussed in detail, highlighting advances in bone regeneration, muscle repair, neural interfaces, cardiac tissue engineering, and wound healing. Overall, conducting polymer-based biomaterials represent a versatile platform for developing bioactive scaffolds that support tissue regeneration through both structural and electrical cues.

title: Conductivity engineering of graphene by defect formation
abstract: Transport measurements have revealed several exotic electronic properties of graphene. The possibility to influence the electronic structure and hence control the conductivity by adsorption or doping with adatoms is crucial in view of electronics applications. Here, we show that in contrast to expectation, the conductivity of graphene increases with increasing concentration of vacancy defects, by more than one order of magnitude. We obtain a pronounced enhancement of the conductivity after insertion of defects by both quantum mechanical transport calculations as well as experimental studies of carbon nano-sheets. Our finding is attributed to the defect induced mid-gap states, which create a region exhibiting metallic behaviour around the vacancy defects. The modification of the conductivity of graphene by the implementation of stable defects is crucial for the creation of electronic junctions in graphene-based electronics devices.

title: Conductivity engineering of graphene by defect formation
abstract: This study demonstrates that the electrical conductivity of graphene can be significantly enhanced through the controlled introduction of vacancy defects. Contrary to conventional expectations that defects reduce conductivity, both quantum mechanical transport calculations and experimental measurements on carbon nanosheets reveal an increase in conductivity by more than an order of magnitude with rising defect concentration. Theoretical modeling shows that vacancy defects induce mid-gap states, resulting in localized regions of metallic behavior around the vacancies. Ab-initio density functional theory and tight-binding calculations, supported by coherent potential approximation, confirm that these mid-gap states increase carrier density and shift the Fermi level away from the Dirac point, thereby enhancing conductivity. Experimental verification using chemically treated carbon nanosheets corroborates the theoretical predictions. These findings highlight defect engineering as a viable strategy for tailoring graphene’s electronic properties and enabling the fabrication of electronic junctions in graphene-based devices.

title: Controlling the porosity and microarchitecture of hydrogels for tissue engineering.
abstract: Tissue engineering holds great promise for regeneration and repair of diseased tissues, making the development of tissue engineering scaffolds a topic of great interest in biomedical research. Because of their biocompatibility and similarities to native extracellular matrix, hydrogels have emerged as leading candidates for engineered tissue scaffolds. However, precise control of hydrogel properties, such as porosity, remains a challenge. Traditional techniques for creating bulk porosity in polymers have demonstrated success in hydrogels for tissue engineering; however, often the conditions are incompatible with direct cell encapsulation. Emerging technologies have demonstrated the ability to control porosity and the microarchitectural features in hydrogels, creating engineered tissues with structure and function similar to native tissues. In this review, we explore the various technologies for controlling the porosity and microarchitecture within hydrogels, and demonstrate successful applications of combining these techniques.

title: Controlling the porosity and microarchitecture of hydrogels for tissue engineering.
abstract: Hydrogels are increasingly utilized as scaffolds in tissue engineering due to their biocompatibility and structural similarity to native extracellular matrix, but precise control over their porosity and microarchitecture remains a significant challenge. Porosity and pore architecture critically influence cell distribution, nutrient diffusion, vascularization, and the mechanical properties of engineered tissues. This review examines established and emerging techniques for modulating hydrogel porosity, including solvent casting/particle leaching, freeze-drying, gas foaming, electrospinning, micropatterning, and micromolding. The advantages and limitations of these methods are discussed with respect to their ability to tune pore size, interconnectivity, and orientation, as well as their compatibility with cell encapsulation and scalability for clinical applications. The review highlights how advances in controlling hydrogel microarchitecture enable the fabrication of scaffolds that better support cell survival, proliferation, migration, and extracellular matrix secretion, ultimately improving the structural and functional integration of engineered tissues. By combining multiple fabrication strategies, it is possible to create hydrogels with tailored properties that address the diverse requirements of different tissue engineering applications.

title: Deep Mining: A Rock Engineering Challenge
abstract: Increasing demand for metals caused by global economic growth and exploitation of shallow mineral deposits forces mineral extraction to go deeper. A direct consequence of this development is an increase in rock pressure-related mining problems. The role of rock engineering in the design and operation of deep mines is discussed in detail. Critical issues are the rock fracturing around mining excavations, the support and control of the fractured rock, and the rock mechanics design of mine infrastructure and extraction (stoping) systems. Progress of the science of rock mechanics in the areas related to these issues is highlighted and critically examined. Specific areas are the prediction and assessment of the mechanical properties of rock mass, the mechanics of controlling fractured rock around deep mining excavations and the resulting demands on support systems. Rock engineering aspects of stoping systems and the regional stress changes resulting from the extraction of large mineral bodies are discussed in detail. The progress in design concepts for open stopes and stopes with caving of the roof strata is illustrated. It is shown that the stress environment in deep mines does not favour the highly productive caving systems of stoping. The value of energy-based design concepts for very deep mines exploiting tabular mineral deposits is shown. Despite the considerable progress that has been made in the science of rock mechanics since the 1950s, progress in applying this knowledge to solve rock pressure problems in deep mines has been rather slow. The tools are available. What is needed is the development of robust design criteria for mine infrastructure, excavations and support systems for dynamic and changing stress environments. The second critical issue is the lack of highly qualified rock engineering personnel on the mines. This has been recognized by the European mining industry through supporting a continued education programme in rock engineering for deep mines.

title: Deep Mining: A Rock Engineering Challenge
abstract: The increasing global demand for metals and the depletion of shallow mineral resources have driven mining operations to greater depths, presenting significant rock engineering challenges. This paper examines the critical role of rock engineering in addressing the complex issues associated with deep mining, including rock fracturing around excavations, support and control of fractured rock, and the design of mine infrastructure and extraction systems. Advances in rock mechanics, particularly in predicting rock mass properties and developing support systems for fractured ground, are reviewed and critically assessed. The study discusses the implications of regional stress changes due to large-scale mineral extraction and evaluates design concepts for various stoping systems, highlighting the limitations of caving methods in high-stress deep mine environments. The effectiveness of energy-based design approaches for deep tabular deposits is demonstrated. Despite substantial progress in rock mechanics research since the 1950s, the practical application of this knowledge to solve deep mining problems remains limited, primarily due to a lack of robust design criteria and a shortage of highly qualified rock engineering professionals. The paper concludes by emphasizing the need for improved design standards and enhanced education programs to address these challenges in deep mining operations.

title: Direct human cartilage repair using three-dimensional bioprinting technology.
abstract: Current cartilage tissue engineering strategies cannot as yet fabricate new tissue that is indistinguishable from native cartilage with respect to zonal organization, extracellular matrix composition, and mechanical properties. Integration of implants with surrounding native tissues is crucial for long-term stability and enhanced functionality. In this study, we developed a bioprinting system with simultaneous photopolymerization capable for three-dimensional (3D) cartilage tissue engineering. Poly(ethylene glycol) dimethacrylate (PEGDMA) with human chondrocytes were printed to repair defects in osteochondral plugs (3D biopaper) in layer-by-layer assembly. Compressive modulus of printed PEGDMA was 395.73±80.40 kPa, which was close to the range of the properties of native human articular cartilage. Printed human chondrocytes maintained the initially deposited positions due to simultaneous photopolymerization of surrounded biomaterial scaffold, which is ideal in precise cell distribution for anatomic cartilage engineering. Viability of printed human chondrocytes increased 26% in simultaneous polymerization than polymerized after printing. Printed cartilage implant attached firmly with surrounding tissue and greater proteoglycan deposition was observed at the interface of implant and native cartilage in Safranin-O staining. This is consistent with the enhanced interface failure strength during the culture assessed by push-out testing. Printed cartilage in 3D biopaper had elevated glycosaminoglycan (GAG) content comparing to that without biopaper when normalized to DNA. These observations were consistent with gene expression results. This study indicates the importance of direct cartilage repair and promising anatomic cartilage engineering using 3D bioprinting technology.

title: Direct human cartilage repair using three-dimensional bioprinting technology.
abstract: This study demonstrates the feasibility of direct human cartilage repair using a three-dimensional bioprinting system with simultaneous photopolymerization. Human chondrocytes suspended in poly(ethylene glycol) dimethacrylate (PEGDMA) were precisely deposited into osteochondral defects via layer-by-layer assembly, resulting in constructs with compressive modulus comparable to native articular cartilage. Simultaneous photopolymerization during printing enhanced chondrocyte viability by 26% compared to post-printing polymerization and maintained accurate cell positioning for anatomical tissue engineering. The printed cartilage implants exhibited firm integration with surrounding native tissue, as evidenced by increased proteoglycan deposition at the interface and improved interface failure strength. Additionally, constructs printed within three-dimensional biopaper showed elevated glycosaminoglycan content normalized to DNA and supported chondrogenic gene expression. These findings highlight the potential of 3D bioprinting technology for precise, minimally invasive, and anatomically relevant cartilage repair that promotes functional integration with host tissue.

title: Discontinuity Analysis for Rock Engineering
abstract: Introduction to discontinuities. Measurement of discontinuity characteristics. Discontinuity orientation. Discontinuity frequency. Discontinuity spacing. Discontinuity size. Stresses on discontinuities. Analysis of rigid blocks. Discontinuities and rock strength. Discontinuities and rock deformability. Fluid flow in discontinuities.

title: Discontinuity Analysis for Rock Engineering
abstract: Discontinuity Analysis for Rock Engineering provides a comprehensive examination of the identification, measurement, and analysis of discontinuities in rock masses and their implications for engineering practice. The book systematically addresses the origins and types of discontinuities, methods for characterizing their orientation, frequency, spacing, and size, and the application of geostatistical techniques to analyze discontinuity data. It explores the mechanical behavior of discontinuities under stress, including their influence on rock strength, deformability, and fluid flow, and presents analytical approaches for assessing the stability of rigid blocks and the impact of discontinuities on engineering structures. Designed for advanced undergraduate and postgraduate students in civil, mining, and geological engineering, the text integrates theoretical principles with practical methodologies, supported by illustrative case studies and exercises. Appendices provide foundational guidance on stereographic projection, statistical analysis, rock mass classification, and force and stress analysis. This work consolidates dispersed knowledge into a coherent framework that supports both academic study and practical application in rock engineering.

title: Dynamics of Structures: Theory and Applications to Earthquake Engineering
abstract: Designed for senior-level and graduate courses in Dynamics of Structures and Earthquake Engineering. Structural dynamics and earthquake engineering for both students and professional engineers An expert on structural dynamics and earthquake engineering, Anil K. Chopra fills an important niche, explaining the material in an approachable style with his Fifth Edition of Dynamics of Structures: Theory and Applications to Earthquake Engineering. No prior knowledge of structural dynamics is assumed, and the presentation is detailed and integrated enough to make the text suitable for self-study.   As a textbook on vibrations and structural dynamics, this book has no competition. The material includes many topics in the theory of structural dynamics, along with applications of this theory to earthquake analysis, response, design, and evaluation of structures, with an emphasis on presenting this often difficult subject in as simple a manner as possible through numerous worked-out illustrative examples. The Fifth Edition includes new sections, figures, and examples, along with relevant updates and revisions.

title: Dynamics of Structures: Theory and Applications to Earthquake Engineering
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive exploration of structural dynamics with a focus on applications to earthquake engineering. It systematically develops the theoretical foundations and analytical methods for both single-degree-of-freedom (SDF) and multi-degree-of-freedom (MDF) systems, covering equations of motion, free and forced vibration, damping mechanisms, and numerical evaluation of dynamic response. The work details the response of linear and inelastic systems to various excitations, including harmonic, periodic, arbitrary, and seismic inputs, and introduces advanced topics such as generalized SDF systems, distributed mass and elasticity, and the finite element method. Special emphasis is placed on the earthquake response and design of multistory buildings, including linearly elastic, inelastic, and base-isolated structures, as well as the integration of structural dynamics principles into building codes and evaluation guidelines. Through rigorous analysis and practical examples, this study provides essential methodologies for predicting and mitigating earthquake-induced structural responses, supporting resilient design in civil engineering practice.

title: Emerging learning environments in engineering education
abstract: Three major challenges, sustainability, the fourth industrial revolution, and employability, will require new types of engineering programs, to help students develop skills in cross-disciplinarity, complexity, and contextual understanding. Future engineering students should be able to understand the needs for technological, sustainable solutions in context. The engineering graduates should be able to act in complex and chaotic situations. The question is how engineering institutions are responding now and how they should respond in the future. This article analyses the general responses from engineering education over the last 20 years. These responses are student-centred learning, integration of theory and practice, digital and online learning, and the definition of professional competencies. Examples are given of institutions that are already applying several of these components in the curriculum. On the long-term horizon, more personalised curriculum models are emerging based on students developing and documenting their own learning and career trajectories, as part of their lifelong learning strategy.

title: Emerging learning environments in engineering education
abstract: This paper examines the evolving landscape of engineering education in response to three major challenges: sustainability, the fourth industrial revolution, and employability. It analyzes how these drivers necessitate new educational models that foster cross-disciplinary skills, systems thinking, and contextual understanding. The study reviews trends over the past two decades, highlighting shifts toward student-centered learning, integration of theory and practice, digital and online modalities, and a redefinition of professional competencies. Institutional examples illustrate early adoption of these approaches. The paper also explores the increasing complexity of engineering problems and the need for graduates to operate effectively in complex, interdisciplinary environments. Looking ahead, it identifies emerging personalized curriculum models that support lifelong learning and adaptability. The findings underscore the importance of integrating societal context, digital skills, and human values into engineering curricula to prepare graduates for rapidly changing technological and social landscapes.

title: Energy band-gap engineering of graphene nanoribbons.
abstract: We investigate electronic transport in lithographically patterned graphene ribbon structures where the lateral confinement of charge carriers creates an energy gap near the charge neutrality point. Individual graphene layers are contacted with metal electrodes and patterned into ribbons of varying widths and different crystallographic orientations. The temperature dependent conductance measurements show larger energy gaps opening for narrower ribbons. The sizes of these energy gaps are investigated by measuring the conductance in the nonlinear response regime at low temperatures. We find that the energy gap scales inversely with the ribbon width, thus demonstrating the ability to engineer the band gap of graphene nanostructures by lithographic processes.

title: Energy band-gap engineering of graphene nanoribbons.
abstract: We report experimental evidence of energy band-gap engineering in graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) fabricated via lithographic patterning of single-layer graphene. By systematically varying the width and crystallographic orientation of over two dozen GNRs, we observe that lateral confinement induces an energy gap near the charge neutrality point, with narrower ribbons exhibiting larger gaps. Temperature-dependent conductance measurements reveal strong suppression of conductance at low temperatures for narrow GNRs, indicating the opening of a band gap. Nonlinear transport measurements allow direct extraction of the energy gap, which scales inversely with ribbon width, consistent with theoretical predictions. No systematic dependence on crystallographic orientation is observed. Our findings demonstrate that lithographic techniques enable precise control over the electronic properties of graphene nanostructures through width modulation, providing a viable route for band-gap engineering in graphene-based nanoelectronic devices.

title: Engineering and Economic Applications of Complementarity Problems
abstract: This paper gives an extensive documentation of applications of finite-dimensional nonlinear complementarity problems in engineering and equilibrium modeling. For most applications, we describe the problem briefly, state the defining equations of the model, and give functional expressions for the complementarity formulations. The goal of this documentation is threefold: (i) to summarize the essential applications of the nonlinear complementarity problem known to date, (ii) to provide a basis for the continued research on the nonlinear complementarity problem, and (iii) to supply a broad collection of realistic complementarity problems for use in algorithmic experimentation and other studies.

title: Engineering and Economic Applications of Complementarity Problems
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of finite-dimensional nonlinear complementarity problems and their diverse applications in engineering and economic equilibrium modeling. It systematically presents a wide range of real-world problems, detailing their mathematical formulations and the functional expressions that define their complementarity structures. The documentation serves three main purposes: to summarize the principal applications of nonlinear complementarity problems identified to date, to offer a foundation for ongoing research in this area, and to assemble an extensive set of realistic test problems for use in algorithmic development and experimental studies. By highlighting applications such as frictional contact in structural engineering, traffic network equilibria, and general economic equilibrium models, the paper demonstrates the centrality of complementarity concepts in modeling system equilibria. It also reviews advances in computational algorithms and modeling languages that facilitate the practical solution of large-scale complementarity problems, underscoring the interplay between theoretical developments and computational practice. This work aims to support researchers and practitioners by providing both a reference for established applications and a resource for future methodological innovation.

title: Engineering hydrogels as extracellular matrix mimics.
abstract: Extracellular matrix (ECM) is a complex cellular environment consisting of proteins, proteoglycans, and other soluble molecules. ECM provides structural support to mammalian cells and a regulatory milieu with a variety of important cell functions, including assembling cells into various tissues and organs, regulating growth and cell-cell communication. Developing a tailored in vitro cell culture environment that mimics the intricate and organized nanoscale meshwork of native ECM is desirable. Recent studies have shown the potential of hydrogels to mimic native ECM. Such an engineered native-like ECM is more likely to provide cells with rational cues for diagnostic and therapeutic studies. The research for novel biomaterials has led to an extension of the scope and techniques used to fabricate biomimetic hydrogel scaffolds for tissue engineering and regenerative medicine applications. In this article, we detail the progress of the current state-of-the-art engineering methods to create cell-encapsulating hydrogel tissue constructs as well as their applications in in vitro models in biomedicine.

title: Engineering hydrogels as extracellular matrix mimics.
abstract: The extracellular matrix (ECM) plays a critical role in regulating cell behavior and tissue architecture, yet traditional two-dimensional (2D) cell culture systems fail to replicate the complex three-dimensional (3D) microenvironment found in vivo. Hydrogels, with their tunable physicochemical and mechanical properties, have emerged as promising biomaterials for engineering ECM-mimetic scaffolds that better support cell growth, differentiation, and function. This paper reviews the advances in hydrogel-based scaffold design, highlighting both natural and synthetic polymers, hybrid materials, and surface modification strategies to enhance biocompatibility and mimic native ECM features. State-of-the-art fabrication techniques, including microfluidics and biopatterning, are discussed for their ability to create intricate, cell-encapsulating constructs with controlled porosity and embedded microchannels for improved nutrient and gas exchange. The challenges of characterizing hydrogel mechanical properties in situ are addressed through novel noninvasive measurement methods. Finally, the potential applications of engineered hydrogel scaffolds in tissue engineering, regenerative medicine, and in vitro drug testing models are explored, emphasizing the need for interdisciplinary approaches to overcome current limitations and achieve functional tissue mimics.

title: Engineering of functional tendon.
abstract: Surgical tendon repair is limited by the availability of viable tissue for transplantation. Because of its relatively avascular nature, tendon is a prime candidate for engineered tissue replacement. To address this problem, cells isolated from rat Achilles tendon were grown to confluence in culture and allowed to self-assemble into a cylinder between two anchor points. The resulting scaffold-free tissue was composed of aligned, small-diameter collagen fibrils, a large number of cells, and an excess of noncollagenous extracellular matrix; all characteristics of embryonic tendon. The stress-strain response of the constructs also resembles the nonlinear behavior of immature tendons, and the ultimate tensile strength is approximately equal to that of embryonic chick tendon, roughly 2 MPa. These physical and mechanical properties indicate that these constructs are the first viable tendons engineered in vitro, without the aid of artificial scaffolding.

title: Engineering of functional tendon.
abstract: This study addresses the limitations of current tendon repair strategies by engineering functional tendon constructs in vitro using primary rat Achilles tendon fibroblasts. Cells were cultured to confluence and induced to self-assemble into three-dimensional, scaffold-free cylindrical constructs anchored between two points. The resulting tissues exhibited morphological characteristics of embryonic tendon, including aligned, small-diameter collagen fibrils, high cellularity, and abundant noncollagenous extracellular matrix. Mechanical testing demonstrated a nonlinear stress–strain response and ultimate tensile strength comparable to embryonic chick tendon (approximately 2 MPa). These findings indicate that self-organized tendon constructs can recapitulate key structural and mechanical properties of native tendon without artificial scaffolding, representing a significant advance toward biologically compatible tendon replacements.

title: Engineering organoids
abstract: Organoids are in vitro miniaturized and simplified model systems of organs that have gained enormous interest for modelling tissue development and disease, and for personalized medicine, drug screening and cell therapy. Despite considerable success in culturing physiologically relevant organoids, challenges remain to achieve real-life applications. In particular, the high variability of self-organizing growth and restricted experimental and analytical access hamper the translatability of organoid systems. In this Review, we argue that many limitations of traditional organoid culture can be addressed by engineering approaches at all levels of organoid systems. We investigate cell surface and genetic engineering approaches, and discuss stem cell niche engineering based on the design of matrices that allow spatiotemporal control of organoid growth and shape-guided morphogenesis. We examine how microfluidic approaches and lessons learnt from organs-on-a-chip enable the integration of mechano-physiological parameters and increase accessibility of organoids to improve functional readouts. Applying engineering principles to organoids increases reproducibility and provides experimental control, which will, ultimately, be required to enable clinical translation. Organoids are cellular 3D models of organs, which provide powerful in vitro platforms for the investigation of tissue and disease biology. In this Review, the authors investigate engineering approaches, including cellular engineering, designer matrices and microfluidics, to improve the reproducibility and physiological relevance of organoids.

title: Engineering organoids
abstract: Organoids are three-dimensional, in vitro culture systems derived from stem cells that recapitulate key structural and functional features of native organs, offering advanced models for studying tissue development, disease mechanisms, personalized medicine, and drug screening. While organoids surpass traditional two-dimensional cultures in mimicking organ complexity and physiological function, their translational potential is limited by challenges such as high variability, restricted experimental access, incomplete maturation, and lack of full organ functionality. This review explores how engineering approaches—including cell surface and genetic modifications, niche-mimetic matrix design for spatiotemporal control, and integration of microfluidic technologies—can address these limitations by enhancing reproducibility, experimental control, and functional readouts. By applying bioengineering principles at multiple levels of organoid culture systems, researchers can improve the reliability and clinical applicability of organoids, ultimately advancing their use in regenerative medicine and therapeutic development.

title: Engineering orthopedic tissue interfaces.
abstract: While a wide variety of approaches to engineering orthopedic tissues have been proposed, less attention has been paid to the interfaces, the specialized areas that connect two tissues of different biochemical and mechanical properties. The interface tissue plays an important role in transitioning mechanical load between disparate tissues. Thus, the relatively new field of interfacial tissue engineering presents new challenges--to not only consider the regeneration of individual orthopedic tissues, but also to design the biochemical and cellular composition of the linking tissue. Approaches to interfacial tissue engineering may be distinguished based on if the goal is to recreate the interface itself, or generate an entire integrated tissue unit (such as an osteochondral plug). As background for future efforts in engineering orthopedic interfaces, a brief review of the biology and mechanics of each interface (cartilage-bone, ligament-bone, meniscus-bone, and muscle-tendon) is presented, followed by an overview of the state-of-the-art in engineering each tissue, including advances and challenges specific to regenerating the interfaces.

title: Engineering orthopedic tissue interfaces.
abstract: Orthopedic tissue interfaces, which connect tissues with distinct biochemical and mechanical properties, play a critical role in load transfer and functional integration within the musculoskeletal system. Despite significant advances in engineering individual orthopedic tissues, the regeneration of these specialized interfaces has received comparatively less attention. This review highlights the unique biological and mechanical characteristics of key orthopedic interfaces—including cartilage–bone, ligament–bone, meniscus–bone, and muscle–tendon—and discusses their importance in restoring native function following injury or disease. Current strategies in interfacial tissue engineering are examined, distinguishing between approaches that aim to recreate the interface itself versus those that generate integrated tissue units such as osteochondral plugs. The paper summarizes state-of-the-art scaffold designs, cell sources, and bioactive factors used to engineer these complex regions, emphasizing the challenges of achieving proper biochemical gradients, mechanical transitions, and tissue integration. Advances and ongoing challenges specific to regenerating orthopedic interfaces are reviewed to inform future research directions in this emerging field.

title: Engineering Systems Multiple‐Domain Matrix: An organizing framework for modeling large‐scale complex systems
abstract: The scope and complexity of engineered systems are ever‐increasing as burgeoning global markets, unprecedented technological capabilities, rising consumer expectations, and ever‐changing social requirements present difficult design challenges that often extend beyond the traditional engineering paradigm. These challenges require engineers and technical managers to treat the technological systems as a part of a larger whole. Existing system modeling frameworks are limited in scope for representing the information about engineering systems. This paper presents a conceptual framework and an improved modeling framework for engineering systems. Its value is that it allows engineers and managers an improved means to visually arrange information and structure discourse in a way that facilitates better systems engineering. It augments the existing literature by providing a clear and concise framework for an engineering system, and provides a methodology for engineers to tag and organize systems information in ways that allow for better collection, storage, processing, and analysis of systems engineering data. © 2011 Wiley Periodicals, Inc.

title: Engineering Systems Multiple‐Domain Matrix: An organizing framework for modeling large‐scale complex systems
abstract: The increasing complexity and scale of modern engineering systems, driven by evolving technological, social, and market demands, challenge traditional modeling approaches and require new frameworks for effective analysis and management. This paper introduces the Engineering Systems Multiple-Domain Matrix (ESM), a conceptual and organizing framework designed to address theoretical gaps in representing and understanding large-scale complex systems. Building on a review of systems theory, socio-technical systems, and large technological systems literature, the ESM provides a structured methodology for identifying, tagging, and organizing diverse system information across technical, organizational, and social domains. The framework facilitates holistic knowledge capture, improved visualization, and enhanced discourse among engineers and managers. By enabling better collection, storage, processing, and analysis of systems engineering data, the ESM supports the development of a comprehensive knowledge basis that advances both scholarship and practice in engineering systems modeling.

title: Factors of Safety and Reliability in Geotechnical Engineering
abstract: Simple reliability analyses, involving neither complex theory nor unfamiliar terms, can be used in routine geotechnical engineering practice. These simple reliability analyses require little effort beyond that involved in conventional geotechnical analyses. They provide a means of evaluating the combined effects of uncertainties in the parameters involved in the calculations, and they offer a useful supplement to conventional analyses. The additional parameters needed for the reliability analyses—standard deviations of the parameters—can be evaluated using the same amount of data and types of correlations that are widely used in geotechnical engineering practice. Example applications to stability and settlement problems illustrate the simplicity and practical usefulness of the method.

title: Factors of Safety and Reliability in Geotechnical Engineering
abstract: This paper examines the factors of safety and reliability in geotechnical engineering through the analysis of a real case involving the collapse of a diaphragm wall during construction. The study details the sequence of events leading up to the failure, highlighting deficiencies in the original geotechnical investigation, such as insufficient sampling and optimistic parameter selection. The methodology involves a chronological assessment of design and construction parameters, emphasizing the impact of using average rather than characteristic geotechnical values in structural calculations. The findings demonstrate that inadequate consideration of soil variability and insufficient safety factors contributed to the collapse, and that adherence to more rigorous geotechnical characterization and conservative design approaches could have prevented the incident. The paper underscores the complexity and high cost of technical solutions following structural failures, as well as the importance of robust geotechnical studies and appropriate safety margins in ensuring reliability in geotechnical engineering projects.

title: Guidelines for conducting and reporting case study research in software engineering
abstract: Case study is a suitable research methodology for software engineering research since it studies contemporary phenomena in its natural context. However, the understanding of what constitutes a case study varies, and hence the quality of the resulting studies. This paper aims at providing an introduction to case study methodology and guidelines for researchers conducting case studies and readers studying reports of such studies. The content is based on the authors’ own experience from conducting and reading case studies. The terminology and guidelines are compiled from different methodology handbooks in other research domains, in particular social science and information systems, and adapted to the needs in software engineering. We present recommended practices for software engineering case studies as well as empirically derived and evaluated checklists for researchers and readers of case study research.

title: Guidelines for conducting and reporting case study research in software engineering
abstract: Case study research is increasingly recognized as a valuable methodology for investigating complex, real-world phenomena in software engineering, yet inconsistencies in terminology and methodological rigor have led to variability in study quality and reporting. This paper synthesizes guidance from social science and information systems literature, adapting it to the specific needs of software engineering, to provide comprehensive guidelines for conducting and reporting case studies. Drawing on the authors’ extensive experience and established methodology handbooks, the paper defines key concepts, situates case studies among other empirical methods, and outlines a structured research process. It offers practical recommendations for study design, data collection, analysis, and reporting, supplemented by empirically derived checklists for researchers and readers. By clarifying terminology and presenting best practices, this work aims to enhance the quality, transparency, and credibility of case study research in software engineering.

title: Handbook of Corrosion Engineering
abstract: Handbook of Corrosion Engineering: Modern Theory, Fundamentals and Practical Applications explores recent progress in metals corrosion and associated protection processes, spanning all corrosion-related characteristics utilized in natural and industrial environments, including monitoring and testing. The book combines the science and engineering of corrosion to assist readers in conducting exact corrosion evaluations in the design and plant management phases, including optimal protection methods. The book examines the basics of corrosion science, including the electrochemical mechanism, thermodynamic and kinetic aspects, different corrosion forms—such as uniform, localized, and stress corrosion phenomena—and protection systems adopted to combat corrosion, including inhibitors, coatings, and cathodic protection.

title: Handbook of Corrosion Engineering
abstract: The Handbook of Corrosion Engineering provides a comprehensive and practical reference for understanding, assessing, and mitigating corrosion in engineering materials. Organized into twelve chapters across three thematic sections, the handbook covers fundamental corrosion principles, environmental factors, and high-temperature effects; advanced techniques for modeling, life prediction, inspection, monitoring, and failure analysis; and strategies for prevention and control including materials selection, protective coatings, inhibitors, and cathodic and anodic protection. Emphasizing both theoretical foundations and real-world applications, this second edition integrates recent advances in materials science, computer-aided analysis, and corrosion management. Designed for practicing engineers and professionals, it offers detailed guidance on detection, maintenance, testing methodologies, and design considerations to enhance the durability and reliability of structures exposed to corrosive environments.

title: Heart Valve Tissue Engineering: Concepts, Approaches, Progress, and Challenges
abstract: Potential applications of tissue engineering in regenerative medicine range from structural tissues to organs with complex function. This review focuses on the engineering of heart valve tissue, a goal which involves a unique combination of biological, engineering, and technological hurdles. We emphasize basic concepts, approaches and methods, progress made, and remaining challenges. To provide a framework for understanding the enabling scientific principles, we first examine the elements and features of normal heart valve functional structure, biomechanics, development, maturation, remodeling, and response to injury. Following a discussion of the fundamental principles of tissue engineering applicable to heart valves, we examine three approaches to achieving the goal of an engineered tissue heart valve: (1) cell seeding of biodegradable synthetic scaffolds, (2) cell seeding of processed tissue scaffolds, and (3) in-vivo repopulation by circulating endogenous cells of implanted substrates without prior in-vitro cell seeding. Lastly, we analyze challenges to the field and suggest future directions for both preclinical and translational (clinical) studies that will be needed to address key regulatory issues for safety and efficacy of the application of tissue engineering and regenerative approaches to heart valves. Although modest progress has been made toward the goal of a clinically useful tissue engineered heart valve, further success and ultimate human benefit will be dependent upon advances in biodegradable polymers and other scaffolds, cellular manipulation, strategies for rebuilding the extracellular matrix, and techniques to characterize and potentially non-invasively assess the speed and quality of tissue healing and remodeling.

title: Heart Valve Tissue Engineering: Concepts, Approaches, Progress, and Challenges
abstract: Heart valve tissue engineering represents a promising frontier in regenerative medicine, aiming to overcome the limitations of current prosthetic and bioprosthetic valve replacements, particularly for pediatric and young adult patients. This review synthesizes the fundamental concepts underlying heart valve structure, function, and biomechanics, and examines the principles of tissue engineering as applied to heart valves. Three primary approaches are discussed: cell seeding of biodegradable synthetic scaffolds, cell seeding of processed tissue scaffolds, and in-vivo repopulation by endogenous cells without prior in-vitro seeding. Progress in these areas is evaluated alongside persistent challenges such as achieving appropriate mechanical properties, durability, biocompatibility, and the capacity for growth and remodeling. The review highlights the need for advances in scaffold materials, cellular manipulation, extracellular matrix reconstruction, and non-invasive assessment techniques. It also addresses regulatory considerations crucial for clinical translation. Ultimately, the successful development of engineered heart valves will depend on multidisciplinary integration of biological, engineering, and technological innovations to meet clinical demands and improve patient outcomes.

title: Injectable hydrogels for cartilage and bone tissue engineering
abstract: Tissue engineering has become a promising strategy for repairing damaged cartilage and bone tissue. Among the scaffolds for tissue-engineering applications, injectable hydrogels have demonstrated great potential for use as three-dimensional cell culture scaffolds in cartilage and bone tissue engineering, owing to their high water content, similarity to the natural extracellular matrix (ECM), porous framework for cell transplantation and proliferation, minimal invasive properties, and ability to match irregular defects. In this review, we describe the selection of appropriate biomaterials and fabrication methods to prepare novel injectable hydrogels for cartilage and bone tissue engineering. In addition, the biology of cartilage and the bony ECM is also summarized. Finally, future perspectives for injectable hydrogels in cartilage and bone tissue engineering are discussed.

title: Injectable hydrogels for cartilage and bone tissue engineering
abstract: Injectable hydrogels have emerged as promising scaffolds for cartilage and bone tissue engineering due to their high water content, structural similarity to the extracellular matrix, and ability to conform to irregular defects through minimally invasive delivery. This review summarizes the selection of biomaterials—both natural and synthetic—and fabrication methods, such as physical and chemical cross-linking, for developing novel injectable hydrogels tailored to cartilage and bone regeneration. The biological characteristics of cartilage and bone extracellular matrices are discussed to highlight the importance of mimicking native tissue architecture and composition. Despite advances in hydrogel design, challenges remain in achieving optimal biocompatibility, mechanical properties, and integration with host tissue for clinical applications. Future perspectives emphasize the need for innovative materials and fabrication strategies to realize the full therapeutic potential of injectable hydrogels in cartilage and bone tissue engineering.

title: International Journal for Numerical Methods in Engineering
abstract: The Journal is known for welcoming contributions in a wide range of areas in computational engineering, including computational issues in model reduction, uncertainty quantification, verification and validation, inverse analysis and stochastic methods, optimisation, element technology, solution techniques and parallel computing, damage and fracture, mechanics at micro and nano-scales, lowspeed fluid dynamics, fluid-structure interaction, electromagnetics, coupled diffusion phenomena, and error estimation and mesh generation. It is emphasized that this is by no means an exhaustive list, and particularly papers on multi-scale, multi-physics or multidisciplinary problems, and on new, emerging topics are welcome.

title: International Journal for Numerical Methods in Engineering
abstract: This paper presents novel algorithms for automated meshing and unit cell analysis of periodic composites using hierarchical tri-quadratic tetrahedral elements. Addressing the challenges of accurately modeling complex material arrangements and ensuring compatibility at matrix-reinforcement interfaces, the proposed methods begin with a hierarchical quad-tree (2D) or oc-tree (3D) mesh of pixel or voxel elements. Through successive element splitting and nodal shifting, these algorithms generate final meshes that precisely capture constituent volume fractions and material-scale stress and strain fields under various loading conditions. The approach effectively resolves both the two-way meshing problem—achieving full displacement compatibility between phases—and the external face-matching problem required for periodic boundary conditions. Performance and convergence behavior are demonstrated on densely packed fiber, particulate, and 3D textile-reinforced composites, showing that the techniques enable efficient, accurate finite element modeling for computational homogenization of complex heterogeneous materials.

title: Introduction to chemical engineering thermodynamics
abstract: Introduction to Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics presents comprehensive coverage of the subject of thermodynamics from a chemical engineering viewpoint. The text provides a thorough exposition of the principles of thermodynamics, and details their application to chemical processes. The content is structured to alternate between the development of thermodynamic principles and the correlation and use of thermodynamic properties as well as between theory and applications. The chapters are written in a clear, logically organized manner, and contain an abundance of realistic problems, examples, and illustrations to help students understand complex concepts. New ideas, terms, and symbols constantly challenge the readers to think and encourage them to apply this fundamental body of knowledge to the solution of practical problems.  McGraw-Hill's Connect, is also available as an optional, add on item. Connect is the only integrated learning system that empowers students by continuously adapting to deliver precisely what they need, when they need it, how they need it, so that class time is more effective. Connect allows the professor to assign homework, quizzes, and tests easily and automatically grades and records the scores of the student's work. Problems are randomized to prevent sharing of answers an may also have a "multi-step solution" which helps move the students' learning along if they experience difficulty.

title: Introduction to chemical engineering thermodynamics
abstract: This comprehensive text provides a foundational and advanced exploration of chemical engineering thermodynamics, systematically covering the principles, laws, and applications essential to the discipline. Beginning with fundamental concepts such as energy, work, heat, and state functions, the book progresses through the first and second laws of thermodynamics, volumetric properties of pure fluids, heat effects, and entropy. It addresses the thermodynamic properties of fluids, flow processes, power generation from heat, refrigeration, and liquefaction. The treatment extends to solution thermodynamics, phase equilibria, vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE), and chemical-reaction equilibria, integrating theoretical frameworks with practical applications. Emphasis is placed on the use of equations of state, property correlations, and computational methods for analyzing real-world chemical processes. The text is supported by extensive tables, diagrams, and example problems to facilitate understanding and application in engineering practice. This work serves as both an instructional resource for students and a reference for practicing engineers seeking a thorough grounding in chemical engineering thermodynamics.

title: Manufacturing Engineering
abstract: Manufacturing Engineering is concerned with designing, building, planning, operating, and managing economical production systems for discrete manufacturing. Manufacturing engineers need to have a thorough knowledge of materials and manufacturing processes. They should also be able to design, operate and manage integrated systems that include people, materials, machine tools, material handling equipment, robots, quality measuring equipment, controls and computers.
venue: Lecture Notes on Multidisciplinary Industrial Engineering

title: Manufacturing Engineering
abstract: This study presents a multi-scale mathematical model to investigate the impact of surface roughness on the adhesion and friction of microfibers in side contact, inspired by gecko-inspired adhesive systems. The model incorporates nanoscale roughness and preload effects, extending beyond previous analytic approximations based on linear elastic contact mechanics. By numerically solving for contact area, adhesion, and friction forces between rough microfiber arrays and glass substrates, the analysis reveals that increased surface roughness significantly reduces adhesive forces while only moderately affecting the limiting friction force. The results highlight the importance of surface topography, fabrication-induced roughness, and the interplay between adhesion and friction at the microscale. These findings provide insights for optimizing synthetic adhesive materials and contribute to a better understanding of contact mechanics in micro-engineered systems.
venue: Lecture Notes on Multidisciplinary Industrial Engineering

title: Metabolic engineering for the production of natural products.
abstract: Natural products and their derivatives play an important role in modern healthcare as frontline treatments for many diseases and as inspiration for chemically synthesized therapeutics. With advances in sequencing and recombinant DNA technology, many of the biosynthetic pathways responsible for the production of these chemically complex yet valuable compounds have been elucidated. With an ever-expanding toolkit of biosynthetic components, metabolic engineering is an increasingly powerful method to improve natural product titers and generate novel compounds. Heterologous production platforms have enabled access to pathways from difficult to culture strains, systems biology and metabolic modeling tools have resulted in increasing predictive and analytic capabilities, advances in expression systems and regulation have enabled the fine-tuning of pathways for increased efficiency, and characterization of individual pathway components has facilitated the construction of hybrid pathways for the production of new compounds. These advances in the many aspects of metabolic engineering not only have yielded fascinating scientific discoveries but also make it an increasingly viable approach for the optimization of natural product biosynthesis.
venue: Annual Review of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering

title: Metabolic engineering for the production of natural products.
abstract: Natural products are a vital source of bioactive compounds for pharmaceuticals and other applications, yet their structural complexity and low natural abundance often limit commercial production. Recent advances in sequencing, recombinant DNA technology, and systems biology have enabled the elucidation and manipulation of biosynthetic pathways responsible for these compounds. Metabolic engineering, which involves the rational modification of an organism’s genetic and metabolic networks, has emerged as a powerful strategy to enhance natural product titers and generate novel analogs. This review discusses key approaches in metabolic engineering for strain improvement, including increasing precursor supply, optimizing bottleneck enzymes, altering regulatory mechanisms, minimizing byproduct formation, and reconstructing pathways in heterologous hosts. The use of heterologous production platforms, particularly in well-characterized bacterial strains such as Streptomyces and Escherichia coli, has expanded access to natural products from genetically intractable or slow-growing organisms. Advances in protein engineering and genome-scale metabolic modeling further facilitate pathway optimization and the design of hybrid biosynthetic routes. Collectively, these developments have transformed metabolic engineering into a robust tool for both improving yields of existing natural products and enabling the discovery and production of new bioactive molecules.
venue: Annual Review of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering

title: Model-Driven Software Engineering in Practice
abstract: Model based software development differs from the conventional software development process and used in conjunction with a range of agile techniques. Despite improvements in third generation programming languages and runtime platforms, the levels of abstraction at which PLAs are developed today remains low-level relative to the concepts and concerns within the application domains themselves, such as manually tracking the library dependency or ensuring component composition syntactical and semantic correctness. [1] A promising means to address this problem involves developing PLAs using model-driven engineering (MDE) [2] which involves systematic use of models as key design and implementation artifacts throughout the software lifecycle. Thus to induce the works on architectures and models, researchers have been working to create structured models. The literature in this area hence proliferates; where the current edition [3] tries to address some of the significant aspects.

title: Model-Driven Software Engineering in Practice
abstract: This book provides a comprehensive introduction to Model-Driven Software Engineering (MDSE), emphasizing its practical application in modern software development. It explores the foundational concepts of modeling, model transformations, and metamodeling, and examines how MDSE methodologies can enhance efficiency, automation, and quality in software engineering processes. The text covers both general-purpose and domain-specific modeling languages, with detailed discussions on standards such as UML and the Model-Driven Architecture (MDA) initiative by OMG. It also addresses the integration of MDSE with established development practices including agile, test-driven development, and software product lines. The second edition features expanded coverage of domain-specific languages, new modeling language examples such as IFML, and updated content for improved clarity and usability. By combining theoretical foundations with real-world scenarios and tool support, the book serves as an agile guide for practitioners seeking to adopt or deepen their use of model-driven approaches in software projects.

title: Modular Tissue Engineering: Engineering Biological Tissues from the Bottom Up.
abstract: Tissue engineering creates biological tissues that aim to improve the function of diseased or damaged tissues. To enhance the function of engineered tissues there is a need to generate structures that mimic the intricate architecture and complexity of native organs and tissues. With the desire to create more complex tissues with features such as developed and functional microvasculature, cell binding motifs and tissue specific morphology, tissue engineering techniques are beginning to focus on building modular microtissues with repeated functional units. The emerging field known as modular tissue engineering focuses on fabricating tissue building blocks with specific microarchitectural features and using these modular units to engineer biological tissues from the bottom up. In this review we will examine the promise and shortcomings of 'bottom-up' approaches to creating engineered biological tissues. Specifically, we will survey the current techniques for controlling cell aggregation, proliferation and extracellular matrix deposition, as well as approaches to generating shape-controlled tissue modules. We will then highlight techniques utilized to create macroscale engineered biological tissues from modular microscale units.

title: Modular Tissue Engineering: Engineering Biological Tissues from the Bottom Up.
abstract: Modular tissue engineering represents a bottom-up approach to creating biological tissues by assembling microscale building blocks with defined architectures, aiming to better replicate the complexity and functionality of native tissues compared to traditional top-down methods. This review examines the principles and techniques underlying modular tissue engineering, including strategies for controlling cell aggregation, proliferation, and extracellular matrix deposition, as well as the fabrication of shape-specific tissue modules using methods such as micromolding, cell sheet stacking, and cell-laden hydrogels. Approaches for assembling these modules into larger, macroscale tissues are discussed, highlighting advances in additive photocrosslinking, directed assembly, and integration of functional microvasculature. The review also addresses the challenges of achieving robust mechanical properties, scalability, and in vivo functionality. By leveraging modular design inspired by native tissue organization, bottom-up tissue engineering holds promise for generating more biomimetic and clinically relevant engineered tissues.

title: Next Generation Science Standards
abstract: Science and Engineering Practices that connect to garden-based education (all 8): • Asking questions (for science) and defining problems (for engineering) • Developing and using models • Planning and carrying out investigations • Analyzing and interpreting data • Using mathematics and computational thinking • Constructing explanations (for science) and designing solutions (for engineering) • Engaging in argument from evidence • Obtaining, evaluating, and communicating information

title: Next Generation Science Standards
abstract: This policy brief examines the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS), a set of voluntary K-12 science performance expectations designed to enhance science education in the United States. The brief outlines the rationale for new standards, citing low national and international science achievement and the need to update outdated state standards. It details the collaborative development process of the NGSS, involving national organizations and state partners, and discusses their slower adoption compared to other standards due to the absence of federal incentives. Supporters argue that the NGSS promote critical thinking, inquiry-based learning, and better preparation for STEM careers, while critics question their rigor, content clarity, and treatment of topics such as climate change and evolution. The brief also reviews Arkansas’s current science standards, which have been rated higher than the NGSS in terms of content and rigor, and describes Arkansas’s ongoing consideration of adopting adapted NGSS as its own K-12 science standards. The analysis provides a balanced overview of the opportunities and challenges associated with NGSS implementation at the state level.

title: Pharmaceutical Particle Engineering via Spray Drying
abstract: This review covers recent developments in the area of particle engineering via spray drying. The last decade has seen a shift from empirical formulation efforts to an engineering approach based on a better understanding of particle formation in the spray drying process. Microparticles with nanoscale substructures can now be designed and their functionality has contributed significantly to stability and efficacy of the particulate dosage form. The review provides concepts and a theoretical framework for particle design calculations. It reviews experimental research into parameters that influence particle formation. A classification based on dimensionless numbers is presented that can be used to estimate how excipient properties in combination with process parameters influence the morphology of the engineered particles. A wide range of pharmaceutical application examples—low density particles, composite particles, microencapsulation, and glass stabilization—is discussed, with specific emphasis on the underlying particle formation mechanisms and design concepts.

title: Pharmaceutical Particle Engineering via Spray Drying
abstract: This review examines recent advances in pharmaceutical particle engineering through spray drying, highlighting the transition from empirical formulation to a more systematic, engineering-based approach grounded in an improved understanding of particle formation mechanisms. The paper introduces a theoretical framework and practical equations for predicting particle properties based on material characteristics and process parameters, with a focus on the use of dimensionless numbers to classify and estimate the impact of excipient and process variables on particle morphology. Key concepts in structured microparticle terminology, particle size analysis, and the relevance of various equivalent diameters—particularly aerodynamic diameter for respiratory delivery—are discussed. The review also surveys experimental research on factors influencing particle formation and presents a range of pharmaceutical applications, including low-density particles, composite structures, microencapsulation, and glass stabilization. Emphasis is placed on how engineered microparticles with tailored nanoscale substructures enhance stability and efficacy in drug delivery systems, underscoring the central role of rational particle design in meeting complex therapeutic requirements.

title: Property-Based Software Engineering Measurement
abstract: Little theory exists in the field of software system measurement. Concepts such as complexity, coupling, cohesion or even size are very often subject to interpretation and appear to have inconsistent definitions in the literature. As a consequence, there is little guidance provided to the analyst attempting to define proper measures for specific problems. Many controversies in the literature are simply misunderstandings and stem from the fact that some people talk about different measurement concepts under the same label (complexity is the most common case). There is a need to define unambiguously the most important measurement concepts used in the measurement of software products. One way of doing so is to define precisely what mathematical properties characterize these concepts, regardless of the specific software artifacts to which these concepts are applied. Such a mathematical framework could generate a consensus in the software engineering community and provide a means for better communication among researchers, better guidelines for analysts, and better evaluation methods for commercial static analyzers for practitioners. We propose a mathematical framework which is generic, because it is not specific to any particular software artifact, and rigorous, because it is based on precise mathematical concepts. We use this framework to propose definitions of several important measurement concepts (size, length, complexity, cohesion, coupling). It does not intend to be complete or fully objective; other frameworks could have been proposed and different choices could have been made. However, we believe that the formalisms and properties we introduce are convenient and intuitive. This framework contributes constructively to a firmer theoretical ground of software measurement.

title: Property-Based Software Engineering Measurement
abstract: This paper addresses the lack of theoretical foundations in software engineering measurement by proposing a property-based mathematical framework for defining and distinguishing key measurement concepts such as size, length, complexity, cohesion, and coupling. The authors argue that ambiguities and inconsistencies in the literature stem from imprecise definitions and overlapping use of terminology, which hinder both academic progress and practical application. The proposed framework is generic, applying to a wide range of software artifacts beyond code, and is grounded in precise mathematical properties that characterize each concept independently. By formalizing these properties, the framework enables more rigorous validation of software measures, facilitates clearer communication among researchers, and provides practical guidance for analysts and practitioners evaluating or developing measurement tools. The paper reviews existing literature, compares alternative approaches, and illustrates the application of the framework with well-known measures, ultimately contributing to a more robust theoretical basis for software measurement and supporting more objective assessment of software quality attributes.

title: Quantum-state engineering with Josephson-junction devices
abstract: Quantum-state engineering, i.e., active control over the coherent dynamics of suitable quantum-mechanical systems, has become a fascinating prospect of modern physics. With concepts developed in atomic and molecular physics and in the context of NMR, the field has been stimulated further by the perspectives of quantum computation and communication. Low-capacitance Josephson tunneling junctions offer a promising way to realize quantum bits (qubits) for quantum information processing. The article reviews the properties of these devices and the practical and fundamental obstacles to their use. Two kinds of device have been proposed, based on either charge or phase (flux) degrees of freedom. Single- and two-qubit quantum manipulations can be controlled by gate voltages in one case and by magnetic fields in the other case. Both kinds of device can be fabricated with present technology. In flux qubit devices, an important milestone, the observation of superpositions of different flux states in the system eigenstates, has been achieved. The Josephson charge qubit has even demonstrated coherent superpositions of states readable in the time domain. There are two major problems that must be solved before these devices can be used for quantum information processing. One must have a long phase coherence time, which requires that external sources of dephasing be minimized. The review discusses relevant parameters and provides estimates of the decoherence time. Another problem is in the readout of the final state of the system. This issue is illustrated with a possible realization by a single-electron transistor capacitively coupled to the Josephson device, but general properties of measuring devices are also discussed. Finally, the review describes how the basic physical manipulations on an ideal device can be combined to perform useful operations.

title: Quantum-state engineering with Josephson-junction devices
abstract: This paper reviews the principles and experimental progress of quantum-state engineering using low-capacitance Josephson-junction devices, focusing on their application as qubits for quantum information processing. Two main types of superconducting qubits are discussed: charge qubits, where the quantum degree of freedom is the number of Cooper pairs on a small island, and flux qubits, based on the phase or magnetic flux in a ring geometry near degeneracy points. The authors analyze methods for coherent control and coupling of qubits via gate voltages or magnetic fields, drawing on techniques from single-charge systems and SQUID technology. Recent experiments demonstrating coherent oscillations and superpositions in both charge and flux qubits are highlighted, underscoring the feasibility of solid-state quantum logic operations. The paper addresses environmental decoherence and dissipation, providing estimates for phase coherence times and discussing strategies to mitigate dephasing. Quantum measurement processes are examined in detail, particularly the use of single-electron transistors (SETs) and dc-SQUIDs as readout devices, with an analysis of their impact on qubit coherence and measurement efficiency. The review concludes that Josephson-junction devices offer a promising platform for scalable quantum computation, with ongoing advances in fabrication, control, and measurement bringing practical quantum logic elements within reach.

title: Requirements for Traffic Engineering Over MPLS
abstract: This document presents a set of requirements for Traffic Engineering over Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS). It identifies the functional capabilities required to implement policies that facilitate efficient and reliable network operations in an MPLS domain. These capabilities can be used to optimize the utilization of network resources and to enhance traffic oriented performance characteristics.

title: Requirements for Traffic Engineering Over MPLS
abstract: This paper defines the functional requirements for implementing effective traffic engineering within Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) networks. It analyzes the limitations of existing interior gateway protocols (IGPs) in managing traffic and resources, motivating the need for enhanced capabilities in MPLS domains. The document details key performance objectives—both traffic-oriented, such as minimizing packet loss and delay, and resource-oriented, such as optimizing bandwidth utilization and minimizing congestion. It specifies necessary attributes for traffic trunks and network resources, including support for constraint-based routing, explicit path selection, load distribution, resilience, and performance monitoring. The requirements outlined aim to enable efficient, reliable, and scalable network operations in both large Internet backbones and enterprise environments by leveraging MPLS mechanisms to achieve advanced traffic engineering goals.

title: Review of collagen I hydrogels for bioengineered tissue microenvironments: characterization of mechanics, structure, and transport.
abstract: Type I collagen hydrogels have been used successfully as three-dimensional substrates for cell culture and have shown promise as scaffolds for engineered tissues and tumors. A critical step in the development of collagen hydrogels as viable tissue mimics is quantitative characterization of hydrogel properties and their correlation with fabrication parameters, which enables hydrogels to be tuned to match specific tissues or fulfill engineering requirements. A significant body of work has been devoted to characterization of collagen I hydrogels; however, due to the breadth of materials and techniques used for characterization, published data are often disjoint and hence their utility to the community is reduced. This review aims to determine the parameter space covered by existing data and identify key gaps in the literature so that future characterization and use of collagen I hydrogels for research can be most efficiently conducted. This review is divided into three sections: (1) relevant fabrication parameters are introduced and several of the most popular methods of controlling and regulating them are described, (2) hydrogel properties most relevant for tissue engineering are presented and discussed along with their characterization techniques, (3) the state of collagen I hydrogel characterization is recapitulated and future directions are proposed. Ultimately, this review can serve as a resource for selection of fabrication parameters and material characterization methodologies in order to increase the usefulness of future collagen-hydrogel-based characterization studies and tissue engineering experiments.

title: Review of collagen I hydrogels for bioengineered tissue microenvironments: characterization of mechanics, structure, and transport.
abstract: Type I collagen hydrogels are widely used as three-dimensional scaffolds in tissue engineering due to their biocompatibility and structural similarity to native extracellular matrix; however, variability in fabrication protocols and characterization methods has led to inconsistent data across studies, limiting their utility as standardized tissue mimics. This review systematically examines the parameter space of collagen I hydrogel fabrication—including source, solubilization method, polymerization conditions, and concentration—and correlates these with key hydrogel properties such as mechanics, structure, and transport. By surveying over 50 research articles, the review highlights significant gaps in the literature, particularly regarding comprehensive multidimensional characterization and standardization of protocols. The discussion emphasizes how fabrication parameters influence hydrogel properties relevant to cellular behavior and tissue function, identifies the most commonly used methods and their limitations, and proposes future directions for more effective characterization. Ultimately, this review serves as a resource for researchers seeking to optimize collagen I hydrogels for bioengineered tissue microenvironments by guiding the selection of fabrication parameters and characterization methodologies.

title: Risk Assessment in Geotechnical Engineering
abstract: This text presents a thorough examination of the theories and methodologies available for risk assessment in geotechnical engineering, spanning the full range from established single-variable and "first order" methods to the most recent, advanced numerical developments. In response to the growing application of LRFD methodologies in geotechnical design, coupled with increased demand for risk assessments from clients ranging from regulatory agencies to insurance companies, authors Fenton and Griffiths have introduced an innovative reliability-based risk assessment method, the Random Finite Element Method (RFEM). The authors have spent more than fifteen years developing this statistically based method for modeling the real spatial variability of soils and rocks. As demonstrated in the book, RFEM performs better in real-world applications than traditional risk assessment tools that do not properly account for the spatial variability of geomaterials.

title: Risk Assessment in Geotechnical Engineering
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive framework for risk assessment in geotechnical engineering by integrating probabilistic theory, random processes, and advanced statistical methods with practical applications. It systematically reviews foundational concepts in probability, random variables, and stochastic processes, extending to the modeling of spatial variability through random fields. Estimation techniques, simulation methods—including Monte Carlo approaches—and reliability-based design principles are developed to quantify and manage uncertainty in geotechnical systems. The practical component applies these methodologies to groundwater modeling, flow through earth dams, settlement and bearing capacity of foundations, slope stability, earth pressures, mine pillar capacity, and soil liquefaction. Through case studies and parametric analyses, the paper demonstrates how probabilistic modeling and random finite-element methods improve the prediction of performance and safety in geotechnical structures. The work emphasizes the importance of risk-based decision making and reliability assessment to achieve more robust and cost-effective designs in the face of inherent soil and loading uncertainties.

title: Scaffolds based bone tissue engineering: the role of chitosan.
abstract: As life expectancy increases, malfunction or loss of tissue caused by injury or disease leads to reduced quality of life in many patients at significant socioeconomic cost.
