Even though major progress has been made in the field of bone tissue engineering, present therapies, such as bone grafts, still have limitations. Current research on biodegradable polymers is emerging, combining these structures with osteogenic cells, as an alternative to autologous bone grafts. Different types of biodegradable materials have been proposed for the preparation of three-dimensional porous scaffolds for bone tissue engineering. Among them, natural polymers are one of the most attractive options, mainly due to their similarities with extracellular matrix, chemical versatility, good biological performance, and inherent cellular interactions. In this review, special attention is given to chitosan as a biomaterial for bone tissue engineering applications. An extensive literature survey was performed on the preparation of chitosan scaffolds and their in vitro biological performance as well as their potential to facilitate in vivo bone regeneration. The present review also aims to offer the reader a general overview of all components needed to engineer new bone tissue. It gives a brief background on bone biology, followed by an explanation of all components in bone tissue engineering, as well as describing different tissue engineering strategies. Moreover, also discussed are the typical models used to evaluate in vitro functionality of a tissue-engineered construct and in vivo models to assess the potential to regenerate bone tissue are discussed.

title: Scaffolds based bone tissue engineering: the role of chitosan.
abstract: As the demand for effective bone regeneration therapies rises with an aging population, limitations of current clinical approaches such as autologous and allogeneic bone grafts have driven the development of bone tissue engineering strategies. This review provides a comprehensive overview of scaffold-based bone tissue engineering, emphasizing the critical role of chitosan as a biomaterial. Chitosan’s structural similarity to extracellular matrix, biocompatibility, biodegradability, and ability to support cellular interactions make it an attractive candidate for scaffold fabrication. The article discusses key concepts in bone biology, requirements for scaffold design, and the integration of osteogenic cells with three-dimensional scaffolds to promote bone regeneration. An extensive literature survey highlights various methods for preparing chitosan-based scaffolds, their in vitro biological performance, and their potential to facilitate in vivo bone repair. The review also examines current in vitro and in vivo models used to evaluate the functionality and regenerative capacity of tissue-engineered constructs. Overall, chitosan-based scaffolds demonstrate significant promise as substrates for supporting osteogenic differentiation and advancing the field of bone tissue engineering.

title: Sedimentation engineering : processes, measurements, modeling, and practice
abstract: Sedimentation Engineering: Theories, Measurements, Modeling, and Practice (ASCE Manuals and Reports on Engineering Practice No. 110) is intended to supplement ''Sedimentation Engineering: Classic Edition'' (ASCE Manuals and Reports on Engineering Practice No. 54), a seminal text on the nature and scope of sedimentation problems, methods for their investigation, and practical approaches to their solution.''Sedimentation Engineering: Theories, Measurements, Modeling, and Practice'' updates selected topics in the original manual and addresses new topics, such as the hydraulic action of flowing water in the context of rivers and inland water bodies.

title: Sedimentation engineering : processes, measurements, modeling, and practice
abstract: Sedimentation Engineering: Processes, Measurements, Modeling, and Practice provides a comprehensive overview of current research and practical approaches to understanding sedimentation processes in diverse aquatic environments. Edited by Ata Amini, this volume compiles ten chapters contributed by international experts, addressing sediment dynamics in marshes, harbor estuaries, offshore regions, hydraulic turbines, and volcanic areas. The book emphasizes the integration of watershed management with sedimentation engineering and explores both the physical and chemical aspects of sediment transport and contamination, including case studies on persistent organic pollutants and heavy metals. By combining theoretical frameworks, measurement techniques, modeling strategies, and real-world applications, the book aims to enhance problem-solving capabilities for researchers, professionals, and students in water resources, environmental science, and related fields.

title: Semiconductor nanocrystals: structure, properties, and band gap engineering.
abstract: Semiconductor nanocrystals are tiny light-emitting particles on the nanometer scale. Researchers have studied these particles intensely and have developed them for broad applications in solar energy conversion, optoelectronic devices, molecular and cellular imaging, and ultrasensitive detection. A major feature of semiconductor nanocrystals is the quantum confinement effect, which leads to spatial enclosure of the electronic charge carriers within the nanocrystal. Because of this effect, researchers can use the size and shape of these 'artificial atoms' to widely and precisely tune the energy of discrete electronic energy states and optical transitions. As a result, researchers can tune the light emission from these particles throughout the ultraviolet, visible, near-infrared, and mid-infrared spectral ranges. These particles also span the transition between small molecules and bulk crystals, instilling novel optical properties such as carrier multiplication, single-particle blinking, and spectral diffusion. In addition, semiconductor nanocrystals provide a versatile building block for developing complex nanostructures such as superlattices and multimodal agents for molecular imaging and targeted therapy. In this Account, we discuss recent advances in the understanding of the atomic structure and optical properties of semiconductor nanocrystals. We also discuss new strategies for band gap and electronic wave function engineering to control the location of charge carriers. New methodologies such as alloying, doping, strain-tuning, and band-edge warping will likely play key roles in the further development of these particles for optoelectronic and biomedical applications.

title: Semiconductor nanocrystals: structure, properties, and band gap engineering.
abstract: Semiconductor nanocrystals, or quantum dots, are nanoscale crystalline materials that exhibit unique size- and shape-dependent optical and electronic properties due to quantum confinement effects. This review discusses recent advances in the understanding of their atomic structure, surface chemistry, and the mechanisms underlying their tunable band gaps. By manipulating nanocrystal dimensions and employing strategies such as alloying, doping, strain-tuning, and surface passivation, researchers can precisely control electronic wave functions and band gap energies, enabling emission across a broad spectral range from ultraviolet to mid-infrared. The interplay between internal crystal structure and surface states is highlighted as a key factor influencing fluorescence efficiency and stability. Advances in synthetic methods have enabled the fabrication of nanocrystals with diverse morphologies and high monodispersity, facilitating their integration into optoelectronic devices, solar energy conversion systems, and biomedical imaging applications. The ability to engineer band structure at the nanoscale positions semiconductor nanocrystals as versatile building blocks for next-generation technologies in electronics, photonics, and medicine.

title: Solar Engineering of Thermal Processes
abstract: Over several editions, Solar Engineering of Thermal Processes has become a classic solar engineering text and reference. This revised Fourth Edition offers current coverage of solar energy theory, systems design, and applications in different market sectors along with an emphasis on solar system design and analysis using simulations to help readers translate theory into practice.

title: Solar Engineering of Thermal Processes
abstract: This paper examines the Demand-Driven Acquisition (DDA) model for library ebook collections, highlighting its evolution, operational mechanisms, and benefits for academic institutions. DDA enables libraries to provide immediate access to a vast selection of ebooks, with purchases or loans triggered by actual user engagement, thereby aligning collection development with real-time user needs and optimizing budget efficiency. The model offers flexible purchasing options, including traditional DDA, Short-Term Loans (STL), and Access-to-Own (ATO), allowing libraries to tailor acquisition strategies and maintain control over content selection. Integration with platforms like Ebook Central, Rialto, and OASIS facilitates seamless management and scalability, while enriched metadata and discovery integration enhance user experience. The study underscores DDA’s capacity to increase usage, ensure cost-effectiveness, and support the dynamic needs of academic communities by leveraging data-driven insights and customizable workflows. User-centric collection building and innovative access models position DDA as a sustainable solution for modern library resource management.

title: Strain engineering of graphene's electronic structure.
abstract: We explore the influence of local strain on the electronic structure of graphene. We show that strain can be easily tailored to generate electron beam collimation, 1D channels, surface states, and confinement. These can be seen as basic elements for all-graphene electronics which, by suitable engineering of local strain profiles, could be integrated on a single graphene sheet. In addition this proposal has the advantage that patterning can be made on substrates rather than on graphene, thereby protecting the integrity of the latter.

title: Strain engineering of graphene's electronic structure.
abstract: We demonstrate that strain engineering offers a versatile and non-destructive approach to modulate the electronic properties of graphene, enabling the realization of all-graphene integrated circuits. By inducing controlled strain profiles via substrate patterning rather than direct modification of the graphene sheet, we show that key device functionalities—such as electron beam collimation, one-dimensional channels, surface states, and quantum confinement—can be achieved within a continuous graphene layer. Using a tight-binding framework, we analyze how strain-induced changes in hopping amplitudes manifest as effective gauge fields, leading to direction-dependent tunneling, transport gaps, and confined electronic modes analogous to those in nanoribbons. Our results highlight the potential of substrate-mediated strain engineering as a scalable platform for graphene-based electronics, circumventing the limitations associated with edge patterning and preserving the intrinsic quality of graphene.

title: Strategic directions in tissue engineering.
abstract: The field of tissue engineering is developing rapidly. Given its ultimate importance to clinical care, the time is appropriate to assess the field's strategic directions to optimize research and development activities. To characterize strategic directions in tissue engineering, a distant but reachable clinical goal was proposed and a worldwide body of 24 leaders in tissue engineering was queried systematically to determine the best paths toward that goal. Using a modified Hoshin process, we identified 14 critical activity categories and then stratified them by their immediate priority for the field. The result of the analysis illustrates a highly interdependent set of activities that are dominated by the need for an understanding of angiogenesis, stem cell science, and the utilization of molecular biology and systems biology tools to enable a deeper comprehension of tissue development and control.

title: Strategic directions in tissue engineering.
abstract: This study systematically assessed the strategic directions of tissue engineering by engaging 24 global leaders in the field to identify and prioritize critical activity areas necessary for achieving broad clinical success by 2021. Using a modified Hoshin planning process, 145 expert-generated ideas were clustered into 14 key concepts, which were then ranked based on their interrelationships, dominance, and current progress. The analysis revealed a highly interdependent network of priorities, with particular emphasis on angiogenic control, stem cell science, molecular and systems biology, and cell/tissue characterization as immediate focal points. These findings provide a strategic framework to guide research, funding, policy, and development efforts in tissue engineering, aiming to enhance the efficiency and impact of future advancements.

title: The Art, Science, and Engineering of Fuzzing: A Survey
abstract: Among the many software testing techniques available today, fuzzing has remained highly popular due to its conceptual simplicity, its low barrier to deployment, and its vast amount of empirical evidence in discovering real-world software vulnerabilities. At a high level, fuzzing refers to a process of repeatedly running a program with generated inputs that may be syntactically or semantically malformed. While researchers and practitioners alike have invested a large and diverse effort towards improving fuzzing in recent years, this surge of work has also made it difficult to gain a comprehensive and coherent view of fuzzing. To help preserve and bring coherence to the vast literature of fuzzing, this paper presents a unified, general-purpose model of fuzzing together with a taxonomy of the current fuzzing literature. We methodically explore the design decisions at every stage of our model fuzzer by surveying the related literature and innovations in the art, science, and engineering that make modern-day fuzzers effective.

title: The Art, Science, and Engineering of Fuzzing: A Survey
abstract: Fuzzing has emerged as a cornerstone technique for software vulnerability discovery due to its simplicity, effectiveness, and widespread adoption in both industry and academia. Despite significant advances and a rapidly expanding body of research, the field suffers from fragmented terminology, inconsistent documentation, and a lack of unified frameworks, which impede systematic progress. This survey addresses these challenges by presenting a comprehensive model and taxonomy of fuzzing, consolidating terminology, and analyzing the design decisions that underpin modern fuzzers. Drawing from an extensive review of recent literature and major security conferences, the paper systematically explores the art, science, and engineering aspects of fuzzing, highlighting key innovations, trade-offs, and engineering practices that contribute to its success. The result is a coherent synthesis that aims to guide future research and practice in automated software testing for security.

title: The effect of nanoparticle size, shape, and surface chemistry on biological systems.
abstract: An understanding of the interactions between nanoparticles and biological systems is of significant interest. Studies aimed at correlating the properties of nanomaterials such as size, shape, chemical functionality, surface charge, and composition with biomolecular signaling, biological kinetics, transportation, and toxicity in both cell culture and animal experiments are under way. These fundamental studies will provide a foundation for engineering the next generation of nanoscale devices. Here, we provide rationales for these studies, review the current progress in studies of the interactions of nanomaterials with biological systems, and provide a perspective on the long-term implications of these findings.

title: The effect of nanoparticle size, shape, and surface chemistry on biological systems.
abstract: This study investigates the influence of silver nanoparticle size, shape, and surface chemistry on their biocidal activity against biological systems, focusing on Candida albicans. Silver nanoparticles were synthesized using sodium citrate as a reducing agent and sodium dodecyl sulfate as a surfactant, yielding particles with diameters ranging from 10 to 50 nm. A 2³ factorial design was employed to correlate reagent concentrations and surface plasmon resonance with nanoparticle size. The biocidal efficacy of nanoparticles, particularly those in the 10–14 nm range, was evaluated against C. albicans in both planktonic and biofilm forms, comparing silver suspensions and liposome-encapsulated formulations. Results demonstrate that nanoparticle size and formulation significantly affect antimicrobial activity, with both suspension and liposomal forms exhibiting effective biocidal action against C. albicans in different growth environments. These findings highlight the critical role of nanoparticle physicochemical properties in modulating biological interactions and antimicrobial efficacy.

title: The role of tissue engineering in articular cartilage repair and regeneration.
abstract: Articular cartilage repair and regeneration continue to be largely intractable because of the poor regenerative properties of this tissue. The field of articular cartilage tissue engineering, which aims to repair, regenerate, and/or improve injured or diseased articular cartilage functionality, has evoked intense interest and holds great potential for improving articular cartilage therapy. This review provides an overall description of the current state of and progress in articular cartilage repair and regeneration. Traditional therapies and related problems are introduced. More importantly, a variety of promising cell sources, biocompatible tissue engineered scaffolds, scaffoldless techniques, growth factors, and mechanical stimuli used in current articular cartilage tissue engineering are reviewed. Finally, the technical and regulatory challenges of articular cartilage tissue engineering and possible future directions are also discussed.

title: The role of tissue engineering in articular cartilage repair and regeneration.
abstract: Articular cartilage possesses limited self-repair capacity, making injuries and degenerative conditions such as osteoarthritis difficult to treat with conventional methods like autografts, allografts, and joint replacement, which are associated with significant limitations and complications. Tissue engineering has emerged as a promising alternative by aiming to restore or regenerate articular cartilage through the use of various cell sources, biocompatible scaffolds, scaffoldless techniques, growth factors, and mechanical stimuli to mimic native tissue structure and function. This review summarizes the unique composition and structure of articular cartilage, evaluates traditional repair strategies and their shortcomings, and discusses recent advances in tissue engineering approaches for cartilage repair and regeneration. Key challenges such as limited cell migration, immune responses, regulatory hurdles, and the need for functional tissue integration are highlighted. The review concludes by outlining future directions for research and clinical translation in articular cartilage tissue engineering to improve therapeutic outcomes.

title: Three-dimensional scaffolds for tissue engineering applications: role of porosity and pore size.
abstract: Tissue engineering applications commonly encompass the use of three-dimensional (3D) scaffolds to provide a suitable microenvironment for the incorporation of cells or growth factors to regenerate damaged tissues or organs. These scaffolds serve to mimic the actual in vivo microenvironment where cells interact and behave according to the mechanical cues obtained from the surrounding 3D environment. Hence, the material properties of the scaffolds are vital in determining cellular response and fate. These 3D scaffolds are generally highly porous with interconnected pore networks to facilitate nutrient and oxygen diffusion and waste removal. This review focuses on the various fabrication techniques (e.g., conventional and rapid prototyping methods) that have been employed to fabricate 3D scaffolds of different pore sizes and porosity. The different pore size and porosity measurement methods will also be discussed. Scaffolds with graded porosity have also been studied for their ability to better represent the actual in vivo situation where cells are exposed to layers of different tissues with varying properties. In addition, the ability of pore size and porosity of scaffolds to direct cellular responses and alter the mechanical properties of scaffolds will be reviewed, followed by a look at nature's own scaffold, the extracellular matrix. Overall, the limitations of current scaffold fabrication approaches for tissue engineering applications and some novel and promising alternatives will be highlighted.

title: Three-dimensional scaffolds for tissue engineering applications: role of porosity and pore size.
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) scaffolds are essential in tissue engineering for providing a biomimetic microenvironment that supports cell growth, differentiation, and tissue regeneration. This review examines the critical roles of porosity and pore size in scaffold design, highlighting their influence on nutrient diffusion, waste removal, vascularization, and mechanical stability. Various conventional and rapid prototyping fabrication techniques are discussed with respect to their ability to control scaffold architecture, porosity, and pore size. Methods for measuring these parameters are also reviewed. The impact of graded porosity on replicating native tissue complexity and the interplay between scaffold structure and cellular response are analyzed. Limitations of current fabrication methods, including challenges in achieving optimal mechanical properties and biocompatibility, are addressed alongside emerging alternatives such as modular assembly and electrospinning. Overall, optimizing porosity and pore size is crucial for developing functional 3D scaffolds that closely mimic the extracellular matrix and enhance tissue engineering outcomes.

title: Tumor engineering: the other face of tissue engineering.
abstract: Advances in tissue engineering have been accomplished for years by employing biomimetic strategies to provide cells with aspects of their original microenvironment necessary to reconstitute a unit of both form and function for a given tissue. We believe that the most critical hallmark of cancer is loss of integration of architecture and function; thus, it stands to reason that similar strategies could be employed to understand tumor biology. In this commentary, we discuss work contributed by Fischbach-Teschl and colleagues to this special issue of Tissue Engineering in the context of 'tumor engineering', that is, the construction of complex cell culture models that recapitulate aspects of the in vivo tumor microenvironment to study the dynamics of tumor development, progression, and therapy on multiple scales. We provide examples of fundamental questions that could be answered by developing such models, and encourage the continued collaboration between physical scientists and life scientists not only for regenerative purposes, but also to unravel the complexity that is the tumor microenvironment.

title: Tumor engineering: the other face of tissue engineering.
abstract: Tumor engineering, as the counterpart to traditional tissue engineering, leverages biomimetic strategies to construct complex in vitro models that recapitulate the architecture and function of the in vivo tumor microenvironment. This approach addresses critical limitations of conventional two-dimensional cultures and animal models, enabling more physiologically relevant studies of tumor development, progression, and therapeutic response. By integrating advances in patterning techniques, materials science, and imaging modalities, tumor engineering facilitates the investigation of dynamic interactions among tumor cells, stromal components, extracellular matrix, and vasculature. Such models allow researchers to dissect fundamental questions regarding angiogenesis, invasion, metastasis, and microenvironmental heterogeneity—questions that are difficult to answer using existing in vivo or in vitro systems. The commentary highlights recent progress in engineering perfused microvasculature within hydrogels and combinatorial microenvironment arrays to study spatial and temporal aspects of tumor biology. Ultimately, the authors advocate for increased collaboration between physical and life scientists to further develop tumor engineering as a discipline, not only to advance regenerative medicine but also to unravel the complexity of cancer biology and improve therapeutic strategies.

title: Vascularization strategies for tissue engineering.
abstract: Tissue engineering is currently limited by the inability to adequately vascularize tissues in vitro or in vivo. Issues of nutrient perfusion and mass transport limitations, especially oxygen diffusion, restrict construct development to smaller than clinically relevant dimensions and limit the ability for in vivo integration. There is much interest in the field as researchers have undertaken a variety of approaches to vascularization, including material functionalization, scaffold design, microfabrication, bioreactor development, endothelial cell seeding, modular assembly, and in vivo systems. Efforts to model and measure oxygen diffusion and consumption within these engineered tissues have sought to quantitatively assess and improve these design strategies. This review assesses the current state of the field by outlining the prevailing approaches taken toward producing vascularized tissues and highlighting their strengths and weaknesses.

title: Vascularization strategies for tissue engineering.
abstract: Tissue engineering faces critical challenges due to insufficient vascularization, which limits nutrient and oxygen transport and restricts construct size and integration in vivo. This review examines current strategies to overcome these barriers, including scaffold functionalization with angiogenic factors, advanced scaffold design, bioreactor systems, microfabrication approaches, endothelial cell seeding, modular assembly, and in vivo vascularization techniques. Quantitative modeling and measurement of oxygen diffusion and consumption are highlighted as essential tools for optimizing these strategies and ensuring cell viability throughout engineered tissues. The strengths and limitations of each approach are discussed with emphasis on their capacity to promote functional vascular networks and facilitate anastomosis with host vasculature. By integrating advances in material science, cellular engineering, and quantitative analysis, this review outlines the fundamental requirements for achieving clinically relevant vascularized tissues both in vitro and in vivo.

title: Actionable Knowledge for Environmental Decision Making: Broadening the Usability of Climate Science
abstract: Despite the rapid evolution and growing complexity in models of science-society interaction, the rate and breadth of use of scientific knowledge in environmental decision making, especially related to climate variability and change, remain below expectations. This suggests a persistent gap between production and use that, to date, efforts to rethink and restructure science production have not been able to surmount. We review different models of science-policy interfaces to understand how they have influenced the organization of knowledge production and application. We then explore how new approaches to the creation of knowledge have emerged, involving both growing integration across disciplines and greater interaction with users. Finally, we review climate information use in the United States and United Kingdom to explore how the structure of knowledge production and the characteristics of users and their decision environments expose the challenges of broadening usable climate science.

title: Actionable Knowledge for Environmental Decision Making: Broadening the Usability of Climate Science
abstract: This paper reviews the evolution of science-policy models and their implications for the usability of climate science in environmental decision making. Despite advances in participatory approaches and boundary organizations designed to bridge the gap between scientific knowledge production and its application, the uptake of climate information by decision makers remains limited. The authors synthesize empirical research on factors influencing the use of scientific information, highlighting how perceptions, institutional contexts, and producer-user interactions shape usability. They argue that current efforts often focus too narrowly on individual users or small groups, overlooking the need to address a broader diversity of decision makers. To address this gap, the paper proposes a conceptual framework based on a typology of users at the aggregate level, offering a pathway to scale up the provision of actionable climate information while maintaining or enhancing its relevance and usability. The review concludes by identifying key challenges and opportunities for advancing the co-production and institutionalization of usable climate knowledge, with particular attention to supporting adaptation decisions in the face of accelerating climate change.

title: Advancing environmental exposure assessment science to benefit society
abstract: Awareness of the human health impacts of exposure to air pollution is growing rapidly. For example, it has become evident that the adverse health effects of air pollution are more pronounced in disadvantaged populations. Policymakers in many jurisdictions have responded to this evidence by enacting initiatives that lead to lower concentrations of air pollutants, such as urban traffic restrictions. In this review, we focus on the interplay between advances in environmental exposure assessment and developments in policy. We highlight recent progress in the granular measurement of air pollutants and individual-level exposures, and how this has enabled focused local policy actions. Finally, we detail an illustrative study designed to link individual-level health-relevant exposures with economic, behavioral, biological, familial, and environmental variables. How can scientists and policymakers work together to reduce the health impacts of air pollution? In this review paper, the authors discuss the interplay between advances in environmental exposure assessment and policy advances to tackle pollution in a focused way.

title: Advancing environmental exposure assessment science to benefit society
abstract: Growing evidence links air pollution exposure to significant adverse health outcomes, particularly among disadvantaged populations who often experience higher pollutant levels and greater susceptibility. This review examines recent advances in environmental exposure assessment, highlighting the shift from coarse, community-level monitoring to granular, individual-level measurements that capture personal exposures and contextual factors. These technological developments have enabled more targeted policy interventions, such as urban traffic restrictions and cleaner fuel mandates, which are increasingly informed by detailed exposure data. The paper also presents an illustrative study in New York City that integrates individual exposure monitoring with economic, behavioral, biological, familial, and environmental variables to better understand health impacts and inform policy. While challenges remain in translating personal exposure data into regulatory action, the integration of advanced assessment methods with policy initiatives holds promise for reducing health disparities and improving public health outcomes on both local and global scales.

title: Advancing environmental risk assessment for transgenic biofeedstock crops
abstract: Transgenic modification of plants is a key enabling technology for developing sustainable biofeedstocks for biofuels production. Regulatory decisions and the wider acceptance and development of transgenic biofeedstock crops are considered from the context of science-based risk assessment. The risk assessment paradigm for transgenic biofeedstock crops is fundamentally no different from that of current generation transgenic crops, except that the focus of the assessment must consider the unique attributes of a given biofeedstock crop and its environmental release. For currently envisioned biofeedstock crops, particular emphasis in risk assessment will be given to characterization of altered metabolic profiles and their implications relative to non-target environmental effects and food safety; weediness and invasiveness when plants are modified for abiotic stress tolerance or are domesticated; and aggregate risk when plants are platforms for multi-product production. Robust risk assessments for transgenic biofeedstock crops are case-specific, initiated through problem formulation, and use tiered approaches for risk characterization.

title: Advancing environmental risk assessment for transgenic biofeedstock crops
abstract: Transgenic modification is increasingly central to the development of sustainable biofeedstock crops for biofuels, necessitating robust environmental risk assessment frameworks to guide regulatory decisions and public acceptance. This review examines how established risk assessment paradigms for transgenic crops can be adapted to address the unique characteristics of biofeedstock crops, including altered metabolic profiles, potential non-target environmental effects, weediness and invasiveness, and aggregate risks from multi-product platforms. Emphasizing case-specific, science-based assessments initiated through problem formulation and employing tiered approaches, the paper highlights the importance of integrating scientific evidence with decision-making processes. Ultimately, advancing risk assessment methodologies for transgenic biofeedstock crops is critical to enabling their safe and effective deployment in sustainable biofuel production systems.

title: Assessing data quality in citizen science (preprint)
abstract: Ecological and environmental citizen science projects have enormous potential to advance science, influence policy, and guide resource management by producing datasets that are otherwise infeasible to generate. This potential can only be realized, though, if the datasets are of high quality. While scientists are often skeptical of the ability of unpaid volunteers to produce accurate datasets, a growing body of publications clearly shows that diverse types of citizen science projects can produce data with accuracy equal to or surpassing that of professionals. Successful projects rely on a suite of methods to boost data accuracy and account for bias, including iterative project development, volunteer training and testing, expert validation, replication across volunteers, and statistical modeling of systematic error. Each citizen science dataset should therefore be judged individually, according to project design and application, rather than assumed to be substandard simply because volunteers generated it.

title: Assessing data quality in citizen science (preprint)
abstract: Citizen science projects in ecology and environmental science have the potential to generate large, valuable datasets that can inform research, policy, and resource management, but concerns about data quality—particularly accuracy and bias—have limited their acceptance. This paper reviews evidence from a range of citizen science initiatives, demonstrating that volunteer-collected data can match or exceed the quality of professional datasets when appropriate project design and quality assurance measures are implemented. Effective strategies include iterative project development, comprehensive volunteer training and testing, expert validation, replication across volunteers, and statistical modeling to address systematic error and bias. The variability in individual volunteer performance is comparable to that observed among professionals, and most biases present in citizen science data are also found in professionally collected datasets and can be mitigated using established statistical tools. The authors argue that citizen science data should be evaluated on the basis of methodological rigor and data stewardship rather than the involvement of volunteers alone, encouraging a shift toward more nuanced assessments of data quality in citizen science.

title: A basic guide for empirical environmental social science
abstract: In this paper, I address a gap in the literature on environmental social science by providing a basic rubric for the conduct of empirical research in this interdisciplinary field. Current literature displays a healthy diversity of methods and techniques, but this has also been accompanied by a lack of consistency in the way in which research in this area is done. In part this can be seen as resulting from a lack in supporting texts that would provide a basis for this consistency. Although relevant methods texts do exist, these are not written with this type of research explicitly in mind, and so translating them to this field can be awkward. This paper is designed to fill this gap and enable more consistency in the conduct of empirical environmental social science. Basic types of research designs and methods are covered, as are criteria for evaluating these methods.

title: A basic guide for empirical environmental social science
abstract: This paper provides a foundational overview of empirical research methods in environmental social science, aiming to guide newcomers and practitioners in designing, conducting, and interpreting empirical studies. It outlines the key principles of empirical inquiry, including the formulation of research questions, selection of appropriate methodologies, data collection strategies, and approaches to data analysis. The guide emphasizes the importance of integrating social and ecological perspectives, recognizing the complexity and interdependence inherent in environmental issues. Practical considerations such as ethical research practices, stakeholder engagement, and the challenges of working across disciplinary boundaries are addressed. By synthesizing best practices and common pitfalls, this guide serves as a practical resource for students and researchers seeking to contribute robust empirical evidence to inform environmental policy and management decisions.

title: A conceptual framework for integrated STEM education
abstract: The global urgency to improve STEM education may be driven by environmental and social impacts of the twenty-first century which in turn jeopardizes global security and economic stability. The complexity of these global factors reach beyond just helping students achieve high scores in math and science assessments. Friedman (The world is flat: A brief history of the twenty-first century, 2005) helped illustrate the complexity of a global society, and educators must help students prepare for this global shift. In response to these challenges, the USA experienced massive STEM educational reforms in the last two decades. In practice, STEM educators lack cohesive understanding of STEM education. Therefore, they could benefit from a STEM education conceptual framework. The process of integrating science, technology, engineering, and mathematics in authentic contexts can be as complex as the global challenges that demand a new generation of STEM experts. Educational researchers indicate that teachers struggle to make connections across the STEM disciplines. Consequently, students are often disinterested in science and math when they learn in an isolated and disjoined manner missing connections to crosscutting concepts and real-world applications. The following paper will operationalize STEM education key concepts and blend learning theories to build an integrated STEM education framework to assist in further researching integrated STEM education.

title: A conceptual framework for integrated STEM education
abstract: This paper addresses the pressing global need for improved STEM education by proposing a conceptual framework for integrated STEM learning. Recognizing that traditional, siloed approaches to science, technology, engineering, and mathematics fail to engage students or prepare them for complex real-world challenges, the authors highlight the limitations of current educational reforms and the ongoing ambiguity surrounding effective STEM integration. Drawing on recent research and policy developments, the paper operationalizes key concepts in integrated STEM education and synthesizes relevant learning theories to construct a framework that emphasizes authentic contexts, cross-disciplinary connections, and the application of scientific inquiry and engineering design. The proposed framework aims to support educators and researchers in designing coherent curricula that foster student interest, enhance learning outcomes, and better equip future generations to address global economic, environmental, and societal challenges.

title: A methodology for systematic mapping in environmental sciences
abstract: Systematic mapping was developed in social sciences in response to a lack of empirical data when answering questions using systematic review methods, and a need for a method to describe the literature across a broad subject of interest. Systematic mapping does not attempt to answer a specific question as do systematic reviews, but instead collates, describes and catalogues available evidence (e.g. primary, secondary, theoretical, economic) relating to a topic or question of interest. The included studies can be used to identify evidence for policy-relevant questions, knowledge gaps (to help direct future primary research) and knowledge clusters (sub-sets of evidence that may be suitable for secondary research, for example systematic review). Evidence synthesis in environmental sciences faces similar challenges to those found in social sciences. Here we describe the translation of systematic mapping methodology from social sciences for use in environmental sciences. We provide the first process-based methodology for systematic maps, describing the stages involved: establishing the review team and engaging stakeholders; setting the scope and question; setting inclusion criteria for studies; scoping stage; protocol development and publication; searching for evidence; screening evidence; coding; production of a systematic map database; critical appraisal (optional); describing and visualising the findings; report production and supporting information. We discuss the similarities and differences in methodology between systematic review and systematic mapping and provide guidance for those choosing which type of synthesis is most suitable for their requirements. Furthermore, we discuss the merits and uses of systematic mapping and make recommendations for improving this evolving methodology in environmental sciences.

title: A methodology for systematic mapping in environmental sciences
abstract: Systematic mapping, originally developed in the social sciences, offers a structured approach to collating, describing, and cataloguing diverse evidence across broad topics, addressing challenges where systematic reviews are limited by data availability or question specificity. This paper presents the first process-based methodology tailored for systematic mapping in environmental sciences, detailing each stage from team formation and stakeholder engagement to protocol development, evidence searching, coding, database production, and reporting. The methodology enables identification of knowledge gaps and clusters, supports evidence-based policy-making, and guides selection between systematic review and mapping approaches. By adapting rigorous, transparent processes from social science to environmental contexts, this work provides practical guidance and recommendations for improving systematic mapping as an evolving tool for evidence synthesis in environmental sciences.

title: A Reconsideration of Environmental Federalism
abstract: This paper provides a review and assessment of the debate over environmental federalism-the issue of the roles of different levels of government in environmental management. The paper begins with the presentation of three benchmark cases that provide a framework for thinking about the issue. It then offers a review, first of the theoretical literature and second of some new, provocative empirical literature on the race to the bottom. The paper contends that there remains, under certain circumstances, an important role for decentralized government in the setting of environmental standards and the design of regulatory programs. The central government, in addition to setting standards for 'national' pollutants, has a fundamental contribution to make in supporting research in environmental science and pollution control technology and in providing needed information and guidance to state and local governments.

title: A Reconsideration of Environmental Federalism
abstract: This paper critically examines the theory and practice of environmental federalism, focusing on the allocation of responsibilities for environmental standard-setting and regulation among different levels of government. Through the development of three benchmark cases—pure public goods, local public goods, and cases with interjurisdictional spillovers—the analysis provides a conceptual framework for evaluating when centralization or decentralization is most appropriate. The paper reviews both theoretical arguments and recent empirical evidence, particularly regarding concerns about a 'race to the bottom' in environmental standards under decentralized governance. Findings suggest that while central governments play a crucial role in addressing national or global pollutants and supporting research and information dissemination, there remain significant circumstances where decentralized standard-setting yields efficiency gains and better matches local preferences. The study concludes with reflections on the need for flexible, context-dependent approaches to environmental policymaking that balance the benefits of both centralized and decentralized governance structures.

title: A typology of Indigenous engagement in Australian environmental management: Implications for knowledge integration and social-ecological system sustainability
abstract: Indigenous peoples now engage with many decentralized approaches to environmental management that offer opportunities for integration of Indigenous Ecological Knowledge (IEK) and western science to promote cultural diversity in the management of social-ecological system sustainability. Nevertheless, processes of combining IEK with western science are diverse and affected by numerous factors, including the adaptive co-management context, the intrinsic characteristics of the natural resources, and the governance systems. We present a typology of Indigenous engagement in environmental management, derived through comparative analysis of 21 Australian case studies, and consider its implications for the integration of IEK with western science. Sociological and rational choice institutionalism underpin our analytical framework, which differentiates on three axes: (1) power sharing, incorporating decision making, rules definition, resource values and property rights; (2) participation, incorporating participatory processes, organizations engaged, and coordination approaches; (3) intercultural purpose, incorporating purposes of environmental management, Indigenous engagement, Indigenous development and capacity building. Our typology groups engagement into four types: Indigenous governed collaborations; Indigenous-driven co-governance; agency-driven co-governance; and agency governance. From our analysis of manifestations of knowledge integration across the types, we argue that Indigenous governance and Indigenous-driven co-governance provides better prospects for integration of IEK and western science for sustainability of social-ecological systems. Supporting Indigenous governance without, or with only a limited requirement for power sharing with other agencies sustains the distinct Indigenous cultural purposes underpinning IEK, and benefits knowledge integration. We conclude by advocating that the typology be applied to test its general effectiveness in guiding practitioners and researchers to develop robust governance for Indigenous knowledge integration in environmental management.

title: A typology of Indigenous engagement in Australian environmental management: Implications for knowledge integration and social-ecological system sustainability
abstract: This paper develops a typology of Indigenous engagement in Australian environmental management and examines its implications for integrating Indigenous Ecological Knowledge (IEK) with western science to enhance social-ecological system sustainability. Drawing on comparative analysis of 21 case studies, the authors identify four types of engagement—Indigenous governed collaborations, Indigenous-driven co-governance, agency-driven co-governance, and agency governance—differentiated by power sharing, participation, and intercultural purpose. The analysis demonstrates that Indigenous governance and Indigenous-driven co-governance provide the most favorable conditions for effective knowledge integration, supporting both sustainability outcomes and the maintenance of distinct Indigenous cultural values. The typology offers a practical framework for practitioners and researchers to assess and design governance arrangements that foster robust integration of IEK in environmental management, with broader relevance for advancing sustainability in complex social-ecological systems.

title: Biochar Aging: Mechanisms, Physicochemical Changes, Assessment, And Implications for Field Applications.
abstract: Biochar has triggered a black gold rush in environmental studies as a carbon-rich material with well-developed porous structure and tunable functionality. While much attention has been placed on its apparent ability to store carbon in the ground, immobilize soil pollutants, and improve soil fertility, its temporally evolving in situ performance in these roles must not be overlooked. After field application, various environmental factors, such as temperature variations, precipitation events and microbial activities, can lead to its fragmentation, dissolution, and oxidation, thus causing drastic changes to the physicochemical properties. Direct monitoring of biochar-amended soils can provide good evidence of its temporal evolution, but this requires long-term field trials. Various artificial aging methods, such as chemical oxidation, wet-dry cycling and mineral modification, have therefore been designed to mimic natural aging mechanisms. Here we evaluate the science of biochar aging, critically summarize aging-induced changes to biochar properties, and offer a state-of-the-art for artificial aging simulation approaches. In addition, the implications of biochar aging are also considered regarding its potential development and deployment as a soil amendment. We suggest that for improved simulation and prediction, artificial aging methods must shift from qualitative to quantitative approaches. Furthermore, artificial preaging may serve to synthesize engineered biochars for green and sustainable environmental applications.

title: Biochar Aging: Mechanisms, Physicochemical Changes, Assessment, And Implications for Field Applications.
abstract: Biochar, a carbon-rich material with promising applications in soil amendment, pollutant remediation, and climate change mitigation, undergoes significant physicochemical transformations after field application due to environmental factors such as temperature fluctuations, precipitation, and microbial activity. These aging processes alter biochar’s structure, surface chemistry, and functionality, impacting its long-term effectiveness and stability in soils. This critical review synthesizes current understanding of natural and artificial biochar aging mechanisms—including physical fragmentation, chemical oxidation, mineral interactions, and biological processes—and evaluates their effects on key biochar properties such as porosity, surface area, elemental composition, and contaminant sorption capacity. The review also assesses artificial aging methods designed to simulate natural weathering and highlights the need for more quantitative approaches to better predict field performance. Implications for the deployment of biochar as a sustainable soil amendment are discussed, emphasizing that engineered pre-aging strategies could enhance biochar’s environmental benefits. Future research directions are proposed to bridge knowledge gaps in long-term field behavior and optimize biochar design for agricultural and remediation applications.

title: Bladder cancer, a review of the environmental risk factors
abstract: BackgroundMany epidemiological studies and reviews have been performed to identify the causes of bladder cancer. The aim of this review is to investigate the links between various environmental risk factors and cancer of the bladder.MethodsA systematic literature search was performed using PubMed, Science Direct, Scopus, Scholar Google and Russian Google databases to identify reviews and epidemiological studies on bladder cancer risk factors associated with the environment published between 1998 and 2010. Only literature discussing human studies was considered.ResultsSmoking, mainly cigarette smoking, is a well known risk factor for various diseases, including bladder cancer. Another factor strongly associated with bladder cancer is exposure to arsenic in drinking water at concentrations higher than 300 µg/l. The most notable risk factor for development of bladder cancer is occupational exposure to aromatic amines (2-naphthylamine, 4-aminobiphenyl and benzidine) and 4,4'-methylenebis(2-chloroaniline), which can be found in the products of the chemical, dye and rubber industries as well as in hair dyes, paints, fungicides, cigarette smoke, plastics, metals and motor vehicle exhaust. There are also data suggesting an effect from of other types of smoking besides cigarettes (cigar, pipe, Egyptian waterpipe, smokeless tobacco and environmental tobacco smoking), and other sources of arsenic exposure such as air, food, occupational hazards, and tobacco. Other studies show that hairdressers and barbers with occupational exposure to hair dyes experience enhanced risk of bladder cancer. For example, a study related to personal use of hair dyes demonstrates an elevated bladder cancer risk for people who used permanent hair dyes at least once a month, for one year or longer.ConclusionSmoking, in particular from cigarettes, exposure to arsenic in drinking water, and occupational exposure to aromatic amines and 4,4'-methylenebis(2-chloroaniline) are well known risk factors for various diseases including bladder cancer. Although the number of chemicals related to occupational exposure is still growing, it is worth noting that it may take several years or decades between exposure and the subsequent cancer.

title: Bladder cancer, a review of the environmental risk factors
abstract: This review systematically examines the environmental risk factors associated with bladder cancer, focusing on epidemiological evidence from studies published between 1998 and 2010. The analysis identifies cigarette smoking as the primary risk factor, with current smokers exhibiting a threefold increased risk compared to non-smokers, and highlights additional risks from other forms of tobacco use, including cigars, pipes, and environmental tobacco smoke. Occupational exposure to aromatic amines—such as 2-naphthylamine, 4-aminobiphenyl, benzidine, and 4,4’-methylenebis(2-chloroaniline)—commonly found in chemical, dye, and rubber industries, as well as in hair dyes and other products, is strongly linked to bladder cancer. Exposure to arsenic in drinking water at concentrations above 300 µg/l is also associated with elevated risk, with some evidence suggesting synergistic effects with smoking and nutritional factors even at lower concentrations. The review underscores the multifactorial nature of bladder cancer etiology and emphasizes the importance of reducing exposure to these environmental carcinogens to mitigate disease incidence.

title: Citizen Science and Biological Invasions: A Review
abstract: Biological invasions are among the most challenging ecological and conservation riddles of our times. Fortunately, citizen science projects became a valuable tool to detect non-indigenous species (NIS), document their spread, prevent dispersion, and eradicate localized populations. We evaluated the most undisputed definitions of citizen science and proposed that a combination of two of them is a better reflection of what citizen science has become. Thus, citizen science is any environmental and/or biological data collection and analysis, including data quality control, undertaken by members of the general public, as individuals or as organized groups of citizens, with the guidance and/or assistance of scientists toward solving environmental and/or community questions. With this review, we also assessed how citizen science has been advancing biological invasions research and its focus, by analyzing 126 peer-reviewed articles that used citizen science methods or data concerning NIS. Most of the articles studied terrestrial species (68%) and terrestrial plants were the most studied group (22.7%). Surprisingly, most first detection reports were of non-indigenous marine fish probably due to the constraints in accessing aquatic ecosystems which delays the detection of new NIS. Citizen science projects running over broad geographical areas are very cost-effective for the early detection of NIS, regardless of the studied environment. We also discuss the applicability and need to adapt the methods and approaches toward the studied ecosystem and species, but also the profile of the participating citizens, their motivations, level of engagement, or social status. We recommend authors to better acknowledge the work done by contributing citizens, and the putative limitations of data generated by citizen science projects. The outreach planning of citizen science projects is also evaluated, including the use of dedicated web platforms vs. pre-existent and disseminated web platforms, while discussing how such outreach actions can be maximized. Lastly, we present a framework that contextualizes the contributions of citizen science, scientific research, and regional and national stakeholders toward the integrated management of biological invasions.

title: Citizen Science and Biological Invasions: A Review
abstract: Biological invasions pose significant ecological and economic challenges, necessitating effective detection and management strategies. This review synthesizes the role of citizen science in advancing research on non-indigenous species (NIS), analyzing 126 peer-reviewed articles to assess trends, effectiveness, and methodological considerations. The majority of studies focused on terrestrial environments, particularly plants, while first detections were most frequently reported for marine fish, highlighting ecosystem-specific detection biases. Citizen science initiatives demonstrated cost-effectiveness and broad geographic coverage, facilitating early detection and monitoring of NIS across diverse habitats. The review underscores the importance of adapting citizen science approaches to ecosystem characteristics, target species, and participant profiles, as well as ensuring data quality through verification and audit procedures. Outreach strategies, including the use of dedicated versus existing web platforms, are evaluated for their potential to maximize engagement and data collection. The authors propose a refined definition of citizen science that emphasizes collaboration between citizens and scientists in data collection and analysis for environmental problem-solving. Finally, a framework is presented to integrate citizen science, scientific research, and stakeholder involvement for improved management of biological invasions, with recommendations for acknowledging citizen contributions and addressing data limitations in future projects.

title: Components of Environmental Literacy in Elementary Science Education Curriculum in Bulgaria and Turkey.
abstract: The purpose of this study was to analyze the extent to which science education objectives in elementary schools addressed to the six basic components of environmental literacy (EL), and how this attention differed from Bulgaria to Turkey. The main method in the study involved comparative content analysis of these objectives. The courses sampled for Bulgaria include “The Human Being and Nature”, “Biology and Health Education”, “Chemistry and Environmental Protection” and “Physics and Astronomy”. The course sampled for Turkey is “Science and Technology Education”. Content analysis of these objectives reveals that all components of environmental literacy did not receive the same attention. For example in both countries most attention was given to knowledge, less to skills and attitudes, and little to environmentally responsible behavior (ERB).

title: Components of Environmental Literacy in Elementary Science Education Curriculum in Bulgaria and Turkey.
abstract: This study examines the extent to which elementary science education curricula in Bulgaria and Turkey address the six fundamental components of environmental literacy: ecological knowledge, socio-political knowledge, knowledge of environmental issues, affect, cognitive skills, and environmentally responsible behaviors. Using comparative content analysis, the research analyzes objectives from Bulgarian courses such as “The Human Being and Nature,” “Biology and Health Education,” “Chemistry and Environmental Protection,” and “Physics and Astronomy,” alongside Turkey’s “Science and Technology Education” course. Findings reveal an uneven emphasis on environmental literacy components in both countries, with the greatest focus on knowledge-related objectives, less attention to skills and affective components, and minimal emphasis on fostering environmentally responsible behaviors. The results highlight the need for a more balanced integration of all environmental literacy components in elementary science curricula to better support the development of environmentally literate citizens.

title: Data Science of the Natural Environment: A Research Roadmap
abstract: Data science is the science of extracting meaning from potentially complex data. This is a fast moving field, drawing principles and techniques from a number of different disciplinary areas including computer science, statistics and complexity science. Data science is having a profound impact on a number of areas including commerce, health and smart cities. This paper argues that data science can have an equal if not greater impact in the area of earth and environmental sciences, offering a rich tapestry of new techniques to support both a deeper understanding of the natural environment in all its complexities, as well as the development of well-founded mitigation and adaptation strategies in the face of climate change. The paper argues that data science for the natural environment brings about new challenges for data science, particularly around complexity, spatial and temporal reasoning, and managing uncertainty. The paper also describes a case study in environmental data science which offers up insights into the promise of the area. The paper concludes with a research roadmap highlighting ten top challenges of environmental data science and also an invitation to become part of an international community working collaboratively on these problems.

title: Data Science of the Natural Environment: A Research Roadmap
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive research roadmap for the emerging field of environmental data science, emphasizing its potential to transform our understanding and management of the natural environment. Drawing on interdisciplinary expertise and a strategic partnership between Lancaster University’s Data Science Institute and the Centre for Ecology and Hydrology, the authors define environmental data science, systematically analyze its unique challenges—including complexity, spatial and temporal reasoning, and uncertainty—and highlight the need for integrative, collaborative approaches. The paper includes a case study on modeling extreme melt events on the Greenland Ice Sheet to illustrate the promise of data-driven methods in addressing pressing environmental issues. Concluding with a prioritized list of ten key research challenges, the authors call for the creation of an international, cross-disciplinary community to advance environmental data science and address global challenges such as climate change through innovative data-centric solutions.

title: Discovering indigenous science: Implications for science education†
abstract: Indigenous science relates to both the science knowledge of long-resident, usually oral culture peoples, as well as the science knowledge of all peoples who as participants in culture are affected by the worldview and relativist interests of their home communities. This article explores aspects of multicultural science and pedagogy and describes a rich and well-documented branch of indigenous science known to biologists and ecologists as traditional ecological knowledge (TEK). Although TEK has been generally inaccessible, educators can now use a burgeoning science-based TEK literature that documents numerous examples of time-proven, ecologically relevant, and cost effective indigenous science. Disputes regarding the universality of the standard scientific account are of critical importance for science educators because the definition of science is a de facto “gatekeeping” device for determining what can be included in a school science curriculum and what cannot. When Western modern science (WMS) is defined as universal it does displace revelation-based knowledge (i.e., creation science); however, it also displaces pragmatic local indigenous knowledge that does not conform with formal aspects of the “standard account.” Thus, in most science classrooms around the globe, Western modern science has been taught at the expense of indigenous knowledge. However, because WMS has been implicated in many of the world's ecological disasters, and because the traditional wisdom component of TEK is particularly rich in time-tested approaches that foster sustainability and environmental integrity, it is possible that the universalist “gatekeeper” can be seen as increasingly problematic and even counter productive. This paper describes many examples from Canada and around the world of indigenous people's contributions to science, environmental understanding, and sustainability. The authors argue the view that Western or modern science is just one of many sciences that need to be addressed in the science classroom. We conclude by presenting instructional strategies that can help all science learners negotiate border crossings between Western modern science and indigenous science. © 2000 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Sci Ed85:6–34, 2001.

title: Discovering indigenous science: Implications for science education†
abstract: This paper examines the significance of indigenous science, particularly traditional ecological knowledge (TEK), and its implications for science education. By analyzing the epistemological and pedagogical dimensions of multicultural science, the authors highlight how TEK—rooted in the long-standing practices and worldviews of oral cultures—offers time-tested, context-specific, and sustainable approaches to understanding nature. The paper discusses challenges in integrating TEK into mainstream science curricula, including differing knowledge systems, cultural assumptions, and historical marginalization of indigenous perspectives. It argues that the dominance of Western modern science in education often excludes valuable local knowledge, which is increasingly recognized by scientists and policymakers for its relevance to contemporary environmental crises. The authors advocate for a more inclusive science education that bridges cultural borders, enabling students to engage with both Western and indigenous sciences. Through an extensive review of TEK literature and concrete examples, the paper provides recommendations for curriculum development that respects cultural diversity and supports sustainability, ultimately calling for a reconceptualization of science education to better serve diverse learners and address global ecological challenges.

title: Environmental DNA for biomonitoring
abstract: This special issue addresses some of these challenges by present- ing the latest advances in eDNA field and discussing their strengths and limitations when applied to routine biomonitoring.

title: Environmental DNA for biomonitoring
abstract: Environmental DNA (eDNA) has rapidly transformed biomonitoring by enabling high-resolution, cost-effective biodiversity assessments across diverse ecosystems. Over the past decade, advances in high-throughput sequencing and analytical methods, including machine learning and taxonomy-free approaches, have expanded the scope of eDNA applications from single-species detection to comprehensive community analyses and environmental impact assessments. Despite these technological breakthroughs, routine implementation of eDNA-based biomonitoring remains limited due to challenges in standardization, legislative integration, and reconciling discrepancies with traditional methods. This special issue of Molecular Ecology presents 29 papers that address methodological innovations, particularly in the use of novel bioindicators and analytical tools, with a focus on fish eDNA surveys and the integration of environmental genomics for ecosystem diagnostics. The collection highlights both the strengths and limitations of current eDNA approaches, emphasizing the need for further development in calibration, reference databases, and regulatory frameworks to fully realize the potential of eDNA in routine biomonitoring.

title: Environmental noise in hospitals: a systematic review
abstract: Environmental noise has been growing in recent years, causing numerous health problems. Highly sensitive environments such as hospitals deserve special attention, since noise can aggravate patients’ health issues and impair the performance of healthcare professionals. This work consists of a systematic review of scientific articles describing environmental noise measurements taken in hospitals between the years 2015 and 2020. The researchers started with a consultation of three databases, namely, Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect. The results indicate that for the most part, these studies are published in journals in the fields of medicine, engineering, environmental sciences, acoustics, and nursing and that most of their authors work in the fields of architecture, engineering, medicine, and nursing. These studies, which are concentrated in Europe, the Americas, and Asia, use as reference values sound levels recommended by the World Health Organization. Leq measured in hospital environments showed daytime values ranging from 37 to 88.6 dB (A) and nighttime values of 38.7 to 68.8 dB (A). Leq values for outdoor noise were 74.3 and 56.6 dB (A) for daytime and nighttime, respectively. The measurements were taken mainly inside hospitals, prioritizing more sensitive departments such as intensive care units. There is a potential for growth in work carried out in this area, but research should also include discussions about guidelines for improvement measures aimed at reducing noise in hospitals.
venue: Environmental science and pollution research international

title: Environmental noise in hospitals: a systematic review
abstract: This systematic review examines scientific literature published between 2015 and 2020 on environmental noise measurements in hospitals, focusing on studies indexed in Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect. The review identifies a predominance of research published in medical, engineering, environmental sciences, acoustics, and nursing journals, with most authors affiliated with architecture, engineering, medicine, or nursing. Geographically, studies are concentrated in Europe, the Americas, and Asia, with a notable absence of research from Africa. The majority reference World Health Organization guidelines for acceptable noise levels. Measured equivalent continuous sound levels (Leq) in hospital environments ranged from 37 to 88.6 dB(A) during the day and 38.7 to 68.8 dB(A) at night—frequently exceeding recommended limits. Measurements were primarily conducted in sensitive hospital areas such as intensive care units. The findings highlight the interdisciplinary nature of hospital noise research and underscore the need for further studies that address both measurement and effective mitigation strategies to reduce environmental noise in healthcare settings.
venue: Environmental science and pollution research international

title: Environmental Policy Attitudes: Issues, Geographical Scale, and Political Trust
abstract: This article examines environmental policy attitudes, focusing on the differences in preferences across issue type (i.e., pollution, resource preservation) and geographical scale (i.e., local, national, global). In addition, we study whether an individual's trust in government influences environmental policy attitudes. Copyright (c) 2008 by the Southwestern Social Science Association.

title: Environmental Policy Attitudes: Issues, Geographical Scale, and Political Trust
abstract: This study investigates how public attitudes toward environmental policy vary by issue type, geographical scale, and political trust. Using data from the 2007 Cooperative Congressional Election Study, we analyze support for government action across pollution and resource preservation issues at local, national, and global levels. Our findings reveal that Americans express stronger support for government intervention on pollution issues, particularly at local and national scales, than for resource preservation or global environmental challenges. Political ideology and party affiliation consistently predict environmental policy preferences, with Republicans and conservatives less supportive of increased government action regardless of their trust in government. Higher trust in government is associated with greater support for addressing pollution and global issues. These results highlight the importance of distinguishing between specific environmental issues and scales when assessing public opinion and underscore the persistent influence of political orientation on environmental policy attitudes.

title: Establishing a baseline of science communication skills in an undergraduate environmental science course
abstract: Seminal reports, based on recommendations by educators, scientists, and in collaboration with students, have called for undergraduate curricula to engage students in some of the same practices as scientists—one of which is communicating science with a general, non-scientific audience (SciComm). Unfortunately, very little research has focused on helping students develop these skills. An important early step in creating effective and efficient curricula is understanding what baseline skills students have prior to instruction. Here, we used the Essential Elements for Effective Science Communication (EEES) framework to survey the SciComm skills of students in an environmental science course in which they had little SciComm training. Results Our analyses revealed that, despite not being given the framework, students included several of the 13 elements, especially those which were explicitly asked for in the assignment instructions. Students commonly targeted broad audiences composed of interested adults, aimed to increase the knowledge and awareness of their audience, and planned and executed remote projects using print on social media. Additionally, students demonstrated flexibility in their skills by slightly differing their choices depending on the context of the assignment, such as creating more engaging content than they had planned for. Conclusions The students exhibited several key baseline skills, even though they had minimal training on the best practices of SciComm; however, more support is required to help students become better communicators, and more work in different contexts may be beneficial to acquire additional perspectives on SciComm skills among a variety of science students. The few elements that were not well highlighted in the students’ projects may not have been as intuitive to novice communicators. Thus, we provide recommendations for how educators can help their undergraduate science students develop valuable, prescribed SciComm skills. Some of these recommendations include helping students determine the right audience for their communication project, providing opportunities for students to try multiple media types, determining the type of language that is appropriate for the audience, and encouraging students to aim for a mix of communication objectives. With this guidance, educators can better prepare their students to become a more open and communicative generation of scientists and citizens.

title: Establishing a baseline of science communication skills in an undergraduate environmental science course
abstract: This study investigates the baseline science communication (SciComm) skills of undergraduate students enrolled in an environmental science course with minimal prior SciComm training. Using the Essential Elements for Effective Science Communication (EEES) framework, we analyzed student projects to assess their ability to communicate scientific concepts to non-expert audiences. Results indicate that, without explicit instruction in the framework, students incorporated several key elements of effective SciComm, particularly those emphasized in assignment guidelines. Students typically targeted broad, interested adult audiences, aimed to increase knowledge and awareness, and utilized remote communication methods such as social media. They also demonstrated adaptability by modifying their approaches based on assignment context. However, some elements of effective SciComm were less intuitive for novice communicators and were underrepresented in student work. Our findings suggest that while students possess foundational SciComm skills, additional support and targeted instruction are needed to develop more comprehensive communication abilities. We provide recommendations for educators to enhance SciComm training, including audience identification, exposure to diverse media types, appropriate language selection, and balancing communication objectives. These strategies can better prepare undergraduates to become effective science communicators and informed citizens.

title: Evolution of DOHaD: the impact of environmental health sciences.
