title: Water quality remediation faces unprecedented challenges from 'legacy phosphorus'.
abstract: Efforts to remediate water quality in agricultural landscapes are increasingly challenged by the persistent influence of 'legacy phosphorus'—phosphorus accumulated in soils, sediments, and water bodies from decades of fertilizer and manure application. Despite significant advances in conservation practices and nutrient management that have reduced phosphorus losses at the field scale, improvements in downstream water quality remain limited due to the chronic release of legacy phosphorus. This paper examines how shifts in agricultural systems have disrupted phosphorus cycling, leading to inefficient use and long-term environmental storage, and explores the complex interplay between source and transport controls that can inadvertently exacerbate legacy phosphorus accumulation. The authors highlight the need for strategies that prioritize drawing down existing phosphorus reserves and improving recycling efficiency, while acknowledging the socio-economic and policy challenges inherent in addressing legacy phosphorus at watershed to global scales. Ultimately, resolving legacy phosphorus issues requires coordinated changes in agricultural policy, market incentives, and land management to achieve sustainable water quality improvements and phosphorus security.

title: What Is Citizen Science? – A Scientometric Meta-Analysis
abstract: The concept of citizen science (CS) is currently referred to by many actors inside and outside science and research. Several descriptions of this purportedly new approach of science are often heard in connection with large datasets and the possibilities of mobilizing crowds outside science to assists with observations and classifications. However, other accounts refer to CS as a way of democratizing science, aiding concerned communities in creating data to influence policy and as a way of promoting political decision processes involving environment and health. Objective In this study we analyse two datasets (N = 1935, N = 633) retrieved from the Web of Science (WoS) with the aim of giving a scientometric description of what the concept of CS entails. We account for its development over time, and what strands of research that has adopted CS and give an assessment of what scientific output has been achieved in CS-related projects. To attain this, scientometric methods have been combined with qualitative approaches to render more precise search terms. Results Results indicate that there are three main focal points of CS. The largest is composed of research on biology, conservation and ecology, and utilizes CS mainly as a methodology of collecting and classifying data. A second strand of research has emerged through geographic information research, where citizens participate in the collection of geographic data. Thirdly, there is a line of research relating to the social sciences and epidemiology, which studies and facilitates public participation in relation to environmental issues and health. In terms of scientific output, the largest body of articles are to be found in biology and conservation research. In absolute numbers, the amount of publications generated by CS is low (N = 1935), but over the past decade a new and very productive line of CS based on digital platforms has emerged for the collection and classification of data.

title: What Is Citizen Science? – A Scientometric Meta-Analysis
abstract: This study presents a scientometric meta-analysis of the concept of citizen science (CS), examining its evolution, disciplinary adoption, and scientific output using two datasets from the Web of Science. By combining quantitative scientometric methods with qualitative analysis to refine search terms, the research identifies three primary strands of CS: biology and conservation, where CS is predominantly used for data collection and classification; geographic information research, involving citizen participation in spatial data gathering; and social sciences and epidemiology, focusing on public engagement in environmental and health issues. The analysis reveals that while the overall volume of CS-related publications remains modest, there has been significant growth in recent years, particularly driven by digital platforms facilitating large-scale data collection. The findings highlight both the diversity of interpretations and applications of CS across disciplines and the methodological challenges in mapping its full scope due to varying terminology and publication practices. This study contributes a more nuanced understanding of what constitutes citizen science and underscores the need for clearer definitions to enhance recognition and analysis of volunteer contributions in scientific research.

title: 2D materials for future heterogeneous electronics
abstract: Graphene and two-dimensional materials (2DM) remain an active field of research in science and engineering over 15 years after the first reports of 2DM. The vast amount of available data and the high performance of device demonstrators leave little doubt about the potential of 2DM for applications in electronics, photonics and sensing. So where are the integrated chips and enabled products? We try to answer this by summarizing the main challenges and opportunities that have thus far prevented 2DM applications. Graphene and related two-dimensional (2D) materials have remained an active field of research in science and engineering for over fifteen years. Here, the authors investigate why the transition from laboratories to fabrication plants appears to lag behind expectations, and summarize the main challenges and opportunities that have thus far prevented the commercialisation of these materials.

title: 2D materials for future heterogeneous electronics
abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) materials such as graphene have demonstrated exceptional electronic, photonic, and sensing properties, positioning them as promising candidates for next-generation heterogeneous electronics. Despite significant progress in device performance and a wealth of research data, the integration of 2D materials into commercial semiconductor technologies remains limited by key manufacturing challenges. These include the lack of turnkey wafer-scale processes compatible with silicon CMOS, difficulties in achieving defect-free growth and transfer, atomic precision in etching, reliable dielectric and contact interfaces, and precise doping control. Addressing these bottlenecks is critical for both “More Moore” applications—where 2D semiconductors could enable further transistor scaling and performance gains—and “More than Moore” domains such as advanced sensing and neuromorphic computing, where 2D materials’ unique properties offer new functionalities. Progress in manufacturing readiness and integration strategies will be essential to unlock the full potential of 2D materials as enablers of future heterogeneous electronic systems.

title: Active learning in materials science with emphasis on adaptive sampling using uncertainties for targeted design
abstract: One of the main challenges in materials discovery is efficiently exploring the vast search space for targeted properties as approaches that rely on trial-and-error are impractical. We review how methods from the information sciences enable us to accelerate the search and discovery of new materials. In particular, active learning allows us to effectively navigate the search space iteratively to identify promising candidates for guiding experiments and computations. The approach relies on the use of uncertainties and making predictions from a surrogate model together with a utility function that prioritizes the decision making process on unexplored data. We discuss several utility functions and demonstrate their use in materials science applications, impacting both experimental and computational research. We summarize by indicating generalizations to multiple properties and multifidelity data, and identify challenges, future directions and opportunities in the emerging field of materials informatics.

title: Active learning in materials science with emphasis on adaptive sampling using uncertainties for targeted design
abstract: This review examines the role of active learning and adaptive sampling strategies in accelerating materials discovery, with a focus on leveraging uncertainties for targeted design. Traditional trial-and-error approaches are inefficient given the vast, high-dimensional search space of possible materials. We discuss how concepts from information science, such as surrogate modeling, utility functions, and Bayesian optimization, enable systematic exploration by prioritizing experiments or calculations that maximize expected information gain. The review outlines the integration of uncertainty quantification into decision-making processes, compares various utility functions, and demonstrates their application in both experimental and computational materials research. We highlight advances in adaptive sampling for optimizing material properties, address challenges related to multi-property and multi-fidelity data, and identify future opportunities for materials informatics to transform the discovery process through optimal experimental design.

title: Advanced Materials
abstract: Materials with new or improved functionalities have always had great importance for humanity, evidenced by the fact that certain periods of time have been named after the available materials which shaped life (e.g. the Stone Age, Bronze Age, and Iron Age). Nowadays, rapid technological advances are resulting in material innovations at an even faster pace, i.e. the so-called advanced materials – a term that has been in use in the field of materials science for more than thirty years1 – which bring about new functionalities and thus new possibilities, but also uncertainties in terms of their effects on humans and the environment. Because of their novel and advanced properties, it has often been pointed out that advanced materials can provide attractive solutions to global challenges, such as the need for continuous renewable energy, clean water, and transition to a low-carbon economy.

title: Advanced Materials
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in the field of advanced materials, with a particular focus on nanostructured systems and their technological applications. Drawing on data from over 1000 literature references and updates to previous monographs, it highlights the development of correlating equations for the temperature dependence of heat capacities in liquids and reviews progress in agricultural formulation science, emphasizing the critical role of surfactants. The report also summarizes key outcomes from major international conferences, including the IUPAC Workshop on Nanostructured Advanced Materials and the International Conference on Solution Chemistry, which showcased interdisciplinary research spanning quantum structures, biological templating of nanomaterials, and solution chemistry. The paper underscores the importance of international collaboration, the integration of theoretical and experimental approaches, and the promotion of young scientists in advancing the field of advanced materials.

title: Anomalous small-angle X-ray scattering in materials science
abstract: After the exploratory studies of the 1980s, anomalous small-angle X-ray scattering (ASAXS) is now a mature technique to disentangle complex subjects in materials science: this is illustrated through selected examples.

title: Anomalous small-angle X-ray scattering in materials science
abstract: Anomalous small-angle X-ray scattering (ASAXS) has evolved into a powerful, element-specific technique for probing complex materials systems, enabled by synchrotron radiation sources and optimized beamlines. This paper presents instructive examples illustrating the unique capabilities of ASAXS in materials science, including contrast enhancement for distinguishing different nanostructures, determination of phase composition and specific volumes in multiphase materials, and coupling with complementary anomalous scattering methods. Applications discussed include the analysis of supported platinum catalyst nanoparticles in fuel cell electrodes, where ASAXS enables in situ monitoring of particle size distributions and oxidation states under electrochemical conditions, and the determination of precipitate composition in age-hardenable aluminum alloys. The results demonstrate that ASAXS provides critical information inaccessible to conventional SAXS, particularly for systems where selective sensitivity to specific elements or phases is required. The technique’s maturity is reflected in its routine use at dedicated European synchrotron beamlines, though experiments remain experimentally demanding. Overall, ASAXS offers novel opportunities for elucidating nanoscale structure and composition in advanced materials.

title: Atomistic to continuum limits for computational materials science
abstract: The present article is an overview of some mathematical results, which provide elements of rigorous basis for some multiscale computations in materials science. The emphasis is laid upon atomistic to continuum limits for crystalline materials. Various mathematical approaches are addressed. The setting is stationary. The relation to existing techniques used in the engineering literature is investigated.

title: Atomistic to continuum limits for computational materials science
abstract: This article provides a comprehensive overview of mathematical approaches that rigorously underpin multiscale computational methods in materials science, with a focus on the transition from atomistic to continuum models for crystalline solids. The authors examine the derivation of continuum limits from discrete atomistic descriptions, highlighting the challenges and open questions in establishing reliable constitutive laws and assessing their impact on numerical simulations. Various mathematical frameworks, including homogenization theory, Γ-convergence, and variational principles, are discussed as tools for analyzing these limits. The review situates these developments within the broader context of engineering practice and existing computational techniques, emphasizing the need for further mathematical and numerical analysis to enhance the reliability and efficiency of multiscale simulations. The stationary setting is considered throughout, and connections to both foundational and recent literature are made to illustrate the current state and future directions of research in this rapidly evolving field.

title: A data ecosystem to support machine learning in materials science
abstract: Facilitating the application of machine learning (ML) to materials science problems requires enhancing the data ecosystem to enable discovery and collection of data from many sources, automated dissemination of new data across the ecosystem, and the connecting of data with materials-specific ML models. Here, we present two projects, the Materials Data Facility (MDF) and the Data and Learning Hub for Science (DLHub), that address these needs. We use examples to show how MDF and DLHub capabilities can be leveraged to link data with ML models and how users can access those capabilities through web and programmatic interfaces.

title: A data ecosystem to support machine learning in materials science
abstract: The integration of machine learning into materials science is hindered by challenges in accessing, sharing, and utilizing diverse and complex datasets and tools. This paper presents a data ecosystem comprising the Materials Data Facility (MDF) and the Data and Learning Hub for Science (DLHub), designed to address these challenges by enabling seamless data discovery, automated metadata extraction, and linking of materials data with machine learning models. Through detailed examples, we demonstrate how MDF and DLHub facilitate data publication, search, and model deployment via user-friendly web and programmatic interfaces, thereby accelerating materials research and supporting the broader adoption of machine learning in the field.

title: A materials-science perspective on tackling COVID-19
abstract: The ongoing SARS-CoV-2 pandemic highlights the importance of materials science in providing tools and technologies for antiviral research and treatment development. In this Review, we discuss previous efforts in materials science in developing imaging systems and microfluidic devices for the in-depth and real-time investigation of viral structures and transmission, as well as material platforms for the detection of viruses and the delivery of antiviral drugs and vaccines. We highlight the contribution of materials science to the manufacturing of personal protective equipment and to the design of simple, accurate and low-cost virus-detection devices. We then investigate future possibilities of materials science in antiviral research and treatment development, examining the role of materials in antiviral-drug design, including the importance of synthetic material platforms for organoids and organs-on-a-chip, in drug delivery and vaccination, and for the production of medical equipment. Materials-science-based technologies not only contribute to the ongoing SARS-CoV-2 research efforts but can also provide platforms and tools for the understanding, protection, detection and treatment of future viral diseases. Materials science provides tools and technologies for the protection against viral infections, as well as for the understanding, diagnosis, treatment and prevention of viral diseases. This Review discusses present and future directions in antiviral materials-science research, with a focus on COVID-19.

title: A materials-science perspective on tackling COVID-19
abstract: This review examines the pivotal role of materials science in addressing the COVID-19 pandemic, highlighting how advances in materials have enabled breakthroughs in viral detection, protection, and treatment. The authors discuss the development of imaging and microfluidic technologies for real-time investigation of viral structure and transmission, as well as material-based platforms for rapid and accurate virus detection and targeted drug and vaccine delivery. The review details contributions to personal protective equipment design and the creation of low-cost diagnostic devices, emphasizing the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration. Looking forward, the paper explores future opportunities for materials science in antiviral research, including synthetic platforms for organoids and organs-on-a-chip, improved drug delivery systems, and scalable production of medical equipment. The authors argue that materials-science-based technologies are essential not only for combating SARS-CoV-2 but also for preparing for future viral outbreaks by enabling universal platforms for understanding, protecting against, detecting, and treating infectious diseases.

title: A Review of the Application of Machine Learning and Data Mining Approaches in Continuum Materials Mechanics
abstract: Machine learning tools represent key enablers for empowering material scientists and engineers to accelerate the development of novel materials, processes and techniques. One of the aims of using such approaches in the field of materials science is to achieve high-throughput identification and quantification of essential features along the process-structure-property-performance chain. In this contribution, machine learning and statistical learning approaches are reviewed in terms of their successful application to specific problems in the field of continuum materials mechanics. They are categorized with respect to their type of task designated to be either descriptive, predictive or prescriptive; thus to ultimately achieve identification, prediction or even optimization of essential characteristics. The respective choice of the most appropriate machine learning approach highly depends on the specific use-case, type of material, kind of data involved, spatial and temporal scales, formats, and desired knowledge gain as well as affordable computational costs. Different examples are reviewed involving case-by-case dependent application of different types of artificial neural networks and other data-driven approaches such as support vector machines, decision trees and random forests as well as Bayesian learning, and model order reduction procedures such as principal component analysis, among others. These techniques are applied to accelerate the identification of material parameters or salient features for materials characterization, to support rapid design and optimization of novel materials or manufacturing methods, to improve and correct complex measurement devices, or to better understand and predict fatigue behavior, among other examples. Besides experimentally obtained datasets, numerous studies draw required information from simulation-based data mining. Altogether, it is shown that experiment- and simulation-based data mining in combination with machine leaning tools provide exceptional opportunities to enable highly reliant identification of fundamental interrelations within materials for characterization and optimization in a scale-bridging manner. Potentials of further utilizing applied machine learning in materials science and empowering significant acceleration of knowledge output are pointed out.

title: A Review of the Application of Machine Learning and Data Mining Approaches in Continuum Materials Mechanics
abstract: This review examines the growing role of machine learning and data mining approaches in continuum materials mechanics, focusing on their ability to accelerate materials discovery, characterization, and optimization along the process-structure-property-performance chain. The paper categorizes machine learning applications into descriptive, predictive, and prescriptive tasks, highlighting their use in identifying patterns, forecasting material behavior, and optimizing processes. A range of methods—including artificial neural networks, support vector machines, decision trees, random forests, Bayesian learning, and principal component analysis—are discussed in the context of specific case studies addressing diverse materials challenges. The review emphasizes the importance of selecting appropriate algorithms based on data type, scale, and computational constraints. Both experimental and simulation-based data sources are considered, demonstrating how integrated data-driven approaches can uncover complex interrelations within materials systems. The paper concludes by outlining the significant potential for further leveraging machine learning to enhance knowledge discovery and accelerate innovation in materials mechanics.

title: Benchmarking the performance of Bayesian optimization across multiple experimental materials science domains
abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) has been leveraged for guiding autonomous and high-throughput experiments in materials science. However, few have evaluated the efficiency of BO across a broad range of experimental materials domains. In this work, we quantify the performance of BO with a collection of surrogate model and acquisition function pairs across five diverse experimental materials systems. By defining acceleration and enhancement metrics for materials optimization objectives, we find that surrogate models such as Gaussian Process (GP) with anisotropic kernels and Random Forest (RF) have comparable performance in BO, and both outperform the commonly used GP with isotropic kernels. GP with anisotropic kernels has demonstrated the most robustness, yet RF is a close alternative and warrants more consideration because it is free from distribution assumptions, has smaller time complexity, and requires less effort in initial hyperparameter selection. We also raise awareness about the benefits of using GP with anisotropic kernels in future materials optimization campaigns.

title: Benchmarking the performance of Bayesian optimization across multiple experimental materials science domains
abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is increasingly used to accelerate experimental materials discovery, yet its comparative performance across diverse real-world materials domains remains underexplored. Here, we systematically benchmark BO using various surrogate model and acquisition function combinations on five experimental datasets spanning carbon nanotube-polymer blends, silver nanoparticles, lead-halide perovskites, and additively manufactured polymer structures. Employing pool-based active learning and quantitative metrics such as enhancement and acceleration factors, we find that BO with Gaussian Process (GP) models featuring anisotropic kernels and Random Forest (RF) surrogates consistently outperform the commonly used isotropic GP models. While GP with anisotropic kernels demonstrates the greatest robustness, RF offers comparable performance with advantages in computational efficiency and reduced hyperparameter tuning effort. Our results provide practical guidelines for surrogate model selection in autonomous materials optimization campaigns and are supported by open-source benchmarking code and datasets to facilitate future algorithm development in the field.

title: Composite Materials Science And Engineering
abstract: This comprehensive text provides an integrated and up-to-date exploration of composite materials, emphasizing the critical relationship between structure and properties at both micro- and macro-scales. Covering fundamental aspects of fabrication, properties, and mechanics, the book addresses the roles of various reinforcement and matrix materials, interfaces, and the resulting behavior of composites. Recent advances such as nanocomposites, biocomposites, self-healing systems, fiber/metal laminates, and high-temperature superconducting composites are discussed alongside traditional polymer, metal, and ceramic matrix composites. The work highlights significant industrial applications—particularly in aerospace—and incorporates new solved examples, problems, and a dedicated chapter on nonconventional composites. Designed as both a reference for researchers and a textbook for advanced students, this edition reflects the multidisciplinary nature of composite materials science and engineering while providing extensive resources for further study.

title: Coupled Cluster Theory in Materials Science
abstract: In this tutorial-style review we discuss basic concepts of coupled cluster theory and recent developments that increase its computational efficiency for calculations of molecules, solids and materials in general. We will touch upon the connection between coupled cluster theory and the random-phase approximation that is widely used in the field of solid-state physics. We will discuss various approaches to improve the computational performance without compromising on accuracy. These approaches include large-scale parallel design as well as techniques that reduce the pre-factor of the computational complexity. A central part of this article discusses the convergence of calculated properties to the thermodynamic limit, which is of significant importance for reliable predictions of materials properties and constitutes an additional challenge compared to calculations of large molecules. We mention technical aspects of computer code implementations of periodic coupled cluster theories in different numerical frameworks of the one-electron orbital basis; the projector-augmented-wave formalism using a plane wave basis set and the numeric atom-centered-orbital (NAO) with resolution-of-identity. We will discuss results and the possible scope of these implementations and how they can help advance the current state of the art in electronic structure theory calculations of materials.

title: Coupled Cluster Theory in Materials Science
abstract: Coupled cluster (CC) theory, a quantum chemical wavefunction-based approach, offers a systematically improvable and highly accurate alternative to density functional theory (DFT) for electronic structure calculations in materials science. While DFT remains the standard due to its balance of accuracy and computational efficiency, its limitations in treating strong correlation and non-local interactions motivate the exploration of CC methods. This review introduces the fundamental concepts of CC theory, recent algorithmic advances that enhance its computational feasibility for molecules and periodic solids, and its connection to the random-phase approximation. We discuss strategies for improving computational performance, including parallelization and reduced scaling techniques, as well as challenges related to achieving convergence to the thermodynamic limit. The implementation of periodic CC methods in different numerical frameworks, such as plane-wave projector-augmented-wave and numeric atom-centered orbital bases, is examined alongside their respective advantages. Applications of CC theory to cohesive energies, phase diagrams, defect formation, surface reactions, and excited-state properties demonstrate its potential for benchmark-quality predictions in materials simulations. The review highlights how ongoing developments are expanding the practical scope of CC theory, enabling more reliable and user-friendly high-accuracy electronic structure calculations for complex materials systems.

title: Deep materials informatics: Applications of deep learning in materials science
abstract: The growing application of data-driven analytics in materials science has led to the rise of materials informatics. Within the arena of data analytics, deep learning has emerged as a game-changing technique in the last few years, enabling numerous real-world applications, such as self-driving cars. In this paper, the authors present an overview of deep learning, its advantages, challenges, and recent applications on different types of materials data. The increasingly availability of materials databases and big data in general, along with groundbreaking advances in deep learning offers a lot of promise to accelerate the discovery, design, and deployment of next-generation materials.

title: Deep materials informatics: Applications of deep learning in materials science
abstract: The rapid expansion of data-driven approaches in materials science has given rise to materials informatics, with deep learning emerging as a transformative tool for extracting knowledge from complex, high-volume materials data. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of deep learning fundamentals, highlighting its advantages—such as automated feature extraction, improved accuracy with large datasets, and fast predictions—as well as challenges including data and computational requirements, network architecture selection, and model interpretability. Recent advances in deep materials informatics are discussed through illustrative applications such as property prediction from composition, crystal structure determination, multiscale modeling in composites, microstructure characterization and reconstruction, and materials design. The increasing availability of large-scale materials datasets, coupled with ongoing developments in deep learning methodologies, holds significant promise for accelerating the discovery, design, and deployment of next-generation materials. The paper concludes with a perspective on the future impact of deep learning in advancing materials science.

title: Digital Transformation in Materials Science: A Paradigm Change in Material's Development
abstract: The ongoing digitalization is rapidly changing and will further revolutionize all parts of life. This statement is currently omnipresent in the media as well as in the scientific community; however, the exact consequences of the proceeding digitalization for the field of materials science in general and the way research will be performed in the future are still unclear. There are first promising examples featuring the potential to change discovery and development approaches toward new materials. Nevertheless, a wide range of open questions have to be solved in order to enable the so‐called digital‐supported material research. The current state‐of‐the‐art, the present and future challenges, as well as the resulting perspectives for materials science are described.

title: Digital Transformation in Materials Science: A Paradigm Change in Material's Development
abstract: Digital transformation is fundamentally reshaping materials science by integrating automation, artificial intelligence, and data-driven methodologies throughout the material development process. This review examines current advancements in the digitalization of materials research, emphasizing the automation of synthesis, characterization, and data analysis across diverse material classes. Key technologies such as robotic synthesis, flow chemistry, and high-throughput characterization are highlighted for their ability to increase experimental efficiency, reproducibility, and data quality while reducing human bias. The paper discusses the challenges of adapting automated systems to accommodate varied reaction conditions and material types, as well as the need for standardized data management and interoperability among analytical tools. The authors outline future perspectives for a fully digitalized materials research ecosystem, where integrated workflows enable accelerated discovery and optimization of new materials. Ultimately, this paradigm shift promises to transform traditional research approaches, fostering innovation and collaboration in the field of materials science.

title: Machine learning and artificial neural network accelerated computational discoveries in materials science
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been referred to as the “fourth paradigm of science,” and as part of a coherent toolbox of data‐driven approaches, machine learning (ML) dramatically accelerates the computational discoveries. As the machinery for ML algorithms matures, significant advances have been made not only by the mainstream AI researchers, but also those work in computational materials science. The number of ML and artificial neural network (ANN) applications in the computational materials science is growing at an astounding rate. This perspective briefly reviews the state‐of‐the‐art progress in some supervised and unsupervised methods with their respective applications. The characteristics of primary ML and ANN algorithms are first described. Then, the most critical applications of AI in computational materials science such as empirical interatomic potential development, ML‐based potential, property predictions, and molecular discoveries using generative adversarial networks (GAN) are comprehensively reviewed. The central ideas underlying these ML applications are discussed, and future directions for integrating ML with computational materials science are given. Finally, a discussion on the applicability and limitations of current ML techniques and the remaining challenges are summarized.

title: Machine learning and artificial neural network accelerated computational discoveries in materials science
abstract: Artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning (ML) and artificial neural networks (ANN), is rapidly transforming computational materials science by enabling accelerated discoveries and predictive modeling. This paper reviews recent advances in the application of supervised and unsupervised ML methods within the field, highlighting their roles in empirical interatomic potential development, ML-based potentials for molecular dynamics simulations, and direct property prediction from data. The characteristics and workflows of primary ML and ANN algorithms are outlined, with special attention given to generative adversarial networks (GANs) for molecular discovery. Key challenges related to model selection, data representation, generalization, and overfitting are discussed, alongside the limitations of current techniques. The review concludes with perspectives on future integration of ML approaches in computational materials science, emphasizing the need for continued methodological innovation and interdisciplinary collaboration to address outstanding challenges and fully realize the potential of AI-driven materials discovery.

title: Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials as Emerging Tools for Materials Science
abstract: Atomic‐scale modeling and understanding of materials have made remarkable progress, but they are still fundamentally limited by the large computational cost of explicit electronic‐structure methods such as density‐functional theory. This Progress Report shows how machine learning (ML) is currently enabling a new degree of realism in materials modeling: by “learning” electronic‐structure data, ML‐based interatomic potentials give access to atomistic simulations that reach similar accuracy levels but are orders of magnitude faster. A brief introduction to the new tools is given, and then, applications to some select problems in materials science are highlighted: phase‐change materials for memory devices; nanoparticle catalysts; and carbon‐based electrodes for chemical sensing, supercapacitors, and batteries. It is hoped that the present work will inspire the development and wider use of ML‐based interatomic potentials in diverse areas of materials research.

title: Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials as Emerging Tools for Materials Science
abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are rapidly transforming atomistic modeling in materials science by bridging the gap between the accuracy of quantum-mechanical methods and the efficiency of classical force fields. This progress report reviews the principles underpinning MLIPs, including the construction of reference databases, atomic structure representations, and regression techniques for learning potential energy surfaces from electronic-structure data. The report highlights recent advances and key applications of MLIPs in simulating complex materials systems, such as phase-change materials for memory devices, nanoparticle catalysts, and carbon-based electrodes for energy storage and sensing. By enabling large-scale molecular dynamics simulations with near first-principles accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost, MLIPs are poised to become indispensable tools for exploring structure-property relationships and guiding materials discovery. The report also discusses current challenges and future directions, emphasizing the need for robust datasets, transferable models, and integration with existing computational frameworks. Overall, MLIPs represent a significant step forward in predictive materials modeling, with broad implications for both fundamental research and technological innovation.

title: Materials Cloud, a platform for open computational science
abstract: Materials Cloud is a platform designed to enable open and seamless sharing of resources for computational science, driven by applications in materials modelling. It hosts (1) archival and dissemination services for raw and curated data, together with their provenance graph, (2) modelling services and virtual machines, (3) tools for data analytics, and pre-/post-processing, and (4) educational materials. Data is citable and archived persistently, providing a comprehensive embodiment of entire simulation pipelines (calculations performed, codes used, data generated) in the form of graphs that allow retracing and reproducing any computed result. When an AiiDA database is shared on Materials Cloud, peers can browse the interconnected record of simulations, download individual files or the full database, and start their research from the results of the original authors. The infrastructure is agnostic to the specific simulation codes used and can support diverse applications in computational science that transcend its initial materials domain.

title: Materials Cloud, a platform for open computational science
abstract: Materials Cloud is an open-science platform designed to advance reproducibility, transparency, and collaboration in computational materials science. Integrating archival services, simulation tools, data analytics, and educational resources, Materials Cloud supports the full research lifecycle and enables FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable) data sharing. The platform’s modular structure—comprising LEARN, WORK, DISCOVER, EXPLORE, and ARCHIVE sections—facilitates seamless access to curated datasets, interactive provenance graphs, and persistent data storage with globally unique identifiers. By supporting diverse simulation codes and workflows through open-source frameworks such as AiiDA, Materials Cloud empowers researchers to publish, browse, and reuse computational results with minimal technical barriers. The ARCHIVE ensures long-term preservation and accessibility of research data in compliance with major funding agencies’ requirements. Materials Cloud thus provides a comprehensive infrastructure that fosters open computational science and accelerates discovery across materials research and related domains.

title: Materials science aspects of zinc–air batteries: a review
abstract: Metal–air batteries are becoming of particular interest, from both fundamental and industrial viewpoints, for their high specific energy density compared to other energy storage devices, in particular the Li-ion systems. Among metal–air batteries, the zinc–air option represents a safe, environmentally friendly and potentially cheap and simple way to store and deliver electrical energy for both portable and stationary devices as well as for electric vehicles. Zinc–air batteries can be classified into primary (including also the mechanically rechargeable), electrically rechargeable (secondary), and fuel cells. Research on primary zinc–air batteries is well consolidated since many years. On the contrary, research on the electrically rechargeable ones still requires further efforts to overcome materials science and electrochemical issues related to charge and discharge processes. In addition, zinc–air fuel cells are also of great potential interest for smart grid energy storage and production. This review aims to report on the latest progresses and state-of-the-art of primary, secondary and mechanically rechargeable zinc–air batteries, and zinc–air fuel cells. In particular, this review focuses on the critical aspects of materials science, engineering, electrochemistry and mathematical modeling related to all zinc–air systems.
venue: Materials for Renewable and Sustainable Energy

title: Materials science aspects of zinc–air batteries: a review
abstract: Zinc–air batteries are emerging as promising candidates for next-generation energy storage due to their high specific energy density, safety, environmental compatibility, and cost-effectiveness compared to conventional systems such as lithium-ion batteries. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of the materials science aspects underpinning zinc–air battery technologies, including primary, secondary (electrically rechargeable), mechanically rechargeable batteries, and zinc–air fuel cells. The paper discusses the critical roles of anode, cathode, and electrolyte materials in determining battery performance and longevity, highlighting the well-established nature of primary zinc–air batteries and the ongoing challenges faced by secondary systems, such as zinc dendrite formation, air cathode degradation, and electrolyte carbonation. Advances in catalyst development, electrode engineering, and understanding of electrochemical processes are examined alongside recent progress in mathematical modeling. The review also contextualizes zinc–air batteries within the broader landscape of energy storage solutions for portable electronics, electric vehicles, and grid applications, emphasizing their potential to support renewable energy integration. Key obstacles to widespread adoption are identified, with a focus on materials-related limitations that must be addressed to realize efficient, durable, and scalable zinc–air energy storage devices.
venue: Materials for Renewable and Sustainable Energy

title: MatSciBERT: A materials domain language model for text mining and information extraction
abstract: A large amount of materials science knowledge is generated and stored as text published in peer-reviewed scientific literature. While recent developments in natural language processing, such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) models, provide promising information extraction tools, these models may yield suboptimal results when applied on materials domain since they are not trained in materials science specific notations and jargons. Here, we present a materials-aware language model, namely, MatSciBERT, trained on a large corpus of peer-reviewed materials science publications. We show that MatSciBERT outperforms SciBERT, a language model trained on science corpus, and establish state-of-the-art results on three downstream tasks, named entity recognition, relation classification, and abstract classification. We make the pre-trained weights of MatSciBERT publicly accessible for accelerated materials discovery and information extraction from materials science texts.

title: MatSciBERT: A materials domain language model for text mining and information extraction
abstract: We present MatSciBERT, a domain-specific language model designed for materials science text mining and information extraction. Trained on a curated corpus of approximately 150,000 peer-reviewed materials science publications spanning diverse subfields, MatSciBERT leverages domain-adaptive pre-training to capture the unique terminology and context of materials literature. We evaluate MatSciBERT on three key downstream tasks—named entity recognition, relation classification, and abstract classification—demonstrating significant performance improvements over SciBERT and establishing new state-of-the-art results in the domain. By making the pre-trained model and associated resources publicly available, our work addresses the lack of specialized language models for materials science and enables automated knowledge extraction to accelerate research and discovery in the field.

title: Named Entity Recognition and Normalization Applied to Large-Scale Information Extraction from the Materials Science Literature
abstract: The number of published materials science articles has increased manyfold over the past few decades. Now, a major bottleneck in the materials discovery pipeline arises in connecting new results with the previously established literature. A potential solution to this problem is to map the unstructured raw-text of published articles onto structured database entries that allows for programmatic querying. To this end, we apply text-mining with named entity recognition (NER) for large-scale information extraction from the published materials science literature. The NER model is trained to extract summary-level information from materials science documents, including: inorganic material mentions, sample descriptors, phase labels, material properties and applications, as well as any synthesis and characterization methods used. Our classifier achieves an accuracy (f1) of 87%, and is applied to information extraction from 3.27 million materials science abstracts. We extract more than 80 million materials-science-related named entities, and the content of each abstract is represented as a database entry in a structured format. We demonstrate that simple database queries can be used to answer complex ``meta-questions' of the published literature that would have previously required laborious, manual literature searches to answer. All of our data and functionality has been made freely available (https://github.com/materialsintelligence/matscholar), and we expect these results to accelerate the pace of future materials science discovery.
venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling

title: Named Entity Recognition and Normalization Applied to Large-Scale Information Extraction from the Materials Science Literature
abstract: The exponential growth of materials science literature has created significant challenges in efficiently accessing and connecting new research with existing knowledge. This study presents a large-scale information extraction framework that applies supervised machine learning-based named entity recognition (NER) and entity normalization to over 3.27 million materials science abstracts. Using a recurrent neural network architecture, the NER model achieves an F1 score of 87%, extracting key summary-level entities such as inorganic material mentions, sample descriptors, phase labels, material properties, applications, and synthesis or characterization methods. Entity normalization, with an F1 score of 95%, enables the consolidation of synonymous terms, greatly enhancing recall in document retrieval compared to traditional keyword searches. The resulting structured database comprises more than 80 million materials-science-related entities and supports complex queries that previously required extensive manual effort. All data, models, and tools are made publicly available through bulk downloads, an API, and a web interface, providing unprecedented access to targeted information and accelerating materials discovery by enabling rapid, programmatic exploration of the literature.
venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling

title: Nanofluidics: A New Arena for Materials Science
abstract: A significant growth of research in nanofluidics is achieved over the past decade, but the field is still facing considerable challenges toward the transition from the current physics‐centered stage to the next application‐oriented stage. Many of these challenges are associated with materials science, so the field of nanofluidics offers great opportunities for materials scientists to exploit. In addition, the use of unusual effects and ultrasmall confined spaces of well‐defined nanofluidic environments would offer new mechanisms and technologies to manipulate nanoscale objects as well as to synthesize novel nanomaterials in the liquid phase. Therefore, nanofluidics will be a new arena for materials science. In the past few years, burgeoning progress has been made toward this trend, as overviewed in this article, including materials and methods for fabricating nanofluidic devices, nanofluidics with functionalized surfaces and functional material components, as well as nanofluidics for manipulating nanoscale materials and fabricating new nanomaterials. Many critical challenges as well as fantastic opportunities in this arena lie ahead. Some of those, which are of particular interest, are also discussed.

title: Nanofluidics: A New Arena for Materials Science
abstract: Nanofluidics, the study of fluid behavior in nanoscale environments, has rapidly advanced in the past decade, revealing unique physical phenomena and offering new opportunities for materials science. This progress report highlights how nanofluidic systems—characterized by ultra-high surface-to-volume ratios and confined geometries—enable novel mechanisms for manipulating and synthesizing nanoscale materials. The article reviews recent developments in five key areas: fabrication methods for nanofluidic devices, integration of functionalized surfaces and material components, manipulation of biological and nanoscale objects, and the synthesis of new nanomaterials within nanofluidic environments. While significant challenges remain, particularly in device fabrication, measurement, and functional integration, these hurdles also present exciting opportunities for materials scientists to drive the field toward application-oriented research. The convergence of nanofluidics and materials science promises to unlock unprecedented control over matter at the nanoscale, paving the way for innovative technologies and multidisciplinary applications.

title: Neural Networks in Materials Science
abstract: There are difficult problems in materials science where the general concepts might be understood but which are not as yet amenable to scientific treatment. We are at the same time told that good engineering has the responsibility to reach objectives in a cost and time-effective way. Any model which deals with only a small part of the required technology is therefore unlikely to be treated with respect. Neural network analysis is a form of regression or classification modelling which can help resolve these difficulties whilst striving for longer term solutions. This paper begins with an introduction to neural networks and contains a review of some applications of the technique in the context of materials science.

title: Neural Networks in Materials Science
abstract: This paper reviews the application of neural networks in materials science, focusing on their ability to address complex problems where traditional physical models are insufficient or unavailable. After introducing the fundamental concepts of neural networks and contrasting them with linear regression and physical modeling approaches, the review highlights how neural networks can capture highly non-linear relationships among numerous variables that influence material properties. The discussion includes the advantages of neural networks in modeling mechanical properties such as yield strength, toughness, fatigue life, and creep resistance, which depend on intricate interactions between compositional and processing parameters. The paper also addresses challenges such as overfitting and model validation, emphasizing the importance of balancing model complexity with predictive accuracy. Through illustrative examples, it is demonstrated that neural networks provide a flexible and powerful empirical modeling tool for quantitative prediction and analysis in materials science, particularly when conventional theoretical frameworks are inadequate.

title: New frontiers for the materials genome initiative
abstract: The Materials Genome Initiative (MGI) advanced a new paradigm for materials discovery and design, namely that the pace of new materials deployment could be accelerated through complementary efforts in theory, computation, and experiment. Along with numerous successes, new challenges are inviting researchers to refocus the efforts and approaches that were originally inspired by the MGI. In May 2017, the National Science Foundation sponsored the workshop “Advancing and Accelerating Materials Innovation Through the Synergistic Interaction among Computation, Experiment, and Theory: Opening New Frontiers” to review accomplishments that emerged from investments in science and infrastructure under the MGI, identify scientific opportunities in this new environment, examine how to effectively utilize new materials innovation infrastructure, and discuss challenges in achieving accelerated materials research through the seamless integration of experiment, computation, and theory. This article summarizes key findings from the workshop and provides perspectives that aim to guide the direction of future materials research and its translation into societal impacts.

title: New frontiers for the materials genome initiative
abstract: The Materials Genome Initiative (MGI) has transformed materials discovery by integrating theory, computation, and experiment to accelerate the development and deployment of new materials. This review summarizes insights from a 2017 National Science Foundation workshop that assessed MGI’s achievements and identified emerging challenges and opportunities. Key advances enabled by MGI include high-throughput screening, data-driven modeling, and collaborative infrastructure that have led to breakthroughs in areas such as polymeric self-assembly, polar metals, and organic light-emitting diodes. The workshop highlighted six priority domains—health and consumer applications, information technologies, new functional materials, efficient separation processes, energy and catalysis, and multicomponent materials with additive manufacturing—as critical for future progress. The article discusses technical successes, infrastructural needs, and cultural shifts required to fully realize MGI’s vision, emphasizing the importance of open data sharing, interdisciplinary collaboration, and new incentive structures. By outlining unifying themes and aspirational perspectives, this review charts a course for advancing the MGI paradigm to address societal needs through accelerated materials innovation.

title: On the application of x-ray microtomography in the field of materials science
abstract: The principle of the tomography technique and the different possible set-ups, which can be used to obtain medium-(10 lm) and high(1 lm) resolution, three-dimensional, non-destructive images, are shown in this paper. Illustrations are made of the applications of the technique in the field of materials science. Examples are given for medium-resolution images of metallic foams and model metal matrix composites that are reinforced with spherical particles. High-resolution examples are shown for aluminium alloys. For low-absorbent materials we show that the phase contrast obtained using synchrotron radiation can provide a valuable solution. The quantitative use of these images, coupled with in-situ tensile tests or used for the simple analysis of the initial microstructure of several structural materials, is also described.

title: On the application of x-ray microtomography in the field of materials science
abstract: This paper presents the principles and applications of x-ray microtomography in materials science, highlighting its ability to provide non-destructive, three-dimensional imaging at both medium (10 μm) and high (1 μm) resolutions. The technique is demonstrated through examples involving metallic foams, model metal matrix composites reinforced with spherical particles, and high-resolution studies of aluminum alloys. For low-absorbent materials, the use of phase contrast with synchrotron radiation is shown to enhance image quality. The study also discusses the quantitative analysis enabled by microtomography, including its integration with in-situ tensile testing and its use in characterizing the initial microstructure of various structural materials. Overall, x-ray microtomography is established as a powerful tool for investigating the internal structure and properties of materials in a non-destructive manner.

title: Opportunities and Challenges for Machine Learning in Materials Science
abstract: Advances in machine learning have impacted myriad areas of materials science, such as the discovery of novel materials and the improvement of molecular simulations, with likely many more important developments to come. Given the rapid changes in this field, it is challenging to understand both the breadth of opportunities and the best practices for their use. In this review, we address aspects of both problems by providing an overview of the areas in which machine learning has recently had significant impact in materials science, and then we provide a more detailed discussion on determining the accuracy and domain of applicability of some common types of machine learning models. Finally, we discuss some opportunities and challenges for the materials community to fully utilize the capabilities of machine learning.

title: Opportunities and Challenges for Machine Learning in Materials Science
abstract: Machine learning (ML) is rapidly transforming materials science by enabling accelerated materials discovery, improved property prediction, and enhanced design capabilities. This review surveys recent advances in the integration of ML within materials science and engineering (MS&E), highlighting key application areas such as materials informatics, molecular simulations, and the development of new computational tools. The paper discusses both supervised and unsupervised learning approaches, emphasizing their respective roles in handling complex datasets and extracting meaningful patterns without explicit programming. It also addresses best practices for model development, including assessment of model accuracy, applicability domains, and error estimation. The review identifies significant opportunities arising from increased computational power, data availability, and open-source software, while also outlining persistent challenges such as data quality, model interpretability, and the need for robust benchmarking. By providing practical guidance and curated resources for researchers at all levels, this work aims to support the effective adoption of ML in MS&E and foster continued innovation in the field.

title: Random-phase approximation and its applications in computational chemistry and materials science
abstract: The random-phase approximation (RPA) as an approach for computing the electronic correlation energy is reviewed. After a brief account of its basic concept and historical development, the paper is devoted to the theoretical formulations of RPA, and its applications to realistic systems. With several illustrating applications, we discuss the implications of RPA for computational chemistry and materials science. The computational cost of RPA is also addressed which is critical for its widespread use in future applications. In addition, current correction schemes going beyond RPA and directions of further development will be discussed.

title: Random-phase approximation and its applications in computational chemistry and materials science
abstract: The random-phase approximation (RPA) is a foundational method for calculating electronic correlation energies in many-body systems, with significant relevance for computational chemistry and materials science. This paper reviews the historical development, theoretical foundations, and practical implementations of RPA, highlighting its ability to treat exchange-correlation effects with improved accuracy over traditional density functional approximations. RPA’s non-local correlation energy captures long-range van der Waals interactions and dynamic electronic screening, making it applicable to a broad range of systems including metals and small-gap materials. The review discusses illustrative applications that demonstrate RPA’s strengths and current limitations, particularly regarding computational cost, which remains a barrier to widespread adoption. Recent advances in correction schemes beyond RPA, such as renormalized second-order perturbation theory, are also examined as promising directions for further methodological development. Overall, the paper underscores RPA’s growing importance and future prospects in first-principles electronic structure calculations for complex materials and molecular systems.

title: Recent advances and applications of machine learning in solid-state materials science
abstract: One of the most exciting tools that have entered the material science toolbox in recent years is machine learning. This collection of statistical methods has already proved to be capable of considerably speeding up both fundamental and applied research. At present, we are witnessing an explosion of works that develop and apply machine learning to solid-state systems. We provide a comprehensive overview and analysis of the most recent research in this topic. As a starting point, we introduce machine learning principles, algorithms, descriptors, and databases in materials science. We continue with the description of different machine learning approaches for the discovery of stable materials and the prediction of their crystal structure. Then we discuss research in numerous quantitative structure–property relationships and various approaches for the replacement of first-principle methods by machine learning. We review how active learning and surrogate-based optimization can be applied to improve the rational design process and related examples of applications. Two major questions are always the interpretability of and the physical understanding gained from machine learning models. We consider therefore the different facets of interpretability and their importance in materials science. Finally, we propose solutions and future research paths for various challenges in computational materials science.

title: Recent advances and applications of machine learning in solid-state materials science
abstract: This review provides a comprehensive analysis of recent advances and applications of machine learning in solid-state materials science. The authors introduce fundamental machine learning concepts, algorithms, descriptors, and relevant databases, establishing the groundwork for understanding their integration into materials research. The review highlights how machine learning accelerates the discovery of stable materials, predicts crystal structures, and enables quantitative structure–property relationships, often serving as a surrogate for first-principles methods. It discusses the role of active learning and surrogate-based optimization in rational materials design, emphasizing improvements in efficiency and effectiveness. The article also addresses critical issues of interpretability and physical insight derived from machine learning models, underscoring their importance for scientific understanding. Finally, the authors outline current challenges and propose future research directions to overcome limitations in computational materials science, positioning machine learning as a transformative tool for the field.

title: Small data machine learning in materials science
abstract: This review discussed the dilemma of small data faced by materials machine learning. First, we analyzed the limitations brought by small data. Then, the workflow of materials machine learning has been introduced. Next, the methods of dealing with small data were introduced, including data extraction from publications, materials database construction, high-throughput computations and experiments from the data source level; modeling algorithms for small data and imbalanced learning from the algorithm level; active learning and transfer learning from the machine learning strategy level. Finally, the future directions for small data machine learning in materials science were proposed.

title: Small data machine learning in materials science
abstract: This review addresses the challenges and opportunities of applying machine learning to materials science in the context of limited data availability, commonly referred to as the small data problem. The article first analyzes the limitations imposed by small datasets on model performance and reliability. It then outlines the typical workflow for machine learning in materials research, including data collection, feature engineering, model selection, and evaluation. Strategies to mitigate small data issues are discussed at three levels: data source (data extraction from literature, database construction, high-throughput computation and experiments), algorithmic (modeling techniques tailored for small and imbalanced datasets), and machine learning strategy (active learning and transfer learning). The review highlights recent advances in each area and proposes future directions for overcoming small data constraints, emphasizing the need for innovative approaches that maximize information extraction from limited samples to accelerate materials discovery and design.

title: Structural Design Elements in Biological Materials: Application to Bioinspiration
abstract: Eight structural elements in biological materials are identified as the most common amongst a variety of animal taxa. These are proposed as a new paradigm in the field of biological materials science as they can serve as a toolbox for rationalizing the complex mechanical behavior of structural biological materials and for systematizing the development of bioinspired designs for structural applications. They are employed to improve the mechanical properties, namely strength, wear resistance, stiffness, flexibility, fracture toughness, and energy absorption of different biological materials for a variety of functions (e.g., body support, joint movement, impact protection, weight reduction). The structural elements identified are: fibrous, helical, gradient, layered, tubular, cellular, suture, and overlapping. For each of the structural design elements, critical design parameters are presented along with constitutive equations with a focus on mechanical properties. Additionally, example organisms from varying biological classes are presented for each case to display the wide variety of environments where each of these elements is present. Examples of current bioinspired materials are also introduced for each element.

title: Structural Design Elements in Biological Materials: Application to Bioinspiration
abstract: Biological materials exhibit a limited set of recurring structural motifs that have evolved to address diverse functional demands using a constrained palette of biopolymers and biominerals. This review identifies and systematizes eight common structural design elements—fibrous, helical, gradient, layered, tubular, cellular, suture, and overlapping structures—found across a wide range of animal taxa. Each element is analyzed in terms of its hierarchical organization, critical design parameters, and constitutive mechanical equations, with examples drawn from various organisms to illustrate their widespread occurrence and multifunctionality. These elements collectively enhance properties such as strength, stiffness, flexibility, fracture toughness, wear resistance, and energy absorption to fulfill roles including support, protection, mobility, and weight reduction. The unified framework presented here provides a foundational toolbox for understanding the structure–function relationships in biological materials and guides the rational design of bioinspired materials by leveraging these natural strategies for advanced structural applications.

title: Symbolic regression in materials science
abstract: The authors showcase the potential of symbolic regression as an analytic method for use in materials research. First, the authors briefly describe the current state-of-the-art method, genetic programming-based symbolic regression (GPSR), and recent advances in symbolic regression techniques. Next, the authors discuss industrial applications of symbolic regression and its potential applications in materials science. The authors then present two GPSR use-cases: formulating a transformation kinetics law and showing the learning scheme discovers the well-known Johnson–Mehl–Avrami–Kolmogorov form, and learning the Landau free energy functional form for the displacive tilt transition in perovskite LaNiO_3. Finally, the authors propose that symbolic regression techniques should be considered by materials scientists as an alternative to other machine learning-based regression models for learning from data.

title: Symbolic regression in materials science
abstract: Symbolic regression offers a promising alternative to traditional machine learning approaches for discovering governing relationships in materials science, particularly in the era of big data enabled by advanced experimental and computational techniques. This perspective introduces genetic programming-based symbolic regression (GPSR) and recent methodological advances, highlighting its ability to autonomously identify both the functional form and parameters of models directly from data without prior assumptions. We discuss the limited but growing adoption of symbolic regression in materials science compared to other domains, and illustrate its utility through two case studies: learning the Johnson-Mehl-Avrami-Kolmogorov kinetics law for phase transformations and deriving the Landau free energy functional for structural transitions in perovskite LaNiO₃. The results demonstrate that GPSR can recover established physical laws and provide interpretable models, underscoring its potential as a tool for elucidating complex structure-property relationships. We advocate for broader adoption of symbolic regression techniques in materials research as a means to accelerate scientific discovery and advance the automation of knowledge extraction from large-scale materials datasets.

title: Theory-Guided Machine Learning in Materials Science
abstract: Materials scientists are increasingly adopting the use of machine learning tools to discover hidden trends in data and make predictions. Applying concepts from data science without foreknowledge of their limitations and the unique qualities of materials data, however, could lead to errant conclusions. The differences that exist between various kinds of experimental and calculated data require careful choices of data processing and machine learning methods. Here, we outline potential pitfalls involved in using machine learning without robust protocols. We address some problems of overfitting to training data using decision trees as an example, rational descriptor selection in the field of perovskites, and preserving physical interpretability in the application of dimensionality reducing techniques such as principal component analysis. We show how proceeding without the guidance of domain knowledge can lead to both quantitatively and qualitatively incorrect predictive models.

title: Theory-Guided Machine Learning in Materials Science
abstract: The integration of machine learning into materials science offers significant potential for accelerating discovery and understanding of material properties, yet the unique characteristics of materials data necessitate careful methodological choices. This paper examines the challenges and best practices in applying machine learning to materials informatics, emphasizing the importance of theory-guided approaches. We discuss common pitfalls such as overfitting, particularly in data-scarce environments, and highlight the need for robust validation strategies like cross-validation and Bayesian error estimation. The issue of underrepresented classes in classification tasks is addressed, with recommendations for balancing datasets and penalizing misclassification of minority classes. Using decision trees as a case study, we demonstrate how algorithmic choices and feature selection can yield qualitatively different models, underscoring the necessity of incorporating domain knowledge to ensure physical interpretability and meaningful predictions. The paper advocates for rational descriptor selection and simple, interpretable models, providing a workflow that integrates theoretical understanding with data-driven techniques to enhance reliability and insight in materials research.

title: The Development of Local Wisdom-Based Natural Science Module to Improve Science Literation of Students
abstract: The vulnerability of communities in facing volcano disaster is one of the indicators of the low literacy of science. The low knowledge about volcanic material causes it needs to be packed in an attractive learning so that it can tap into the ability of students' science literacy by using teaching materials that are closer to student learning environments. This research aims to develop the local wisdom-based natural science module on the theme of Mount Kelud eruption, which is both theoretical and empirical. The type of this research development is Research and Development (R & D) by adapting the ASSURE instructional design. The results of this research are the validation results of theoretical feasibility of teaching materials based on the components of material feasibility of 87, 5% with very good category, components of presentation feasibility of 91, 7% with very good category, components of language feasibility of 88, 9% with very good category, components of local wisdom values of 87, 5% with very good category, and components of science literacy feasibility of 88, 9% with 88, 9% with very good category. The results of empirical feasibility are the test results of students' science literacy with N-gain variation value of 0,2; 0,3; and 0,4 respectively with low, medium, and medium category. The results show that the developed local wisdom-based natural science module is suitable to improve the ability of students' science literacy either theoretically or empirically.

title: The Development of Local Wisdom-Based Natural Science Module to Improve Science Literation of Students
abstract: This study aims to develop a natural science module based on local wisdom to enhance students’ science literacy, particularly in disaster-prone areas near Mount Kelud. Employing a Research and Development (R&D) approach with the ASSURE instructional design model, the module integrates local knowledge and cultural practices related to volcanic eruptions into science learning materials. Theoretical validation by experts showed high feasibility across material, presentation, language, local wisdom integration, and science literacy components, each scoring above 87% in the “very good” category. Empirical testing with students demonstrated improvements in science literacy, with N-gain values ranging from low to medium categories (0.2–0.4). These results indicate that the developed module is both theoretically sound and empirically effective in fostering students’ understanding of scientific concepts through the context of their local environment and experiences, supporting the integration of local wisdom as a valuable resource in science education.

title: The Materials Science beamline upgrade at the Swiss Light Source
abstract: The wiggler X-ray source of the Materials Science beamline at the Swiss Light Source has been replaced with a 14 mm-period cryogenically cooled in-vacuum undulator. In order to best exploit the increased brilliance of this new source, the entire front-end and optics have been redesigned.

title: The Materials Science beamline upgrade at the Swiss Light Source
abstract: The Materials Science beamline at the Swiss Light Source underwent a major upgrade with the replacement of its original wiggler source by a state-of-the-art in-vacuum cryogenically cooled permanent-magnet undulator (CPMU), enabling access to higher photon energies and significantly increased brilliance in a medium-energy storage ring. This paper details the design, implementation, and performance of the new U14 undulator and associated beamline components, including redesigned front-end and X-ray optics optimized for the reduced beam divergence and enhanced coherent fraction. The upgrade supports advanced experimental techniques such as coherent X-ray diffraction imaging and micro Laue diffraction, while also improving flux, energy resolution, and beam stability for powder and surface diffraction applications. Performance metrics post-upgrade demonstrate substantial gains in photon flux and energy range, establishing the upgraded beamline as a versatile platform for cutting-edge materials science research.

title: The Materials Science of Semiconductors
abstract: The book reviews the most relevant concepts of semiconductor materials and processing including condensed matter physics, electronic device theory, and materials science. It describes the development of energy bands from atomic orbitals and the effect of atomic chemistry on the semiconductor. Semiconductor alloys are described including issues of miscibility, ordering, and electronic properties.
