Defects in semiconductors are described with particular emphasis on point and line defects, their sources and effects. A chapter on amorphous semiconductors is included as well as a chapter on organic materials used in optical and switching devices. The book concludes with chapters on general aspects of thin film nucleation and growth, physical vapor deposition and chemical vapor deposition methods. Examples of the application of the concepts in each chapter to specific problems or situations is included, along with recommended readings and homework problems.

title: The Materials Science of Semiconductors
abstract: This book provides a comprehensive introduction to the materials science underlying semiconductor technology, emphasizing the fundamental atomic and structural principles that govern semiconductor properties and performance. Designed primarily for senior undergraduate and early graduate students in materials science, but also accessible to those in related fields such as electrical engineering, chemical engineering, and physics, the text bridges gaps in prerequisite knowledge by reviewing essential concepts from chemistry, physics, and materials science. The work systematically explores atomic bonding, crystal structure, defects, and processing methods, illustrating how these factors influence electronic behavior and device functionality. Special attention is given to both traditional inorganic semiconductors and emerging materials such as organics and amorphous systems, with practical examples drawn from the author’s research on photovoltaic materials. By integrating scientific theory with engineering applications, the book equips readers with the conceptual tools necessary to understand, design, and improve semiconductor materials for a wide range of technological applications.

title: Three-dimensional coordinates of individual atoms in materials revealed by electron tomography.
abstract: Crystallography, the primary method for determining the 3D atomic positions in crystals, has been fundamental to the development of many fields of science. However, the atomic positions obtained from crystallography represent a global average of many unit cells in a crystal. Here, we report, for the first time, the determination of the 3D coordinates of thousands of individual atoms and a point defect in a material by electron tomography with a precision of ∼19 pm, where the crystallinity of the material is not assumed. From the coordinates of these individual atoms, we measure the atomic displacement field and the full strain tensor with a 3D resolution of ∼1 nm(3) and a precision of ∼10(-3), which are further verified by density functional theory calculations and molecular dynamics simulations. The ability to precisely localize the 3D coordinates of individual atoms in materials without assuming crystallinity is expected to find important applications in materials science, nanoscience, physics, chemistry and biology.

title: Three-dimensional coordinates of individual atoms in materials revealed by electron tomography.
abstract: Crystallography has long enabled the determination of average atomic positions in crystals, but direct three-dimensional (3D) localization of individual atoms without assuming crystallinity has remained elusive. Here, we report the determination of the 3D coordinates of 3,769 individual atoms and a point defect in a tungsten needle using electron tomography with aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy and equal slope tomography reconstruction, achieving a precision of approximately 19 picometers. The atomic displacement field and full strain tensor were measured with a 3D resolution of ~1 nm³ and precision of ~10⁻³, and validated by density functional theory calculations and molecular dynamics simulations. Our approach enables direct visualization of atomic-scale defects and strain in materials without averaging or prior knowledge of crystallinity, representing a significant advance for materials characterization at the single-atom level and offering new opportunities for research in materials science, nanoscience, physics, and chemistry.

title: Tracking materials science data lineage to manage millions of materials experiments and analyses
abstract: In an era of rapid advancement of algorithms that extract knowledge from data, data and metadata management are increasingly critical to research success. In materials science, there are few examples of experimental databases that contain many different types of information, and compared with other disciplines, the database sizes are relatively small. Underlying these issues are the challenges in managing and linking data across disparate synthesis and characterization experiments, which we address with the development of a lightweight data management framework that is generally applicable for experimental science and beyond. Five years of managing experiments with this system has yielded the Materials Experiment and Analysis Database (MEAD) that contains raw data and metadata from millions of materials synthesis and characterization experiments, as well as the analysis and distillation of that data into property and performance metrics via software in an accompanying open source repository. The unprecedented quantity and diversity of experimental data are searchable by experiment and analysis attributes generated by both researchers and data processing software. The search web interface allows users to visualize their search results and download zipped packages of data with full annotations of their lineage. The enormity of the data provides substantial challenges and opportunities for incorporating data science in the physical sciences, and MEAD’s data and algorithm management framework will foster increased incorporation of automation and autonomous discovery in materials and chemistry research.

title: Tracking materials science data lineage to manage millions of materials experiments and analyses
abstract: The management and integration of experimental data and metadata are critical challenges in materials science, particularly as the scale and diversity of experiments increase. This paper presents a lightweight, experiment-centric data management framework designed to track the complete lineage of materials synthesis and characterization experiments, addressing the need for robust protocols that link disparate data types across research phases. Over five years, this approach has enabled the creation of the Materials Experiment and Analysis Database (MEAD), which houses raw data, metadata, and derived metrics from millions of experiments. MEAD’s architecture supports comprehensive searchability by both experimental and analytical attributes, facilitates visualization and download of annotated datasets, and adheres to FAIR data principles to promote accessibility and reuse. The system’s modular design accommodates evolving analysis methods and diverse user interactions, fostering integration with data science workflows and automation in materials research. By ensuring transparent data provenance and scalable management, this framework advances the field’s capacity for high-throughput experimentation, autonomous discovery, and community-driven materials informatics.

title: Ultrafast laser processing of materials: from science to industry
abstract: Processing of materials by ultrashort laser pulses has evolved significantly over the last decade and is starting to reveal its scientific, technological and industrial potential. In ultrafast laser manufacturing, optical energy of tightly focused femtosecond or picosecond laser pulses can be delivered to precisely defined positions in the bulk of materials via two-/multi-photon excitation on a timescale much faster than thermal energy exchange between photoexcited electrons and lattice ions. Control of photo-ionization and thermal processes with the highest precision, inducing local photomodification in sub-100-nm-sized regions has been achieved. State-of-the-art ultrashort laser processing techniques exploit high 0.1–1 μm spatial resolution and almost unrestricted three-dimensional structuring capability. Adjustable pulse duration, spatiotemporal chirp, phase front tilt and polarization allow control of photomodification via uniquely wide parameter space. Mature opto-electrical/mechanical technologies have enabled laser processing speeds approaching meters-per-second, leading to a fast lab-to-fab transfer. The key aspects and latest achievements are reviewed with an emphasis on the fundamental relation between spatial resolution and total fabrication throughput. Emerging biomedical applications implementing micrometer feature precision over centimeter-scale scaffolds and photonic wire bonding in telecommunications are highlighted. The ability of femtosecond lasers to efficiently fabricate complex structures and devices for a wide variety of applications is reviewed. Mangirdas Malinauskas at Vilnius University in Lithuania and co-workers in Japan, Australia and Saudi Arabia describe how state-of-the-art laser processing techniques with ultrashort light pulses can be used to structure materials with a sub-micrometre resolution. Direct laser writing of suitable photoresists and other transparent media can create intricate three-dimensional photonic crystals, micro-optical components, gratings, tissue scaffolds and optical waveguides. Such structures are potentially useful for empowering next-generation applications in telecommunications and bioengineering that rely on the creation of increasingly sophisticated miniature parts. The precision, fabrication speed and versatility of ultrafast laser processing make it well placed to become a vital industrial tool for manufacturing.

title: Ultrafast laser processing of materials: from science to industry
abstract: Ultrafast laser processing, utilizing tightly focused femtosecond and picosecond pulses, has rapidly advanced from fundamental research to industrial applications, enabling precise three-dimensional structuring of materials at sub-100-nanometer scales. This review highlights the unique capabilities of ultrashort laser pulses for localized photomodification through nonlinear light–matter interactions, offering high spatial resolution and flexible control over fabrication parameters such as pulse duration and polarization. Recent technological developments have significantly increased processing speeds and throughput, facilitating the transition from laboratory demonstrations to scalable manufacturing. Key achievements include the fabrication of complex micro- and nano-scale devices, high-density optical memories, photonic structures, and biomedical scaffolds with micrometer precision. The interplay between spatial resolution and fabrication efficiency is examined, along with emerging industrial and biomedical applications that leverage the unrestricted 3D structuring potential of ultrafast lasers. These advances position ultrafast laser processing as a transformative tool for next-generation nanotechnologies and industrial manufacturing.

title: ABC of complementary medicine: herbal medicine.
abstract: The ABC of complementary medicine is edited and written by Catherine Zollman and Andrew Vickers. Catherine Zollman is a general practitioner in Bristol, and Andrew Vickers will shortly take up a post at Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, New York. At the time of writing, both worked for the Research Council for Complementary Medicine, London. The series will be published as a book in spring 2000. The picture of a herbal dispensary is reproduced with permission of Paul Biddle/Science Photo Library. The pictures of Chinese herbal medicine are reproduced with permission of Rex Features/Hafenrichter. The picture of different herbal formulations is reproduced with permission of Alain Dex, Publiphoto Diffusion/Science Photo Library. The pictures of St John’s wort and valerian are reproduced with permission of Glenis Moore/A-Z Botanical and A-Z Botanical. The picture of echinacea is reproduced with permission of NHPA/Stephen Krasemann. The picture of a Western herbalist is reproduced with permission of BMJ/Ulrike Preuss.

title: ABC of complementary medicine: herbal medicine.
abstract: This paper examines the role of herbal medicine within complementary medicine, focusing on the practices, regulation, and training associated with nutritional therapy in the United Kingdom. It highlights the diversity of practitioners offering nutritional consultations, ranging from complementary therapists to medically trained professionals, and discusses the significant costs involved in diagnostic testing, supplements, and dietary changes. The regulatory landscape is explored, noting established bodies for naturopaths and nutritional therapists but less comprehensive oversight for other practitioners. Training pathways vary widely in duration and depth, from short courses to multi-year programs. The paper also references key professional organizations and resources for further education. Historical context is provided through a discussion of honey poisoning, illustrating the longstanding interplay between natural substances and health. The overview underscores the complexity of integrating herbal and nutritional medicine into mainstream healthcare and the need for clear standards in practitioner training and regulation.

title: ABC of Learning and Teaching in Medicine
abstract: In undergoing this life, many people always try to do and get the best. New knowledge, experience, lesson, and everything that can improve the life will be done. However, many people sometimes feel confused to get those things. Feeling the limited of experience and sources to be better is one of the lacks to own. However, there is a very simple thing that can be done. This is what your teacher always manoeuvres you to do this one. Yeah, reading is the answer. Reading a book as this abc of learning and teaching in medicine and other references can enrich your life quality. How can it be?

title: ABC of Learning and Teaching in Medicine
abstract: This review evaluates the second edition of 'ABC of Learning and Teaching in Medicine' by Peter Cantillon and Diana Wood, highlighting its value as an accessible introductory text for new medical educators. The book’s concise format, with 17 chapters spanning just over 80 pages, makes it approachable for beginners while covering essential topics such as curriculum design, collaborative learning, assessment methods, feedback skills, clinical education, professionalism, and support for struggling students. The inclusion of visuals and practical tools enhances comprehension and retention. Each chapter offers further reading to supplement information, addressing potential gaps due to brevity. The reviewer recommends this book as a foundational resource for faculty development and anticipates the publication of a Korean edition to further support local medical educators.

title: Adolescent Medicine: A Practical Guide
abstract: The clinical skills required for the primary care of adolescents encompass the domains of several specialties, but it is the precision with which these skills can be adapted to the unique requirements of adolescents that determines the quality of the clinical outcome. Several texts are now available that attempt to identify unique aspects of adolescence so that primary care clinicians may apply their skills more precisely. The authors of Adolescent Medicine: A Practical Guide use a congenial, informal prose to describe the aspects of adolescence that provide a framework for more detailed discussions of common healthrelated problems of adolescents. The book is intended to serve as an initial guide for clinicians encountering an unfamiliar adolescent problem. Chapters on physical and psychological development and a chapter on seeing adolescents in an office setting provide the framework for addressing other health problems of adolescents. The authors provide some rather uneven discussions of various clinical syndromes, from acne to chronic fatigue syndrome. Chapters dealing with aspects of sexuality—especially contraception and sexually transmitted diseases—are reasonably complete and quite readable. A chapter on adolescent sports medicine is also good and comes closest to the goal of providing a quick guide to commonly encountered health problems of adolescents. Some major problems diminish the book's quality. A continuous appeal is made to a stereotype of the adolescent patient, which, like most stereotypes, is only partially accurate. (For example, most adolescents are said to 'live in a constant state of embarrassment . . .'). This portrayal of adolescents may make them pitiable but not especially attractive as patients. There are also a few factual errors, as in the description of the click of mitral valve prolapse as diastolic. Finally, the quality of many of the figures, especially the microphotographs, is quite poor. This book only partly achieves the goals of its authors. It is difficult to envision the book as a reliable and frequently used quick reference. Other texts are available to better serve this purpose. Clinicians seeking an expanded perspective about their adolescent patients may find the book to be a useful introduction because it is both readable and relatively brief. (J. Dennis Fortenberry, MD, MS, Oklahoma University Health Sciences Center, Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, 73105)

title: Adolescent Medicine: A Practical Guide
abstract: This paper reviews the second edition of Dr. H. Hyde Salter’s treatise on asthma, highlighting its expanded practical content and detailed case records, which now number 223 and provide a robust foundation for clinical conclusions. The work maintains the author’s central thesis that asthma is primarily a nervous disorder, with emphysema as a frequent consequence, and discusses the pathophysiological mechanisms involved. Salter’s additions focus on therapeutic strategies, including the use of stimulants such as coffee, tea, alcohol, and ammonia, as well as the limited efficacy of iodide of potassium. The book offers comprehensive guidance on pharmacological and non-pharmacological management, with extensive discussion of lifestyle modifications and environmental factors. Narrative case histories enrich the clinical perspective and serve as valuable resources for practitioners and students seeking practical approaches to asthma treatment. The review concludes by affirming the enduring significance of Salter’s work as both a scholarly and practical guide for clinicians managing asthma.

title: Adverse drug reactions and off-label and unlicensed medicines in children: a nested case?control study of inpatients in a pediatric hospital
abstract: Off-label and unlicensed (OLUL) prescribing has been prevalent in pediatric practice. Using data from a prospective cohort study of adverse drug reactions (ADRs) among pediatric inpatients, we aimed to test the hypothesis that OLUL status is a risk factor for ADRs.MethodsA nested case?control study was conducted within a prospective cohort study. Details of all medicines administered were recorded, including information about OLUL status. The odds ratio for OLUL medicines being implicated in a probable or definite ADR was calculated. A multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression model was fitted to the data to assess the influence that OLUL medicine use had on the hazard of an ADR occurring.ResultsA total of 10,699 medicine courses were administered to 1,388 patients. The odds ratio (OR) of an OLUL medicine being implicated in an ADR compared with an authorized medicine was 2.25 (95% confidence interval (CI) 1.95 to 2.59). Medicines licensed in children but given to a child below the minimum age or weight had the greatest odds of being implicated in an ADR (19% of courses in this category were implicated, OR 3.54 (95% CI 2.82 to 4.44). Each additional OLUL medicine given significantly increased the hazard of an ADR (hazard ratio (HR) 1.3 95% CI 1.2 to 1.3, P <0.001). Each additional authorized medicine given also significantly increased the hazard (HR 1.2 95% CI 1.2 to 1.3, P <0.001).ConclusionsOLUL medicines are more likely to be implicated in an ADR than authorized medicines. The number of medicines administered is a risk factor for ADRs highlighting the need to use the lowest number of medicines, at the lowest dose for the shortest period, with continual vigilance by prescribers, in order to reduce the risk of ADRs.

title: Adverse drug reactions and off-label and unlicensed medicines in children: a nested case?control study of inpatients in a pediatric hospital
abstract: This nested case–control study investigated the association between adverse drug reactions (ADRs) and the use of off-label and unlicensed (OLUL) medicines in pediatric inpatients. Data were collected prospectively from 1,388 children admitted to a pediatric hospital, documenting 10,699 medicine courses. Cases (patients experiencing at least one probable or definite ADR) were matched to controls without ADRs by admission date and time. Medicines were categorized as authorized, off-label, or unlicensed based on regulatory status. The odds of an OLUL medicine being implicated in an ADR were significantly higher than for authorized medicines (OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.95–2.59), with the highest risk observed when medicines licensed for children were given below the minimum age or weight (OR 3.54, 95% CI 2.82–4.44). Multivariate Cox regression showed that each additional OLUL medicine increased the hazard of an ADR (HR 1.3, 95% CI 1.2–1.3), as did each additional authorized medicine (HR 1.2, 95% CI 1.2–1.3). These findings demonstrate that OLUL prescribing is a significant risk factor for ADRs in hospitalized children and highlight the importance of minimizing polypharmacy and exercising caution when prescribing OLUL medicines in pediatric settings.

title: American Medical Society for Sports Medicine position statement: concussion in sport
abstract: Sport-related concussion (SRC) is a common injury in recreational and organised sport. Over the past 30 years, there has been significant progress in our scientific understanding of SRC, which in turn has driven the development of clinical guidelines for diagnosis, assessment and management of SRC. In addition to a growing need for knowledgeable healthcare professionals to provide evidence-based care for athletes with SRC, media attention and legislation have created awareness and, in some cases, fear about many issues and unknowns surrounding SRC. The American Medical Society for Sports Medicine (AMSSM) formed a writing group to review the existing literature on SRC, update its previous position statement, and to address current evidence and knowledge gaps regarding SRC. The absence of definitive outcomes-based data is challenging and requires relying on the best available evidence integrated with clinical experience and patient values. This statement reviews the definition, pathophysiology and epidemiology of SRC, the diagnosis and management of both acute and persistent concussion symptoms, the short-term and long-term risks of SRC and repetitive head impact exposure, SRC prevention strategies, and potential future directions for SRC research. The AMSSM is committed to best clinical practices, evidence-based research and educational initiatives that positively impact the health and safety of athletes.

title: American Medical Society for Sports Medicine position statement: concussion in sport
abstract: This position statement by the American Medical Society for Sports Medicine provides an evidence-based summary to guide physicians in the evaluation and management of sport-related concussion. Concussion is defined as a traumatically induced, transient disturbance of brain function and is a subset of mild traumatic brain injury. The statement reviews current knowledge on incidence, risk factors, diagnosis, sideline management, neuropsychological testing, return-to-play protocols, and long-term effects. It emphasizes that concussion diagnosis remains clinical, ideally performed by healthcare providers with specific training and experience. The document highlights the importance of cognitive rest, individualized return-to-play decisions, and the need for education among athletes, parents, coaches, and healthcare professionals. It also addresses prevention strategies, legislative efforts, and identifies key knowledge gaps requiring further research, including validation of assessment tools and understanding long-term neurological outcomes. The statement underscores the evolving nature of concussion management and calls for ongoing research to optimize athlete safety and care.

title: Aquaporins in clinical medicine.
abstract: The aquaporins are a family of membrane water channels, some of which also transport glycerol. They are involved in a wide range of physiological functions (including water/salt homeostasis, exocrine fluid secretion, and epidermal hydration) and human diseases (including glaucoma, cancer, epilepsy, and obesity). At the cellular level, aquaporin-mediated osmotic water transport across cell plasma membranes facilitates transepithelial fluid transport, cell migration, and neuroexcitation; aquaporin-mediated glycerol transport regulates cell proliferation, adipocyte metabolism, and epidermal water retention. Genetic diseases caused by loss-of-function mutations in aquaporins include nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and congenital cataracts. The neuroinflammatory demyelinating disease neuromyelitis optica is marked by pathogenic autoantibodies against astrocyte water channel aquaporin-4. There remain broad opportunities for the development of aquaporin-based diagnostics and therapeutics. Disease-relevant aquaporin polymorphisms are beginning to be explored. There is great promise in the development of small-molecule aquaporin modulators for therapy of some types of refractory edema, brain swelling, neuroinflammation, glaucoma, epilepsy, cancer, pain, and obesity.

title: Aquaporins in clinical medicine.
abstract: Aquaporins are a family of membrane water channels, some of which also transport glycerol, that play critical roles in diverse physiological processes including water and salt homeostasis, exocrine fluid secretion, and epidermal hydration. Their dysfunction is implicated in a range of human diseases such as nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, congenital cataracts, neuromyelitis optica, glaucoma, cancer, epilepsy, and obesity. At the cellular level, aquaporins facilitate osmotic water transport essential for transepithelial fluid movement, cell migration, neuroexcitation, and regulate cell proliferation and metabolism through glycerol transport. Genetic mutations and autoimmune targeting of aquaporins can cause or contribute to disease pathogenesis. Advances in understanding aquaporin structure and function have revealed opportunities for the development of novel diagnostics and therapeutics, including small-molecule modulators for treating refractory edema, brain swelling, neuroinflammation, and other conditions. Ongoing research into aquaporin polymorphisms and regulatory mechanisms continues to expand their potential applications in clinical medicine.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Medicine: Today and Tomorrow
abstract: Artificial intelligence-powered medical technologies are rapidly evolving into applicable solutions for clinical practice. Deep learning algorithms can deal with increasing amounts of data provided by wearables, smartphones, and other mobile monitoring sensors in different areas of medicine. Currently, only very specific settings in clinical practice benefit from the application of artificial intelligence, such as the detection of atrial fibrillation, epilepsy seizures, and hypoglycemia, or the diagnosis of disease based on histopathological examination or medical imaging. The implementation of augmented medicine is long-awaited by patients because it allows for a greater autonomy and a more personalized treatment, however, it is met with resistance from physicians which were not prepared for such an evolution of clinical practice. This phenomenon also creates the need to validate these modern tools with traditional clinical trials, debate the educational upgrade of the medical curriculum in light of digital medicine as well as ethical consideration of the ongoing connected monitoring. The aim of this paper is to discuss recent scientific literature and provide a perspective on the benefits, future opportunities and risks of established artificial intelligence applications in clinical practice on physicians, healthcare institutions, medical education, and bioethics.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Medicine: Today and Tomorrow
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the landscape of medicine, offering innovative solutions for clinical practice through advanced data analysis and decision support. This perspective paper reviews current applications of AI-powered technologies across various medical specialties, including cardiology, pulmonology, endocrinology, nephrology, gastroenterology, neurology, and histopathology. Notable examples include AI-driven detection of atrial fibrillation and epilepsy seizures, continuous glucose monitoring for diabetes management, risk prediction in cardiovascular and renal diseases, image analysis in gastroenterology and cancer diagnostics, and wearable sensors for neurological assessment. While patients increasingly embrace these tools for personalized and participatory care, healthcare professionals face challenges related to education gaps, increased administrative burdens, concerns about professional roles, and unresolved legal and ethical issues. The implementation of augmented medicine necessitates rigorous validation through clinical trials and integration of digital health literacy into medical education. This paper discusses the benefits, opportunities, and risks associated with established AI applications in clinical practice, highlighting the need for collaborative efforts among clinicians, educators, institutions, and policymakers to ensure responsible adoption and maximize patient outcomes.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Nuclear Medicine
abstract: Despite the great media attention for artificial intelligence (AI), for many health care professionals the term and the functioning of AI remain a “black box,” leading to exaggerated expectations on the one hand and unfounded fears on the other. In this review, we provide a conceptual classification and a brief summary of the technical fundamentals of AI. Possible applications are discussed on the basis of a typical work flow in medical imaging, grouped by planning, scanning, interpretation, and reporting. The main limitations of current AI techniques, such as issues with interpretability or the need for large amounts of annotated data, are briefly addressed. Finally, we highlight the possible impact of AI on the nuclear medicine profession, the associated challenges and, last but not least, the opportunities.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Nuclear Medicine
abstract: This review explores the evolving role of artificial intelligence (AI) in nuclear medicine, addressing both the conceptual foundations and practical applications within medical imaging workflows. The paper provides a classification of AI methodologies, distinguishing between symbolic and data-driven approaches such as machine learning and deep learning, and summarizes key technical principles relevant to healthcare professionals. Applications of AI are discussed across the stages of imaging—planning, scanning, interpretation, and reporting—highlighting both current capabilities and limitations, including challenges related to interpretability and the need for large annotated datasets. The review also considers the broader impact of AI on the nuclear medicine profession, emphasizing that rather than replacing specialists, AI is poised to transform workflows and create new opportunities for active professional engagement in shaping future healthcare practices.

title: Biomedical informatics and translational medicine
abstract: Biomedical informatics involves a core set of methodologies that can provide a foundation for crossing the 'translational barriers' associated with translational medicine. To this end, the fundamental aspects of biomedical informatics (e.g., bioinformatics, imaging informatics, clinical informatics, and public health informatics) may be essential in helping improve the ability to bring basic research findings to the bedside, evaluate the efficacy of interventions across communities, and enable the assessment of the eventual impact of translational medicine innovations on health policies. Here, a brief description is provided for a selection of key biomedical informatics topics (Decision Support, Natural Language Processing, Standards, Information Retrieval, and Electronic Health Records) and their relevance to translational medicine. Based on contributions and advancements in each of these topic areas, the article proposes that biomedical informatics practitioners ('biomedical informaticians') can be essential members of translational medicine teams.

title: Biomedical informatics and translational medicine
abstract: Biomedical informatics encompasses a range of methodologies and sub-disciplines—including bioinformatics, imaging informatics, clinical informatics, and public health informatics—that are essential for overcoming translational barriers in translational medicine. This review examines how biomedical informatics supports the movement of basic research findings to clinical application, evaluation of interventions at the community level, and assessment of their impact on health policy. Key topics such as decision support, natural language processing, standards, information retrieval, and electronic health records are discussed in relation to their roles in facilitating knowledge integration and management across the translational continuum. The article highlights the importance of trans-disciplinary teams and proposes that biomedical informaticians are critical contributors to translational medicine efforts, enabling effective communication and translation of concepts among diverse experts to advance patient care and public health outcomes.

title: Chemical markers for the quality control of herbal medicines: an overview
abstract: Selection of chemical markers is crucial for the quality control of herbal medicines, including authentication of genuine species, harvesting the best quality raw materials, evaluation of post-harvesting handling, assessment of intermediates and finished products, and detection of harmful or toxic ingredients. Ideal chemical markers should be the therapeutic components of herbal medicines. However, for most herbal medicines, the therapeutic components have not been fully elucidated or easily monitored. Bioactive, characteristic, main, synergistic, correlative, toxic and general components may be selected. This article reviews the effective use of chemical markers in the quality control of herbal medicines including the selection criteria considering the roles and physicochemical factors which may affect the effective use of chemical markers.

title: Chemical markers for the quality control of herbal medicines: an overview
abstract: The quality control of herbal medicines is challenged by their complex and variable chemical compositions, necessitating reliable analytical approaches to ensure consistency, safety, and efficacy. Chemical markers serve as critical tools for the authentication of species, evaluation of raw materials and finished products, and detection of adulterants or toxic substances. This review provides an overview of the selection criteria and classification systems for chemical markers, highlighting their roles in quality assessment. Eight categories of chemical markers are proposed: therapeutic, bioactive, synergistic, characteristic, main, correlative, toxic, and general components used with fingerprint spectra. The article discusses the advantages and limitations of each category, emphasizing the importance of selecting appropriate markers based on therapeutic relevance, specificity, detectability, and physicochemical properties. Case studies illustrate the practical application of chemical markers in quality control protocols for widely used herbal medicines. The review concludes that systematic selection and utilization of chemical markers are essential for standardizing herbal medicines and advancing their research and clinical use.

title: Clinical epigenetics settings for cancer and cardiovascular diseases: real-life applications of network medicine at the bedside
abstract: Despite impressive efforts invested in epigenetic research in the last 50 years, clinical applications are still lacking. Only a few university hospital centers currently use epigenetic biomarkers at the bedside. Moreover, the overall concept of precision medicine is not widely recognized in routine medical practice and the reductionist approach remains predominant in treating patients affected by major diseases such as cancer and cardiovascular diseases. By its’ very nature, epigenetics is integrative of genetic networks. The study of epigenetic biomarkers has led to the identification of numerous drugs with an increasingly significant role in clinical therapy especially of cancer patients. Here, we provide an overview of clinical epigenetics within the context of network analysis. We illustrate achievements to date and discuss how we can move from traditional medicine into the era of network medicine (NM), where pathway-informed molecular diagnostics will allow treatment selection following the paradigm of precision medicine.

title: Clinical epigenetics settings for cancer and cardiovascular diseases: real-life applications of network medicine at the bedside
abstract: Despite significant advances in epigenetic research, the integration of epigenetic biomarkers and therapies into routine clinical practice for cancer and cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remains limited. This review examines the current landscape of clinical epigenetics, highlighting the potential of network medicine (NM) to address the complexity of these diseases by leveraging multi-omics data, systems biology, and artificial intelligence. We discuss the mechanisms and clinical relevance of epigenetic modifications, including DNA methylation and histone modifications, and summarize the development and approval of epi-drugs for hematologic malignancies, with ongoing trials exploring their use in solid tumors and CVDs. The limitations of reductionist approaches underscore the need for NM to enable precision medicine by integrating molecular interaction networks for improved diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy selection. By bridging basic science and clinical application, this review provides insights into how NM can facilitate the translation of epigenetic discoveries to bedside care, ultimately advancing personalized treatment strategies for cancer and CVD patients.

title: Clinical Medicine
abstract: Integrated care systems join up health and care services, so that people have the support they need, in the right place, at the right time. The aims include improving outcomes in healthcare, tackling inequalities in access and enhancing productivity and value for money. This is needed for neuroscience care as the traditional delivery of neuroscience care is inefficient, outdated and expensive, and can involve complex referral pathways and long waiting times. In preparation for the formation of the integrated care system (ICS), a novel innovative collaboration across multiple NHS trusts developed across North Central London in 2021. We developed a model where neuroscience specialists engage in collaborative care with clinicians outside the specialist hospital setting. Pivotal to the pathway is a multidisciplinary meeting, and collaborative working enables joint clinical reviews, diagnostics and medication initiation. This innovative collaboration has already significantly improved access, addressed inequalities due to borough variation and enhanced the delivery and quality of neuroscience care in our ICS. It is a translatable model that can be adapted to suit other regions in the UK. It fulfils many of the objectives of the integrated care system and these benefits are seen without the need for significantly more resource.

title: Clinical Medicine
abstract: Clinical medicine is defined as the practice of medicine grounded in the direct observation and treatment of patients. This paper explores the foundational principles of clinical medicine, emphasizing its distinction from laboratory-based or theoretical approaches. Drawing on definitions from authoritative sources such as the National Cancer Institute Thesaurus, the discussion highlights the centrality of patient interaction, physical examination, and clinical judgment in diagnosis and management. The paper also considers the evolving landscape of clinical medicine in light of technological advancements and changing healthcare paradigms. Ultimately, it underscores the enduring importance of clinician-patient engagement as a cornerstone of effective medical practice.

title: Clinical practice parameters for hemodynamic support of pediatric and neonatal patients in septic shock*
abstract: The Institute of Medicine has called for the development of clinical guidelines and practice parameters to develop “best practice” and potentially improve patient outcome. ObjectiveTo provide American College of Critical Care Medicine clinical guidelines for hemodynamic support of neonates and children with septic shock. SettingIndividual members of the Society of Critical Care Medicine with special interest in neonatal and pediatric septic shock were identified from literature review and general solicitation at Society of Critical Care Medicine Educational and Scientific Symposia (1998–2001). MethodsThe MEDLINE literature database was searched with the following age-specific keywords: sepsis, septicemia, septic shock, endotoxemia, persistent pulmonary hypertension, nitric oxide, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. More than 30 experts graded literature and drafted specific recommendations by using a modified Delphi method. More than 30 more experts then reviewed the compiled recommendations. The task-force chairman modified the document until <10% of experts disagreed with the recommendations. ResultsOnly four randomized controlled trials in children with septic shock could be identified. None of these randomized trials led to a change in practice. Clinical practice has been based, for the most part, on physiologic experiments, case series, and cohort studies. Despite relatively low American College of Critical Care Medicine–graded evidence in the pediatric literature, outcomes in children have improved from 97% mortality in the 1960s to 60% in the 1980s and 9% mortality in 1999. U.S. hospital survival was three-fold better in children compared with adults (9% vs. 27% mortality) in 1999. Shock pathophysiology and response to therapies is age specific. For example, cardiac failure is a predominant cause of death in neonates and children, but vascular failure is a predominant cause of death in adults. Inotropes, vasodilators (children), inhaled nitric oxide (neonates), and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation can be more important contributors to survival in the pediatric populations, whereas vasopressors can be more important contributors to adult survival. ConclusionAmerican College of Critical Care Medicine adult guidelines for hemodynamic support of septic shock have little application to the management of pediatric or neonatal septic shock. Studies are required to determine whether American College of Critical Care Medicine guidelines for hemodynamic support of pediatric and neonatal septic shock will be implemented and associated with improved outcome.

title: Clinical practice parameters for hemodynamic support of pediatric and neonatal patients in septic shock*
abstract: This paper presents clinical practice parameters developed by the American College of Critical Care Medicine for the hemodynamic support of pediatric and neonatal patients in septic shock. A multidisciplinary task force conducted a comprehensive literature review using age-specific search terms and applied a modified Delphi method to develop evidence-based, age-appropriate recommendations. Despite identifying only four randomized controlled trials in pediatric septic shock, which did not alter clinical practice, expert consensus was used to address the predominance of physiologic studies, case series, and cohort data in this field. The guidelines emphasize that the pathophysiology and therapeutic response in septic shock differ significantly between children, neonates, and adults, with cardiac failure being a leading cause of death in younger populations and vascular failure more common in adults. Recommended interventions include inotropes, vasodilators, inhaled nitric oxide, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for pediatric patients. Notably, mortality rates in children have dramatically improved over recent decades, now surpassing adult outcomes. The paper concludes that adult guidelines are not directly applicable to pediatric or neonatal care and highlights the need for further research to validate the implementation and impact of these pediatric-specific recommendations on patient outcomes.

title: Davidson's Principles and practice of medicine
abstract: I first read Davidson 30 years ago: at that time it was already in its 5th edition. A brief comparison shows that it then contained about 440,000 words in 1,100 pages: the current edition has compressed 625,000 words into 800 pages. I think I bought it as a student because it was cheap: but also because it seemed to be comprehensive and straightforward, and I have used it as a basis for my medical knowledge ever since. So I miss some of the old pictures of the acute skin rashes such as scarlet fever: in fact infectious disease has been transferred to the back and genetic factors take the first chapters. But careful linguistic comparison will still uncover the old phrases which some of us know by heart-there are minor changes such as 'alarming reactions to intravenous iron are uncommon, but have occasionally been noted', which becomes 'alarming systemic anaphyllactic reactions can occur'. Sir Stanley Davidson made 'no attempt to describe every rare disease or syndrome, but devoted most of the space available to those disorders most commonly encountered in practice'. I have grown up with successive editions, and have gradually come to appreciate the problems of the authors in the compression of knowledge. Having got to know many of them personally as real people rather than as names I can still recommend the book. It is the essential starting point for the study of internal medicine and for many doctors will remain their base reference work. The present editors have kept up-to-date and been prepared to prune the dead wood. There are many competitors in the market, and the publishers must take care with layout and illustration, although Davidson is still the best value for money. I will continue to recommend it to my clinical students: they will need to read it and know it to pass final MB. Postgraduates will need to remember the facts, but also to be able to place them in a broader perspective. The older consultant will still happily read it, and to get to know the authors themselves is really to complete your medical education. Dr John Macleod and his team have successfully kept alive the primary objective 'to provide a rational and easily comprehensible basis for the practice of medicine'. The book is economical in price and compact in size, but still contains the essential truths for the practice of good medicine.

title: Davidson's Principles and practice of medicine
abstract: This review critically examines the 15th edition of Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, edited by John Macleod, Christopher Edwards, and Ian Bouchier. The reviewer reflects on the evolution of the textbook over three decades, noting its expansion in content yet compression in page count, and highlights changes in the organization of topics such as the repositioning of infectious diseases and the increased emphasis on genetic factors. Despite updates and necessary pruning of outdated material, the book retains its hallmark clarity and comprehensiveness, maintaining its status as an essential reference for medical students, postgraduates, and practicing clinicians. The review commends the editors for preserving the original objective of providing a rational and accessible foundation for internal medicine while ensuring affordability and practical utility. Davidson's continues to be recommended as a foundational text that supports both examination success and lifelong medical education.

title: Dental pulp stem cells: function, isolation and applications in regenerative medicine
abstract: Dental pulp stem cells (DPSCs) are a promising source of cells for numerous and varied regenerative medicine applications. Their natural function in the production of odontoblasts to create reparative dentin support applications in dentistry in the regeneration of tooth structures. However, they are also being investigated for the repair of tissues outside of the tooth. The ease of isolation of DPSCs from discarded or removed teeth offers a promising source of autologous cells, and their similarities with bone marrow stromal cells (BMSCs) suggest applications in musculoskeletal regenerative medicine. DPSCs are derived from the neural crest and, therefore, have a different developmental origin to BMSCs. These differences from BMSCs in origin and phenotype are being exploited in neurological and other applications. This review briefly highlights the source and functions of DPSCs and then focuses on in vivo applications across the breadth of regenerative medicine. © 2014 The Authors. Journal of Tissue Engineering and Regenerative Medicine published by John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.
venue: Journal of Tissue Engineering and Regenerative Medicine

title: Dental pulp stem cells: function, isolation and applications in regenerative medicine
abstract: Dental pulp stem cells (DPSCs) are a unique population of mesenchymal stem cells derived from the neural crest, residing within the dental pulp and exhibiting the capacity for self-renewal and multilineage differentiation. Their primary physiological role involves the generation of odontoblasts for reparative dentin formation, contributing to tooth homeostasis and repair. DPSCs can be efficiently isolated from both permanent and deciduous teeth using enzymatic digestion or tissue outgrowth methods, with advances in culture techniques enabling expansion and cryopreservation for future clinical use. Compared to bone marrow stromal cells, DPSCs display distinct phenotypic markers and enhanced neuroglial differentiation potential, broadening their applicability beyond dental tissue regeneration. In regenerative medicine, DPSCs have demonstrated promise in dental pulp and dentin regeneration, bone repair, neural regeneration, and angiogenesis, supported by in vivo studies showing their ability to generate dentin-pulp-like complexes and vascularized tissues. The accessibility of DPSCs from discarded teeth, their robust proliferative capacity, and their versatility in tissue engineering underscore their significant potential as an autologous cell source for a wide range of regenerative therapies.
venue: Journal of Tissue Engineering and Regenerative Medicine

title: Designing the next generation of medicines for malaria control and eradication
abstract: In the fight against malaria new medicines are an essential weapon. For the parts of the world where the current gold standard artemisinin combination therapies are active, significant improvements can still be made: for example combination medicines which allow for single dose regimens, cheaper, safer and more effective medicines, or improved stability under field conditions. For those parts of the world where the existing combinations show less than optimal activity, the priority is to have activity against emerging resistant strains, and other criteria take a secondary role. For new medicines to be optimal in malaria control they must also be able to reduce transmission and prevent relapse of dormant forms: additional constraints on a combination medicine. In the absence of a highly effective vaccine, new medicines are also needed to protect patient populations. In this paper, an outline definition of the ideal and minimally acceptable characteristics of the types of clinical candidate molecule which are needed (target candidate profiles) is suggested. In addition, the optimal and minimally acceptable characteristics of combination medicines are outlined (target product profiles). MMV presents now a suggested framework for combining the new candidates to produce the new medicines. Sustained investment over the next decade in discovery and development of new molecules is essential to enable the long-term delivery of the medicines needed to combat malaria.

title: Designing the next generation of medicines for malaria control and eradication
abstract: The ongoing challenge of malaria control and eradication necessitates the development of next-generation medicines that address both current and emerging needs. While artemisinin-based combination therapies have significantly reduced malaria morbidity and mortality, the emergence of drug resistance, limitations in treatment regimens, and the need for improved safety, affordability, and stability highlight the urgency for new therapeutic options. This review outlines the ideal and minimally acceptable characteristics for clinical candidate molecules (target candidate profiles) and combination medicines (target product profiles) required to achieve effective malaria control and eventual eradication. Key considerations include activity against resistant strains, single-dose regimens, transmission-blocking potential, relapse prevention, chemoprotection for vulnerable populations, compatibility with co-morbidities such as HIV and tuberculosis, and chemical stability in challenging environments. The Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV) proposes a framework for integrating these attributes into new medicines through sustained investment in discovery and development. Defining clear target profiles is essential to guide research priorities, ensure adaptability to evolving public health landscapes, and optimize the long-term impact of antimalarial interventions.

title: Diagnosis and treatment of diabetic foot infections.
abstract: Foot infections in persons with diabetes are a common, complex, and costly problem [1–4]. In addition to causing severe morbidities, they now account for the largest number of diabetes-related hospital bed—days [5] and are the most common proximate, nontraumatic cause of amputations [6, 7]. Diabetic foot infections require careful attention and coordinated management, preferably by a multidisciplinary foot-care team (A-II) [8–13]. The team managing these infections should preferably include, or have ready access to, an infectious diseases specialist or a medical microbiologist (B-III) [1]. Optimal management of diabetic foot infections can potentially reduce the incidence of infection-related morbidities, the need for and duration of hospitalization, and the incidence of major limb amputation [14, 15]. Unfortunately, these infections are frequently inadequately managed [16]. This may result from a lack of understanding of current diagnostic and therapeutic approaches, insufficient resources devoted to the problem, or a lack of effective multidisciplinary collaboration. The primary purpose of this guideline is to help reduce the medical morbidity, psychological distress, and financial costs associated with diabetic foot infections.

title: Diagnosis and treatment of diabetic foot infections.
abstract: Diabetic foot infections are a significant cause of morbidity and lower-extremity amputations, necessitating prompt and coordinated management. This guideline, developed by the Infectious Diseases Society of America, outlines evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis and treatment of these infections. Key risk factors include peripheral neuropathy, vascular insufficiency, and poor glycemic control, with foot ulceration serving as the primary predisposing condition. Diagnosis relies on clinical assessment, supported by appropriate microbiological cultures and imaging studies, particularly MRI for deep tissue involvement. Empirical antibiotic therapy should be guided by infection severity and likely pathogens, with definitive regimens tailored to culture results and clinical response. Surgical intervention is indicated for deep abscesses, extensive necrosis, or osteomyelitis. Optimal wound care—including debridement and off-loading—is essential alongside antimicrobial therapy. The guideline emphasizes the importance of multidisciplinary care, early follow-up, and individualized treatment duration based on infection resolution rather than wound healing. Adjunctive therapies such as granulocyte colony-stimulating factors or hyperbaric oxygen may be considered in refractory cases. Further research is needed to refine classification systems, diagnostic strategies, and therapeutic approaches for diabetic foot infections.

title: Digital twins to personalize medicine
abstract: Personalized medicine requires the integration and processing of vast amounts of data. Here, we propose a solution to this challenge that is based on constructing Digital Twins. These are high-resolution models of individual patients that are computationally treated with thousands of drugs to find the drug that is optimal for the patient.

title: Digital twins to personalize medicine
abstract: Personalized medicine faces significant challenges in integrating and interpreting the vast, complex data required to tailor treatments for individual patients. This paper proposes the use of digital twins—computational models that replicate the molecular, phenotypic, and environmental characteristics of individual patients—as a scalable solution to this challenge. By constructing high-resolution network models that incorporate multi-omics, clinical, and environmental data, digital twins can be computationally treated with thousands of drugs to identify optimal therapies. Network analysis tools enable the prioritization of key genes, cell types, and tissues involved in disease mechanisms, while machine learning approaches can further enhance model accuracy and predictive power. The integration of diverse data types into multilayer modules allows for comprehensive disease modeling and facilitates the translation of in silico findings to patient care. Although significant technical, ethical, and logistical challenges remain, the implementation of digital twins has the potential to revolutionize personalized medicine by improving diagnostics, guiding targeted therapies, and inspiring new research directions.

title: Do Doctors Practice Defensive Medicine?
abstract: `Defensive medicine' is a potentially serious social problem: if fear of liability drives health care providers to administer treatments that do not have worthwhile medical benefits, then the current liability system may generate inefficiencies many times greater than the costs of compensating malpractice claimants. To obtain direct empirical evidence on this question, we analyze the effects of malpractice liability reforms using data on all elderly Medicare beneficiaries treated for serious heart disease in 1984, 1987, and 1990. We find that malpractice reforms that directly reduce provider liability pressure lead to reductions of 5 to 9 percent in medical expenditures without substantial effects on mortality or medical complications. We conclude that liability reforms can reduce defensive medical practices.

title: Do Doctors Practice Defensive Medicine?
abstract: This paper investigates whether doctors engage in defensive medicine, defined as the practice of recommending tests, procedures, or visits, or avoiding high-risk patients or procedures, primarily to reduce exposure to malpractice liability rather than to benefit the patient. Drawing on a review of empirical studies and survey data from multiple countries and healthcare systems, the analysis finds substantial evidence that defensive medicine is prevalent among physicians, particularly in high-liability specialties such as obstetrics and surgery. The findings indicate that fear of litigation leads to increased use of diagnostic tests and referrals, as well as avoidance of certain procedures or patients perceived as high risk. Defensive practices contribute to higher healthcare costs without clear improvements in patient outcomes. The paper concludes that tort reform and changes in malpractice liability environments may reduce the incidence of defensive medicine, but must be carefully designed to avoid compromising patient safety.

title: Drug repositioning for personalized medicine
abstract: Human diseases can be caused by complex mechanisms involving aberrations in numerous proteins and pathways. With recent advances in genomics, elucidating the molecular basis of disease on a personalized level has become an attainable goal. In many cases, relevant molecular targets will be identified for which approved drugs already exist, and the potential repositioning of these drugs to a new indication can be investigated. Repositioning is an accelerated route for drug discovery because existing drugs have established clinical and pharmacokinetic data. Personalized medicine and repositioning both aim to improve the productivity of current drug discovery pipelines, which expend enormous time and cost to develop new drugs, only to have them fail in clinical trials because of lack of efficacy or toxicity. Here, we discuss the current state of research in these two fields, focusing on recent large-scale efforts to systematically find repositioning candidates and elucidate individual disease mechanisms in cancer. We also discuss scenarios in which personalized drug repositioning could be particularly rewarding, such as for diseases that are rare or have specific mutations, as well as current challenges in this field. With an increasing number of drugs being approved for rare cancer subtypes, personalized medicine and repositioning approaches are poised to significantly alter the way we diagnose diseases, infer treatments and develop new drugs.

title: Drug repositioning for personalized medicine
abstract: Drug repositioning, the process of identifying new therapeutic uses for existing drugs, has emerged as a promising strategy to address the high cost, lengthy timelines, and low success rates associated with traditional drug development. In parallel, personalized medicine leverages advances in genomics to stratify patients and diseases into molecular subtypes, enabling more effective and tailored treatments. This review examines the intersection of these two approaches, highlighting how repositioning can accelerate drug discovery by utilizing established safety and pharmacokinetic data, while personalized medicine can improve efficacy by targeting therapies to specific patient populations. We discuss recent successes in oncology, such as the repositioning of crizotinib for ALK-positive non-small-cell lung cancer, and explore various mechanisms by which repositioning occurs, including serendipitous clinical observations, high-throughput screening, pathway analysis, and side effect profiling. The integration of drug repositioning with personalized medicine is particularly advantageous for rare diseases and cancers with distinct molecular drivers. Despite challenges such as disease heterogeneity and incomplete understanding of drug mechanisms, ongoing large-scale efforts in computational drug design and high-throughput screening are expanding the repertoire of repositioned drugs. Together, these strategies are poised to transform drug discovery and clinical practice by enabling faster, safer, and more precise therapeutic interventions.

title: Effects and treatment methods of acupuncture and herbal medicine for premenstrual syndrome/premenstrual dysphoric disorder: systematic review
abstract: During their reproductive years about 10% of women experience some kind of symptoms before menstruation (PMS) in a degree that affects their quality of life (QOL). Acupuncture and herbal medicine has been a recent favorable therapeutic approach. Thus we aimed to review the effects of acupuncture and herbal medicine in the past decade as a preceding research in order to further investigate the most effective Korean Medicine treatment for PMS/PMDD.MethodsA systematic literature search was conducted using electronic databases on studies published between 2002 and 2012. Our review included randomized controlled clinical trials (RCTs) of acupuncture and herbal medicine for PMS/PMDD. Interventions include acupuncture or herbal medicine. Clinical information including statistical tests was extracted from the articles and summarized in tabular form or in the text. Study outcomes were presented as the rate of improvement (%) and/or end-of-treatment scores.ResultsThe search yielded 19 studies. In screening the RCTs, 8 studies in acupuncture and 11 studies in herbal medicine that matched the criteria were identified. Different acupuncture techniques including traditional acupuncture, hand acupuncture and moxibustion, and traditional acupuncture technique with auricular points, have been selected for analysis. In herbal medicine, studies on Vitex Agnus castus, Hypericum perforatum, Xiao yao san, Elsholtzia splendens, Cirsium japonicum, and Gingko biloba L. were identified. Experimental groups with Acupuncture and herbal medicine treatment (all herbal medicine except Cirsium japonicum) had significantly improved results regarding PMS/PMDD.ConclusionsLimited evidence supports the efficacy of alternative medicinal interventions such as acupuncture and herbal medicine in controlling premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder. Acupuncture and herbal medicine treatments for premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder showed a 50% or better reduction of symptoms compared to the initial state. In both acupuncture and herbal medical interventions, there have been no serious adverse events reported, proving the safety of the interventions while most of the interventions provided over 50% relief of symptoms associated with PMS/PMDD. Stricter diagnostic criteria may have excluded many participants from some studies. Also, depending on the severity of symptoms, the rate of improvement in the outcomes of the studies may have greatly differed.

title: Effects and treatment methods of acupuncture and herbal medicine for premenstrual syndrome/premenstrual dysphoric disorder: systematic review
abstract: This systematic review evaluated the efficacy and safety of acupuncture and herbal medicine in the treatment of premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) by analyzing randomized controlled trials published between 2002 and 2012. Nineteen studies met inclusion criteria, comprising eight on acupuncture and eleven on various herbal medicines, including Vitex Agnus castus, Hypericum perforatum, Xiao yao san, Elsholtzia splendens, Cirsium japonicum, and Ginkgo biloba L. The interventions demonstrated significant improvement in PMS/PMDD symptoms, with most studies reporting a 50% or greater reduction in symptom severity compared to baseline. No serious adverse events were associated with either acupuncture or herbal medicine treatments. Despite some limitations related to diagnostic criteria and heterogeneity in symptom severity among participants, the findings suggest that both acupuncture and herbal medicine are effective and safe complementary approaches for managing PMS and PMDD symptoms. Further research with standardized methodologies is recommended to confirm these results and identify optimal treatment protocols.

title: Evaluating Drug Prices, Availability, Affordability, and Price Components: Implications for Access to Drugs in Malaysia
abstract: Malaysia's stable health care system is facing challenges with increasing medicine costs. To investigate these issues a survey was carried out to evaluate medicine prices, availability, affordability, and the structure of price components. Methods and Findings The methodology developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) and Health Action International (HAI) was used. Price and availability data for 48 medicines was collected from 20 public sector facilities, 32 private sector retail pharmacies and 20 dispensing doctors in four geographical regions of West Malaysia. Medicine prices were compared with international reference prices (IRPs) to obtain a median price ratio. The daily wage of the lowest paid unskilled government worker was used to gauge the affordability of medicines. Price component data were collected throughout the supply chain, and markups, taxes, and other distribution costs were identified. In private pharmacies, innovator brand (IB) prices were 16 times higher than the IRPs, while generics were 6.6 times higher. In dispensing doctor clinics, the figures were 15 times higher for innovator brands and 7.5 for generics. Dispensing doctors applied high markups of 50%–76% for IBs, and up to 316% for generics. Retail pharmacy markups were also high—25%–38% and 100%–140% for IBs and generics, respectively. In the public sector, where medicines are free, availability was low even for medicines on the National Essential Drugs List. For a month's treatment for peptic ulcer disease and hypertension people have to pay about a week's wages in the private sector. Conclusions The free market by definition does not control medicine prices, necessitating price monitoring and control mechanisms. Markups for generic products are greater than for IBs. Reducing the base price without controlling markups may increase profits for retailers and dispensing doctors without reducing the price paid by end users. To increase access and affordability, promotion of generic medicines and improved availability of medicines in the public sector are required.

title: Evaluating Drug Prices, Availability, Affordability, and Price Components: Implications for Access to Drugs in Malaysia
abstract: This study assessed medicine prices, availability, affordability, and price components in Malaysia to evaluate their impact on access to essential drugs. Using the World Health Organization and Health Action International methodology, data were collected on 48 medicines from public sector facilities, private retail pharmacies, and dispensing doctors across four regions of West Malaysia. Prices were compared to international reference prices, and affordability was measured using the daily wage of the lowest-paid government worker. The findings revealed that private sector prices for innovator brands and generics were significantly higher than international reference prices, with substantial markups at both retail pharmacies and dispensing doctors’ clinics. Public sector availability was low even for essential medicines, while out-of-pocket costs in the private sector often equated to a week’s wages for common treatments. The analysis of price components indicated that markups on generics exceeded those on innovator brands, suggesting that reducing base prices without controlling markups may not benefit consumers. The study concludes that Malaysia’s free-market approach necessitates price monitoring and control mechanisms to improve access and affordability, emphasizing the need for greater promotion of generics and enhanced public sector medicine availability.

title: Evoked potentials in clinical medicine.
abstract: Recent technological advances have facilitated the conduct of evoked potential studies, and permitted their wider use in a clinical context. Evoked potential studies are performed to determine the presence, extent and site of disease of the peripheral and central sensory pathways. This may be helpful for diagnostic purposes, and for characterizing more completely the changes occurring in various diseases. Certain evoked potential components have also been used in the evaluation of cognitive function. The major uses and limitations of evoked potential studies in clinical medicine are reviewed, but technical details are not provided in the interest of simplicity.

title: Evoked potentials in clinical medicine.
abstract: This book provides a comprehensive overview of the use of evoked potentials in clinical medicine, targeting medical and paramedical professionals involved in clinical diagnosis and evaluation. Organized into sections on visual, brainstem auditory, and somatosensory evoked potentials, the text emphasizes methodology and clinical findings, offering extensive references primarily from recent decades. While the methodological chapters are somewhat repetitive and less detailed than other sources, the strength of the book lies in its thorough compilation of clinical data, particularly in somatosensory evoked potentials and their application to conditions such as multiple sclerosis. The text is well-illustrated with clear figures and captions, facilitating independent understanding. However, the book is limited by an inadequate index, making topic-specific searches challenging, and by a tendency to present findings without synthesizing their implications for clinical decision-making. Despite these shortcomings, the volume serves as a valuable starting point for clinicians seeking to familiarize themselves with the field of evoked potentials and provides a solid foundation for further exploration of the literature.

title: Facilitators and barriers of herbal medicine use in Accra, Ghana: an inductive exploratory study
abstract: The use of complementary and alternative medicine including herbal medicine is increasing in many countries including Ghana. However, there is paucity of research on the perspectives of patrons of herbal medicine regarding the facilitators and barriers of herbal medicine use. This study sought to investigate the facilitators and barriers of herbal medicine among Ghanaian adults who use one form of herbal medicine or the other.MethodsThe study employed an inductive exploratory qualitative approach. It was conducted at a private herbal clinic in Accra. Purposive sampling was employed to recruit 16 participants. Data collection was through individual face-to-face interviews and these were transcribed and analysed using content analysis procedures.ResultsIt was realized that the factors that enhanced the use of herbal medicine included use of convincing information to enhance the initiation of herbal medicine use, effectiveness of herbal medicine, personal preference for herbal medicine, perceived ineffectiveness of western medicine and integration of spirituality in herbal medicine. The factors that hindered herbal medicine use included negative perceptions and attitudes about herbal medicine, poor vending environment, poor knowledge of vendors, high cost of herbal products at credible herbal clinics and inconsistent effectiveness of some herbal products. Participants desired that the national health insurance scheme will cover the cost of herbal medicine to alleviate the financial burden associated with herbal medicine use.ConclusionAlthough some Ghanaians patronize herbal medicine, the negative perceptions about herbal medicine resulting from deceitful producers and vendors call for enhanced education and monitoring to ensure that effective herbal products are used.

title: Facilitators and barriers of herbal medicine use in Accra, Ghana: an inductive exploratory study
abstract: This inductive exploratory qualitative study investigated the facilitators and barriers to herbal medicine use among adults attending a private herbal clinic in Accra, Ghana. Sixteen participants were purposively sampled and interviewed face-to-face, with data analyzed using content analysis. Facilitators identified included convincing information promoting initiation, perceived effectiveness of herbal medicine, personal preference, dissatisfaction with western medicine, and the integration of spirituality. Barriers encompassed negative perceptions and attitudes, poor vending environments, inadequate knowledge among vendors, high costs at reputable clinics, and inconsistent product effectiveness. Participants expressed a desire for national health insurance coverage of herbal medicine to reduce financial burdens. The findings highlight the need for enhanced public education and regulatory monitoring to address negative perceptions and ensure the safety and efficacy of herbal products in Ghana’s healthcare landscape.

title: Factors related to the choice of family medicine: a reassessment and literature review.
abstract: Recent decreases in the number of students entering family medicine has prompted reconsideration of what is known about the factors affecting specialty choice. METHODS Thirty-six articles on family medicine specialty choice published since 1993 were reviewed and rated for quality. RESULTS Rural background related positively and parents' socioeconomic status relates negatively to choice of family medicine. Career intentions at entry to medical school predict specialty choice. Students who believe primary care is important, have low income expectations, and do not plan a research career are more likely to choose family medicine. The school characteristic related to choice of family medicine is public ownership. Large programs to increase numbers entering primary care seem effective. Required family medicine time in clinical years is related to higher numbers selecting family medicine. Faculty role models serve both as positive and negative influences. Students rejecting family medicine are concerned about prestige, low income, and breadth of knowledge required. Students planning on a career in a disadvantaged or rural area are more likely to enter family medicine. CONCLUSIONS Multiple factors are consistently shown to be related to the choice of the specialty of family medicine.
venue: The Journal of the American Board of Family Practice

title: Factors related to the choice of family medicine: a reassessment and literature review.
abstract: This literature review reassesses factors influencing medical students’ choice of family medicine as a specialty by analyzing 36 articles published since 1993. The findings indicate that a rural background and lower parental socioeconomic status are positively associated with selecting family medicine, while higher parental socioeconomic status has a negative association. Early career intentions toward primary care, valuing the importance of primary care, lower income expectations, and lack of interest in research careers also predict a greater likelihood of choosing family medicine. Publicly owned medical schools and required family medicine clinical experiences increase the number of students entering the field, and comprehensive primary care programs are effective in boosting interest.
