Faculty role models can exert both positive and negative influences. Students who do not choose family medicine often cite concerns about prestige, income, and the broad knowledge base required. Those intending to practice in rural or underserved areas are more likely to select family medicine. The review concludes that multiple, consistent factors—including student background, values, school characteristics, and educational experiences—shape specialty choice, highlighting areas for targeted interventions to address declining interest in family medicine.
venue: The Journal of the American Board of Family Practice

title: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology in General Medicine
abstract: New knowledge drives medical progress and improves patient care. The rapid growth of this knowledge in skin diseases and skin biology makes publication of the eighth edition of Fitzpatrick's Dermatology in General Medicine (DIGM) particularly timely. Forty years ago, the first edition of “Fitz” was a critical textbook devoted to providing a comprehensive knowledge of dermatology. The relevance of dermatology to general medicine and the basic science foundations of the specialty were defining elements of the new text. This edition, more than ever, reinforces those earlier goals and is designed to be easily accessible to those interested in the clinical and basic science of dermatology. This reference text also highlights the relevance of dermatology to general internal medicine and other disciplines of medicine and surgery. It is written for experienced clinicians and skin biologists worldwide as well as for those in training.

title: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology in General Medicine
abstract: The seventh edition of Fitzpatrick’s Dermatology in General Medicine represents a comprehensive and thoroughly updated resource reflecting the rapid advancements in dermatological science and clinical practice. This edition features significant reorganization, integrating basic sciences within relevant clinical sections to enhance continuity and learning. New chapters address emerging topics such as public health, complementary and alternative dermatology, drug interactions, and dermatology in bioterrorism, broadening the scope for modern practitioners. Enhanced visual aids—including color plates, figures, tables, and summary boxes—facilitate efficient assimilation of complex information. The inclusion of concise differential diagnoses and treatment protocols, along with user-friendly design elements like color-coded headings and margin thumbnails, further supports quick reference and retention. Overall, this edition solidifies Fitzpatrick’s status as an essential, authoritative text for both trainees and experienced dermatologists seeking current, accessible knowledge in the field.

title: Franklin H. Epstein Lecture: Sirtuins, aging, and medicine.
abstract: In this year's Franklin H. Epstein Lecture, Leonard Guarente summarizes the many biologic properties of the sirtuin family of deacetylases and explains why enhancement or inhibition of specific sirtuins may influence many common diseases and longevity.

title: Franklin H. Epstein Lecture: Sirtuins, aging, and medicine.
abstract: This review examines the role of sirtuins, a family of NAD-dependent protein deacetylases, in the regulation of aging and age-related diseases, highlighting their evolutionary conservation from yeast to mammals. Sirtuins, particularly SIRT1, modulate key metabolic pathways, stress responses, circadian rhythms, and inflammation by deacetylating a range of transcription factors and cofactors. Evidence from model organisms and mammalian studies suggests that sirtuins contribute to increased lifespan and mediate beneficial effects of calorie restriction. In mammals, SIRT1 influences metabolic health by promoting insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial biogenesis, and adaptive responses to energy limitation, while also exerting anti-inflammatory and DNA repair functions. Pharmacological activation of sirtuins, notably through compounds such as resveratrol and synthetic activators, has shown promise in mitigating metabolic decline and protecting against diabetes, obesity, bone loss, and certain cancers in animal models. However, the direct mechanisms of action for these compounds remain under investigation. The review underscores the therapeutic potential of targeting sirtuin pathways to delay aging and treat age-associated diseases but emphasizes the need for further research to clarify their complex roles in human health and disease.

title: From big data analysis to personalized medicine for all: challenges and opportunities
abstract: Recent advances in high-throughput technologies have led to the emergence of systems biology as a holistic science to achieve more precise modeling of complex diseases. Many predict the emergence of personalized medicine in the near future. We are, however, moving from two-tiered health systems to a two-tiered personalized medicine. Omics facilities are restricted to affluent regions, and personalized medicine is likely to widen the growing gap in health systems between high and low-income countries. This is mirrored by an increasing lag between our ability to generate and analyze big data. Several bottlenecks slow-down the transition from conventional to personalized medicine: generation of cost-effective high-throughput data; hybrid education and multidisciplinary teams; data storage and processing; data integration and interpretation; and individual and global economic relevance. This review provides an update of important developments in the analysis of big data and forward strategies to accelerate the global transition to personalized medicine.

title: From big data analysis to personalized medicine for all: challenges and opportunities
abstract: Advances in high-throughput omics technologies and systems biology have accelerated the promise of personalized medicine, yet significant challenges remain in translating big data into equitable healthcare solutions. This review examines the socioeconomic and scientific barriers impeding the global adoption of personalized medicine, highlighting disparities between high- and low-income countries in access to omics infrastructure, data analysis capabilities, and multidisciplinary expertise. The transition from conventional to personalized medicine is slowed by bottlenecks in data generation, storage, integration, interpretation, and economic evaluation. While technological innovations continue to improve data acquisition efficiency, the costs and complexities of data analysis pose persistent obstacles. The review discusses strategies such as micro-grants, interdisciplinary training, and global collaborations to foster innovation and bridge gaps in resource-limited settings. Ultimately, achieving personalized medicine for all will require coordinated efforts to address economic inequalities, enhance translational research capacity, and develop sustainable models for integrating big data into diverse healthcare systems.

title: From Big Data to Precision Medicine
abstract: For over a decade the term “Big data” has been used to describe the rapid increase in volume, variety and velocity of information available, not just in medical research but in almost every aspect of our lives. As scientists, we now have the capacity to rapidly generate, store and analyse data that, only a few years ago, would have taken many years to compile. However, “Big data” no longer means what it once did. The term has expanded and now refers not to just large data volume, but to our increasing ability to analyse and interpret those data. Tautologies such as “data analytics” and “data science” have emerged to describe approaches to the volume of available information as it grows ever larger. New methods dedicated to improving data collection, storage, cleaning, processing and interpretation continue to be developed, although not always by, or for, medical researchers. Exploiting new tools to extract meaning from large volume information has the potential to drive real change in clinical practice, from personalized therapy and intelligent drug design to population screening and electronic health record mining. As ever, where new technology promises “Big Advances,” significant challenges remain. Here we discuss both the opportunities and challenges posed to biomedical research by our increasing ability to tackle large datasets. Important challenges include the need for standardization of data content, format, and clinical definitions, a heightened need for collaborative networks with sharing of both data and expertise and, perhaps most importantly, a need to reconsider how and when analytic methodology is taught to medical researchers. We also set “Big data” analytics in context: recent advances may appear to promise a revolution, sweeping away conventional approaches to medical science. However, their real promise lies in their synergy with, not replacement of, classical hypothesis-driven methods. The generation of novel, data-driven hypotheses based on interpretable models will always require stringent validation and experimental testing. Thus, hypothesis-generating research founded on large datasets adds to, rather than replaces, traditional hypothesis driven science. Each can benefit from the other and it is through using both that we can improve clinical practice.

title: From Big Data to Precision Medicine
abstract: The advent of big data has transformed biomedical research by enabling the rapid generation, storage, and analysis of vast and complex datasets, fostering a shift from traditional hypothesis-driven approaches to hypothesis-generating, data-driven methodologies. This review explores the evolving definition of big data in medicine, emphasizing its role in uncovering novel disease pathways and informing precision medicine strategies aimed at delivering tailored treatments to individual patients. Key challenges are identified, including the need for standardized data formats, robust technical infrastructure, enhanced data sharing and collaboration, and improved analytic training for medical researchers. The review highlights the contrast between the open data environments of successful industries and the siloed, sensitive nature of medical data, underscoring barriers to widespread adoption of big data analytics in healthcare. Ultimately, the synergy between big data-driven discovery and classical experimental validation is essential for translating large-scale biomedical insights into clinical practice, with each approach complementing and strengthening the other in the pursuit of improved patient outcomes.

title: Guidelines for Field Surveys of the Quality of Medicines: A Proposal
abstract: Paul Newton and colleagues propose guidelines for conducting and reporting field surveys of the quality of medicines.

title: Guidelines for Field Surveys of the Quality of Medicines: A Proposal
abstract: Poor-quality medicines, including counterfeit, substandard, and degraded products, pose significant threats to public health, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where regulatory oversight is limited. Despite the global importance of this issue, reliable data on the prevalence and distribution of poor-quality medicines are scarce, largely due to methodological shortcomings in field surveys. This paper reviews existing literature and expert opinion to propose guidelines for conducting statistically valid field surveys of medicine quality. It highlights the limitations of convenience sampling, which is prone to bias and lacks representativeness, and advocates for standardized random sampling strategies that enable accurate estimation of the prevalence of poor-quality medicines and outlets selling them. The authors also introduce a draft checklist—the Medicine Quality Assessment Reporting Guidelines (MEDQUARG)—to improve transparency and consistency in reporting survey methodologies and findings. By providing practical recommendations for sampling design, data collection, and reporting, this proposal aims to facilitate robust surveillance of medicine quality and inform policy interventions to safeguard public health.

title: Herbal Medicines in African Traditional Medicine
abstract: African traditional medicine is a form of holistic health care system organized into three levels of specialty, namely divination, spiritualism, and herbalism. The traditional healer provides health care services based on culture, religious background, knowledge, attitudes, and beliefs that are prevalent in his community. Illness is regarded as having both natural and supernatural causes and thus must be treated by both physical and spiritual means, using divination, incantations, animal sacrifice, exorcism, and herbs. Herbal medicine is the cornerstone of traditional medicine but may include minerals and animal parts. The adjustment is ok, but may be replaced with –‘ Herbal medicine was once termed primitive by western medicine but through scientific investigations there is a better understanding of its therapeutic activities such that many pharmaceuticals have been modeled on phytochemicals derived from it. Major obstacles to the use of African medicinal plants are their poor quality control and safety. Traditional medical practices are still shrouded with much secrecy, with few reports or documentations of adverse reactions. However, the future of African traditional medicine is bright if viewed in the context of service provision, increase of health care coverage, economic potential, and poverty reduction. Formal recognition and integration of traditional medicine into conventional medicine will hold much promise for the future.

title: Herbal Medicines in African Traditional Medicine
abstract: African traditional medicine represents a holistic healthcare system that integrates divination, spiritualism, and herbalism, with herbal medicine serving as its cornerstone. This chapter explores the historical development, cultural context, and therapeutic practices of herbal medicine within African traditional medicine, highlighting the roles of traditional healers and the complex interplay between physical and spiritual approaches to illness. Herbal medicines, derived from diverse plant parts and sometimes combined with minerals or animal products, are widely used due to their accessibility, affordability, and cultural acceptance. Despite being historically marginalized by colonial and Western medical paradigms, scientific research has increasingly validated the efficacy of many African medicinal plants, leading to the development of pharmaceuticals based on their phytochemicals. Challenges persist regarding quality control, safety, standardization, and documentation of adverse effects. Nevertheless, the integration of traditional medicine into formal healthcare systems presents significant opportunities for expanding healthcare coverage, supporting economic development, and preserving indigenous knowledge in Africa.

title: Herbal medicine research and global health: an ethical analysis.
abstract: Governments, international agencies and corporations are increasingly investing in traditional herbal medicine research. Yet little literature addresses ethical challenges in this research. In this paper, we apply concepts in a comprehensive ethical framework for clinical research to international traditional herbal medicine research. We examine in detail three key, underappreciated dimensions of the ethical framework in which particularly difficult questions arise for international herbal medicine research: social value, scientific validity and favourable risk-benefit ratio. Significant challenges exist in determining shared concepts of social value, scientific validity and favourable risk-benefit ratio across international research collaborations. However, we argue that collaborative partnership, including democratic deliberation, offers the context and process by which many of the ethical challenges in international herbal medicine research can, and should be, resolved. By 'cross-training' investigators, and investing in safety-monitoring infrastructure, the issues identified by this comprehensive framework can promote ethically sound international herbal medicine research that contributes to global health.
venue: Bulletin of the World Health Organization

title: Herbal medicine research and global health: an ethical analysis.
abstract: As global investment in traditional herbal medicine research grows, critical ethical challenges remain underexplored. This paper applies a comprehensive ethical framework for clinical research to international herbal medicine studies, focusing on the dimensions of social value, scientific validity, and favourable risk–benefit ratio. We analyze how differing cultural perspectives and regulatory standards complicate consensus on these ethical requirements in global collaborations. Using a case study of an HIV treatment trial involving a traditional African remedy, we illustrate the complexities inherent in evaluating efficacy, safety, and community benefit. We argue that collaborative partnerships—characterized by mutual respect, democratic deliberation, and capacity-building—are essential for addressing these challenges. By fostering cross-disciplinary training and investing in safety-monitoring infrastructure, stakeholders can ensure that international herbal medicine research is ethically robust and contributes meaningfully to global health.
venue: Bulletin of the World Health Organization

title: Herbal medicine use among urban residents in Lagos, Nigeria
abstract: Over three-quarter of the world's population is using herbal medicines with an increasing trend globally. Herbal medicines may be beneficial but are not completely harmless.This study aimed to assess the extent of use and the general knowledge of the benefits and safety of herbal medicines among urban residents in Lagos, Nigeria.MethodsThe study involved 388 participants recruited by cluster and random sampling techniques. Participants were interviewed with a structured open- and close-ended questionnaire.The information obtained comprises the demography and types of herbal medicines used by the respondents; indications for their use; the sources, benefits and adverse effects of the herbal medicines they used.ResultsA total of 12 herbal medicines (crude or refined) were used by the respondents, either alone or in combination with other herbal medicines. Herbal medicines were reportedly used by 259 (66.8%) respondents. 'Agbo jedi-jedi' (35%) was the most frequently used herbal medicine preparation, followed by 'agbo-iba' (27.5%) and Oroki herbal mixture® (9%). Family and friends had a marked influence on 78.4% of the respondents who used herbal medicine preparations. Herbal medicines were considered safe by half of the respondents despite 20.8% of those who experienced mild to moderate adverse effects.ConclusionsHerbal medicine is popular among the respondents but they appear to be ignorant of its potential toxicities. It may be necessary to evaluate the safety, efficacy and quality of herbal medicines and their products through randomised clinical trial studies. Public enlightenment programme about safe use of herbal medicines may be necessary as a means of minimizing the potential adverse effects.

title: Herbal medicine use among urban residents in Lagos, Nigeria
abstract: This study investigated the prevalence, patterns, and perceptions of herbal medicine use among 388 urban residents in Surulere Local Government Area, Lagos, Nigeria, using structured interviews and questionnaires. Results showed that 66.8% of respondents reported using herbal medicines, with 'agbo jedi-jedi' being the most commonly used preparation. Family and friends significantly influenced usage decisions for 78.4% of users. Despite half of the respondents perceiving herbal medicines as safe, 20.8% reported experiencing mild to moderate adverse effects. The findings highlight widespread use and limited awareness of potential toxicities associated with herbal medicines among urban Lagos residents, underscoring the need for public education on safe use and further evaluation of the safety and efficacy of these products through clinical studies.

title: Herbal medicine use in pregnancy: results of a multinational study
abstract: The use of complementary and alternative medicines (CAM) is growing in the general population. Herbal medicines are used in all countries of the world and are included in the top CAM therapies used.MethodsA multinational study on how women treat disease and pregnancy-related health ailments was conducted between October 2011 and February 2012 in Europe, North and South America and Australia. In this study, the primary aim was to determine the prevalence of herbal medicine use in pregnancy and factors related to such use across participating countries and regions. The secondary aim was to investigate who recommended the use of herbal medication in pregnancy.ResultsThere were 9,459 women from 23 countries participating in the study. Of these, 28.9% reported the use of herbal medicines in pregnancy. Most herbal medicines were used for pregnancy-related health ailments such as cold and nausea. Ginger, cranberry, valerian and raspberry were the most commonly used herbs in pregnancy. The highest reported rate of herbal use medicines was in Russia (69%). Women from Eastern Europe (51.8%) and Australia (43.8%) were twice as likely to use an herbal medicine versus other regions. Women using herbal medicines were characteristically having their first child, non-smokers, using folic acid and consuming some alcohol in pregnancy. Also, women who were currently students and women with an education other than a high school degree were more likely to use herbal medicines than other women. Although 1 out of 5 women stated that a physician had recommended the herbal use, most women used herbal medicine in pregnancy on their own initiative.ConclusionsIn this multinational study herbal medicine use in pregnancy was high although there were distinct differences in the herbs and users of herbal medicines across regions. Most commonly the women self-medicated with herbal medicine to treat pregnancy-related health ailments. More knowledge regarding the efficacy and safety of herbal medicines in pregnancy is warranted.

title: Herbal medicine use in pregnancy: results of a multinational study
abstract: This multinational, cross-sectional, internet-based study investigated the prevalence and determinants of herbal medicine use during pregnancy among 9,459 women from 23 countries across Europe, North and South America, and Australia. The findings revealed that 28.9% of participants reported using herbal medicines during pregnancy, with significant regional variation—highest in Russia (69%), Eastern Europe (51.8%), and Australia (43.8%). Herbal medicines were most commonly used to manage pregnancy-related ailments such as colds and nausea, with ginger, cranberry, valerian, and raspberry being the most frequently reported herbs. Women more likely to use herbal medicines tended to be first-time mothers, non-smokers, users of folic acid, occasional alcohol consumers, students, or those with education beyond high school. While one in five women received a physician’s recommendation for herbal use, most initiated use independently. The study highlights widespread self-medication with herbal products during pregnancy and underscores the need for further research on their safety and efficacy in this population.

title: History of cannabis as a medicine: a review.
abstract: Cannabis as a medicine was used before the Christian era in Asia, mainly in India. The introduction of cannabis in the Western medicine occurred in the midst of the 19th century, reaching the climax in the last decade of that century, with the availability and usage of cannabis extracts or tinctures. In the first decades of the 20th century, the Western medical use of cannabis significantly decreased largely due to difficulties to obtain consistent results from batches of plant material of different potencies. The identification of the chemical structure of cannabis components and the possibility of obtaining its pure constituents were related to a significant increase in scientific interest in such plant, since 1965. This interest was renewed in the 1990's with the description of cannabinoid receptors and the identification of an endogenous cannabinoid system in the brain. A new and more consistent cycle of the use of cannabis derivatives as medication begins, since treatment effectiveness and safety started to be scientifically proven.

title: History of cannabis as a medicine: a review.
abstract: Cannabis has a long history of medicinal use, originating in Asia before the Christian era, particularly in India, where it was integral to both medical and religious practices. Its introduction into Western medicine occurred in the mid-19th century, reaching peak usage by the late 1800s through extracts and tinctures. However, medical use declined in the early 20th century due to inconsistent potency in plant material and challenges in standardization. Scientific interest was renewed after the identification of cannabis’ chemical constituents in 1965 and further intensified in the 1990s with the discovery of cannabinoid receptors and the endogenous cannabinoid system in the brain. These advances have led to a new era of research and more consistent therapeutic applications, as efficacy and safety of cannabis derivatives are increasingly supported by scientific evidence. This review traces the historical trajectory of cannabis as a medicine, highlighting its shifting roles across cultures and time periods, and underscores the recent resurgence of interest based on modern pharmacological discoveries.

title: Hormesis and medicine.
abstract: Evidence is presented which supports the conclusion that the hormetic dose-response model is the most common and fundamental in the biological and biomedical sciences, being highly generalizable across biological model, endpoint measured and chemical class and physical agent. The paper provides a broad spectrum of applications of the hormesis concept for clinical medicine including anxiety, seizure, memory, stroke, cancer chemotherapy, dermatological processes such as hair growth, osteoporosis, ocular diseases, including retinal detachment, statin effects on cardiovascular function and tumour development, benign prostate enlargement, male sexual behaviours/dysfunctions, and prion diseases.

title: Hormesis and medicine.
abstract: This paper presents comprehensive evidence that the hormetic dose–response model, characterized by low-dose stimulation and high-dose inhibition, is a fundamental and highly generalizable principle in biological and biomedical sciences. Drawing from an extensive database of approximately 8000 dose–responses across diverse biological models, endpoints, and agents, the paper details the quantitative features, mechanistic underpinnings, and clinical implications of hormesis. The hormetic response is shown to be modest in magnitude yet consistent across species, organ systems, and endpoints, suggesting an adaptive evolutionary strategy. Mechanistic explanations include receptor subtype interactions and adaptive/preconditioning responses. The paper discusses the independence of hormetic responses from interindividual variation in susceptibility and highlights the relevance of hormesis to drug interactions, therapeutic windows, and adverse effect profiles. Applications span a wide range of medical conditions including anxiety, seizures, memory, stroke, cancer chemotherapy, osteoporosis, ocular diseases, cardiovascular function, prostate enlargement, sexual dysfunctions, and prion diseases. The findings challenge traditional dose–response assumptions and underscore the need to integrate hormesis into clinical pharmacology for improved drug development and patient care strategies.

title: Hospital Readmission in General Medicine Patients: A Prediction Model
abstract: Previous studies of hospital readmission have focused on specific conditions or populations and generated complex prediction models.ObjectiveTo identify predictors of early hospital readmission in a diverse patient population and derive and validate a simple model for identifying patients at high readmission risk.DesignProspective observational cohort study.PatientsParticipants encompassed 10,946 patients discharged home from general medicine services at six academic medical centers and were randomly divided into derivation (n = 7,287) and validation (n = 3,659) cohorts.MeasurementsWe identified readmissions from administrative data and 30-day post-discharge telephone follow-up. Patient-level factors were grouped into four categories: sociodemographic factors, social support, health condition, and healthcare utilization. We performed logistic regression analysis to identify significant predictors of unplanned readmission within 30 days of discharge and developed a scoring system for estimating readmission risk.ResultsApproximately 17.5% of patients were readmitted in each cohort. Among patients in the derivation cohort, seven factors emerged as significant predictors of early readmission: insurance status, marital status, having a regular physician, Charlson comorbidity index, SF12 physical component score, ≥1 admission(s) within the last year, and current length of stay >2 days. A cumulative risk score of ≥25 points identified 5% of patients with a readmission risk of approximately 30% in each cohort. Model discrimination was fair with a c-statistic of 0.65 and 0.61 for the derivation and validation cohorts, respectively.ConclusionsSelect patient characteristics easily available shortly after admission can be used to identify a subset of patients at elevated risk of early readmission. This information may guide the efficient use of interventions to prevent readmission.

title: Hospital Readmission in General Medicine Patients: A Prediction Model
abstract: This study aimed to identify predictors of early hospital readmission among general medicine patients and to develop and validate a simple risk prediction model. In a prospective cohort of 10,946 patients discharged home from six academic medical centers, patients were randomly assigned to derivation (n=7,287) and validation (n=3,659) cohorts. Readmissions within 30 days were identified using administrative data and post-discharge telephone follow-up. Logistic regression analysis examined patient-level factors across sociodemographic, social support, health condition, and healthcare utilization domains. Seven variables—insurance status, marital status, having a regular physician, Charlson comorbidity index, SF12 physical component score, prior admissions in the past year, and current length of stay >2 days—were significant predictors of readmission. A cumulative risk score of ≥25 points identified 5% of patients with a 30% readmission risk in both cohorts. Model discrimination was fair (c-statistic 0.65 derivation; 0.61 validation). Easily obtainable patient characteristics shortly after admission can identify those at elevated risk for early readmission and may inform targeted interventions to reduce readmissions.

title: Hydrogels for Regenerative Medicine
abstract: Regenerative medicine requires materials that are biodegradable, biocompatible, struc‐ turally and chemically stable, and that can mimic the properties of the native extracellular matrix (ECM). Hydrogels are hydrophilic three-dimensional networks that have long re‐ ceived attention in the field of regenerative medicine due to their unique properties. Hy‐ drogels have a potential to be the future of regenerative medicine due to their desirable mechanical and chemical properties, ease of their synthesis, and their multiple applicabil‐ ity as drug delivery vehicles, scaffolds, and constructs for cell culture. In this chapter, we have described hydrogels in terms of their cross-linking and then discussed the most re‐ cent developments in the use of hydrogels for peripheral nerve regeneration, tooth regen‐ eration, and 3D bioprinting.

title: Hydrogels for Regenerative Medicine
abstract: Hydrogels, as hydrophilic three-dimensional polymer networks, have emerged as promising materials in regenerative medicine due to their ability to mimic the native extracellular matrix, support cell adhesion and proliferation, and provide tunable mechanical and chemical properties. This chapter reviews the classification of hydrogels based on physical and chemical cross-linking mechanisms, highlighting their structural stability, biocompatibility, and biodegradability. Advances in hydrogel design, including the development of stimuli-responsive and nanocomposite hydrogels, are discussed with a focus on their application as scaffolds for tissue engineering, drug delivery systems, and constructs for cell culture. Particular emphasis is placed on recent innovations in using hydrogels for peripheral nerve regeneration, tooth regeneration, and 3D bioprinting. The versatility and adaptability of hydrogels underscore their potential to address key challenges in regenerative medicine by providing physiologically relevant environments that closely resemble in vivo conditions.

title: Hygiene, Sanitation, and Water: Forgotten Foundations of Health
abstract: As the first article in a four-part PLoS Medicine series on water and sanitation, Jamie Bartram and Sandy Cairncross argue that the massive burden of ill health associated with poor hygiene, sanitation, and water supply demands more attention from health professionals and policymakers.

title: Hygiene, Sanitation, and Water: Forgotten Foundations of Health
abstract: Deficiencies in hygiene, sanitation, and water (HSW) remain major but often overlooked contributors to global disease burden, particularly among children in developing countries. This introductory article to a PLoS Medicine series highlights that inadequate HSW is responsible for millions of preventable deaths and a significant proportion of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), primarily through diarrhoeal diseases and malnutrition-related conditions. Despite proven, cost-effective interventions capable of reducing diarrhoeal disease by up to two-thirds, HSW receives insufficient attention from the public health community compared to higher-profile diseases. The paper reviews the extensive health impacts of poor HSW, including its role in infectious diseases, malnutrition, and broader child mortality, and emphasizes the need for effective behaviour change strategies and policy prioritization. The authors argue that the benefits of improving HSW extend beyond health outcomes to economic and social gains, underscoring the critical importance of renewed commitment from health professionals and policymakers to address these foundational determinants of health.

title: Implementing the 27 PRISMA 2020 Statement items for systematic reviews in the sport and exercise medicine, musculoskeletal rehabilitation and sports science fields: the PERSiST (implementing Prisma in Exercise, Rehabilitation, Sport medicine and SporTs science) guidance
abstract: Poor reporting of medical and healthcare systematic reviews is a problem from which the sports and exercise medicine, musculoskeletal rehabilitation, and sports science fields are not immune. Transparent, accurate and comprehensive systematic review reporting helps researchers replicate methods, readers understand what was done and why, and clinicians and policy-makers implement results in practice. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Statement and its accompanying Explanation and Elaboration document provide general reporting examples for systematic reviews of healthcare interventions. However, implementation guidance for sport and exercise medicine, musculoskeletal rehabilitation, and sports science does not exist. The Prisma in Exercise, Rehabilitation, Sport medicine and SporTs science (PERSiST) guidance attempts to address this problem. Nineteen content experts collaborated with three methods experts to identify examples of exemplary reporting in systematic reviews in sport and exercise medicine (including physical activity), musculoskeletal rehabilitation (including physiotherapy), and sports science, for each of the PRISMA 2020 Statement items. PERSiST aims to help: (1) systematic reviewers improve the transparency and reporting of systematic reviews and (2) journal editors and peer reviewers make informed decisions about systematic review reporting quality.

title: Implementing the 27 PRISMA 2020 Statement items for systematic reviews in the sport and exercise medicine, musculoskeletal rehabilitation and sports science fields: the PERSiST (implementing Prisma in Exercise, Rehabilitation, Sport medicine and SporTs science) guidance
abstract: Poor reporting of systematic reviews remains a significant challenge in sport and exercise medicine, musculoskeletal rehabilitation, and sports science, limiting the utility and reproducibility of research findings. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 Statement provides general guidance for systematic review reporting but lacks field-specific implementation support. To address this gap, the PERSiST (implementing Prisma in Exercise, Rehabilitation, Sport medicine and SporTs science) guidance was developed through collaboration among 19 content experts and three methodologists. The team identified exemplary reporting examples for each of the 27 PRISMA 2020 items, tailored to the contexts of sport and exercise medicine, musculoskeletal rehabilitation, and sports science. PERSiST aims to enhance transparency, accuracy, and comprehensiveness in systematic review reporting within these fields by providing practical, context-specific examples. This guidance supports systematic reviewers in improving their reporting practices and assists journal editors and peer reviewers in assessing the quality of systematic reviews. By facilitating the implementation of PRISMA 2020 standards, PERSiST seeks to strengthen evidence synthesis and promote informed decision-making in clinical practice and research.

title: Internationalization of traditional Chinese medicine: current international market, internationalization challenges and prospective suggestions
abstract: Through reviewing the current international market for traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), this paper identified the internationalization challenges for TCM, including unclear therapeutic material basis and mechanism, difficulty of quality control, low preparation level, registration/policy barriers, and shortage of intellectual property. To deal with these challenges, suggestions were given including: (1) product innovation of TCM (study the TCM by using the methods and means of western medicine; innovate the basic theory of TCM; develop TCM health product); (2) standard innovation of TCM; (3) building big data platform of Chinese medicine (big data platform of TCM preparation; big data platform on the quality of TCM).

title: Internationalization of traditional Chinese medicine: current international market, internationalization challenges and prospective suggestions
abstract: This review examines the current state of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) in the international market, highlighting recent declines in export volume and value despite growing global interest. Analysis reveals that TCM exports are concentrated in Asia and the United States, with significant barriers to entry including stringent regulatory requirements, high policy thresholds, and technical trade barriers. Additional challenges impeding TCM internationalization include unclear therapeutic mechanisms, difficulties in quality control, low levels of product innovation, and insufficient intellectual property protection. To address these issues, the paper proposes strategies such as integrating Western scientific methods to clarify TCM mechanisms, innovating both products and standards, and leveraging big data platforms for quality assurance and research. These approaches aim to enhance the global competitiveness and sustainable development of TCM in international markets.

title: Joint EANM/EANO/RANO practice guidelines/SNMMI procedure standards for imaging of gliomas using PET with radiolabelled amino acids and [18F]FDG: version 1.0
abstract: These joint practice guidelines, or procedure standards, were developed collaboratively by the European Association of Nuclear Medicine (EANM), the Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging (SNMMI), the European Association of Neurooncology (EANO), and the working group for Response Assessment in Neurooncology with PET (PET-RANO). Brain PET imaging is being increasingly used to supplement MRI in the clinical management of glioma. The aim of these standards/guidelines is to assist nuclear medicine practitioners in recommending, performing, interpreting and reporting the results of brain PET imaging in patients with glioma to achieve a high-quality imaging standard for PET using FDG and the radiolabelled amino acids MET, FET and FDOPA. This will help promote the appropriate use of PET imaging and contribute to evidence-based medicine that may improve the diagnostic impact of this technique in neurooncological practice. The present document replaces a former version of the guidelines published in 2006 (Vander Borght et al. Eur J Nucl Med Mol Imaging. 33:1374–80, 2006), and supplements a recent evidence-based recommendation by the PET-RANO working group and EANO on the clinical use of PET imaging in patients with glioma (Albert et al. Neuro Oncol. 18:1199–208, 2016). The information provided should be taken in the context of local conditions and regulations.
venue: European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging

title: Joint EANM/EANO/RANO practice guidelines/SNMMI procedure standards for imaging of gliomas using PET with radiolabelled amino acids and [18F]FDG: version 1.0
abstract: These joint guidelines, developed by the EANM, EANO, RANO, and SNMMI, provide updated recommendations and procedure standards for imaging gliomas using PET with radiolabelled amino acids (MET, FET, FDOPA) and [18F]FDG. Recognizing the increasing clinical use of PET to complement MRI in the management of glioma, these guidelines aim to assist nuclear medicine practitioners in the appropriate selection, performance, interpretation, and reporting of PET studies to ensure high-quality imaging and evidence-based patient care. The document addresses technical aspects of PET acquisition, highlights the limitations of MRI in certain clinical scenarios, and underscores the value of PET in diagnosis, treatment planning, and response assessment. These guidelines replace previous versions and should be applied in conjunction with local regulations and clinical judgment to optimize neurooncological practice.
venue: European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging

title: Joint practice guidelines for radionuclide lymphoscintigraphy for sentinel node localization in oral/oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma
abstract: Involvement of the cervical lymph nodes is the most important prognostic factor for patients with oral/oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), and the decision whether to electively treat patients with clinically negative necks remains a controversial topic. Sentinel node biopsy (SNB) provides a minimally invasive method of determining the disease status of the cervical node basin, without the need for a formal neck dissection. This technique potentially improves the accuracy of histological nodal staging and avoids over-treating three-quarters of this patient population, minimizing associated morbidity. The technique has been validated for patients with OSCC, and larger-scale studies are in progress to determine its exact role in the management of this patient population. This article was designed to outline the current best practice guidelines for the provision of SNB in patients with early-stage OSCC, and to provide a framework for the currently evolving recommendations for its use. These guidelines were prepared by a multidisciplinary surgical/nuclear medicine/pathology expert panel under the joint auspices of the European Association of Nuclear Medicine (EANM) Oncology Committee and the Sentinel European Node Trial Committee.
venue: European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging

title: Joint practice guidelines for radionuclide lymphoscintigraphy for sentinel node localization in oral/oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma
abstract: Cervical lymph node status is the most significant prognostic factor in oral and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), yet management of the clinically node-negative neck remains controversial. Sentinel node biopsy (SNB) offers a minimally invasive alternative to elective neck dissection, enabling accurate histological staging while reducing overtreatment and associated morbidity. This article presents joint evidence-based guidelines for radionuclide lymphoscintigraphy in sentinel node localization for early-stage OSCC, developed by a multidisciplinary expert panel under the European Association of Nuclear Medicine Oncology Committee and the European Sentinel Node Biopsy Trial Committee. The guidelines review current literature, define the sentinel node concept, outline clinical indications and contraindications, and provide practical recommendations for patient selection, imaging protocols, surgical technique, and pathological assessment. These recommendations aim to standardize SNB practice, optimize diagnostic accuracy, and inform ongoing research into its role in OSCC management.
venue: European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging

title: Lifestyle Medicine: The Health Promoting Power of Daily Habits and Practices
abstract: There is no longer any serious doubt that daily habits and actions profoundly affect both short-term and long-term health and quality of life. This concept is supported by literally thousands of research articles and incorporated in multiple evidence-based guidelines for the prevention and/or treatment of chronic metabolic diseases. The study of how habits and actions affect both prevention and treatment of diseases has coalesced around the concept of “lifestyle medicine.” The purpose of this review is to provide an up-to-date summary of many of the modalities fundamental to lifestyle medicine, including physical activity, proper nutrition, weight management, and cigarette smoking cessation. This review will also focus specifically on how these modalities are employed both in the prevention and treatment of chronic diseases including coronary heart disease, diabetes, obesity, and cancer. The review concludes with a Call to Action challenging the medical community to embrace the modalities of lifestyle medicine in the daily practice of medicine.

title: Lifestyle Medicine: The Health Promoting Power of Daily Habits and Practices
abstract: This review examines the robust evidence supporting the significant impact of daily habits and practices—such as regular physical activity, sound nutrition, weight management, and tobacco avoidance—on both the prevention and treatment of chronic diseases including coronary heart disease, diabetes, obesity, and cancer. The concept of lifestyle medicine has emerged as a distinct discipline focused on leveraging these health-promoting behaviors to improve quality of life and reduce disease risk. Despite widespread inclusion of lifestyle recommendations in clinical guidelines and strong consensus within the medical community regarding their benefits, adoption rates among the general population remain low. The review highlights key research findings, summarizes current guidelines, and discusses strategies for integrating lifestyle medicine into routine clinical practice. It concludes with a call to action for healthcare professionals to prioritize lifestyle interventions as foundational components of patient care.

title: Machine Learning and Prediction in Medicine - Beyond the Peak of Inflated Expectations.
abstract: Big data, we have all heard, promise to transform health care. But in the “hype cycle” of emerging technologies, machine learning now rides atop the “peak of inflated expectations,” and we need to better appreciate the technology’s capabilities and limitations.

title: Machine Learning and Prediction in Medicine - Beyond the Peak of Inflated Expectations.
abstract: Machine learning and predictive analytics are heralded as transformative tools in medicine, promising to revolutionize clinical decision-making through the analysis of vast and diverse health data. However, this enthusiasm often overlooks critical limitations inherent in real-world data sources, including bias, confounding, and the rapid obsolescence of historical information. While machine learning can enhance risk stratification and diagnostic accuracy beyond traditional models, its predictive power is constrained by the quality and relevance of available data, as well as the inherent unpredictability of complex biological and social systems. Moreover, accurate prediction does not equate to actionable intervention, as many models identify associations rather than causal relationships amenable to change. The integration of machine learning with clinical expertise holds potential for improved resource allocation and patient outcomes, but expectations must be tempered by a realistic understanding of both the technology’s capabilities and its boundaries. Moving beyond inflated expectations requires a nuanced approach that leverages machine learning as a complement to human judgment, aiming for incremental improvements in care rather than unattainable perfection.

title: Machine Learning in Medicine
abstract: Spurred by advances in processing power, memory, storage, and an unprecedented wealth of data, computers are being asked to tackle increasingly complex learning tasks, often with astonishing success. Computers have now mastered a popular variant of poker, learned the laws of physics from experimental data, and become experts in video games - tasks that would have been deemed impossible not too long ago. In parallel, the number of companies centered on applying complex data analysis to varying industries has exploded, and it is thus unsurprising that some analytic companies are turning attention to problems in health care. The purpose of this review is to explore what problems in medicine might benefit from such learning approaches and use examples from the literature to introduce basic concepts in machine learning. It is important to note that seemingly large enough medical data sets and adequate learning algorithms have been available for many decades, and yet, although there are thousands of papers applying machine learning algorithms to medical data, very few have contributed meaningfully to clinical care. This lack of impact stands in stark contrast to the enormous relevance of machine learning to many other industries. Thus, part of my effort will be to identify what obstacles there may be to changing the practice of medicine through statistical learning approaches, and discuss how these might be overcome.
venue: Mach. Learn. under Resour. Constraints Vol. 3

title: Machine Learning in Medicine
abstract: Machine learning has emerged as a transformative approach in medicine, driven by advances in computational power and the availability of large-scale data. This review examines the potential applications of machine learning in healthcare, distinguishing between tasks where computers approximate physician performance and those where they may uncover novel insights beyond human capability. Key concepts such as supervised and unsupervised learning are introduced, with examples including automated electrocardiogram interpretation, risk prediction models, and the identification of disease subtypes through pattern recognition. Despite the proliferation of research applying machine learning to medical data, few algorithms have meaningfully impacted clinical practice, highlighting significant barriers to implementation. The paper explores technical challenges such as feature selection, model choice, and parameter optimization, and discusses why these obstacles have limited the integration of machine learning into routine care. Strategies to overcome these challenges are considered, emphasizing the need for robust validation and careful translation of computational advances into clinical benefit.
venue: Mach. Learn. under Resour. Constraints Vol. 3

title: Machine learning in medicine: Addressing ethical challenges
abstract: Effy Vayena and colleagues argue that machine learning in medicine must offer data protection, algorithmic transparency, and accountability to earn the trust of patients and clinicians.

title: Machine learning in medicine: Addressing ethical challenges
abstract: Machine learning (ML) is rapidly transforming the field of medicine, offering unprecedented opportunities for improved diagnostics, personalized treatment, and healthcare efficiency. However, the integration of ML technologies into clinical practice raises significant ethical challenges that must be addressed to ensure responsible and equitable use. This paper examines key ethical issues associated with ML in medicine, including concerns about data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, accountability, and informed consent. We analyze how these challenges can impact patient trust, exacerbate health disparities, and complicate clinical decision-making. The paper also explores current frameworks and guidelines aimed at mitigating ethical risks and highlights the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration among clinicians, data scientists, ethicists, and policymakers. By critically evaluating existing approaches and proposing strategies for ethical oversight, we underscore the need for ongoing vigilance and adaptive governance as ML becomes increasingly embedded in healthcare systems. Our findings emphasize that addressing ethical challenges is essential not only for safeguarding patient rights but also for realizing the full potential of machine learning to advance medical care.

title: Machine learning in medicine: a practical introduction
abstract: Following visible successes on a wide range of predictive tasks, machine learning techniques are attracting substantial interest from medical researchers and clinicians. We address the need for capacity development in this area by providing a conceptual introduction to machine learning alongside a practical guide to developing and evaluating predictive algorithms using freely-available open source software and public domain data.MethodsWe demonstrate the use of machine learning techniques by developing three predictive models for cancer diagnosis using descriptions of nuclei sampled from breast masses. These algorithms include regularized General Linear Model regression (GLMs), Support Vector Machines (SVMs) with a radial basis function kernel, and single-layer Artificial Neural Networks. The publicly-available dataset describing the breast mass samples (N=683) was randomly split into evaluation (n=456) and validation (n=227) samples.We trained algorithms on data from the evaluation sample before they were used to predict the diagnostic outcome in the validation dataset. We compared the predictions made on the validation datasets with the real-world diagnostic decisions to calculate the accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of the three models. We explored the use of averaging and voting ensembles to improve predictive performance. We provide a step-by-step guide to developing algorithms using the open-source R statistical programming environment.ResultsThe trained algorithms were able to classify cell nuclei with high accuracy (.94 -.96), sensitivity (.97 -.99), and specificity (.85 -.94). Maximum accuracy (.96) and area under the curve (.97) was achieved using the SVM algorithm. Prediction performance increased marginally (accuracy =.97, sensitivity =.99, specificity =.95) when algorithms were arranged into a voting ensemble.ConclusionsWe use a straightforward example to demonstrate the theory and practice of machine learning for clinicians and medical researchers. The principals which we demonstrate here can be readily applied to other complex tasks including natural language processing and image recognition.

title: Machine learning in medicine: a practical introduction
abstract: Machine learning techniques are increasingly being adopted in medicine due to their success in predictive tasks and the growing availability of large datasets. This paper provides a conceptual and practical introduction to machine learning for medical researchers and clinicians, demonstrating the development and evaluation of predictive algorithms using open-source software and public domain data. Using a breast cancer dataset, we developed and compared three classification models—regularized General Linear Model regression, Support Vector Machines with a radial basis function kernel, and single-layer Artificial Neural Networks—achieving high accuracy (0.94–0.96), sensitivity (0.97–0.99), and specificity (0.85–0.94). The best performance was observed with the SVM model, and further improvement was achieved through a voting ensemble approach. We offer a step-by-step guide to implementing these methods in the R programming environment, emphasizing their applicability to other complex medical tasks such as natural language processing and image recognition. This work aims to build capacity in the medical community for applying machine learning techniques to enhance diagnostic accuracy and clinical decision-making.

title: Medicine 2.0: Social Networking, Collaboration, Participation, Apomediation, and Openness
abstract: In a very significant development for eHealth, a broad adoption of Web 2.0 technologies and approaches coincides with the more recent emergence of Personal Health Application Platforms and Personally Controlled Health Records such as Google Health, Microsoft HealthVault, and Dossia. “Medicine 2.0” applications, services, and tools are defined as Web-based services for health care consumers, caregivers, patients, health professionals, and biomedical researchers, that use Web 2.0 technologies and/or semantic web and virtual reality approaches to enable and facilitate specifically 1) social networking, 2) participation, 3) apomediation, 4) openness, and 5) collaboration, within and between these user groups. The Journal of Medical Internet Research (JMIR) publishes a Medicine 2.0 theme issue and sponsors a conference on “How Social Networking and Web 2.0 changes Health, Health Care, Medicine, and Biomedical Research”, to stimulate and encourage research in these five areas.

title: Medicine 2.0: Social Networking, Collaboration, Participation, Apomediation, and Openness
abstract: The advent of Medicine 2.0 marks a transformative phase in health care, characterized by the integration of Web 2.0 technologies, social networking, and participatory approaches into medical practice, research, and patient engagement. This editorial explores how Medicine 2.0 applications—encompassing personal health platforms, collaborative tools, and semantic web innovations—are redefining interactions among patients, health professionals, and researchers by fostering social networking, participation, apomediation, collaboration, and openness. The shift towards patient-controlled health records and open data exchange challenges traditional hierarchical models, empowering consumers to take an active role in their health management and knowledge production. By highlighting the convergence of technological advances and evolving user expectations, this paper frames Medicine 2.0 as both a set of web-based tools and a broader movement towards a more collaborative, transparent, and patient-centered health system. The Journal of Medical Internet Research’s theme issue and conference aim to stimulate further research and dialogue on the implications of these developments for the future of health care and biomedical science.

title: Mental Health Strategies to Combat the Psychological Impact of COVID-19 Beyond Paranoia and Panic.
abstract: It is urgent to identify the effective measures to cope with the psychological stress triggered by the precipitate coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. Objective: The present study aimed at examining the levels and links of the anxiety and coping strategies, and then exploring the coping predictors in anxiety in the crisis. Methods: An online survey was conducted using stratified random sampling method among 2640 Chinese university students from 21 February to 24 February 2020. The students’ anxiety and coping strategies were measured by the Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS) and the Coping Strategy Questionnaire (CSQ), respectively. Results: The students expressed high levels of coping strategies and comparatively low level of anxiety. Multiple stepwise regression analysis showed that cognitive coping, emotional coping, and social support had a significantly negative predictive effect on anxiety, social support being the most powerful predictor, whereas behavioral coping predicted anxiety positively. Conclusion: The findings suggest that the enhancement of cognitive coping, emotional coping, and social support should be highlighted and the potentially destructive impact of behavioral coping is noteworthy, and the pedagogical implications in health education are hereby addressed.
venue: Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore

title: Mental Health Strategies to Combat the Psychological Impact of COVID-19 Beyond Paranoia and Panic.
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has triggered widespread psychological distress, manifesting as heightened paranoia, panic, and other mental health challenges across affected populations. This commentary examines the multifaceted psychological impact of the outbreak, drawing on early experiences in Singapore and global data. It highlights how fear, uncertainty, and extensive media coverage have contributed to anxiety, depression, and stress among the general public, patients, and healthcare workers. The paper discusses the exacerbation of pre-existing mental health conditions, the emergence of new psychiatric symptoms, and the role of stigma and social disruption in intensifying psychological morbidity. It further explores the unique vulnerabilities of healthcare workers due to occupational exposure and stresses the importance of targeted mental health support. In response, the authors advocate for comprehensive mental health strategies that extend beyond crisis management to include clear communication, community engagement, psychological defense mechanisms, and accessible support services. The commentary underscores the necessity of integrating mental health considerations into public health responses to pandemics to foster resilience and mitigate long-term psychological consequences.
venue: Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore

title: Nanotechnology and its Applications in Medicine
abstract: Nanotechnologyis the study of extremely small structures, having size of 0.1 to 100 nm. Nano medicine is a relatively new field of science and technology. Brief explanation of various types of pharmaceutical nano systems is given. Classification of nano materials based on their dimensions is given. An application of Nanotechnology in various fields such as health and medicine, electronics, energy and environment, is discussed in detail. Applications of nano particles in drug delivery, protein and peptide delivery, cancer are explained. Applications of various nano systems in cancer therapy such as carbon nano tube, dendrimers, nano crystal, nano wire, nano shells etc. are given. The advancement in nano technology helps in the treatment of neuro degenerative disorders such as Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease. Applications of nano technology in tuberculosis treatment, the clinical application of nanotechnology in operative dentistry, in ophthalmology, in surgery, visualization, tissue engineering, antibiotic resistance, immune response are discussed in this article. Nano pharmaceuticals can be used to detect diseases at much earlier stages.

title: Nanotechnology and its Applications in Medicine
abstract: Nanotechnology, defined as the manipulation of matter at the nanometer scale (0.1–100 nm), has emerged as a transformative field with significant implications for medicine and pharmaceuticals. This paper reviews the fundamental concepts of nanotechnology, including its historical development, classification of nanomaterials by dimension and phase, and manufacturing approaches such as top-down and bottom-up techniques. The unique physical, chemical, and biological properties of nanomaterials enable the design of novel nano devices and systems—such as carbon nanotubes, dendrimers, liposomes, metallic nanoparticles, and quantum dots—that have advanced drug delivery, diagnostics, and therapeutic strategies. Applications discussed include targeted drug delivery systems for cancer therapy, protein and peptide delivery, treatment of neurodegenerative disorders like Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s diseases, tuberculosis management, and innovations in surgery, ophthalmology, tissue engineering, and combating antibiotic resistance. The integration of nanotechnology in medicine enables earlier disease detection, improved therapeutic efficacy, and reduced side effects. The review highlights both current clinical applications and future prospects of nanomedicine in revolutionizing healthcare.

title: Naturally occurring anti-cancer compounds: shining from Chinese herbal medicine
abstract: Numerous natural products originated from Chinese herbal medicine exhibit anti-cancer activities, including anti-proliferative, pro-apoptotic, anti-metastatic, anti-angiogenic effects, as well as regulate autophagy, reverse multidrug resistance, balance immunity, and enhance chemotherapy in vitro and in vivo. To provide new insights into the critical path ahead, we systemically reviewed the most recent advances (reported since 2011) on the key compounds with anti-cancer effects derived from Chinese herbal medicine (curcumin, epigallocatechin gallate, berberine, artemisinin, ginsenoside Rg3, ursolic acid, silibinin, emodin, triptolide, cucurbitacin B, tanshinone I, oridonin, shikonin, gambogic acid, artesunate, wogonin, β-elemene, and cepharanthine) in scientific databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Medline, Scopus, and Clinical Trials). With a broader perspective, we focused on their recently discovered and/or investigated pharmacological effects, novel mechanism of action, relevant clinical studies, and their innovative applications in combined therapy and immunomodulation. In addition, the present review has extended to describe other promising compounds including dihydroartemisinin, ginsenoside Rh2, compound K, cucurbitacins D, E, I, tanshinone IIA and cryptotanshinone in view of their potentials in cancer therapy. Up to now, the evidence about the immunomodulatory effects and clinical trials of natural anti-cancer compounds from Chinese herbal medicine is very limited, and further research is needed to monitor their immunoregulatory effects and explore their mechanisms of action as modulators of immune checkpoints.

title: Naturally occurring anti-cancer compounds: shining from Chinese herbal medicine
abstract: Chinese herbal medicine is a rich source of naturally occurring compounds with significant anti-cancer activities, including anti-proliferative, pro-apoptotic, anti-metastatic, and anti-angiogenic effects, as well as the ability to regulate autophagy, reverse multidrug resistance, modulate immunity, and enhance chemotherapy. This review systematically summarizes recent advances since 2011 in the pharmacological effects, mechanisms of action, clinical studies, and innovative therapeutic applications of key bioactive compounds such as curcumin, epigallocatechin gallate, berberine, artemisinin, ginsenoside Rg3, ursolic acid, silibinin, emodin, triptolide, cucurbitacin B, tanshinone I, oridonin, shikonin, gambogic acid, artesunate, wogonin, β-elemene, and cepharanthine. Additional promising agents including dihydroartemisinin, ginsenoside Rh2, compound K, cucurbitacins D/E/I, tanshinone IIA and cryptotanshinone are also discussed for their emerging roles in cancer therapy. The review highlights both the advantages and limitations of these compounds across various cancer types and emphasizes the need for further research into their immunomodulatory effects and mechanisms as immune checkpoint modulators. Despite growing evidence supporting their potential clinical utility, more comprehensive studies are required to fully elucidate their therapeutic value and optimize their integration into modern oncology.

title: New evidence pyramid
abstract: A pyramid has expressed the idea of hierarchy of medical evidence for so long, that not all evidence is the same. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses have been placed at the top of this pyramid for several good reasons. However, there are several counterarguments to this placement. We suggest another way of looking at the evidence-based medicine pyramid and explain how systematic reviews and meta-analyses are tools for consuming evidence—that is, appraising, synthesising and applying evidence.

title: New evidence pyramid
abstract: The traditional evidence pyramid has long depicted a hierarchy of medical evidence, placing systematic reviews and meta-analyses at its apex. However, this model oversimplifies the complex nature of evidence quality and fails to account for methodological nuances and limitations inherent in different study designs. This paper proposes two key modifications to the evidence pyramid: first, replacing the rigid boundaries between study types with wavy lines to reflect the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, which considers factors beyond study design such as risk of bias, imprecision, inconsistency, and indirectness; second, repositioning systematic reviews and meta-analyses as tools—lenses through which evidence is appraised and synthesized—rather than as the highest tier of evidence. These changes better capture the dynamic process of evaluating certainty in evidence and acknowledge that systematic reviews’ value depends on the quality of included studies. The revised pyramid serves as a more accurate teaching tool for evidence-based medicine, guiding practitioners to critically assess both primary studies and syntheses, and ultimately supports more nuanced clinical decision-making.

title: Osteoarthritis: a disease of the joint as an organ.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis and a major cause of pain and disability in older adults (1). OA is often referred to as degenerative joint disease. This is a misnomer because OA is not simply a process of wear and tear, but rather, an abnormal remodeling of joint tissues driven by a host of inflam- matory mediators within the affected joint. The most common risk factors for OA include age, sex, prior joint injury, obesity, genetic predisposition, and mechanical factors, including malalignment and abnormal joint shape (2,3). Despite the multifactorial nature of OA, the pathologic changes seen in osteoarthritic joints have common features that affect the entire joint structure, resulting in pain, deformity, and loss of function. The pathologic changes seen in OA joints (Fig- ures 1 and 2) include degradation of the articular cartilage, thickening of the subchondral bone, formation of osteophytes, variable degrees of inflammation of the synovium, degeneration of ligaments and, in the knee, the menisci, and hypertrophy of the joint capsule. There can also be changes in periarticular muscles, nerves, bursa, and local fat pads that may contribute to OA or to the symptoms of OA. The findings of pathologic changes in all of the joint tissues are the impetus for considering OA as a disease of the joint as an organ that can result in “joint failure.” In this review, we summarize the key features of OA in the various joint tissues affected and provide an overview of the basic mechanisms currently thought to contribute to the pathologic changes seen in these tissues.

title: Osteoarthritis: a disease of the joint as an organ.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent and disabling joint disorder traditionally mischaracterized as mere degenerative wear and tear, but is now recognized as a complex disease involving the entire joint as an organ. This review synthesizes current understanding of OA pathogenesis, highlighting how pathological changes extend beyond articular cartilage to include subchondral bone thickening, osteophyte formation, synovial inflammation, ligament and meniscal degeneration, and alterations in periarticular tissues. Central to OA progression are activated chondrocytes that drive matrix remodeling and degradation through upregulation of matrix metalloproteinases and inflammatory mediators, influenced by mechanical stress, cytokine signaling, and epigenetic modifications. Inflammatory pathways, including NF-κB and MAPK cascades, Toll-like receptor activation by damage-associated molecular patterns, and complement system involvement, further amplify tissue catabolism. Age-related changes such as cellular senescence, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy, and increased cell death exacerbate joint degeneration. The interplay of these mechanisms underscores OA as a multifactorial disease process resulting in joint failure, emphasizing the need for therapeutic strategies targeting the whole joint environment rather than isolated tissues.

title: Overview of natural hydrogels for regenerative medicine applications
abstract: Hydrogels from different materials can be used in biomedical field as an innovative approach in regenerative medicine. Depending on the origin source, hydrogels can be synthetized through chemical and physical methods. Hydrogel can be characterized through several physical parameters, such as size, elastic modulus, swelling and degradation rate. Lately, research is focused on hydrogels derived from biologic materials. These hydrogels can be derived from protein polymers, such as collage, elastin, and polysaccharide polymers like glycosaminoglycans or alginate among others. Introduction of decellularized tissues into hydrogels synthesis displays several advantages compared to natural or synthetic based hydrogels. Preservation of natural molecules such as growth factors, glycans, bioactive cryptic peptides and natural proteins can promote cell growth, function, differentiation, angiogenesis, anti-angiogenesis, antimicrobial effects, and chemotactic effects. Versatility of hydrogels make possible multiple applications and combinations with several molecules on order to obtain the adequate characteristic for each scope. In this context, a lot of molecules such as cross link agents, drugs, grow factors or cells can be used. This review focuses on the recent progress of hydrogels synthesis and applications in order to classify the most recent and relevant matters in biomedical field.
venue: Journal of Materials Science: Materials in Medicine

title: Overview of natural hydrogels for regenerative medicine applications
abstract: This review provides a comprehensive overview of natural hydrogels and their applications in regenerative medicine, emphasizing their synthesis, characterization, and functional properties. Natural hydrogels, derived from protein-based materials such as collagen, elastin, fibrin, and silk fibroin, as well as polysaccharide-based materials like glycosaminoglycans, alginate, and chitosan, offer significant advantages including biocompatibility, biodegradability, and similarity to native extracellular matrix. The review discusses various methods for hydrogel preparation—both chemical and physical crosslinking—and highlights the importance of characterizing mechanical properties, swelling behavior, and degradation kinetics to tailor hydrogels for specific biomedical uses. Additionally, the incorporation of decellularized tissues into hydrogels is explored for its potential to preserve bioactive molecules that promote cell growth and tissue regeneration. Despite challenges such as limited mechanical strength and batch-to-batch variability, natural hydrogels remain highly versatile platforms for applications in drug delivery, tissue engineering, and cell culture systems. The article concludes by summarizing recent advances and future perspectives in the development of natural hydrogels for regenerative medicine.
venue: Journal of Materials Science: Materials in Medicine

title: P4 medicine: how systems medicine will transform the healthcare sector and society.
abstract: Ten years ago, the proposition that healthcare is evolving from reactive disease care to care that is predictive, preventive, personalized and participatory was regarded as highly speculative. Today, the core elements of that vision are widely accepted and have been articulated in a series of recent reports by the US Institute of Medicine. Systems approaches to biology and medicine are now beginning to provide patients, consumers and physicians with personalized information about each individual's unique health experience of both health and disease at the molecular, cellular and organ levels. This information will make disease care radically more cost effective by personalizing care to each person's unique biology and by treating the causes rather than the symptoms of disease. It will also provide the basis for concrete action by consumers to improve their health as they observe the impact of lifestyle decisions. Working together in digitally powered familial and affinity networks, consumers will be able to reduce the incidence of the complex chronic diseases that currently account for 75% of disease-care costs in the USA.

title: P4 medicine: how systems medicine will transform the healthcare sector and society.
abstract: P4 medicine, defined by its predictive, preventive, personalized, and participatory approach, is poised to transform healthcare and society through the integration of systems biology, digital technologies, and active consumer engagement. This paper examines the convergence of these megatrends—advances in systems medicine, the digital revolution’s capacity for big data management, and empowered patients—to outline a new paradigm for disease care and wellness. Systems medicine leverages high-throughput omics technologies and computational modeling to stratify individuals and diseases, enabling earlier interventions, targeted therapies, and more cost-effective care by addressing disease causes rather than symptoms. The proliferation of personal health data tools and networked consumer communities further accelerates this shift by generating essential data for continuous innovation and supporting lifestyle changes that can reduce the incidence of complex chronic diseases. As patients become active participants in their health management, P4 medicine facilitates the emergence of a learning healthcare system that integrates discovery science with clinical practice.
