The resulting transformation promises not only improved health outcomes and reduced costs but also a redefinition of the roles of patients, providers, and society in healthcare.

title: Participatory medicine: a driving force for revolutionizing healthcare
abstract: Healthcare is undergoing a profound revolution as a consequence of three contemporary thrusts: systems medicine [1-4], big data and patient involvement in their own health through social networks. This convergence is leading to a medicine that is predictive, preventive, personalized and participatory (P4) [4-7]. The first three Ps, predictive, preventive and personalized, were delineated in the early 2000s [1,2], whereas the fourth P, participatory, was added later. To achieve a participatory healthcare system, major technical and societal challenges will need to be overcome, and this will require close integration with systems medicine and big data. Before commenting further on participatory medicine, let us first delineate the essence of systems medicine and big data and their implications for P4 medicine. Systems medicine, the application of systems biology approaches to disease [3,4,6,8,9], is already changing how healthcare is practiced (Table 1). We predict that in 5 to 10 years each patient will be surrounded by a virtual cloud of billions of data points - molecular, clinical chemistries, cellular, organ, phenotypic, imaging, social networks, and so on. We also predict that we will have the analytical tools to reduce this big data cloud to simple models that will guide improvements in health and minimize disease. This requires addressing two grand challenges: the signal-to-noise issues intrinsic to big data and integration of multi-scale data into predictive models. Table 1 How systems medicine is transforming healthcare In addition, for each individual patient we foresee that we will be able to integrate an individual’s genetic, molecular, cellular, organ and social networks into an overall 'network of networks’ [10]. Disease leads to the perturbation of the network of networks and this alters the information the network manages. The availability of a personal data cloud will allow one to characterize an individual’s network of networks in its normal or disease-perturbed states. This altered, disease-perturbed information will provide deep insights into disease mechanisms, new approaches to diagnostics and therapeutics, and a platform for participatory medicine.

title: Participatory medicine: a driving force for revolutionizing healthcare
abstract: Participatory medicine, as a core component of predictive, preventive, personalized, and participatory (P4) medicine, is revolutionizing healthcare by integrating systems medicine, big data, and active patient involvement. This editorial explores how systems biology approaches and the aggregation of vast personal data clouds are enabling individualized models for health optimization and disease prevention. The transition to participatory medicine presents significant technical and societal challenges, including the development of advanced analytical tools, addressing ethical and privacy concerns, redefining the roles of patients and healthcare professionals, and fostering educational initiatives for all stakeholders. Patient-activated social networks and robust information technology infrastructures are highlighted as key drivers for empowering individuals and decentralizing care. The authors propose pilot programs focused on wellness and advocate for new professional roles, such as healthcare and wellness coaches, to interpret complex data for patients. Ultimately, participatory medicine promises to transform healthcare into a more collaborative, data-driven, and patient-centered system.

title: Patient safety in genomic medicine: an exploratory study
abstract: Concerns about patient safety and the potential for medical error are largely unexplored for genetic testing, despite the expansion of test use. In this preliminary qualitative study, we sought the views of genetics professionals about error and patient safety concerns in genomic medicine and factors that might mitigate them.Methods:Twelve semistructured interviews with experienced genetics professionals were conducted. Transcripts were analyzed using selective coding for issues related to error definition, mitigation, and communication. Additional thematic analysis captured themes across content categories.Results:Key informants suggested that the potential for adverse events exists in all phases of genetic testing, from ordering to analysis, interpretation, and follow-up. A perceived contributor was lack of physician knowledge about genetics, resulting in errors in test ordering and interpretation. The limitations and uncertainty inherent to rapidly evolving technology were also seen as contributing factors. Strategies to prevent errors included physician education, availability of genetic experts for consultation, and enhanced communication such as improved test reports and electronic decision support.Conclusion:Genetic testing poses concerns for patient safety due to errors and the limitations of current tests. As genomic tests are integrated into medical care, anticipating and addressing patient safety concerns identified by these key informants will be crucial.Genet Med 18 11, 1136–1142.

title: Patient safety in genomic medicine: an exploratory study
abstract: This exploratory study examines patient safety in the rapidly evolving field of genomic medicine, with a focus on the challenges and risks associated with the clinical application of genetic information. The research highlights the need for diagnostic guidelines that reflect human diversity, as illustrated by the development of the Atlas of Human Malformation Syndromes in Diverse Populations, which provides a resource for clinicians working in underresourced settings. The study also addresses the identification of new clinically significant genetic variants through next-generation sequencing, emphasizing the importance of accurate diagnosis in conditions such as Ehlers–Danlos syndrome to prevent life-threatening complications. Ethical considerations related to patient privacy and representation are discussed, particularly regarding the use of identifiable images in global resources. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of equitable access to genomic medicine, robust diagnostic tools, and careful ethical oversight to enhance patient safety as genomic technologies become more widely implemented.

title: Personalized medicine and human genetic diversity.
abstract: Human genetic diversity has long been studied both to understand how genetic variation influences risk of disease and infer aspects of human evolutionary history. In this article, we review historical and contemporary views of human genetic diversity, the rare and common mutations implicated in human disease susceptibility, and the relevance of genetic diversity to personalized medicine. First, we describe the development of thought about diversity through the 20th century and through more modern studies including genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and next-generation sequencing. We introduce several examples, such as sickle cell anemia and Tay-Sachs disease that are caused by rare mutations and are more frequent in certain geographical populations, and common treatment responses that are caused by common variants, such as hepatitis C infection. We conclude with comments about the continued relevance of human genetic diversity in medical genetics and personalized medicine more generally.
venue: Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Medicine

title: Personalized medicine and human genetic diversity.
abstract: Human genetic diversity plays a critical role in understanding disease susceptibility, evolutionary history, and the development of personalized medicine. This paper reviews the evolution of scientific thought regarding human genetic variation, from early 20th-century theories and biased physical measurements to modern genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and next-generation sequencing. Landmark discoveries, such as the ABO blood group system and Lewontin’s demonstration that most genetic diversity exists within rather than between populations, have shifted perspectives on race and genetics. The paper highlights how both rare and common genetic variants contribute to disease risk and treatment response, using examples like sickle cell anemia, Tay–Sachs disease, and hepatitis C. It also addresses the limitations of current genomics research, which is disproportionately focused on populations of European ancestry, potentially exacerbating health disparities. The authors argue that a comprehensive understanding of human genetic diversity is essential for advancing medical genetics, reducing health inequities, and realizing the full potential of personalized medicine.
venue: Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Medicine

title: Personalized Medicine and the Practice of Medicine in the 21st Century
abstract: The renowned Canadian physician and McGill alumnus got it right. Much of medical science over the past century has documented intra-and inter-individual variability, however the rationale for this variability is not well understood and not often applied in clinical practice. Indeed most therapeutic strategies rely on data derived from randomized clinical trials (RCTs) and large observational studies, and applied to the so-called 'statistically average' patient. Although medicine will continue to remain very much an art, just over a hundred years after Osler's observation, we are beginning to understand the factors driving interindividual variability. Armed with details of individual variation, physicians could divide patients into subgroups and predict which are likely to have an aggressive or indolent form of a disease and which would respond to one drug rather than another. The emergence and continued growth of personalized medicine will catalyze fundamental changes at many different levels in the future of health care and health systems. The objective of this special focus article is to describe the role and increasing importance of personalized medicine in health care, as well as discuss some of the ongoing challenges for integrating personalized medicine into contemporary medicine.

title: Personalized Medicine and the Practice of Medicine in the 21st Century
abstract: Personalized medicine, driven by advances in genomics and pharmacogenomics, is transforming the practice of medicine in the 21st century by enabling more precise, individualized therapeutic strategies. This review examines the historical development and current applications of personalized medicine, highlighting how genetic variability among individuals influences drug response and disease progression. Key examples such as HER-2/neu testing for trastuzumab in breast cancer, genotyping for warfarin dosing, and CYP450 enzyme testing illustrate the clinical integration of pharmacogenomic information. The article discusses the impact of these innovations on drug development, regulatory practices, and patient care, while also addressing ongoing challenges related to implementation, cost, and clinical utility. Ultimately, personalized medicine holds promise for improving treatment efficacy, reducing adverse drug reactions, and optimizing healthcare delivery, but its widespread adoption will require overcoming scientific, logistical, and ethical barriers.

title: Personalized medicine in psychiatry: problems and promises
abstract: The central theme of personalized medicine is the premise that an individual’s unique physiologic characteristics play a significant role in both disease vulnerability and in response to specific therapies. The major goals of personalized medicine are therefore to predict an individual’s susceptibility to developing an illness, achieve accurate diagnosis, and optimize the most efficient and favorable response to treatment. The goal of achieving personalized medicine in psychiatry is a laudable one, because its attainment should be associated with a marked reduction in morbidity and mortality. In this review, we summarize an illustrative selection of studies that are laying the foundation towards personalizing medicine in major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia. In addition, we present emerging applications that are likely to advance personalized medicine in psychiatry, with an emphasis on novel biomarkers and neuroimaging.

title: Personalized medicine in psychiatry: problems and promises
abstract: Personalized medicine in psychiatry aims to tailor prevention, diagnosis, and treatment strategies to individual biological and environmental profiles, with the promise of improving outcomes in major psychiatric disorders such as major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia. This review examines the current state of personalized approaches in psychiatry, highlighting advances in genetic, epigenetic, and biomarker research that contribute to understanding disease susceptibility and therapeutic response. Despite notable progress, particularly in identifying genetic variants and neurobiological markers associated with psychiatric conditions, significant challenges remain due to the complex interplay of genetic, environmental, and clinical factors underlying these disorders. The review also discusses emerging technologies such as neuroimaging and pharmacogenomics that may enhance individualized care. Ultimately, while personalized medicine holds considerable promise for reducing morbidity and mortality in psychiatric populations, further research is needed to overcome barriers related to heritability, biomarker validation, and clinical implementation.

title: Practice Guidelines for the Management of Community-Acquired Pneumonia in Adults
abstract: Lower respiratory tract infections are the major cause of death in the world and the major cause of death due to infectious diseases in the United States. Recent advances in the field include the identification of new pathogens (Chlamydia pneumoniae and hantavirus), new methods of microbial detection (PCR), and new antimicrobial agents (macrolides, β-lactam agents, fluoroquinolones, oxazolidinones, and streptogramins). Despite extensive studies, there are few conditions in medicine that are so controversial in terms of management. Guidelines for management were published in 1993 by the American Thoracic Society [1], the British Thoracic Society [2], and the Canadian Infectious Disease Society [3], as well as the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) in 1998 [4]. The present guidelines represent revised recommendations of the IDSA. Compared with previous guidelines, these guidelines are intended to reflect updated information, provide more extensive recommendations in selected areas, and indicate an evolution of opinion. These therapeutic guidelines are restricted to community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in immunocompetent adults.

title: Practice Guidelines for the Management of Community-Acquired Pneumonia in Adults
abstract: This paper presents updated practice guidelines from the Infectious Diseases Society of America for the management of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in immunocompetent adults. The guidelines address diagnostic evaluation, site-of-care decisions, laboratory testing, antimicrobial therapy, and prevention strategies, incorporating recent advances in pathogen identification, diagnostic methods, and antimicrobial agents. Recommendations are graded by strength and quality of supporting evidence. Key elements include the use of chest radiography for diagnosis, risk stratification for hospitalization based on clinical prediction rules, and targeted laboratory studies to guide pathogen-specific therapy and reduce inappropriate antibiotic use. Empirical antimicrobial regimens are tailored to illness severity, likely pathogens, resistance patterns, and comorbidities, with specific guidance for outpatient, inpatient, and intensive care unit settings. The guidelines emphasize early initiation of appropriate antibiotics, switching to oral therapy when clinically indicated, and monitoring for treatment response. Prevention measures focus on influenza and pneumococcal vaccination. Performance indicators are proposed to assess adherence to recommended practices. These evidence-based recommendations aim to optimize clinical outcomes, minimize antibiotic resistance, and standardize care for adults with CAP.

title: Pulmonary complications of sickle cell disease.
abstract: From the Division of Pulmonary, Allergy, and Critical Care Medicine and the Hemostasis and Vascular Biology Research Institute, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, (M.T.G.); and Children’s Hospital and Research Center at Oakland, Oakland, CA (E.V.). Address reprint requests to Dr. Gladwin at the Division of Pulmonary, Allergy, and Critical Care Medicine, University of Pittsburgh, NW 168 Montefiore Hospital, 354 Fifth Ave., Pittsburgh, PA, 15213, or at gladwinmt@upmc.edu.

title: Pulmonary complications of sickle cell disease.
abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a prevalent inherited hemoglobinopathy associated with significant morbidity and mortality, particularly due to pulmonary complications such as acute chest syndrome (ACS) and pulmonary hypertension (PH). This review examines the pathophysiology, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and management of major pulmonary manifestations in both adult and pediatric SCD populations. ACS, a leading cause of hospitalization and premature death in SCD, arises from multifactorial etiologies including infection, fat embolism, and pulmonary infarction. PH, often developing with age, further contributes to high mortality rates. Additional comorbidities such as asthma and restrictive lung disease are also discussed. Early recognition and targeted treatment of these pulmonary complications are essential to improving outcomes in patients with SCD.

title: Quantifying the Impoverishing Effects of Purchasing Medicines: A Cross-Country Comparison of the Affordability of Medicines in the Developing World
abstract: Laurens Niëns and colleagues estimate the impoverishing effects of four medicines in 16 low- and middle-income countries using the impoverishment method as a metric of affordability and show that medicine purchases could impoverish large numbers of people.

title: Quantifying the Impoverishing Effects of Purchasing Medicines: A Cross-Country Comparison of the Affordability of Medicines in the Developing World
abstract: This study assesses the impoverishing effects of purchasing essential medicines in 16 low- and middle-income countries by quantifying the proportion of the population pushed below international poverty lines (US$1.25 and US$2 per day) after buying four commonly used medicines. Using standardized facility-based price surveys and World Bank household expenditure data, the analysis reveals that medicine purchases can impoverish significant portions of national populations, with up to 86% affected in some settings. Originator brand medicines are consistently less affordable than lowest-priced generics, with marked differences observed in countries such as the Philippines. The findings highlight the widespread unaffordability of essential medicines and underscore the urgent need for policy interventions to promote access, including increased use of quality-assured generics and expansion of health insurance coverage.

title: Reconciling evidence-based medicine and precision medicine in the era of big data: challenges and opportunities
abstract: This era of groundbreaking scientific developments in high-resolution, high-throughput technologies is allowing the cost-effective collection and analysis of huge, disparate datasets on individual health. Proper data mining and translation of the vast datasets into clinically actionable knowledge will require the application of clinical bioinformatics. These developments have triggered multiple national initiatives in precision medicine—a data-driven approach centering on the individual. However, clinical implementation of precision medicine poses numerous challenges. Foremost, precision medicine needs to be contrasted with the powerful and widely used practice of evidence-based medicine, which is informed by meta-analyses or group-centered studies from which mean recommendations are derived. This “one size fits all” approach can provide inadequate solutions for outliers. Such outliers, which are far from an oddity as all of us fall into this category for some traits, can be better managed using precision medicine. Here, we argue that it is necessary and possible to bridge between precision medicine and evidence-based medicine. This will require worldwide and responsible data sharing, as well as regularly updated training programs. We also discuss the challenges and opportunities for achieving clinical utility in precision medicine. We project that, through collection, analyses and sharing of standardized medically relevant data globally, evidence-based precision medicine will shift progressively from therapy to prevention, thus leading eventually to improved, clinician-to-patient communication, citizen-centered healthcare and sustained well-being.

title: Reconciling evidence-based medicine and precision medicine in the era of big data: challenges and opportunities
abstract: The convergence of high-throughput technologies, advanced bioinformatics, and empowered patients is transforming medicine by enabling the collection and analysis of vast, multidimensional health datasets. This evolution underpins precision medicine, which aims to tailor healthcare to individual variability, yet presents significant challenges when contrasted with the established paradigm of evidence-based medicine that relies on population-level data and generalized recommendations. This paper explores the conceptual and practical tensions between these approaches, highlighting the inadequacy of one-size-fits-all solutions for individual outliers and advocating for a synergistic model that integrates both frameworks. Achieving evidence-based precision medicine will require global data sharing, standardized clinical bioinformatics, and updated training for healthcare professionals. The authors argue that overcoming these challenges will shift healthcare from reactive treatment to proactive prevention, fostering improved patient outcomes, citizen-centered care, and sustained well-being in the era of big data.

title: Regional Anesthesia in the Patient Receiving Antithrombotic or Thrombolytic Therapy: American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine Evidence-Based Guidelines (Fourth Edition)
abstract: The American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine (ASRA) convened its Fourth Consensus Conference on Regional Anesthesia and Anticoagulation in conjunction with the European Society of Anesthesiology (ESA) in response to emerging patient safety issue

title: Regional Anesthesia in the Patient Receiving Antithrombotic or Thrombolytic Therapy: American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine Evidence-Based Guidelines (Fourth Edition)
abstract: This fourth edition of the American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine (ASRA) evidence-based guidelines addresses the management of regional anesthesia in patients receiving antithrombotic or thrombolytic therapy, reflecting evolving standards in perioperative venous thromboembolism prevention and the introduction of new anticoagulant and antiplatelet agents. Developed in collaboration with the European Society of Anaesthesiology and other organizations, these guidelines synthesize literature from 2010 to 2017, incorporating pharmacologic data, clinical studies, and expert consensus to provide recommendations for neuraxial and peripheral nerve blocks, including in obstetric and interventional pain settings. Emphasizing patient safety, the guidelines recommend conservative time intervals for interruption of antithrombotic therapy prior to regional anesthesia, with adjustments based on drug pharmacokinetics, patient comorbidities, and procedural risk. The grading system reflects the strength and quality of available evidence, which is often limited due to the rarity of complications such as spinal hematoma. These recommendations aim to support anesthesiologists and other healthcare providers in optimizing perioperative care for anticoagulated patients while acknowledging the need for individualized clinical judgment and ongoing revision as new evidence emerges.

title: Revolutionizing medicine in the 21st century through systems approaches.
abstract: Personalized medicine is a term for a revolution in medicine that envisions the individual patient as the central focus of healthcare in the future. The term 'personalized medicine', however, fails to reflect the enormous dimensionality of this new medicine that will be predictive, preventive, personalized, and participatory-a vision of medicine we have termed P4 medicine. This reflects a paradigm change in how medicine will be practiced that is revolutionary rather than evolutionary. P4 medicine arises from the confluence of a systems approach to medicine and from the digitalization of medicine that creates the large data sets necessary to deal with the complexities of disease. We predict that systems approaches will empower the transition from conventional reactive medical practice to a more proactive P4 medicine focused on wellness, and will reverse the escalating costs of drug development an will have enormous social and economic benefits. Our vision for P4 medicine in 10 years is that each patient will be associated with a virtual data cloud of billions of data points and that we will have the information technology for healthcare to reduce this enormous data dimensionality to simple hypotheses about health and/or disease for each individual. These data will be multi-scale across all levels of biological organization and extremely heterogeneous in type - this enormous amount of data represents a striking signal-to-noise (S/N) challenge. The key to dealing with this S/N challenge is to take a 'holistic systems approach' to disease as we will discuss in this article.

title: Revolutionizing medicine in the 21st century through systems approaches.
abstract: This paper explores the transformative potential of systems approaches in 21st-century medicine, arguing that the integration of high-dimensional data and holistic network analysis will drive a shift from reactive, disease-focused care to proactive, predictive, preventive, personalized, and participatory (P4) medicine. By conceptualizing biology as an information science and leveraging advances in digitalization, systems medicine enables the comprehensive mapping of biological parts, their interactions, and dynamic behaviors across multiple scales. Case studies in neurodegeneration and chronic respiratory disease illustrate how systems biology can unravel complex disease mechanisms, improve signal-to-noise ratios in large datasets, and identify novel diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. The authors envision a future where each patient’s health is characterized by a vast, multi-layered data cloud distilled into actionable insights through advanced information technologies. This paradigm promises not only to enhance clinical outcomes and patient engagement but also to reduce healthcare costs and deliver significant societal benefits.

title: Role of platelet-derived growth factors in physiology and medicine.
abstract: Platelet-derived growth factors (PDGFs) and their receptors (PDGFRs) have served as prototypes for growth factor and receptor tyrosine kinase function for more than 25 years. Studies of PDGFs and PDGFRs in animal development have revealed roles for PDGFR-alpha signaling in gastrulation and in the development of the cranial and cardiac neural crest, gonads, lung, intestine, skin, CNS, and skeleton. Similarly, roles for PDGFR-beta signaling have been established in blood vessel formation and early hematopoiesis. PDGF signaling is implicated in a range of diseases. Autocrine activation of PDGF signaling pathways is involved in certain gliomas, sarcomas, and leukemias. Paracrine PDGF signaling is commonly observed in epithelial cancers, where it triggers stromal recruitment and may be involved in epithelial-mesenchymal transition, thereby affecting tumor growth, angiogenesis, invasion, and metastasis. PDGFs drive pathological mesenchymal responses in vascular disorders such as atherosclerosis, restenosis, pulmonary hypertension, and retinal diseases, as well as in fibrotic diseases, including pulmonary fibrosis, liver cirrhosis, scleroderma, glomerulosclerosis, and cardiac fibrosis. We review basic aspects of the PDGF ligands and receptors, their developmental and pathological functions, principles of their pharmacological inhibition, and results using PDGF pathway-inhibitory or stimulatory drugs in preclinical and clinical contexts.

title: Role of platelet-derived growth factors in physiology and medicine.
abstract: Platelet-derived growth factors (PDGFs) and their receptors (PDGFRs) are key regulators of cell proliferation, migration, and survival, serving as paradigms for growth factor and receptor tyrosine kinase biology. This review synthesizes current understanding of PDGF biochemistry, receptor interactions, and signaling mechanisms, highlighting their essential roles in embryonic development, particularly in neural crest formation, organogenesis, and vascular development. Dysregulated PDGF signaling is implicated in a spectrum of human diseases, including cancers, fibrotic disorders, and vascular pathologies, through both autocrine and paracrine mechanisms. The discovery of additional PDGF family members and their evolutionary relationship to vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGFs) has expanded the functional landscape of these ligands across species. Recent advances in pharmacological modulation of PDGF pathways have led to clinical applications in oncology and regenerative medicine, with PDGF antagonists and recombinant ligands showing therapeutic promise. This review provides an integrated overview of PDGF structure-function relationships, developmental and pathological roles, regulatory mechanisms controlling ligand bioavailability, and the translational potential of targeting PDGF signaling in disease.

title: Sanitation and Health
abstract: As one article in a four-part PLoS Medicine series on water and sanitation, David Trouba and colleagues discuss the importance of improved sanitation to health and the role that the health sector can play in its advocacy.

title: Sanitation and Health
abstract: Adequate sanitation is fundamental to public health, yet over 2.6 billion people worldwide lack access to safe disposal of human excreta, contributing to approximately 10% of the global disease burden, primarily through diarrhoeal diseases. This paper reviews the latest evidence on the health impacts of poor sanitation, highlighting its strong association with diarrhoeal diseases, neglected tropical diseases, acute respiratory infections, and undernutrition, particularly among children in developing countries. Improved sanitation can reduce rates of diarrhoeal disease by up to 37% and plays a crucial role in controlling diseases such as trachoma, soil-transmitted helminthiases, and schistosomiasis. Despite these benefits, progress in sanitation coverage has been slow due to insufficient policy focus and reliance on infrastructure provision rather than behavior change. The paper argues for a multidisciplinary approach involving engineers, social scientists, health professionals, and communities themselves to achieve sustainable improvements. Beyond health, improved sanitation yields significant social and economic benefits, including enhanced privacy, dignity, and safety—especially for women. The health sector has a vital role in policy development and program implementation to accelerate progress toward universal sanitation coverage and maximize its broad benefits for society.

title: Structural Violence and Clinical Medicine
abstract: Structural violence refers to the social structures that put people in harm's way. Farmer and colleagues describe the impact of social violence upon people living with HIV in the US and Rwanda.

title: Structural Violence and Clinical Medicine
abstract: Structural violence, defined as social arrangements embedded in political and economic systems that harm individuals and populations, profoundly shapes patterns of disease and access to care. Despite clinicians’ awareness of social determinants such as poverty, racism, and gender inequality, these insights are rarely integrated into clinical frameworks, contributing to a desocialized approach to medicine that overlooks the biosocial nature of illness. This article argues for the necessity of biosocial perspectives in clinical practice, illustrating how structural violence influences the distribution and outcomes of diseases like HIV/AIDS in both the United States and Rwanda. The authors demonstrate that disparities in care and health outcomes are not solely the result of individual behaviors but are deeply rooted in social forces that limit access to prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. By examining interventions that address these inequities—ranging from proximal clinical actions to broader structural changes—the paper highlights actionable strategies for health professionals and policymakers. Ultimately, integrating an understanding of structural violence into clinical medicine is essential for preventing premature death and disability, improving patient outcomes, and advancing social justice in health care globally.

title: Techniques for extraction and isolation of natural products: a comprehensive review
abstract: Natural medicines were the only option for the prevention and treatment of human diseases for thousands of years. Natural products are important sources for drug development. The amounts of bioactive natural products in natural medicines are always fairly low. Today, it is very crucial to develop effective and selective methods for the extraction and isolation of those bioactive natural products. This paper intends to provide a comprehensive view of a variety of methods used in the extraction and isolation of natural products. This paper also presents the advantage, disadvantage and practical examples of conventional and modern techniques involved in natural products research.

title: Techniques for extraction and isolation of natural products: a comprehensive review
abstract: Natural products have long served as a foundation for drug discovery, yet their low abundance in natural sources poses significant challenges for their extraction and isolation. This comprehensive review examines both conventional and modern techniques employed in the extraction and isolation of bioactive compounds from natural medicines, including methods such as maceration, percolation, decoction, reflux extraction, Soxhlet extraction, pressurized liquid extraction, supercritical fluid extraction, ultrasound-assisted extraction, and microwave-assisted extraction. The review discusses the principles, advantages, disadvantages, and practical applications of each method, highlighting factors that influence extraction efficiency such as solvent selection, particle size, temperature, duration, and solvent-to-solid ratio. Emphasis is placed on the growing adoption of greener and more selective techniques to improve yield and purity while reducing time and solvent consumption. By providing a critical evaluation of these methodologies, this review aims to guide researchers in selecting appropriate strategies for phytochemical investigation and drug development from natural products.

title: Telocytes in regenerative medicine
abstract: Telocytes (TCs) are a distinct type of interstitial cells characterized by a small cell body and extremely long and thin telopodes (Tps). The presence of TCs has been documented in many tissues and organs (go to http://www.telocytes.com). Functionally, TCs form a three‐dimensional (3D) interstitial network by homocellular and heterocellular communication and are involved in the maintenance of tissue homeostasis. As important interstitial cells to guide or nurse putative stem and progenitor cells in stem cell niches in a spectrum of tissues and organs, TCs contribute to tissue repair and regeneration. This review focuses on the latest progresses regarding TCs in the repair and regeneration of different tissues and organs, including heart, lung, skeletal muscle, skin, meninges and choroid plexus, eye, liver, uterus and urinary system. By targeting TCs alone or in tandem with stem cells, we might promote regeneration and prevent the evolution to irreversible tissue damage. Exploring pharmacological or non‐pharmacological methods to enhance the growth of TCs would be a novel therapeutic strategy besides exogenous transplantation for many diseased disorders.
venue: Journal of Cellular and Molecular Medicine

title: Telocytes in regenerative medicine
abstract: Telocytes (TCs) are a recently identified type of interstitial cell distinguished by their small cell bodies and extremely long, thin telopodes, with a presence documented across numerous tissues and organs. Characterized by unique ultrastructural and immunohistochemical features, TCs form extensive three-dimensional networks through homo- and heterocellular junctions, facilitating intercellular communication and the maintenance of tissue homeostasis. TCs interact closely with stem and progenitor cells within tissue niches, supporting their role in tissue repair and regeneration. This review summarizes current knowledge on the identification, distribution, and functional implications of TCs, highlighting their involvement in regenerative processes in organs such as the heart, lungs, skeletal muscle, skin, meninges, eye, liver, uterus, and urinary system. The therapeutic potential of targeting TCs—either alone or in combination with stem cells—is discussed as a novel strategy to enhance tissue regeneration and prevent irreversible damage. Further exploration of methods to promote TC growth may offer innovative approaches in regenerative medicine beyond traditional stem cell transplantation.
venue: Journal of Cellular and Molecular Medicine

title: The cost of defensive medicine on 3 hospital medicine services.
abstract: The overuse of tests and procedures due to fear of malpractice litigation, known as defensive medicine,1 is estimated to cost $46 billion annually in the US,2 but these costs have been measured only indirectly. We estimated the cost of defensive medicine on three hospital medicine services in a health system by having physicians assess the defensiveness of their own orders. We hypothesized that physicians who were concerned about being targeted by litigation would practice more defensively and have higher overall costs.

title: The cost of defensive medicine on 3 hospital medicine services.
abstract: This study assessed the cost of defensive medicine on three hospital medicine services by having physicians rate the defensiveness of their own orders. Hospitalists at one tertiary and two community hospitals evaluated 4,215 orders for 769 patients, indicating the degree to which each order was motivated by concerns about malpractice liability. Results showed that 28% of orders were at least partially defensive, accounting for 13% of total hospital costs, while only 2.9% of costs were due to completely defensive orders, primarily from additional hospital days. Physician characteristics and attitudes toward litigation were not associated with defensive ordering or costs. The findings suggest that although a significant proportion of hospital orders have some defensive component, only a small fraction of overall costs are attributable to fully defensive practices, indicating limited potential for cost savings through tort reform.

title: The EANM practice guidelines for bone scintigraphy
abstract: PurposeThe radionuclide bone scan is the cornerstone of skeletal nuclear medicine imaging. Bone scintigraphy is a highly sensitive diagnostic nuclear medicine imaging technique that uses a radiotracer to evaluate the distribution of active bone formation in the skeleton related to malignant and benign disease, as well as physiological processes.MethodsThe European Association of Nuclear Medicine (EANM) has written and approved these guidelines to promote the use of nuclear medicine procedures of high quality.ConclusionThe present guidelines offer assistance to nuclear medicine practitioners in optimizing the diagnostic procedure and interpreting bone scintigraphy. These guidelines describe the protocols that are currently accepted and used routinely, but do not include all existing procedures. They should therefore not be taken as exclusive of other nuclear medicine modalities that can be used to obtain comparable results. It is important to remember that the resources and facilities available for patient care may vary.
venue: European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging

title: The EANM practice guidelines for bone scintigraphy
abstract: These EANM practice guidelines provide comprehensive recommendations for the performance, interpretation, and reporting of bone scintigraphy, a highly sensitive nuclear medicine imaging technique essential for evaluating skeletal pathology. The guidelines address the use of technetium-99m-labeled phosphate analogues, describe standard imaging protocols including planar, SPECT, and SPECT/CT acquisitions, and outline multiphase imaging approaches. They emphasize the importance of bone scintigraphy in detecting metabolic changes associated with malignant and benign bone diseases, often before radiological alterations become apparent. The document discusses clinical indications, technical considerations, and the complementary role of bone scintigraphy alongside other imaging modalities. Developed through consensus by EANM committees and informed by international standards, these guidelines aim to support practitioners in delivering high-quality, standardized care while acknowledging variability in resources and clinical scenarios.
venue: European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging

title: The future landscape of large language models in medicine
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are artificial intelligence (AI) tools specifically trained to process and generate text. LLMs attracted substantial public attention after OpenAI’s ChatGPT was made publicly available in November 2022. LLMs can often answer questions, summarize, paraphrase and translate text on a level that is nearly indistinguishable from human capabilities. The possibility to actively interact with models like ChatGPT makes LLMs attractive tools in various fields, including medicine. While these models have the potential to democratize medical knowledge and facilitate access to healthcare, they could equally distribute misinformation and exacerbate scientific misconduct due to a lack of accountability and transparency. In this article, we provide a systematic and comprehensive overview of the potentials and limitations of LLMs in clinical practice, medical research and medical education.

title: The future landscape of large language models in medicine
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly emerged as transformative artificial intelligence tools capable of generating human-like text and engaging in complex language tasks. Their integration into medicine offers significant opportunities to enhance patient care, medical research, and education by facilitating communication, democratizing access to knowledge, and streamlining documentation. However, the adoption of LLMs also presents challenges, including risks of misinformation, privacy concerns, algorithmic biases, and the potential for misuse due to limited transparency and accountability. This perspective provides a comprehensive overview of the development and current capabilities of LLMs, examines their potential applications across clinical practice, research, and education, and discusses critical limitations that must be addressed to ensure their safe and effective use in healthcare. The future landscape of LLMs in medicine will depend on balancing innovation with robust safeguards to maximize benefits while mitigating risks.

title: The Future of Family Medicine: A Collaborative Project of the Family Medicine Community
abstract: Recognizing fundamental flaws in the fragmented US health care systems and the potential of an integrative, generalist approach, the leadership of 7 national family medicine organizations initiated the Future of Family Medicine (FFM) project in 2002. The goal of the project was to develop a strategy to transform and renew the discipline of family medicine to meet the needs of patients in a changing health care environment. METHODS A national research study was conducted by independent research firms. Interviews and focus groups identified key issues for diverse constituencies, including patients, payers, residents, students, family physicians, and other clinicians. Subsequently, interviews were conducted with nationally representative samples of 9 key constituencies. Based in part on these data, 5 task forces addressed key issues to meet the project goal. A Project Leadership Committee synthesized the task force reports into the report presented here. RESULTS The project identified core values, a New Model of practice, and a process for development, research, education, partnership, and change with great potential to transform the ability of family medicine to improve the health and health care of the nation. The proposed New Model of practice has the following characteristics: a patient-centered team approach; elimination of barriers to access; advanced information systems, including an electronic health record; redesigned, more functional offices; a focus on quality and outcomes; and enhanced practice finance. A unified communications strategy will be developed to promote the New Model of family medicine to multiple audiences. The study concluded that the discipline needs to oversee the training of family physicians who are committed to excellence, steeped in the core values of the discipline, competent to provide family medicine’s basket of services within the New Model, and capable of adapting to varying patient needs and changing care technologies. Family medicine education must continue to include training in maternity care, the care of hospitalized patients, community and population health, and culturally effective and proficient care. A comprehensive lifelong learning program for each family physician will support continuous personal, professional, and clinical practice assessment and improvement. Ultimately, systemwide changes will be needed to ensure high-quality health care for all Americans. Such changes include taking steps to ensure that every American has a personal medical home, promoting the use and reporting of quality measures to improve performance and service, advocating that every American have health care coverage for basic services and protection against extraordinary health care costs, advancing research that supports the clinical decision making of family physicians and other primary care clinicians, and developing reimbursement models to sustain family medicine and primary care practices. CONCLUSIONS The leadership of US family medicine organizations is committed to a transformative process. In partnership with others, this process has the potential to integrate health care to improve the health of all Americans.

title: The Future of Family Medicine: A Collaborative Project of the Family Medicine Community
abstract: The Future of Family Medicine (FFM) project, initiated by the leadership of seven national family medicine organizations, aimed to address critical flaws in the fragmented US health care system by developing a strategy to transform and renew the discipline of family medicine. Through a comprehensive national research study involving diverse stakeholders and five dedicated task forces, the project identified core values and proposed a New Model of practice characterized by patient-centered teams, improved access, advanced information systems, redesigned offices, a focus on quality and outcomes, and enhanced practice finance. The report emphasizes the need for unified communication strategies, ongoing education including maternity and hospital care, community health, cultural competence, and lifelong learning for family physicians. Systemwide reforms are recommended to ensure every American has a personal medical home, access to quality care, appropriate coverage, and protection against extraordinary costs. The FFM project concludes that transformative changes in family medicine, supported by collaborative leadership and innovative practice models, have significant potential to improve health care delivery and outcomes for all Americans.

title: The Future of Nuclear Medicine, Molecular Imaging, and Theranostics.
abstract: Wolfgang A. Weber and Johannes Czernin Scientific discoveries published in The Journal of Nuclear Medicine over the past 60 years have shaped the practice of medicine and form the foundation for the future of nuclear medicine, molecular imaging, and theranostics. Nuclear medicine now provides

title: The Future of Nuclear Medicine, Molecular Imaging, and Theranostics.
abstract: This paper reviews the evolving landscape of nuclear medicine, molecular imaging, and theranostics, emphasizing their expanding roles in oncology, cardiology, and neurology. Advances in radiopharmaceutical chemistry, instrumentation—such as total-body and hybrid PET/MR systems—and artificial intelligence are transforming diagnostic and prognostic capabilities. In oncology, the integration of molecular imaging with omics technologies and the shift toward theranostic approaches enable more precise patient selection and targeted therapies. The tumor microenvironment is emerging as a critical focus for new imaging agents, with novel tracers and optical imaging modalities offering deeper insight into tumor biology and therapeutic response. Machine learning promises to automate image interpretation, increasing efficiency and reproducibility. Despite challenges in radiolabeling and radiation exposure, innovations in antibody labeling and total-body PET are enhancing pharmacokinetic studies and target identification. The field is poised to become increasingly integral to patient management by providing comprehensive biomarkers for disease characterization and therapy monitoring across multiple specialties.

title: The incidence of diagnostic error in medicine
abstract: A wide variety of research studies suggest that breakdowns in the diagnostic process result in a staggering toll of harm and patient deaths. These include autopsy studies, case reviews, surveys of patient and physicians, voluntary reporting systems, using standardised patients, second reviews, diagnostic testing audits and closed claims reviews. Although these different approaches provide important information and unique insights regarding diagnostic errors, each has limitations and none is well suited to establishing the incidence of diagnostic error in actual practice, or the aggregate rate of error and harm. We argue that being able to measure the incidence of diagnostic error is essential to enable research studies on diagnostic error, and to initiate quality improvement projects aimed at reducing the risk of error and harm. Three approaches appear most promising in this regard: (1) using ‘trigger tools’ to identify from electronic health records cases at high risk for diagnostic error; (2) using standardised patients (secret shoppers) to study the rate of error in practice; (3) encouraging both patients and physicians to voluntarily report errors they encounter, and facilitating this process.

title: The incidence of diagnostic error in medicine
abstract: Diagnostic errors represent a significant and underappreciated source of patient harm in medicine, with research indicating that diagnoses are incorrect or delayed in approximately 10–15% of cases. This narrative review synthesizes evidence from multiple research methodologies—including autopsy studies, patient and provider surveys, standardized patient encounters, second reviews in visual specialties, diagnostic testing audits, malpractice claim analyses, case reviews, and voluntary reporting systems—to estimate the incidence of diagnostic error. Each approach offers unique insights but also presents methodological limitations that hinder precise measurement of error rates in routine clinical practice. Autopsy studies consistently reveal major diagnostic discrepancies in 10–20% of cases, while standardized patient studies and provider surveys corroborate similar rates of diagnostic inaccuracy. Malpractice data further highlight diagnostic error as the leading cause of paid claims. The lack of a unified, robust method for measuring diagnostic errors impedes efforts to quantify their true incidence and associated harm. The review identifies promising strategies for advancing measurement—including trigger tools in electronic health records, standardized patients, and enhanced voluntary reporting—and underscores the urgent need for accurate data to drive quality improvement initiatives targeting diagnostic safety.

title: The Limits of Reductionism in Medicine: Could Systems Biology Offer an Alternative?
abstract: In the first of a two part series, Ahn and colleagues discuss the reductionist approach pervading medicine and explain how a systems approach (as advocated by systems biology) may complement reductionism.

title: The Limits of Reductionism in Medicine: Could Systems Biology Offer an Alternative?
abstract: Reductionism has long dominated medical science, shaping diagnosis, treatment, and prevention through the analysis of isolated components and singular causal factors. While this approach has yielded significant advances, it often overlooks the complex interactions and contextual factors inherent in human health. This essay critically examines four key manifestations of reductionism in medicine: the focus on singular factors, the emphasis on homeostasis as static stability, the limitations of inexact risk modification, and the additive treatment of coexisting conditions. Each practice illustrates how reductionist thinking can miss dynamic system behaviors, multifactorial risk profiles, and nonlinear treatment effects. The emerging field of systems biology offers a complementary perspective by emphasizing holistic analysis and computational modeling of biological networks. By recognizing the limitations of reductionism and integrating systems-oriented approaches, medicine may better account for complexity and improve patient care. This article lays the groundwork for further exploration of how systems biology could reshape clinical practice.

title: The n-of-1 clinical trial: the ultimate strategy for individualizing medicine?
abstract: N-of-1 or single subject clinical trials consider an individual patient as the sole unit of observation in a study investigating the efficacy or side-effect profiles of different interventions. The ultimate goal of an n-of-1 trial is to determine the optimal or best intervention for an individual patient using objective data-driven criteria. Such trials can leverage study design and statistical techniques associated with standard population-based clinical trials, including randomization, washout and crossover periods, as well as placebo controls. Despite their obvious appeal and wide use in educational settings, n-of-1 trials have been used sparingly in medical and general clinical settings. We briefly review the history, motivation and design of n-of-1 trials and emphasize the great utility of modern wireless medical monitoring devices in their execution. We ultimately argue that n-of-1 trials demand serious attention among the health research and clinical care communities given the contemporary focus on individualized medicine.

title: The n-of-1 clinical trial: the ultimate strategy for individualizing medicine?
abstract: N-of-1 clinical trials, which treat the individual patient as the sole unit of observation, offer a rigorous, data-driven approach for determining optimal therapeutic interventions tailored to unique patient characteristics. While traditional randomized controlled trials (RCTs) remain the gold standard for evaluating treatment efficacy at the population level, they often fail to address the heterogeneity inherent in individual responses, especially in the context of chronic and complex conditions. This review examines the history, design, and implementation of n-of-1 trials, highlighting their potential to advance truly individualized medicine beyond current stratification strategies based on genetic or phenotypic subgroups. Despite their promise and established use in educational and behavioral research, n-of-1 trials are underutilized in clinical practice due to perceived challenges in cost, logistics, and generalizability. However, advances in wireless health monitoring technologies may facilitate broader adoption by enabling objective, real-time data collection and remote assessment. The authors argue that n-of-1 trials warrant greater attention as a practical strategy for personalizing care, improving comparative effectiveness research, and ultimately enhancing patient outcomes in an era increasingly focused on precision medicine.

title: The social transformation of american medicine.
abstract: The Social Transformation of American Medicine is one of the most comprehensive studies on the rise of the medical profession and the development of the health care industry published to date, Starr is able to span the fields of medicine so that he discusses intelligently the economic, political, and historical developments in medical care. His wri ting is clear and succinct, his arguments are copiously footnoted, and the inferences he draws are sound. In Book I, he covers 'the rise of medical authority and the shaping of the medical system'; in Book II, 'doctors, the State, and the coming of the corporation.' Reviews by Daniel Bell of Harvard and George Silver of Yale call Starr's work brilliant-I would agree. I would recommend this book to anyone who wants to understand the current health care system. Starr describes the movement of the medical profession from one that was initially viewed skeptically to one that was later embraced; and now, coming full circle, to one that is viewed critically. Starr maintains that the current status of American medicine is the result of our history of accommodating professional interests while failing to exercise control over health programs, and then needing to adopt piecemeal regulations and cut-backs on programs that become too inflationary, One of the primary messages I take from this book is the importance of a com bination of forces: a profession's authority, the political climate, and the current philosophy about health care. Starr illustrates how these forces coalesce to defeat or achieve medical improvements. As occupational therapists, we are dependent on the development of the health care industry. It is wise for us to understand the forces that have an impact on medical care and what they could mean for our profession, Kay Barbara Schwartz, M.S., OTR

title: The social transformation of american medicine.
abstract: This paper reviews Paul Starr’s influential work, The Social Transformation of American Medicine, which examines the evolution of the American medical profession and health care industry. Starr’s analysis is divided into two main themes: the rise of physicians as a sovereign profession with unprecedented cultural authority, and the subsequent transformation of medicine into an industry increasingly dominated by corporations and state involvement. The review highlights Starr’s compelling account of how physicians consolidated professional power and autonomy, as well as his exploration of the challenges posed by corporatization and shifting state roles. However, it also critiques the book’s omission of key sociological issues, such as the social construction of medical knowledge, the processes of medicalization and demedicalization, and the interplay between medical ideology and broader social structures. The review notes that Starr overlooks important historical dynamics, including the profession’s role in enforcing regressive social norms and the intellectual shifts accompanying changes in medical practice. Despite these limitations, the book is recognized as a significant contribution that encourages readers to view present dilemmas in historical context and provokes critical reflection on the future trajectory of American medicine.

title: The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) Statement: Guidelines for Reporting Observational Studies
abstract: Much biomedical research is observational. The reporting of such research is often inadequate, which hampers the assessment of its strengths and weaknesses and of a study's generalisability. The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) Initiative developed recommendations on what should be included in an accurate and complete report of an observational study. We defined the scope of the recommendations to cover three main study designs: cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional studies. We convened a 2-day workshop in September 2004, with methodologists, researchers, and journal editors to draft a checklist of items. This list was subsequently revised during several meetings of the coordinating group and in e-mail discussions with the larger group of STROBE contributors, taking into account empirical evidence and methodological considerations. The workshop and the subsequent iterative process of consultation and revision resulted in a checklist of 22 items (the STROBE Statement) that relate to the title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, and discussion sections of articles. 18 items are common to all three study designs and four are specific for cohort, case-control, or cross-sectional studies. A detailed Explanation and Elaboration document is published separately and is freely available on the Web sites of PLoS Medicine, Annals of Internal Medicine, and Epidemiology. We hope that the STROBE Statement will contribute to improving the quality of reporting of observational studies.

title: The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) Statement: Guidelines for Reporting Observational Studies
abstract: The STROBE Statement provides a checklist of 22 essential items to guide transparent and comprehensive reporting of observational studies in epidemiology, specifically cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional designs. Developed through a collaborative process involving methodologists, researchers, and journal editors, the checklist addresses key elements across the title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, and discussion sections of research articles. Eighteen items are common to all study types, while four are design-specific. The initiative aims to enhance the clarity and completeness of reporting, facilitating critical appraisal, replication, and synthesis of observational research. An accompanying Explanation and Elaboration document offers detailed guidance and examples. Adoption of the STROBE Statement is expected to improve the quality and utility of published observational studies in biomedical research.

title: The use of herbal medicines during breastfeeding: a population-based survey in Western Australia
abstract: Main concerns for lactating women about medications include the safety of their breastfed infants and the potential effects of medication on quantity and quality of breast milk. While medicine treatments include conventional and complementary medicines, most studies to date have focused on evaluating the safety aspect of conventional medicines. Despite increasing popularity of herbal medicines, there are currently limited data available on the pattern of use and safety of these medicines during breastfeeding. This study aimed to identify the pattern of use of herbal medicines during breastfeeding in Perth, Western Australia, and to identify aspects which require further clinical research.MethodsThis study was conducted using a self-administered questionnaire validated through two pilot studies. Participants were 18 years or older, breastfeeding or had breastfed in the past 12 months. Participants were recruited from various community and health centres, and through advertising in newspapers. Simple descriptive statistics were used to summarise the demographic profile and attitudes of respondents, using the SPSS statistical software.ResultsA total of 304 questionnaires from eligible participants were returned (27.2% response rate) and analysed. Amongst the respondents, 59.9% took at least one herb for medicinal purposes during breastfeeding, whilst 24.3% reported the use of at least one herb to increase breast milk supply. Most commonly used herbs were fenugreek (18.4%), ginger (11.8%), dong quai (7.9%), chamomile (7.2%), garlic (6.6%) and blessed thistle (5.9%). The majority of participants (70.1%) believed that there was a lack of information resources, whilst 43.4% perceived herbal medicines to be safer than conventional medicines. Only 28.6% of users notified their doctor of their decision to use herbal medicine(s) during breastfeeding; 71.6% had previously refused or avoided conventional medicine treatments due to concerns regarding safety of their breastfed infants.ConclusionsThe use of herbal medicines is common amongst breastfeeding women, while information supporting their safety and efficacy is lacking. This study has demonstrated the need for further research into commonly used herbal medicines. Evidence-based information should be available to breastfeeding women who wish to consider use of all medicines, including complementary medicines, to avoid unnecessary cessation of breastfeeding or compromising of pharmacotherapy.

title: The use of herbal medicines during breastfeeding: a population-based survey in Western Australia
abstract: This population-based survey investigated the prevalence, patterns, and attitudes towards herbal medicine use among breastfeeding women in Western Australia. Using a validated self-administered questionnaire, data were collected from 304 women aged 18 years or older who were currently breastfeeding or had breastfed in the previous 12 months. Results showed that 59.9% of respondents used at least one herbal medicine during breastfeeding, with 24.3% specifically using herbs to increase milk supply. The most commonly used herbs included fenugreek, ginger, dong quai, chamomile, garlic, and blessed thistle. Despite widespread use, 70.1% of participants reported a lack of accessible information on herbal medicines during lactation, and only 28.6% informed their doctor about their herbal use. Additionally, 43.4% perceived herbal medicines as safer than conventional medicines, and 71.6% had avoided or refused conventional treatments due to concerns for infant safety. The findings highlight the common use of herbal medicines among breastfeeding women and underscore the need for further research and evidence-based information to support safe decision-making regarding herbal and conventional medicine use during lactation.

title: The Values and Value of Patient-Centered Care
abstract: Patient-centered care has now made it to center stage in discussions of quality. Enshrined by the Institute of Medicine’s “quality chasm” report as 1 of 6 key elements of high-quality care,[1][1] health care institutions, health planners, congressional representatives, and hospital public

title: The Values and Value of Patient-Centered Care
abstract: Patient-centered care has emerged as a central tenet of high-quality healthcare, emphasizing respect for patients as unique individuals and involving them meaningfully in their care. This editorial explores the foundational values and practical value of patient-centered care, clarifying its moral underpinnings, its integration with evidence-based medicine, and the importance of fostering patient-clinician partnerships at personal, professional, and organizational levels. The authors critique superficial implementations that conflate amenities or infrastructural changes with genuine patient-centeredness and highlight the need for robust measures to assess whether interventions truly enhance patient engagement, understanding, and shared decision-making. They identify challenges in current assessment approaches, including the conflation of behaviors with outcomes, reliance on patient self-reporting, and discrepancies between patient, clinician, and expert evaluations of encounters. The editorial calls for the development of more nuanced, context-sensitive tools that capture the complex realities of patient-centered care and provide actionable feedback to improve practice. Ultimately, the authors argue that patient-centered care is both a moral imperative and a pathway to better health outcomes, requiring ongoing commitment to measurement and meaningful engagement at all levels of the healthcare system.

title: Toward precision medicine in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: In Western societies, Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia and the sixth leading cause of death. In recent years, the concept of precision medicine, an approach for disease prevention and treatment that is personalized to an individual's specific pattern of genetic variability, environment and lifestyle factors, has emerged. While for some diseases, in particular select cancers and a few monogenetic disorders such as cystic fibrosis, significant advances in precision medicine have been made over the past years, for most other diseases precision medicine is only in its beginning. To advance the application of precision medicine to a wider spectrum of disorders, governments around the world are starting to launch Precision Medicine Initiatives, major efforts to generate the extensive scientific knowledge needed to integrate the model of precision medicine into every day clinical practice. In this article we summarize the state of precision medicine in AD, review major obstacles in its development, and discuss its benefits in this highly prevalent, clinically and pathologically complex disease.

title: Toward precision medicine in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD), the most prevalent form of dementia and a leading cause of death in Western societies, presents significant clinical, pathological, and genetic heterogeneity that has impeded the development of effective therapies. Precision medicine, which seeks to tailor prevention and treatment strategies to an individual’s unique genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors, has shown promise in other diseases but remains nascent in AD. This review summarizes the current state of precision medicine approaches in AD, highlighting advances in genomics that have identified multiple susceptibility loci and biological pathways involved in disease risk. It also discusses the complex interplay between genetic and non-genetic risk factors, such as cerebrovascular disease and traumatic brain injury, and emphasizes the need for integrating molecular profiling with environmental and behavioral data to better stratify patients. Major challenges include incomplete understanding of pathogenic mechanisms, limited predictive power of known genetic variants, and the need for large-scale data integration. The article concludes that overcoming these obstacles is essential for realizing the potential of precision medicine to improve diagnosis, prevention, and individualized treatment in this complex and burdensome disease.

title: Transparent reporting of a multivariable prediction model for individual prognosis or diagnosis (TRIPOD): the TRIPOD Statement
abstract: Prediction models are developed to aid health care providers in estimating the probability or risk that a specific disease or condition is present (diagnostic models) or that a specific event will occur in the future (prognostic models), to inform their decision making. However, the overwhelming evidence shows that the quality of reporting of prediction model studies is poor. Only with full and clear reporting of information on all aspects of a prediction model can risk of bias and potential usefulness of prediction models be adequately assessed. The Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) Initiative developed a set of recommendations for the reporting of studies developing, validating, or updating a prediction model, whether for diagnostic or prognostic purposes. This article describes how the TRIPOD Statement was developed. An extensive list of items based on a review of the literature was created, which was reduced after a Web-based survey and revised during a 3-day meeting in June 2011 with methodologists, health care professionals, and journal editors. The list was refined during several meetings of the steering group and in e-mail discussions with the wider group of TRIPOD contributors. The resulting TRIPOD Statement is a checklist of 22 items, deemed essential for transparent reporting of a prediction model study. The TRIPOD Statement aims to improve the transparency of the reporting of a prediction model study regardless of the study methods used. The TRIPOD Statement is best used in conjunction with the TRIPOD explanation and elaboration document. To aid the editorial process and readers of prediction model studies, it is recommended that authors include a completed checklist in their submission (also available at www.tripod-statement.org). Editors’ note: In order to encourage dissemination of the TRIPOD Statement, this article is freely accessible on the Annals of Internal Medicine Web site (www.annals.org) and will be also published in BJOG, British Journal of Cancer, British Journal of Surgery, BMC Medicine, British Medical Journal, Circulation, Diabetic Medicine, European Journal of Clinical Investigation, European Urology, and Journal of Clinical Epidemiology. The authors jointly hold the copyright of this article. An accompanying Explanation and Elaboration article is freely available only on www.annals.org; Annals of Internal Medicine holds copyright for that article.

title: Transparent reporting of a multivariable prediction model for individual prognosis or diagnosis (TRIPOD): the TRIPOD Statement
abstract: Prediction models are essential tools in healthcare for estimating the probability of disease presence (diagnosis) or future outcomes (prognosis) to inform clinical decision-making. Despite their increasing development and use, the quality of reporting in prediction model studies remains suboptimal, hindering assessment of bias, reproducibility, and clinical utility. The Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) Initiative was established to address these deficiencies by providing comprehensive recommendations for reporting studies that develop, validate, or update diagnostic or prognostic prediction models. The TRIPOD Statement was developed through literature review, expert surveys, and consensus meetings involving methodologists, clinicians, and journal editors. It consists of a 22-item checklist covering essential aspects of study design, analysis, and results to ensure transparency and completeness in reporting. Adoption of the TRIPOD Statement aims to improve the reliability, interpretability, and application of prediction models in research and practice. Researchers are encouraged to use the checklist alongside the accompanying explanation and elaboration document to facilitate high-quality reporting and enhance the value of prediction model studies in medicine.

title: Use of herbal medicine during pregnancy among women with access to public healthcare in Nairobi, Kenya: a cross-sectional survey
abstract: Maternal health is a public health priority in many African countries, but little is known about herbal medicine use in pregnancy. This study aimed to determine the pattern of use of herbal medicine in an urban setting, where women have relatively high access to public healthcare.MethodsThis cross-sectional study included 333 women attending a childcare clinic in a district public health hospital in Nairobi, Kenya, during January and February, 2012, and who had delivered a baby within the past 9 months. Qualitative and quantitative data on herbal medicine use during their latest pregnancy were collected through an interviewer-administered questionnaire. Data was analysed descriptively and the Chi square test and Fishers’ exact test used to analyse relationships among variables.ResultsAbout 12% of women used herbal medicine during their most recent pregnancy. The use of herbal medicine was associated with a lower level of education (p = 0.007) and use before the index pregnancy (p <0.001). Only 12.5% of users disclosed such use to healthcare professionals, and about 20% used herbal medicine concomitantly with Western medicine for the same illness/condition. Women used herbal medicine for back pain, toothache, indigestion and infectious diseases, such as respiratory tract infections and malaria. A proportion of users took herbal medicine only to boost or maintain health. There were high rates of self-prescribing, as well as sourcing from family and friends. Beliefs about safety and efficacy were consistent with patterns of use or non-use, although both users and non-users were unsure about the safety and contraindications of Western medicine during pregnancy compared with that of herbal medicine.ConclusionHerbal medicine is used by 12% of pregnant women with access to healthcare in an urban context in Kenya, and often occurs without the knowledge of healthcare practitioners. Healthcare professionals should play a role in rational use of both herbal and Western medicine, by discussing contraindications and the potential for drug-herb interactions with patients. More studies are needed into the use of herbal medicines during pregnancy, labour and the postpartum period in different geographical areas, and into the health outcomes associated with their use.

title: Use of herbal medicine during pregnancy among women with access to public healthcare in Nairobi, Kenya: a cross-sectional survey
abstract: This cross-sectional survey investigated the prevalence and patterns of herbal medicine use during pregnancy among 333 women attending a public childcare clinic in Nairobi, Kenya, an urban setting with high access to public healthcare. Data were collected through interviewer-administered questionnaires and analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests. The study found that 12% of respondents used herbal medicine during their most recent pregnancy, with use significantly associated with lower educational attainment and prior experience with herbal remedies.
