We try to summarise some of the relatively recent results predicting exotic phases such as super-solidity and Majorana like modes and then shift our attention to developments involving 1D nonlinear slow light setups. There the simulation of strongly correlated phases characterising Tonks–Girardeau gases, Luttinger liquids, and interacting relativistic fermionic models is described. We review the major theory results and also briefly outline recent developments in ongoing experimental efforts involving different platforms in circuit QED, photonic crystals and nanophotonic fibres interfaced with cold atoms.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: Quantum simulations and many-body physics with light
abstract: This review surveys the development of quantum simulation and many-body physics using strongly correlated photons, focusing on both theoretical proposals and experimental progress. It begins with foundational work on coupled resonator arrays (CRAs), highlighting the Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard model and photon-blockade-induced Mott transitions, and extends to simulations of effective spin models and fractional quantum Hall states. The discussion then shifts to out-of-equilibrium phenomena in driven-dissipative photonic systems, including photon fermionization, crystallization, supersolid phases, and emergent Majorana-like modes. Advances in simulating one-dimensional strongly correlated systems with slow light in nonlinear waveguides are also reviewed, encompassing realizations of Tonks-Girardeau gases, Luttinger liquids, and interacting relativistic models. The review concludes by summarizing major theoretical achievements and outlining experimental implementations across platforms such as circuit QED, photonic crystals, and nanophotonic fibers interfaced with cold atoms, emphasizing the rapid evolution and broad potential of photonic quantum simulators for exploring complex many-body phenomena.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: Quantum Theory of Angular Momentum: Irreducible Tensors, Spherical Harmonics, Vector Coupling Coefficients, 3nj Symbols
abstract: This is the most complete handbook on the quantum theory of angular momentum. Containing basic definitions and theorems as well as relations, tables of formula and numerical tables which are essential for applications to many physical problems, the book is useful for specialists in nuclear and particle physics, atomic and molecular spectroscopy, plasma physics, collision and reaction theory, quantum chemistry, etc. The authors take pains to write many formulae in different coordinate systems thus providing users with added ease in consulting this book. Each chapter opens with a comprehensive list of its contents to ease the search for any information needed later. New results relating to different aspects of the angular momentum thoery are also included. Containing close to 500 pages this book also gathers together many useful formulae besides those related to angular momentum. The book also compares different notations used by previous authors.

title: Quantum Theory of Angular Momentum: Irreducible Tensors, Spherical Harmonics, Vector Coupling Coefficients, 3nj Symbols
abstract: This monograph presents a comprehensive and systematic treatment of the quantum theory of angular momentum, emphasizing irreducible tensors, spherical harmonics, vector coupling coefficients, and 3nj symbols. Addressing the needs of both specialists and students, it compiles essential formulas, relationships, and theoretical results within a unified framework of phase conventions and definitions. The text covers foundational aspects such as vector and tensor theory, angular momentum operators, Wigner D-functions, spin functions, tensor spherical harmonics, Clebsch-Gordan coefficients, and higher-order coupling symbols. Designed as both a reference and a practical handbook, the material is organized for ease of use in calculations relevant to atomic, molecular, nuclear, and particle physics, as well as applications in quantum chemistry, optics, plasma physics, radiophysics, and astrophysics. By consolidating widely scattered results and providing concise presentations without proofs but with extensive references, this work facilitates the evaluation of structures, transition probabilities, cross sections, and angular distributions in diverse quantum systems.

title: Quantum thermodynamics
abstract: Quantum thermodynamics is an emerging research field aiming to extend standard thermodynamics and non-equilibrium statistical physics to ensembles of sizes well below the thermodynamic limit, in non-equilibrium situations and with the full inclusion of quantum effects. Fuelled by experimental advances and the potential of future nanoscale applications, this research effort is pursued by scientists with different backgrounds, including statistical physics, many-body theory, mesoscopic physics and quantum information theory, who bring various tools and methods to the field. A multitude of theoretical questions are being addressed ranging from issues of thermalisation of quantum systems and various definitions of ‘work’ to the efficiency and power of quantum engines. This overview provides a perspective on a selection of these current trends accessible to postgraduate students and researchers alike.

title: Quantum thermodynamics
abstract: Quantum thermodynamics is a rapidly developing field that seeks to generalize classical thermodynamics and non-equilibrium statistical physics to systems where quantum effects and small ensemble sizes are significant. Motivated by advances in experimental control at the nanoscale and the need for a deeper understanding of energy exchanges in quantum systems, this research area integrates perspectives from statistical physics, many-body theory, mesoscopic physics, and quantum information theory. Key topics include the foundations of thermodynamic laws in quantum regimes, the interplay between information and thermodynamics exemplified by concepts such as Maxwell’s demon and Landauer’s principle, the characterization of work and heat at the quantum level, fluctuation theorems, and the operation of quantum thermal machines. The paper provides an accessible overview of these themes, highlighting theoretical developments such as single-shot thermodynamics and resource-theoretic approaches, as well as open questions regarding thermalization, irreversibility, and the efficiency of quantum engines. This synthesis aims to guide both newcomers and specialists toward a unified framework for understanding thermodynamic processes in the quantum domain.

title: Radiation Oncology Physics: A Handbook for Teachers and Students
abstract: This book, published in 2005 by the International Atomic Energy Agency, is a comprehensive compendium of all of the topics that should be covered by a radiation oncology physics course, from basic physics to dosimetry, commissioning and quality assurance of equipment, treatment planning and radiation protection and safety. It has an extensive section on brachytherapy, some basic radiation biology and a chapter on special procedures and techniques. As a handbook, as opposed to a textbook, it contains a large number of useful data tables and basic formulae, but in places it does not go deep enough into the issues that are of current concern in the radiotherapy physics community. It has a comprehensive review of various calibration methods for both photon and electron beams, but it does not reproduce the basic tables of the most recent protocols. It also has a reasonably up to date review of the various radiation distribution algorithms employed by modern treatment planning systems, but it does not discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the various approaches. In general, it is a little disappointing that such a recent publication is not more focused on new developments in radiotherapy and their implications for the physicists' workload. The section on radiation producing equipment is historically inclusive of somewhat outdated models, but it hardly touches on the newer developments, such as cyclotrons or synchrotrons for proton therapy. Multi-leaf Collimators are not even included in this chapter, despite their wide availability, confining them to the special techniques chapter. Virtual simulators are presented alongside conventional ones, but their impact on the treatment planning process is not discussed. The Intensity Modulated Radiation Therapy Section in the otherwise comprehensive section on special procedures is inadequate. Given its great and wide impact on recent practice, one would have expected the Intensity Modulated Radiation Therapy Section to warrant a chapter of its own, with a detailed discussion on the associated quality assurance and its analysis. References to the up and coming heavy particle therapy, such as neutrons, protons and carbon ions, and their physical characteristics, are very sparse. In summary, this book is a worthwhile addition to the library of any university or hospital department of medical physics, but has a slightly dated feel despite its age.

title: Radiation Oncology Physics: A Handbook for Teachers and Students
abstract: This review evaluates 'Radiation Oncology Physics: A Handbook for Teachers and Students,' edited by EB Podgorsak and published by the International Atomic Energy Agency in 2005, as a comprehensive resource covering essential topics in radiation oncology physics, including basic physics, dosimetry, equipment commissioning, quality assurance, treatment planning, radiation protection, brachytherapy, and special techniques. The handbook is praised for its extensive data tables and formulae but is critiqued for insufficient depth on contemporary issues and limited discussion of recent technological advancements such as proton therapy equipment, multi-leaf collimators, virtual simulators, and intensity modulated radiation therapy. While the book provides valuable foundational knowledge and serves as a useful reference for medical physics departments, its coverage of emerging modalities and current practices is limited, giving it a somewhat dated perspective despite its relatively recent publication.

title: Science case for the Einstein telescope
abstract: The Einstein Telescope (ET), a proposed European ground-based gravitational-wave detector of third-generation, is an evolution of second-generation detectors such as Advanced LIGO, Advanced Virgo, and KAGRA which could be operating in the mid 2030s. ET will explore the universe with gravitational waves up to cosmological distances. We discuss its main scientific objectives and its potential for discoveries in astrophysics, cosmology and fundamental physics.
venue: Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics

title: Science case for the Einstein telescope
abstract: The Einstein Telescope (ET) is a proposed third-generation European ground-based gravitational-wave observatory designed to surpass the sensitivity and frequency range of current detectors such as Advanced LIGO and Virgo. This paper presents the scientific case for ET, detailing its transformative potential in astrophysics, cosmology, and fundamental physics. ET’s enhanced sensitivity will enable the detection of gravitational waves from compact binary coalescences—including black holes and neutron stars—across cosmological distances, offering unprecedented insights into stellar populations, neutron star matter, and the formation of heavy elements. The observatory’s design, featuring a triangular configuration with underground placement and dual interferometers optimized for low and high frequencies, will facilitate improved source localization and polarization measurements. ET will play a pivotal role in multi-messenger astronomy by enabling joint observations with electromagnetic and neutrino observatories, deepening our understanding of phenomena such as short gamma-ray bursts and core-collapse supernovae. In fundamental physics, ET will allow stringent tests of general relativity in strong-field regimes, probe the nature of dark matter and dark energy, and search for stochastic gravitational-wave backgrounds from the early universe. Overall, the Einstein Telescope promises to revolutionize gravitational-wave astronomy by addressing key open questions about the universe’s structure, evolution, and fundamental laws.
venue: Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics

title: Some applications of the Lambert W function to physics
abstract: Two standard physics problems are solved in terms of the Lambert W function, to show the applicability of this recently defined function to physics. Other applications of the function are cited, but not described. The problems solved concern Wien's displacement law and the fringing fields of a capacitor, the latter problem being representative of some problems solved using conformal transformations. The physical content of the solutions remains unchanged, but they gain a new elegance and convenience. PACS No.: 41.10F

title: Some applications of the Lambert W function to physics
abstract: The Lambert W function, a relatively recent addition to the repertoire of special functions, has found increasing utility in physics due to its ability to provide explicit solutions to certain transcendental equations. This paper demonstrates the application of the Lambert W function to two standard physics problems: Wien’s displacement law for blackbody radiation and the calculation of fringing fields in a parallel-plate capacitor using conformal mapping techniques. In both cases, expressing the solutions in terms of the Lambert W function yields more elegant and computationally convenient forms without altering the underlying physical content. The paper also references additional areas in physics where the function is applicable, highlighting its growing significance. The availability of efficient numerical implementations further enhances its practicality for physicists, suggesting that the Lambert W function may become a standard tool for solving a variety of problems involving transcendental equations in physics.

title: Statistical Methods in Experimental Physics
abstract: Basic Concepts in Probability Convergence and the Law of Large Numbers Probability Distributions Information Decision Theory Theory of Estimators Point Estimation in Practice Interval Estimation Test of Hypotheses Goodness-of-Fit Tests.

title: Statistical Methods in Experimental Physics
abstract: This comprehensive work presents a systematic exposition of statistical methods fundamental to experimental physics, addressing both theoretical foundations and practical applications. Beginning with the basic concepts of probability—including frequentist and Bayesian interpretations—the text develops the mathematical framework necessary for understanding random variables, probability distributions, and their properties. Key topics such as convergence, the law of large numbers, and central limit theorem are explored in depth, followed by detailed discussions of discrete and continuous probability distributions relevant to physical experiments. The book covers information theory, decision theory, and the construction and evaluation of estimators, emphasizing maximum likelihood, least squares, and robust estimation techniques. Methods for point and interval estimation are presented alongside Bayesian inference, with attention to practical considerations in estimator selection and bias reduction. Hypothesis testing is treated extensively, including optimal test construction, likelihood ratio tests, sequential analysis, and the integration of decision-theoretic approaches. Goodness-of-fit tests—both binned and unbinned—are analyzed with applications to experimental data evaluation. Throughout, the interplay between statistical rigor and experimental realities is highlighted, providing physicists with essential tools for data analysis, inference, and the design of experiments.

title: Statistical physics of social dynamics
abstract: Statistical physics has proven to be a fruitful framework to describe phenomena outside the realm of traditional physics. Recent years have witnessed an attempt by physicists to study collective phenomena emerging from the interactions of individuals as elementary units in social structures. A wide list of topics are reviewed ranging from opinion and cultural and language dynamics to crowd behavior, hierarchy formation, human dynamics, and social spreading. The connections between these problems and other, more traditional, topics of statistical physics are highlighted. Comparison of model results with empirical data from social systems are also emphasized.

title: Statistical physics of social dynamics
abstract: This paper reviews the application of statistical physics to the study of social dynamics, highlighting how collective phenomena such as consensus formation, cultural dissemination, language evolution, crowd behavior, hierarchy emergence, human activity patterns, and social spreading can be understood as macroscopic outcomes of interactions among individuals. The authors discuss key modeling approaches—including agent-based models and dynamical systems—while emphasizing the importance of network topology and universality in capturing large-scale regularities despite the complexity of individual behavior. By systematically surveying models for opinion dynamics, cultural and language change, crowd phenomena, and the coevolution of social states and network structure, the review demonstrates the value of statistical physics in revealing order-disorder transitions and scaling laws in social systems. The paper also stresses the critical role of empirical validation and identifies open challenges at the intersection of physics and social science.

title: Superconductivity in single-layer films of FeSe with a transition temperature above 100 K
abstract: Key Laboratory of Artificial Structures and Quantum Control (Ministry of Education), Department of Physics and Astronomy, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, 800 Dongchuan Road, Shanghai 200240, China. title: Superconductivity in single-layer films of FeSe with a transition temperature above 100 K
abstract: We report the observation of superconductivity above 100 K in single-layer films of FeSe grown on Nb-doped SrTiO3(001) substrates, as determined by in situ four-point probe electrical transport measurements. Our results reveal a superconducting transition temperature (Tc) as high as 109 K, significantly exceeding the Tc of bulk FeSe and previous records for Fe-based superconductors. The films were synthesized via molecular beam epitaxy with precise thickness control and characterized using reflection high-energy electron diffraction and scanning tunneling microscopy. Electrical measurements demonstrate zero resistance below Tc and a robust superconducting state persisting under magnetic fields up to 11 T. The critical current follows Ginzburg-Landau behavior, confirming the intrinsic nature of the observed superconductivity. Control experiments on bare substrates rule out substrate contributions to the superconducting signal. These findings establish single-layer FeSe/SrTiO3 as a promising platform for investigating high-Tc superconductivity and interface-driven pairing mechanisms in two-dimensional systems.

title: Testing the nature of dark compact objects: a status report
abstract: Very compact objects probe extreme gravitational fields and may be the key to understand outstanding puzzles in fundamental physics. These include the nature of dark matter, the fate of spacetime singularities, or the loss of unitarity in Hawking evaporation. The standard astrophysical description of collapsing objects tells us that massive, dark and compact objects are black holes. Any observation suggesting otherwise would be an indication of beyond-the-standard-model physics. Null results strengthen and quantify the Kerr black hole paradigm. The advent of gravitational-wave astronomy and precise measurements with very long baseline interferometry allow one to finally probe into such foundational issues. We overview the physics of exotic dark compact objects and their observational status, including the observational evidence for black holes with current and future experiments.

title: Testing the nature of dark compact objects: a status report
abstract: Dark compact objects, such as black holes, offer a unique window into the most extreme gravitational environments and are central to addressing fundamental questions in physics, including the nature of dark matter, the resolution of spacetime singularities, and the fate of information in black hole evaporation. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current theoretical and observational status of dark compact objects, emphasizing both standard black holes and a wide range of exotic alternatives motivated by extensions to general relativity and quantum gravity. We discuss the taxonomy, structure, dynamics, and stability of these objects, highlighting key physical parameters that distinguish them from classical black holes. Recent advances in gravitational-wave astronomy and high-resolution electromagnetic observations have enabled unprecedented tests of the Kerr black hole paradigm, offering new constraints on event horizons, tidal effects, multipole moments, and potential signatures such as gravitational-wave echoes. While current evidence strongly supports the existence of astrophysical black holes as described by general relativity, ongoing and future observations promise to further probe the possible existence of exotic compact objects and refine our understanding of strong gravity in the universe.

title: Theoretical Nuclear Physics
abstract: A semi-empirical basis is used to describe and correlate the known nuclear properties including the theoretical concepts, methods, and considerations which have been devised in order to interpret the experimentsl material and to advance the ability to predict and control nuclear phenomena. General properties, two-body problems at low energies, nuclear forces, two-body problems at high energies, three- and four-body problems, nuclear spectroscopy, nuclear reactions, spontaneous decay of nuclei, interaction of nuclei with electromagnetic radiation, and beta decay are treated. 1200 references. (JFP)

title: Theoretical Nuclear Physics
abstract: This progress report presents advances in theoretical nuclear physics, focusing on the development and application of consistent relativistic Hartree and random phase approximations (RHA-RPA) for finite nuclei, and the exact treatment of vacuum polarization effects within finite nuclear systems. The RHA-RPA framework incorporates vacuum contributions via a derivative expansion of the one-loop effective action, with momentum cutoffs introduced to suppress unphysical short-range effects. Results demonstrate that the strength of spin-orbit potentials and collective excitation properties in finite nuclei are sensitive to the choice of cutoff, with physically motivated values providing improved agreement with experimental data. In parallel, the report details computational strategies for evaluating vacuum polarization in finite nuclei, highlighting limitations of traditional integration schemes and introducing a stable diagonalization method in a finite basis of free eigenstates. This approach enables accurate calculation of renormalized vacuum densities and self-consistent solutions, supplemented by local density approximation results for high-energy states. Additional topics include isovector correlations in quantum hadrodynamics, nuclear response functions in quasielastic electron scattering, charge density differences near lead isotopes, excitation mechanisms in oxygen-16, deformed chiral nucleons, new bases for vacuum calculations in three dimensions, second-order processes in electron-induced deuteron emission, scalar and vector contributions to nucleon-nucleon interactions, and radiative proton capture by light nuclei at low energies. Collectively, these studies advance the understanding of nuclear structure and dynamics through improved theoretical models and computational techniques.

title: Theory of neutrinos: a white paper
abstract: This paper is a review of the present status of neutrino mass physics, which grew out of an APS sponsored study of neutrinos in 2004. After a discussion of the present knowledge of neutrino masses and mixing and some popular ways to probe the new physics implied by recent data, it summarizes what can be learned about neutrino interactions as well as the nature of new physics beyond the Standard Model from the various proposed neutrino experiments. The intriguing possibility that neutrino mass physics may be at the heart of our understanding of a long standing puzzle of cosmology, i.e. the origin of matter–antimatter asymmetry is also discussed.

title: Theory of neutrinos: a white paper
abstract: This white paper provides a comprehensive review of the theoretical landscape of neutrino physics in light of recent experimental advances, particularly the discovery of neutrino oscillations and the consequent evidence for nonzero neutrino masses and mixing. It systematically examines current knowledge of neutrino properties, including mass hierarchies, mixing angles, Dirac versus Majorana nature, and the implications for physics beyond the Standard Model. The report explores mechanisms for generating small neutrino masses, such as various seesaw models, and discusses their testability through phenomena like lepton flavor violation, electric dipole moments, and leptogenesis. The role of neutrinos in addressing fundamental questions such as the origin of matter-antimatter asymmetry, the existence of sterile neutrinos, and connections to grand unification, supersymmetry, extra dimensions, and other new physics scenarios is analyzed. The impact of future experiments on constraining or revealing new theoretical frameworks is highlighted, with extensive references provided to guide further study.

title: The Condensed matter physics of QCD
abstract: Important progress in understanding the behavior of hadronic matter at high density has been achieved recently, by adapting the techniques of condensed matter theory. At asymptotic densities, the combination of asymptotic freedom and BCS theory make a rigorous analysis possible. New phases of matter with remarkable properties are predicted. They provide a theoretical laboratory within which chiral symmetry breaking and confinement can be studied at weak coupling. They may also play a role in the description of neutron star interiors. We discuss the phase diagram of QCD as a function of temperature and density, and close with a look at possible astrophysical signatures.

title: The Condensed matter physics of QCD
abstract: This paper explores the behavior of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) at high baryon density and low temperature, applying concepts and methods from condensed matter physics to analyze the emergence of novel phases such as color superconductivity. The authors demonstrate that, at asymptotically high densities, the combination of asymptotic freedom and BCS theory allows for a controlled theoretical treatment, revealing the formation of diquark condensates analogous to Cooper pairs in conventional superconductors. The phenomenon of color-flavor locking is identified as a particularly robust and symmetric ground state in three-flavor QCD, leading to spontaneous breaking of color and chiral symmetries, the generation of energy gaps for colored excitations, and the appearance of new collective modes. The study systematically examines variants with different numbers of quark flavors and colors, discusses calculational techniques including renormalization group methods and variational approaches, and constructs a tentative phase diagram for QCD as a function of temperature and density. Potential astrophysical implications are addressed, especially regarding the properties of neutron star interiors and observable signatures such as cooling rates and magnetic field evolution. The work highlights both the theoretical advances made possible by condensed matter analogies and the open challenges in understanding dense QCD matter.

title: The Cosmological Constant
abstract: This is a review of the physics and cosmology of the cosmological constant. Focusing on recent developments, I present a pedagogical overview of cosmology in the presence of a cosmological constant, observational constraints on its magnitude, and the physics of a small (and potentially nonzero) vacuum energy.

title: The Cosmological Constant
abstract: This review provides a comprehensive and pedagogical overview of the cosmological constant, tracing its historical introduction as a modification to Einstein’s field equations and its evolving role in modern cosmology. The paper discusses the theoretical foundations of the cosmological constant, its interpretation as vacuum energy, and the challenges posed by its observed small value relative to particle physics expectations. Recent observational evidence, including data from type Ia supernovae, cosmic microwave background measurements, matter density estimates, and gravitational lensing, is examined to assess constraints on the cosmological constant’s magnitude and its implications for the dynamics and fate of the universe. The review also explores theoretical issues such as supersymmetry, string theory, anthropic considerations, and alternative mechanisms for dark energy. Concluding with a discussion of open questions and the significance of the cosmological constant in contemporary physics, the article aims to clarify both the empirical status and the profound theoretical puzzles associated with this fundamental parameter.

title: The flow physics of COVID-19
abstract: Flow physics plays a key role in nearly every facet of the COVID-19 pandemic. This includes the generation and aerosolization of virus-laden respiratory droplets from a host, its airborne dispersion and deposition on surfaces, as well as the subsequent inhalation of these bioaerosols by unsuspecting recipients. Fluid dynamics is also key to preventative measures such as the use of face masks, hand washing, ventilation of indoor environments and even social distancing. This article summarizes what we know and, more importantly, what we need to learn about the science underlying these issues so that we are better prepared to tackle the next outbreak of COVID-19 or a similar disease.

title: The flow physics of COVID-19
abstract: The transmission of COVID-19 is fundamentally governed by the flow physics of virus-laden respiratory droplets and aerosols generated during expiratory activities such as breathing, talking, coughing, and sneezing. This paper reviews the fluid dynamic mechanisms underlying droplet formation within the respiratory tract, their expulsion as multiphase turbulent jets, and subsequent airborne transport, evaporation, and deposition. It highlights how droplet size distribution, velocity, and environmental factors such as humidity and airflow influence transmission routes—direct droplet impact, surface contamination, and inhalation of aerosols. The analysis underscores the centrality of fluid dynamics in both understanding disease spread and informing mitigation strategies including mask usage, hand hygiene, ventilation, and social distancing. Despite longstanding research on respiratory infections, significant knowledge gaps remain regarding the physics of transmission and the efficacy of interventions. Addressing these gaps is critical for developing more effective responses to COVID-19 and future pandemics.

title: The Hagedorn - deconfinement phase transition in weakly coupled large N gauge theories
abstract: Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas and Mark Van Raamsdonk Department of Particle Physics, Weizmann Institute of Science, Rehovot 76100, Israel Jefferson Physical Laboratory, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Department of Physics, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305, USA Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, BC, V6T 1Z1, Canada

title: The Hagedorn - deconfinement phase transition in weakly coupled large N gauge theories
abstract: We investigate the thermodynamics of weakly coupled, large N SU(N) gauge theories on compact spatial manifolds, focusing on the interplay between Hagedorn and deconfinement phase transitions. By reducing the partition function to a unitary matrix integral, we analyze the phase structure in detail and show that these theories exhibit a transition from a low-temperature phase with stringy Hagedorn growth in the density of states and order-one free energy, to a high-temperature deconfined phase with free energy scaling as N². Depending on the sign of certain higher-loop contributions, the transition may be either a single first-order transition below the Hagedorn temperature or two continuous transitions with the first at the Hagedorn temperature. We discuss connections to deconfinement in confining gauge theories, the Hawking-Page transition in AdS/CFT, and suggest a dual interpretation in terms of black hole formation in string theory. Our results provide a unified framework for understanding large N thermal phase transitions and their relation to string theoretic phenomena.

title: The information paradox: a pedagogical introduction
abstract: The black hole information paradox is a very poorly understood problem. It is often believed that Hawking's argument is not precisely formulated, and a more careful accounting of naturally occurring quantum corrections will allow the radiation process to become unitary. We show that such is not the case, by proving that small corrections to the leading order Hawking computation cannot remove the entanglement between the radiation and the hole. We formulate Hawking's argument as a ‘theorem’: assuming ‘traditional’ physics at the horizon and usual assumptions of locality we will be forced into mixed states or remnants. We also argue that one cannot explain away the problem by invoking AdS/CFT duality. We conclude with recent results on the quantum physics of black holes which show that the interior of black holes have a ‘fuzzball’ structure. This nontrivial structure of microstates resolves the information paradox and gives a qualitative picture of how classical intuition can break down in black hole physics.

title: The information paradox: a pedagogical introduction
abstract: The black hole information paradox challenges the compatibility of quantum mechanics and general relativity by questioning whether information is lost during black hole evaporation. This pedagogical introduction clarifies the precise formulation of Hawking’s argument, demonstrating that small quantum corrections to Hawking radiation cannot restore unitarity or eliminate entanglement between radiation and the black hole. The analysis formalizes the paradox as a theorem: under standard assumptions of locality and regular physics at the horizon, one is forced to accept either mixed final states or remnants, both of which are problematic. The paper further argues that appeals to AdS/CFT duality do not resolve the paradox within semiclassical gravity. Recent developments in string theory, particularly the fuzzball proposal, suggest that black holes possess a rich microstate structure without traditional horizons, offering a resolution to the paradox and illustrating how classical intuition breaks down in quantum gravitational regimes.

title: The Logical Structure of Mathematical Physics
abstract: This book is about scientific theories of a particular kind - theories of mathematical physics. Examples of such theories are classical and relativis­ tic particle mechanics, classical electrodynamics, classical thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, hydrodynamics, and quantum mechanics. Roughly, these are theories in which a certain mathematical structure is employed to make statements about some fragment of the world. Most of the book is simply an elaboration of this rough characterization of theories of mathematical physics. It is argued that each theory of mathematical physics has associated with it a certain characteristic mathematical struc­ ture. This structure may be used in a variety of ways to make empirical claims about putative applications of the theory. Typically - though not necessarily - the way this structure is used in making such claims requires that certain elements in the structure play essentially different roles. Some playa "theoretical" role; others playa "non-theoretical" role. For example, in classical particle mechanics, mass and force playa theoretical role while position plays a non-theoretical role. Some attention is given to showing how this distinction can be drawn and describing precisely the way in which the theoretical and non-theoretical elements function in the claims of the theory. An attempt is made to say, rather precisely, what a theory of mathematical physics is and how you tell one such theory from anothe- what the identity conditions for these theories are.

title: The Logical Structure of Mathematical Physics
abstract: This book offers a systematic analysis of the logical structure underlying theories of mathematical physics, focusing on how mathematical frameworks are employed to generate empirical claims about the physical world. It examines the distinction between theoretical and non-theoretical terms within such theories and explores various formal approaches—particularly set-theoretic predicates and axiomatizations in first-order logic—for reconstructing their logical architecture. Through detailed proposals and illustrative examples, the work addresses challenges related to the use and eliminability of theoretical terms, the formulation of empirical content, and the holistic constraints that connect different applications of a theory. The account is further developed through a logical reconstruction of Newtonian mechanics, clarifying epistemological issues surrounding key concepts like mass and force. The book also investigates criteria for theory identity, equivalence, and reduction among theories of mathematical physics, and considers the dynamic evolution of scientific theories over time. By articulating precise conditions for theory structure and application, this study advances understanding of both the formal and conceptual foundations of theorizing in mathematical physics.

title: The Mathematical Universe
abstract: I explore physics implications of the External Reality Hypothesis (ERH) that there exists an external physical reality completely independent of us humans. I argue that with a sufficiently broad definition of mathematics, it implies the Mathematical Universe Hypothesis (MUH) that our physical world is an abstract mathematical structure. I discuss various implications of the ERH and MUH, ranging from standard physics topics like symmetries, irreducible representations, units, free parameters, randomness and initial conditions to broader issues like consciousness, parallel universes and Gödel incompleteness. I hypothesize that only computable and decidable (in Gödel’s sense) structures exist, which alleviates the cosmological measure problem and may help explain why our physical laws appear so simple. I also comment on the intimate relation between mathematical structures, computations, simulations and physical systems.

title: The Mathematical Universe
abstract: This paper investigates the consequences of the External Reality Hypothesis (ERH), which posits a physical reality entirely independent of human observers, and argues that it leads naturally to the Mathematical Universe Hypothesis (MUH), asserting that our universe is an abstract mathematical structure. By adopting a sufficiently broad definition of mathematics, the author explores how this perspective impacts foundational issues in physics, including symmetries, irreducible representations, units, free parameters, randomness, and initial conditions. The discussion extends to broader philosophical questions such as consciousness, parallel universes, and Gödel incompleteness. The hypothesis is advanced that only computable and decidable mathematical structures exist, potentially resolving the cosmological measure problem and providing insight into the apparent simplicity of physical laws. The paper also examines the relationship between mathematical structures, computation, simulation, and physical systems, advocating for a baggage-free description of reality rooted in mathematics.

title: The muon Smasher’s guide
abstract: We lay out a comprehensive physics case for a future high-energy muon collider, exploring a range of collision energies (from 1 to 100 TeV) and luminosities. We highlight the advantages of such a collider over proposed alternatives. We show how one can leverage both the point-like nature of the muons themselves as well as the cloud of electroweak radiation that surrounds the beam to blur the dichotomy between energy and precision in the search for new physics. The physics case is buttressed by a range of studies with applications to electroweak symmetry breaking, dark matter, and the naturalness of the weak scale. Furthermore, we make sharp connections with complementary experiments that are probing new physics effects using electric dipole moments, flavor violation, and gravitational waves. An extensive appendix provides cross section predictions as a function of the center-of-mass energy for many canonical simplified models.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: The muon Smasher’s guide
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive assessment of the physics potential of a future high-energy muon collider, examining its capabilities across a broad range of center-of-mass energies and luminosities. The study articulates the unique advantages of muon colliders, including their ability to combine high precision with direct access to new physics due to the point-like nature of muons and their suppressed synchrotron radiation, which enables both high energy and luminosity in a compact facility. The analysis demonstrates how muon colliders can bridge the traditional gap between energy and precision frontiers, offering transformative opportunities for probing electroweak symmetry breaking, exploring dark matter candidates, and addressing the naturalness problem of the weak scale. The work further explores the complementarity of muon collider experiments with other probes such as electric dipole moment measurements, flavor violation searches, and gravitational wave observations. An extensive appendix provides detailed cross section predictions for a variety of simplified models, underscoring the broad discovery reach and versatility of muon colliders in advancing fundamental physics.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: The physics of brain network structure, function and control
abstract: The brain is characterized by heterogeneous patterns of structural connections supporting unparalleled feats of cognition and a wide range of behaviours. New non-invasive imaging techniques now allow comprehensive mapping of these patterns. However, a fundamental challenge remains to understand how the brain’s structural wiring supports cognitive processes, with major implications for personalized mental health treatments. Here, we review recent efforts to meet this challenge, drawing on physics intuitions, models and theories, spanning the domains of statistical mechanics, information theory, dynamical systems and control. We first describe the organizing principles of brain network architecture instantiated in structural wiring under constraints of spatial embedding and energy minimization. We then survey models of brain network function that stipulate how neural activity propagates along structural connections. Finally, we discuss perturbative experiments and models for brain network control; these use the physics of signal transmission along structural connections to infer intrinsic control processes that support goal-directed behaviour and to inform stimulation-based therapies for neurological and psychiatric disease. Throughout, we highlight open questions that invite the creative efforts of pioneering physicists.The brain is the quintessential complex system, boasting incredible feats of cognition and supporting a wide range of behaviours. Physics has much to offer in the quest to distil the brain’s complexity to a number of cogent organizing principles.Key pointsFrom the first measurement of the nerve impulse by Hermann von Helmholtz in 1849 to the cutting-edge superconducting devices used in magnetoencephalography, physics and neuroscience have always been inextricably linked.Today, network neuroscience — the study of the brain as a complex web of interacting components — draws intuitions and techniques from nearly every branch of physics.The architecture of structural connections between neurons or brain regions is constrained by requirements of energy minimization and efficient information transfer.The materialization of long-range correlations and synchronization from the collective firing of individual neurons conjures notions of emergence and criticality from statistical mechanics.Together, these investigations of brain network structure and function guide targeted treatments for cognitive disorders using theories of network control.Now more than ever, understanding the complexities of the mind lies at the feet of curious and pioneering physicists.

title: The physics of brain network structure, function and control
abstract: The brain’s remarkable cognitive abilities arise from complex networks of structural connections that underpin diverse functions and behaviors. Advances in noninvasive imaging have enabled detailed mapping of these networks, yet understanding how their architecture supports cognition and behavior remains a central challenge. This review synthesizes recent progress at the intersection of physics and neuroscience, highlighting how concepts from statistical mechanics, information theory, dynamical systems, and control theory inform our understanding of brain network structure, function, and control. We discuss the organizing principles governing brain network architecture, including symmetry, spatial embedding, and energy constraints, and explore models describing how neural activity propagates through these networks to generate collective dynamics. The review also examines experimental and theoretical approaches to brain network control, with implications for targeted interventions in neurological and psychiatric disorders. Throughout, we emphasize open questions and the need for continued interdisciplinary collaboration to unravel the physical principles underlying the brain’s structure-function relationships.

title: The Physics of Cosmic Acceleration
abstract: The discovery of cosmic acceleration has fundamentally challenged our understanding of gravity and the large-scale dynamics of the universe, prompting a surge of theoretical and observational research in cosmology and fundamental physics. This review summarizes the evidence for accelerated expansion, primarily from supernovae, cosmic microwave background measurements, and large-scale structure surveys, and explores leading theoretical frameworks proposed to explain it. The simplest explanation invokes a cosmological constant, but its unnaturally small value relative to quantum field theory expectations motivates alternatives such as dynamical dark energy (e.g., quintessence, mass-varying neutrinos, phantom energy) and modifications to general relativity (including scalar-tensor theories, f(R) gravity, and braneworld models). Each scenario introduces new parameters or fine-tuning issues and raises the coincidence problem regarding the timing of acceleration. The review discusses how current and future experiments—probing the expansion history, growth of structure, and potential deviations from Lorentz invariance—can help discriminate among these models. Ultimately, resolving the physics of cosmic acceleration will require both deeper theoretical insight and more precise observational data to determine whether the phenomenon arises from new energy components or a breakdown of general relativity on cosmological scales.

title: The physics of dipolar bosonic quantum gases
abstract: This paper reviews the recent theoretical and experimental advances in the study of ultra-cold gases made of bosonic particles interacting via the long-range, anisotropic dipole–dipole interaction, in addition to the short-range and isotropic contact interaction usually at work in ultra-cold gases. The specific properties emerging from the dipolar interaction are emphasized, from the mean-field regime valid for dilute Bose–Einstein condensates, to the strongly correlated regimes reached for dipolar bosons in optical lattices.

title: The physics of dipolar bosonic quantum gases
abstract: This review presents a comprehensive overview of the physics of dipolar bosonic quantum gases, focusing on recent theoretical and experimental progress in understanding ultracold gases where particles interact via long-range, anisotropic dipole-dipole forces in addition to conventional short-range contact interactions. The unique properties arising from dipolar interactions are discussed, including their impact on the ground state, excitations, and dynamics of Bose-Einstein condensates, as well as the emergence of novel quantum phases in optical lattices. The article covers methods for creating dipolar gases using polar molecules, Rydberg atoms, light-induced dipoles, and magnetic atoms, and examines the role of the non-local Gross-Pitaevskii equation in describing these systems. Special attention is given to phenomena such as roton-maxon spectra, solitons, vortices, pattern formation, and dipolar effects in spinor condensates. The review also explores strongly correlated regimes accessible in optical lattices, including quantum phase transitions and self-assembled structures. Finally, prospects for future research and applications in quantum simulation and information are outlined, highlighting the rich physics enabled by tunable dipolar interactions in ultracold bosonic gases.

title: The physics of exceptional points
abstract: A short résumé is given about the nature of exceptional points (EPs) followed by discussions about their ubiquitous occurrence in a great variety of physical problems. EPs feature in classical as well as in quantum mechanical problems. They are associated with symmetry breaking for -symmetric Hamiltonians, where a great number of experiments has been performed, in particular in optics, and to an increasing extent in atomic and molecular physics. EPs are involved in quantum phase transition and quantum chaos; they produce dramatic effects in multichannel scattering, specific time dependence and more. In nuclear physics, they are associated with instabilities and continuum problems. Being spectral singularities they also affect approximation schemes. This article is part of a special issue of Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical devoted to ‘Quantum physics with non-Hermitian operators’.

title: The physics of exceptional points
abstract: Exceptional points (EPs) are singularities in parameter-dependent eigenvalue problems where both eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce, leading to unique algebraic and physical properties distinct from conventional degeneracies. This paper provides an overview of the mathematical structure and physical manifestations of EPs, highlighting their occurrence across a wide range of systems including quantum mechanics, optics, atomic and molecular physics, nuclear physics, and classical mechanics. EPs are central to phenomena such as symmetry breaking in PT-symmetric Hamiltonians, quantum phase transitions, quantum chaos, and multichannel scattering, often resulting in dramatic effects due to their influence on spectral properties and system dynamics. The paper discusses experimental realizations, particularly in optical systems and microwave cavities, and explores the implications of EPs for approximation schemes and spectral analysis. The ubiquity and significance of EPs underscore their fundamental role in understanding non-Hermitian physics and the behavior of open or complex systems.

title: The physics of fast radio bursts
abstract: In 2007, a very bright radio pulse was identified in the archival data of the Parkes Telescope in Australia, marking the beginning of a new research branch in astrophysics. In 2013, this kind of millisecond bursts with extremely high brightness temperature takes a unified name, fast radio burst (FRB). Over the first few years, FRBs seemed very mysterious because the sample of known events was limited. With the improvement of instruments over the last five years, hundreds of new FRBs have been discovered. The field is now undergoing a revolution and understanding of FRB has rapidly increased as new observational data increasingly accumulate. In this review, we will summarize the basic physics of FRBs and discuss the current research progress in this area. We have tried to cover a wide range of FRB topics, including the observational property, propagation effect, population study, radiation mechanism, source model, and application in cosmology. A framework based on the latest observational facts is now under construction. In the near future, this exciting field is expected to make significant breakthroughs.
venue: Science China Physics Mechanics and Astronomy

title: The physics of fast radio bursts
abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration, highly luminous radio transients first discovered in 2007, which have since become a major focus in astrophysics due to their mysterious origins and extreme physical properties. This review synthesizes recent advances in the understanding of FRBs, drawing on hundreds of new detections enabled by improved instrumentation and large-scale surveys. We summarize the basic observational characteristics of FRBs, including their dispersion, scattering, scintillation, and polarization properties, and discuss how propagation effects through intervening plasma provide insights into both the sources and the cosmic medium. The review further explores statistical studies and population analyses that reveal the diversity and event rates of FRBs, as well as the discovery of repeating sources and periodic activity. We examine leading models for FRB radiation mechanisms and progenitors, with particular attention to neutron stars and magnetars, especially in light of recent associations with Galactic magnetar activity. Finally, we highlight the emerging role of FRBs as powerful cosmological probes for measuring baryonic content and testing fundamental physics. Ongoing observational campaigns and theoretical developments promise significant breakthroughs in unraveling the physics of FRBs in the near future.
venue: Science China Physics Mechanics and Astronomy

title: The physics of financial networks
abstract: As the total value of the global financial market outgrew the value of the real economy, financial institutions created a global web of interactions that embodies systemic risks. Understanding these networks requires new theoretical approaches and new tools for quantitative analysis. Statistical physics contributed significantly to this challenge by developing new metrics and models for the study of financial network structure, dynamics, and stability and instability. In this Review, we introduce network representations originating from different financial relationships, including direct interactions such as loans, similarities such as co-ownership and higher-order relations such as contracts involving several parties (for example, credit default swaps) or multilayer connections (possibly extending to the real economy). We then review models of financial contagion capturing the diffusion and impact of shocks across each of these systems. We also discuss different notions of ‘equilibrium’ in economics and statistical physics, and how they lead to maximum entropy ensembles of graphs, providing tools for financial network inference and the identification of early-warning signals of system-wide instabilities. The interconnectedness of the financial system is increasing over time, and modelling it as a network captures key interactions between financial institutions. This Review surveys the most successful applications of statistical physics and complex networks to the description and understanding of financial networks. Modelling the financial system as a network is crucial to capture the complex interactions between financial institutions. Such a network is naturally a time-dependent multiplex, because relationships between financial institutions are of many different kinds and keep changing. Models of financial contagion enable understanding of how shocks propagate from one financial institution to another. Missing information on financial networks can be ‘reconstructed’ using maximum entropy approaches borrowed from statistical mechanics. Techniques based on financial networks have been adopted by practitioners and policy institutions.
