title: The physics of financial networks
abstract: This paper addresses the longstanding challenge of achieving energy stability in global radial basis function (RBF) methods for linear advection problems, particularly in the presence of boundary conditions. Traditional RBF approaches that strongly enforce boundary conditions often suffer from stability issues, leading to unreliable numerical solutions. To overcome this, we propose two novel RBF schemes that weakly enforce boundary conditions: one inspired by flux reconstruction (FR) techniques and another based on simultaneous approximation terms (SATs). We rigorously prove that both methods are energy stable for linear advection equations and demonstrate their conservation properties. Numerical experiments in one and two spatial dimensions, for both scalar equations and systems, validate the theoretical findings and highlight the advantages and limitations of each approach. Our results establish a foundation for more robust RBF methods and reveal connections to classical finite difference and finite element schemes, paving the way for further advancements in stable numerical methods for partial differential equations.

title: The physics of higher-order interactions in complex systems
abstract: Complex networks have become the main paradigm for modelling the dynamics of interacting systems. However, networks are intrinsically limited to describing pairwise interactions, whereas real-world systems are often characterized by higher-order interactions involving groups of three or more units. Higher-order structures, such as hypergraphs and simplicial complexes, are therefore a better tool to map the real organization of many social, biological and man-made systems. Here, we highlight recent evidence of collective behaviours induced by higher-order interactions, and we outline three key challenges for the physics of higher-order systems. Network representations of complex systems are limited to pairwise interactions, but real-world systems often involve higher-order interactions. This Perspective looks at the new physics emerging from attempts to characterize these interactions.

title: The physics of higher-order interactions in complex systems
abstract: Complex systems are typically modeled using networks that capture pairwise interactions, yet many real-world systems—from social and biological to technological—exhibit higher-order interactions involving groups of three or more units. This paper reviews recent advances in the physics of higher-order interactions, emphasizing the limitations of traditional network representations and the necessity of frameworks such as hypergraphs and simplicial complexes to accurately describe group-level dynamics. We discuss empirical evidence for collective behaviors uniquely induced by higher-order structures, including abrupt (explosive) transitions in processes like contagion and synchronization that are difficult to achieve with pairwise models alone. The paper also identifies key challenges for the field: characterizing the dynamical consequences of higher-order interactions, developing mathematical tools for their analysis, and inferring meaningful higher-order patterns from empirical data. By outlining these directions, we highlight the transformative potential of higher-order modeling in understanding and predicting the emergent phenomena of complex systems.

title: The Physics of Musical Instruments
abstract: When we wrote the first edition of this book, we directed our presenta­ tion to the reader with a compelling interest in musical instruments who has "a reasonable grasp of physics and who is not frightened by a little mathematics." We are delighted to find how many such people there are. The opportunity afforded by the preparation of this second edition has allowed us to bring our discussion up to date by including those new insights that have arisen from the work of many dedicated researchers over the past decade. We have also taken the opportunity to revise our presentation of some aspects of the subject to make it more general and, we hope, more immediately accessible. We have, of course, corrected any errors that have come to our attention, and we express our thanks to those friends who pointed out such defects in the early printings of the first edition. We hope that this book will continue to serve as a guide, both to those undertaking research in the field and to those who simply have a deep interest in the subject. June 1991 N.H.F and T.D.R.

title: The Physics of Musical Instruments
abstract: This book provides a comprehensive exploration of the physical principles underlying the operation and sound production of Western musical instruments. Emphasizing a quantitative approach, it systematically examines vibrating systems, including strings, bars, membranes, plates, and shells, and analyzes how their mechanical properties and modes of vibration contribute to musical tone and timbre. The authors integrate historical context and cultural considerations with detailed mathematical and physical explanations, highlighting the interplay between tradition, craftsmanship, and acoustical science. By synthesizing decades of research and incorporating recent advances in the field, the text serves as both an authoritative reference for researchers and an accessible resource for readers with a background in physics who seek to understand the scientific foundations of musical instrument design and performance.

title: The Physics of Neutron Stars
abstract: Neutron stars are some of the densest manifestations of massive objects in the universe. They are ideal astrophysical laboratories for testing theories of dense matter physics and provide connections among nuclear physics, particle physics, and astrophysics. Neutron stars may exhibit conditions and phenomena not observed elsewhere, such as hyperon-dominated matter, deconfined quark matter, superfluidity and superconductivity with critical temperatures near 1010 kelvin, opaqueness to neutrinos, and magnetic fields in excess of 1013 Gauss. Here, we describe the formation, structure, internal composition, and evolution of neutron stars. Observations that include studies of pulsars in binary systems, thermal emission from isolated neutron stars, glitches from pulsars, and quasi-periodic oscillations from accreting neutron stars provide information about neutron star masses, radii, temperatures, ages, and internal compositions.

title: The Physics of Neutron Stars
abstract: Neutron stars represent some of the densest forms of matter in the universe and serve as unique astrophysical laboratories for exploring the physics of dense matter, connecting nuclear physics, particle physics, and astrophysics. This paper reviews the formation, structure, internal composition, and evolution of neutron stars, highlighting phenomena such as superfluidity, superconductivity, hyperon-dominated matter, and possible deconfined quark phases. The formation process following core-collapse supernovae is discussed, including neutrino emission and proto-neutron star evolution. The global properties of neutron stars, such as mass-radius relations and their dependence on the equation of state (EOS), are examined with attention to uncertainties arising from the symmetry energy and proton fraction at supra-nuclear densities. Observational constraints from pulsar timing, thermal emission, and rotational limits are considered in relation to theoretical models. The study emphasizes the importance of simultaneous mass and radius measurements for constraining the EOS and discusses scenarios for black hole formation from proto-neutron stars. Overall, neutron stars provide critical insights into fundamental physics under extreme conditions not accessible in terrestrial laboratories.

title: The physics of optical computing
abstract: Optical computing has the potential to be faster and more energy-efficient than conventional digital-electronic computing for certain applications. This Perspective article surveys the differences between optics and electronics that could be exploited, and explores the physics and engineering challenges in realizing useful optical computers. There has been a resurgence of interest in optical computing since the early 2010s, both in academia and in industry, with much of the excitement centred around special-purpose optical computers for neural-network processing. Optical computing has been a topic of periodic study since the 1960s, including for neural networks in the 1980s and early 1990s, and a wide variety of optical-computing schemes and architectures have been proposed. In this Perspective article, we provide a systematic explanation of why and how optics might be able to give speed or energy-efficiency benefits over electronics for computing, enumerating 11 features of optics that can be harnessed when designing an optical computer. One often-mentioned motivation for optical computing — that the speed of light is fast — is emphatically not a key differentiating physical property of optics for computing; understanding where an advantage could come from is more subtle. We discuss how gaining an advantage over state-of-the-art electronic processors will likely only be achievable by careful design that harnesses more than 1 of the 11 features, while avoiding a number of pitfalls that we describe.

title: The physics of optical computing
abstract: This paper examines the renewed interest in optical computing, particularly for special-purpose applications such as neural-network processing, scientific computing, combinatorial optimization, and cryptography. It systematically identifies and analyzes eleven distinct physical features of optics that can be leveraged to achieve computational advantages over traditional electronic processors, emphasizing that the commonly cited speed of light is not the primary differentiator. Instead, potential benefits arise from careful architectural design that combines multiple optical features while mitigating associated pitfalls. The discussion highlights how advances in photonic hardware, the rising computational demands of neural networks, and the limitations of further CMOS scaling have converged to make analog optical computing increasingly viable. The paper also explores the parallels between emerging analog electronic and optical processor architectures, underscoring the importance of robust design to tolerate noise and limited precision inherent to analog computation. Ultimately, it provides a framework for understanding where and how optical computing can outperform electronics for specific tasks, guiding future research and development in this field.

title: The Physics of Pair-Density Waves: Cuprate Superconductors and Beyond
abstract: We review the physics of pair-density wave (PDW) superconductors. We begin with a macroscopic description that emphasizes order induced by PDW states, such as charge-density wave, and discuss related vestigial states that emerge as a consequence of partial melting of the PDW order. We review and critically discuss the mounting experimental evidence for such PDW order in the cuprate superconductors, the status of the theoretical microscopic description of such order, and the current debate on whether the PDW is a mother order or another competing order in the cuprates. In addition, we give an overview of the weak coupling version of PDW order, Fulde–Ferrell–Larkin–Ovchinnikov states, in the context of cold atom systems, unconventional superconductors, and noncentrosymmetric and Weyl materials.
venue: Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics

title: The Physics of Pair-Density Waves: Cuprate Superconductors and Beyond
abstract: This review explores the physics of pair-density wave (PDW) superconductors, focusing on their macroscopic properties, induced orders such as charge density waves and vestigial states, and the theoretical challenges in understanding their microscopic origins. We critically assess experimental evidence for PDW order in cuprate high-temperature superconductors and discuss whether PDW represents a fundamental or competing order in these materials. The phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau-Wilson framework is used to elucidate the symmetry-driven emergence of secondary orders and topological excitations associated with PDW states. Beyond cuprates, we examine PDW phenomena in other strongly correlated systems, including organic, iron-based, and heavy fermion superconductors, as well as cold atomic gases where Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov (FFLO) states are relevant. The review highlights the distinctness of PDW from FFLO phases, the role of lattice effects, and the broader implications for unconventional superconductivity, emphasizing both established findings and open questions in this rapidly evolving field.
venue: Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics

title: The Physics of the B Factories
abstract: We review recent progress at the two e+ e− B factories. The first measurement of CP violation and the prospects for measuring all the angles of the unitarity triangle are discussed.

title: The Physics of the B Factories
abstract: This comprehensive review details the conception, operation, and scientific achievements of the B Factories—two major experimental facilities at SLAC and KEK—built to investigate the origins of matter-antimatter asymmetry through precise studies of CP violation in the B meson system. The book outlines the historical context, detector technologies, data acquisition and analysis methodologies, and provides an in-depth pedagogical discussion of the theoretical framework underpinning CP violation and flavor mixing. It documents how high-luminosity asymmetric electron-positron collisions at the B Factories enabled precise measurements of mixing angles and confirmed that quark flavor mixing is the dominant source of CP violation observed in laboratory experiments, thus validating key aspects of the Standard Model. The review also addresses ongoing challenges, such as the inability of the Standard Model to fully account for the observed matter dominance in the universe, and highlights prospects for future discoveries at next-generation Super B Factories. This work serves as both a reference for experts and an educational resource for students, reflecting collaborative efforts across experimental and theoretical communities.

title: The physics of the colloidal glass transition
abstract: As one increases the concentration of a colloidal suspension, the system exhibits a dramatic increase in viscosity. Beyond a certain concentration, the system is said to be a colloidal glass; structurally, the system resembles a liquid, yet motions within the suspension are slow enough that it can be considered essentially frozen. For several decades, colloids have served as a valuable model system for understanding the glass transition in molecular systems. The spatial and temporal scales involved allow these systems to be studied by a wide variety of experimental techniques. The focus of this review is the current state of understanding of the colloidal glass transition, with an emphasis on experimental observations. A brief introduction is given to important experimental techniques used to study the glass transition in colloids. We describe features of colloidal systems near and in glassy states, including increases in viscosity and relaxation times, dynamical heterogeneity and ageing, among others. We also compare and contrast the glass transition in colloids to that in molecular liquids. Other glassy systems are briefly discussed, as well as recently developed synthesis techniques that will keep these systems rich with interesting physics for years to come.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: The physics of the colloidal glass transition
abstract: The colloidal glass transition occurs when increasing the concentration of particles in a colloidal suspension leads to a dramatic rise in viscosity and a kinetic arrest of particle motion, resulting in an amorphous, solid-like state. This review examines the physics underlying the colloidal glass transition, highlighting its close analogy to the glass transition in molecular systems while emphasizing the unique advantages of colloids as model systems due to their accessible spatial and temporal scales. Key experimental techniques such as video and confocal microscopy, particle tracking, light scattering, and rheology are discussed for their roles in probing structural and dynamical features near the glass transition. The review explores phenomena including viscosity growth, relaxation time increase, dynamical heterogeneity, ageing, and confinement effects as colloidal systems approach and enter glassy states. Comparisons are drawn between colloidal and molecular glasses, and other soft glassy materials such as emulsions and foams are briefly considered. Recent advances in colloid synthesis and future directions, including anisotropic particles, are outlined, underscoring the continued relevance of colloidal suspensions for advancing fundamental understanding of glassy behavior.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: THE PHYSICS OF TRAFFIC
abstract: Traffic jams are a fact of life for many car drivers. Every morning millions of drivers around the world sit motionless in their vehicles for long periods of time as they try to get to work, and then repeat the experience on their journeys home in the evening. The same thing often happens when they are driving to the coast for the weekend or to the airport to go on their holidays. They blame other drivers, increasing volumes of traffic and, inevitably, roadworks. So what has any of this got to do with physics?

title: THE PHYSICS OF TRAFFIC
abstract: This monograph presents a comprehensive investigation into the complex dynamics of freeway traffic, emphasizing empirical spatiotemporal patterns and their theoretical interpretation. Challenging traditional traffic flow models, the author introduces the three-phase traffic theory to explain observed discrepancies between empirical data and earlier theories. The book systematically reviews historical developments in traffic research, details key features of free and congested traffic, and identifies fundamental empirical patterns such as wide moving jams, synchronized flow, and spontaneous breakdown phenomena. Through qualitative analysis accessible to a broad audience, the work elucidates the mechanisms underlying traffic pattern formation and transitions between distinct traffic phases. Subsequent sections develop a microscopic perspective on these patterns and explore practical engineering applications informed by the new theory. By integrating empirical evidence with innovative theoretical frameworks, this study advances understanding of traffic as a paradigmatic complex system and provides actionable insights for traffic management and infrastructure design.

title: The statistical physics of cities
abstract: Challenges due to the rapid urbanization of the world — especially in emerging countries — range from an increasing dependence on energy to air pollution, socio-spatial inequalities and environmental and sustainability issues. Modelling the structure and evolution of cities is therefore critical because policy makers need robust theories and new paradigms for mitigating these problems. Fortunately, the increased data available about urban systems opens the possibility of constructing a quantitative ‘science of cities’, with the aim of identifying and modelling essential phenomena. Statistical physics plays a major role in this effort by bringing tools and concepts able to bridge theory and empirical results. This Perspective illustrates this point by focusing on fundamental objects in cities: the distribution of the urban population; segregation phenomena and spin-like models; the polycentric transition of the activity organization; energy considerations about mobility and models inspired by gravity and radiation concepts; CO2 emitted by transport; and finally, scaling that describes how various socio-economical and infrastructures evolve when cities grow.This Perspective describes how statistical physics helps understand some of the key aspects of cities: their spatial structure and social organization, the distribution of their population, urban mobility and how some critical factors vary with population.

title: The statistical physics of cities
abstract: Rapid urbanization presents complex challenges related to energy use, pollution, inequality, and sustainability, necessitating robust theoretical frameworks for understanding and managing city dynamics. This paper explores how statistical physics provides powerful tools and concepts to model urban systems, leveraging the increasing availability of large-scale urban data. By treating cities as complex systems characterized by emergent collective behaviors, the study examines key urban phenomena including population distribution, segregation dynamics, polycentric transitions in activity organization, mobility patterns, energy consumption, and scaling laws governing socio-economic and infrastructural growth. The analysis highlights the interplay between empirical data and theoretical models, such as those explaining Zipf’s law for city size distributions and diffusion-based approaches that account for migration and internal growth. The paper underscores the interdisciplinary nature of urban science and demonstrates how statistical physics can bridge theory with observation, identify critical parameters, and inform strategies to mitigate urban challenges in a rapidly changing world.

title: The statistical physics of real-world networks
abstract: In the past 15 years, statistical physics has been successful as a framework for modelling complex networks. On the theoretical side, this approach has unveiled a variety of physical phenomena, such as the emergence of mixed distributions and ensemble non-equivalence, that are observed in heterogeneous networks but not in homogeneous systems. At the same time, thanks to the deep connection between the principle of maximum entropy and information theory, statistical physics has led to the definition of null models for networks that reproduce features of real-world systems but that are otherwise as random as possible. We review here the statistical physics approach and the null models for complex networks, focusing in particular on analytical frameworks that reproduce local network features. We show how these models have been used to detect statistically significant structural patterns in real-world networks and to reconstruct the network structure in cases of incomplete information. We further survey the statistical physics models that reproduce more complex, semilocal network features using Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, as well as models of generalized network structures, such as multiplex networks, interacting networks and simplicial complexes. This Review describes advances in the statistical physics of complex networks and provides a reference for the state of the art in theoretical network modelling and applications to real-world systems for pattern detection and network reconstruction. Statistical physics is a powerful framework to explain properties of complex networks, modelled as systems of heterogeneous entities whose degrees of freedom are their interactions rather than their states. The statistical physics of complex networks has brought theoretical insights into physical phenomena that are different in heterogeneous networks than in homogeneous systems. From an applied perspective, statistical physics defines null models for real-world networks that reproduce local features but are otherwise as random as possible. These models have been used, on the one hand, to detect statistically significant patterns in real-world networks and, on the other, to infer the network structure when information is incomplete. These applications are particularly useful in the current information age to make consistent inference from huge streams of continuously produced, high-dimensional, noisy data. The statistical mechanics approach has also been extended using numerical techniques to reproduce semilocal network features and, more recently, to encompass structures such as multilayer networks and simplicial complexes. title: The statistical physics of real-world networks
abstract: Statistical physics has emerged as a powerful framework for modeling and understanding the structure and dynamics of real-world complex networks, which are ubiquitous in technological, social, economic, and biological systems. This review synthesizes recent theoretical developments and empirical applications of statistical physics approaches to network science, with a particular focus on maximum entropy methods and exponential random graph models. We discuss how these frameworks enable the construction of null models that reproduce specific structural features of observed networks while remaining otherwise maximally random, thus providing rigorous baselines for detecting significant patterns and reconstructing network structures from incomplete data. The review highlights the distinction between microcanonical and canonical ensembles in network modeling, emphasizing their non-equivalence in the thermodynamic limit and the implications for practical applications. Furthermore, we survey advanced models that capture semi-local and generalized network features, such as multiplex networks and simplicial complexes, using techniques like Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. Overall, statistical physics offers a unifying language for analyzing complex networks, yielding insights into their universal properties and informing the study of dynamical processes occurring on them.

title: Trans-Planckian problem of inflationary cosmology
abstract: In most current models of inflation based on a weakly self-coupled scalar matter field minimally coupled to gravity, the period of inflation lasts so long that, at the beginning of the inflationary period, the physical wavelengths of comoving scales which correspond to the present large-scale structure of the Universe were smaller than the Planck length. Thus, the usual computations of the spectrum of fluctuations in these models involve extrapolating low-energy physics (both in the matter and gravitational sector) into regions where this physics is not applicable. In this article we study the dependence of the usual predictions of inflation for the spectrum of cosmological fluctuations on the hidden assumptions about super-Planck scale physics. We introduce a class of modified dispersion relations to mimic possible effects of super-Planck scale physics, and find that, given an initial state determined by minimizing the energy density, for dispersions relations introduced by Unruh the spectrum is unchanged, whereas for a class of dispersion relations similar to those used by Corley and Jacobson (which involve a more radical departure from the usual linear relation) important deviations from the usual predictions of inflation can be obtained. Some implications of this result for the unification of fundamental physicsmore » and early Universe cosmology are discussed.« less

title: Trans-Planckian problem of inflationary cosmology
abstract: The trans-Planckian problem in inflationary cosmology arises because, in standard inflationary models, modes corresponding to present-day cosmological structures originate with physical wavelengths smaller than the Planck length, where conventional field theory and general relativity are expected to break down. This paper investigates the sensitivity of inflationary predictions for the spectrum of cosmological fluctuations to assumptions about unknown super-Planckian physics by introducing modified dispersion relations for a scalar field in a de Sitter background. For dispersion relations of the type proposed by Unruh, the usual scale-invariant spectrum is preserved when the initial state minimizes energy density. However, for more radical modifications akin to those of Corley and Jacobson, significant deviations from scale invariance—including spectral tilt, exponential factors, and oscillatory features—can emerge. These results demonstrate that standard predictions of inflation are not robust against changes in trans-Planckian physics, highlighting the need for a deeper understanding of high-energy physics in early universe cosmology and raising important questions for attempts to unify fundamental interactions with cosmological models.

title: Two-dimensional gas of massless Dirac fermions in graphene
abstract: Quantum electrodynamics (resulting from the merger of quantum mechanics and relativity theory) has provided a clear understanding of phenomena ranging from particle physics to cosmology and from astrophysics to quantum chemistry. The ideas underlying quantum electrodynamics also influence the theory of condensed matter, but quantum relativistic effects are usually minute in the known experimental systems that can be described accurately by the non-relativistic Schrödinger equation. Here we report an experimental study of a condensed-matter system (graphene, a single atomic layer of carbon) in which electron transport is essentially governed by Dirac's (relativistic) equation. The charge carriers in graphene mimic relativistic particles with zero rest mass and have an effective ‘speed of light’ c* ≈ 106 m s-1. Our study reveals a variety of unusual phenomena that are characteristic of two-dimensional Dirac fermions. In particular we have observed the following: first, graphene's conductivity never falls below a minimum value corresponding to the quantum unit of conductance, even when concentrations of charge carriers tend to zero; second, the integer quantum Hall effect in graphene is anomalous in that it occurs at half-integer filling factors; and third, the cyclotron mass mc of massless carriers in graphene is described by E = mcc*2. This two-dimensional system is not only interesting in itself but also allows access to the subtle and rich physics of quantum electrodynamics in a bench-top experiment.

title: Two-dimensional gas of massless Dirac fermions in graphene
abstract: We report the experimental observation and characterization of a two-dimensional gas of massless Dirac fermions in graphene, a single atomic layer of carbon arranged in a honeycomb lattice. Our studies reveal that charge carriers in graphene behave as relativistic particles with zero effective mass and a characteristic velocity c* ≈ 10^6 m/s, leading to several unconventional electronic properties. These include an anomalous integer quantum Hall effect manifesting at half-integer filling factors, a minimum conductivity close to the conductance quantum e^2/h even at vanishing carrier concentrations, a cyclotron mass that varies with carrier energy as mc = E/c*^2, and Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations exhibiting a π phase shift due to Berry’s phase. The linear dispersion relation E = ħkc* for both electrons and holes is confirmed by the dependence of cyclotron mass and quantum oscillation frequency on carrier density. Furthermore, the quantum Hall plateaux sequence in graphene is shifted by 1/2 compared to conventional systems, reflecting the unique Landau level structure predicted for massless Dirac fermions and consistent with the Atiyah-Singer index theorem. Our findings establish graphene as an ideal platform for studying relativistic quantum phenomena in condensed matter and provide direct evidence for the existence of a two-dimensional gas of massless Dirac fermions.

title: Ultracold atomic gases in optical lattices: mimicking condensed matter physics and beyond
abstract: We review recent developments in the physics of ultracold atomic and molecular gases in optical lattices. Such systems are nearly perfect realisations of various kinds of Hubbard models, and as such may very well serve to mimic condensed matter phenomena. We show how these systems may be employed as quantum simulators to answer some challenging open questions of condensed matter, and even high energy physics. After a short presentation of the models and the methods of treatment of such systems, we discuss in detail, which challenges of condensed matter physics can be addressed with (i) disordered ultracold lattice gases, (ii) frustrated ultracold gases, (iii) spinor lattice gases, (iv) lattice gases in “artificial” magnetic fields, and, last but not least, (v) quantum information processing in lattice gases. For completeness, also some recent progress related to the above topics with trapped cold gases will be discussed. Motto: There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, Than are dreamt of in your philosophy 1

title: Ultracold atomic gases in optical lattices: mimicking condensed matter physics and beyond
abstract: This review comprehensively examines the rapidly evolving field of ultracold atomic and molecular gases in optical lattices, highlighting their role as highly controllable quantum simulators for condensed matter and beyond. We discuss how these systems provide nearly ideal realizations of various Hubbard and spin models, enabling the exploration of fundamental phenomena such as superfluid–Mott insulator transitions, disorder-induced localization, frustration, and magnetism in both bosonic and fermionic regimes. The review details experimental and theoretical advances in simulating disordered and frustrated systems, spinor gases, and artificial gauge fields, as well as their applications in quantum information processing. By bridging atomic physics, condensed matter, and quantum information science, ultracold lattice gases offer unprecedented opportunities to address open questions in strongly correlated systems and to realize novel phases of matter not accessible in traditional solid-state platforms.

title: Variational autoencoders for new physics mining at the Large Hadron Collider
abstract: Using variational autoencoders trained on known physics processes, we develop a one-sided threshold test to isolate previously unseen processes as outlier events. Since the autoencoder training does not depend on any specific new physics signature, the proposed procedure doesn’t make specific assumptions on the nature of new physics. An event selection based on this algorithm would be complementary to classic LHC searches, typically based on model-dependent hypothesis testing. Such an algorithm would deliver a list of anomalous events, that the experimental collaborations could further scrutinize and even release as a catalog, similarly to what is typically done in other scientific domains. Event topologies repeating in this dataset could inspire new-physics model building and new experimental searches. Running in the trigger system of the LHC experiments, such an application could identify anomalous events that would be otherwise lost, extending the scientific reach of the LHC.

title: Variational autoencoders for new physics mining at the Large Hadron Collider
abstract: We present a novel approach for model-independent searches of physics beyond the Standard Model at the Large Hadron Collider by deploying variational autoencoders (VAEs) trained on known Standard Model processes. Our method leverages the VAE’s ability to learn the underlying distribution of standard events and identifies anomalies as outliers based on reconstruction loss, without assumptions about specific new physics signatures. Using simulated LHC data streams, we demonstrate that a one-sided threshold test on the VAE output can effectively isolate rare or previously unseen event topologies, enabling the selection and cataloging of anomalous events for further scrutiny. This strategy is complementary to traditional model-dependent searches and can be integrated into the LHC trigger system to capture events that might otherwise be missed, thus enhancing the discovery potential for new physics phenomena.

title: Whose Science? Whose Knowledge?: Thinking from Women's Lives
abstract: Sandra Harding here develops further the themes first addressed in her widely influential book, The Science Question in Feminism, and conducts a compelling analysis of feminist theories on the philosophical problem of how we know what we know.  Following a strong narrative line, Harding sets out her arguments in highly readable prose. In Part 1, she discusses issues that will interest anyone concerned with the social bases of scientific knowledge. In Part 2, she modifies some of her views and then pursues the many issues raised by the feminist position which holds that women's social experience provides a unique vantage point for discovering masculine bias and and questioning conventional claims about nature and social life. In Part 3, Harding looks at the insights that people of color, male feminists, lesbians, and others can bring to these controversies, and concludes by outlining a feminist approach to science in which these insights are central. "Women and men cannot understand or explain the world we live in or the real choices we have," she writes, "as long as the sciences describe and explain the world primarily from the perspectives of the lives of the dominant groups."

title: Whose Science? Whose Knowledge?: Thinking from Women's Lives
abstract: This paper critically examines the relationship between science and feminism, interrogating traditional scientific paradigms through the lens of women's lived experiences. It explores how feminist perspectives challenge the presumed objectivity and universality of scientific knowledge, advocating for an epistemology that recognizes the social situatedness of knowers. The analysis addresses the limitations of using physics as a model for all sciences and highlights the contributions of the women's movement to scientific inquiry. By engaging with issues of race, sexuality, and global context, the paper demonstrates how feminist epistemology can broaden and democratize scientific practices. Ultimately, it argues for a reimagined science that incorporates strong objectivity and values diverse standpoints, positioning feminist science as a transformative force in knowledge production.

title: Why Does Deep and Cheap Learning Work So Well?
abstract: We show how the success of deep learning could depend not only on mathematics but also on physics: although well-known mathematical theorems guarantee that neural networks can approximate arbitrary functions well, the class of functions of practical interest can frequently be approximated through “cheap learning” with exponentially fewer parameters than generic ones. We explore how properties frequently encountered in physics such as symmetry, locality, compositionality, and polynomial log-probability translate into exceptionally simple neural networks. We further argue that when the statistical process generating the data is of a certain hierarchical form prevalent in physics and machine learning, a deep neural network can be more efficient than a shallow one. We formalize these claims using information theory and discuss the relation to the renormalization group. title: Why Does Deep and Cheap Learning Work So Well?
abstract: This paper investigates why deep learning is both highly effective and resource-efficient, despite the vast complexity of real-world data. We argue that the remarkable success of deep neural networks stems not only from mathematical universality but also from properties common in physics, such as symmetry, locality, compositionality, and polynomial log-probability, which structure the functions of practical interest. These properties allow neural networks to approximate relevant functions with exponentially fewer parameters than would be required for arbitrary functions—a phenomenon we term 'cheap learning.' We formalize these insights using information theory and draw connections to concepts like the renormalization group. Through a series of 'no-flattening' theorems, we demonstrate that certain hierarchical or compositional functions can be represented much more efficiently by deep rather than shallow networks, with significant efficiency losses incurred by attempts to approximate them in a shallow architecture. Our analysis explains why deep learning is so successful in practice: both the data encountered in natural tasks and the architectures of deep networks exploit similar simplifying structures, enabling powerful yet efficient learning.

title: Analytical sociology and computational social science
abstract: Analytical sociology focuses on social interactions among individuals and the hard-to-predict aggregate outcomes they bring about. It seeks to identify generalizable mechanisms giving rise to emergent properties of social systems which, in turn, feed back on individual decision-making. This research program benefits from computational tools such as agent-based simulations, machine learning, and large-scale web experiments, and has considerable overlap with the nascent field of computational social science. By providing relevant analytical tools to rigorously address sociology’s core questions, computational social science has the potential to advance sociology in a similar way that the introduction of econometrics advanced economics during the last half century. Computational social scientists from computer science and physics often see as their main task to establish empirical regularities which they view as “social laws.” From the perspective of the social sciences, references to social laws appear unfounded and misplaced, however, and in this article we outline how analytical sociology, with its theory-grounded approach to computational social science, can help to move the field forward from mere descriptions and predictions to the explanation of social phenomena.

title: Analytical sociology and computational social science
abstract: Analytical sociology seeks to explain how individual interactions generate complex social phenomena, emphasizing the identification of underlying mechanisms responsible for emergent collective outcomes. This approach contrasts with traditional quantitative methods by prioritizing mechanism-based explanations over mere statistical associations. The recent rise of computational social science, which leverages large-scale data, simulations, and machine learning, offers powerful tools that can advance analytical sociology’s aims. While computational social scientists often focus on uncovering empirical regularities, analytical sociology insists on theory-grounded models that map realistically onto actual social processes. This article surveys the synergies and differences between the two fields, arguing that integrating computational methods with the explanatory ambitions of analytical sociology can move social science beyond description and prediction toward deeper understanding of social dynamics and mechanisms.

title: Applications of social constructivist learning theories in knowledge translation for healthcare professionals: a scoping review
abstract: Use of theory is essential for advancing the science of knowledge translation (KT) and for increasing the likelihood that KT interventions will be successful in reducing existing research-practice gaps in health care. As a sociological theory of knowledge, social constructivist theory may be useful for informing the design and evaluation of KT interventions. As such, this scoping review explored the extent to which social constructivist theory has been applied in the KT literature for healthcare professionals.MethodsSearches were conducted in six databases: Ovid MEDLINE (1948 – May 16, 2011), Ovid EMBASE, CINAHL, ERIC, PsycInfo, and AMED. Inclusion criteria were: publications from all health professions, research methodologies, as well as conceptual and theoretical papers related to KT. To be included in the review, key words such as constructivism, social constructivism, or social constructivist theories had to be included within the title or abstract. Papers that discussed the use of social constructivist theories in the context of undergraduate learning in academic settings were excluded from the review. An analytical framework of quantitative (numerical) and thematic analysis was used to examine and combine study findings.ResultsOf the 514 articles screened, 35 papers published between 1992 and 2011 were deemed eligible and included in the review. This review indicated that use of social constructivist theory in the KT literature was limited and haphazard. The lack of justification for the use of theory continues to represent a shortcoming of the papers reviewed. Potential applications and relevance of social constructivist theory in KT in general and in the specific studies were not made explicit in most papers. For the acquisition, expression and application of knowledge in practice, there was emphasis on how the social constructivist theory supports clinicians in expressing this knowledge in their professional interactions.ConclusionsThis scoping review was the first to examine use of social constructivism in KT studies. While the links between social constructivism and KT have not been fully explored, the Knowledge to Action framework has strong constructivist underpinnings that can be used in moving forward within the broader KT enterprise.

title: Applications of social constructivist learning theories in knowledge translation for healthcare professionals: a scoping review
abstract: This scoping review examines the application of social constructivist learning theories in knowledge translation (KT) for healthcare professionals. Despite the recognized importance of theory in designing effective KT interventions to bridge research-practice gaps, the use of social constructivist theory in KT literature remains limited and inconsistently justified. A systematic search across six databases identified 35 relevant papers published between 1992 and 2011. Analysis revealed that while social constructivist theory has potential to inform KT by emphasizing active, contextually situated knowledge construction among clinicians, its explicit integration and rationale in KT studies are often lacking. The review highlights the need for more deliberate application of social constructivist principles in KT intervention design and evaluation, suggesting that frameworks such as Knowledge to Action may benefit from stronger constructivist underpinnings to enhance evidence uptake and practice change among healthcare professionals.

title: A History of Archaeological Thought
abstract: A History of Archaeological Thought is an intermediate level course intended to introduce students to the development of archaeological theory from the early 19 th century realization that the remote past could be reconstructed solely on the basis of the archaeological record to later developments, such as attempts to identify ethnic/linguistic groups exclusively from material remains. It will trace the emergence of archaeology as a sub-field within anthropology and its continuing close interaction with broader developments in anthropological theory. The course contrasts perspectives that emphasize internal social evolution and adaptation to local environmental settings with post-modern responses that stress multiple perspectives on a contingent past. Students will be introduced to different theoretical approaches to interpreting the archaeological record, such as cultural ecology and neo-evolutionary processual archaeology, archaeologies of identity and place and landscape, Marxist historical materialism and world systems theory, and so-called symbolic/cognitive archaeology. This course reviews different theoretical approaches for explaining the past, emphasizing the positive interaction between accumulating archaeological discoveries and their interpretation and analysis. Social theories, originally formulated in sociology and social anthropology, are evaluated for their adequacy in understanding the material culture record of archaeology. The suitability of these theoretical approaches for interpreting the archaeological record will be critically examined.

title: A History of Archaeological Thought
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive examination of the development of archaeological thought from its origins in antiquarianism to contemporary theoretical debates. It traces the evolution of the discipline through key historical periods, including the influence of classical and text-based approaches, the rise of scientific and prehistoric archaeology, and the impact of evolutionary, culture-historical, and processual paradigms. The analysis highlights how social, political, and intellectual contexts have shaped archaeological interpretation and methodology, with particular attention to issues such as nationalism, colonialism, racism, and the integration of social sciences. The paper also explores the emergence of postprocessualism and alternative theoretical frameworks, culminating in a discussion of current challenges related to subjectivity, relativism, and archaeology’s relevance in broader academic and public spheres. Through this historical overview, the paper underscores the dynamic and contested nature of archaeological inquiry and its ongoing negotiation between scientific rigor and interpretive flexibility.

title: A Risk Society
abstract: “Risk society” is a concept that was first framed by the German sociologist Ulrich Beck in Risk Society in 1986. In Beck’s view, the modern society had deviated from (Karl Marx’s) class society or (Max Weber’s) industrial society and had developed into a social form that is highly modern, known as the “risk society.” Social theories based on unequal distribution of wealth (the functional theory, Marxism, and various kinds of postindustrial or postmodern theories that derived from it) have lost their interpretability when it comes to the crisis and inequality in the distribution of risks. Therefore, there needs to be a turn in social theories, that is to say, “risk sociology” needs to be advanced with problem awareness being “how to avoid, minimize, and direct risks or hazards systematically created as a part of modernization.”

title: A Risk Society
abstract: This paper examines the transformation of rural China through the lens of Ulrich Beck’s “risk society” theory, arguing that traditional social theories centered on class and wealth distribution inadequately explain the new forms of crisis and inequality engendered by modernization. Focusing on the small peasant economy as a foundational element of China’s rural structure, the study traces its evolution from a subsistence-based, autarkic system to its integration into a dual urban-rural social structure shaped by state policies and industrialization. The analysis highlights how state-driven industrial priorities and institutional arrangements, such as the hukou system, reinforced rural-urban segregation and perpetuated the dominance of smallholder agriculture even after industrialization. With market reforms and the breakdown of spatial and institutional barriers, rural areas were exposed to new vulnerabilities as traditional economic practices collided with market mechanisms, leading to persistent disparities in welfare, security, and opportunity. The paper concludes that contemporary rural China exemplifies a risk society in which systemic hazards—rather than class-based inequalities—define social stratification and governance challenges.

title: A Teoria Queer e a Sociologia: o desafio de uma analítica da normalização
abstract: Originated from the American Cultural Studies, Queer Theory has gained a reputation as a critical counterpoint to the sociological studies on sexual minorities and the political identity of the social movements. Based on a creative implementation of post-structuralist philosophy for the understanding of how sexuality shapes the contemporary social order, for more than a decade its affinities and tensions, as related to the social sciences, and particularly to sociology, are in discussion. This article joins the debate, analyzes the similarities and distinctions between those two, and finally presents an overview of the current dialogue, pointing to a possible convergence in the queer project to enable an analysis of normalization.

title: A Teoria Queer e a Sociologia: o desafio de uma analítica da normalização
abstract: Este artigo examina o surgimento e desenvolvimento da Teoria Queer como contraponto crítico à tradição sociológica no estudo das sexualidades e das minorias sexuais, destacando suas origens nos Estudos Culturais norte-americanos e sua fundamentação no pós-estruturalismo francês, especialmente nas obras de Michel Foucault e Jacques Derrida. Analisa as tensões e afinidades entre a Teoria Queer e a Sociologia, enfatizando o desafio de construir uma analítica da normalização que vá além da lógica identitária e minorizante predominante nos estudos sociológicos clássicos. O texto argumenta que a Teoria Queer propõe uma abordagem inovadora ao tratar a sexualidade como dispositivo histórico do poder, questionando as categorias binárias e os processos de naturalização das identidades sociais. Ao mapear o diálogo entre essas correntes, o artigo aponta para possibilidades de convergência teórica e metodológica orientadas à crítica dos regimes de normalização que estruturam a ordem social contemporânea.

title: Climate change and society : sociological perspectives
abstract: Climate change is one of today’s most important issues, presenting an intellectual challenge to the natural and social sciences. While there has been progress in natural science understanding of climate change, social science research has not been as fully developed. This book breaks new theoretical and empirical ground by presenting climate change as a thoroughly social phenomenon, embedded in our institutions and cultural practices. Drawing on a variety of sociological literature, thirty-eight sociologists summarize existing approaches to understanding the social, economic, political, and culture dimensions of climate change, detailing the causes, impacts, and responses. Chapters 2 to 4 focus on factors that drive carbon emissions and situate these factors within social structure and processes. Chapters 5 to 7 examine the impacts of climate change and how sociological perspectives can inform the creation of just and equitable mitigation and adaptation strategies. Chapters 8 to 10 examine the factors that influence how society responds to climate change, including the movements that advocate for or against climate action and public opinion. Chapters 11 and 12 present an overview of debates within social theory about the significance of climate change and how to address it, followed by a review of methodological approaches for studying the relationship between societal and climate phenomena. The concluding chapter takes stock of all these sociological insights and how they fulfill the need for more social science research on climate (and global environmental) change, while also pointing to the importance of further sociological engagement with these topics.

title: Climate change and society : sociological perspectives
abstract: This paper examines the multifaceted impacts of climate change on society through a sociological lens, focusing on critical sectors such as water resources, food production, energy use, coastal communities, and broader economic and social systems. It highlights how shifting weather patterns and rising temperatures are altering water availability and quality, threatening agricultural productivity, and increasing energy demands for cooling while reducing heating needs. The vulnerability of coastal regions to sea level rise and intensified storms is discussed, alongside the heightened risks faced by developing countries and marginalized populations. The analysis underscores that while some short-term benefits may arise in certain regions, the long-term consequences of climate change are likely to exacerbate social inequalities, disrupt infrastructure, and pose significant challenges to public health, national security, and economic stability. The paper calls for comprehensive adaptation strategies that address both environmental changes and their societal ramifications.

title: Cognitive Linguistics
abstract: This chapter aims to show the reader how social cognition also includes language. Neither cognitive sociology nor cognitive linguistics can logically ignore one another’s perspectives and empirical findings. The chapter aims to introduce cognitive sociologists to leading strands of research in cognitive linguistics that have a bearing on the structure and processes of society. In explaining the cognitive basis of language, linguists are now beginning to recognize its dialogic nature, the importance of dialogue in language acquisition, and thus the dependence of language on early socialization. This design feature enables the many social uses of the human language faculty that are termed “discourse.” There are many approaches to “discourse” but here the focus is on the recently developed cognitive approaches that are able to handle the complexities of grammatical detail as well as lexical meaning, without ignoring pragmatics. These approaches include cognitive frame theory, which describes lexical meaning and phenomena such as grammatically triggered attention shifts. A widely used approach analyzes conceptual metaphor, where “metaphor” is understood as a mental framing device that works by linking different conceptual domains, including image schemata. A third cognitive approach to socially relevant conceptualization emphasizes the role of spatial cognition, in particular containing spaces and the dimensions of direction and distance. In all cases, this overview relates the social and linguistic aspects to cognitive science and neuroscience.
venue: The Oxford Handbook of Cognitive Sociology

title: Cognitive Linguistics
abstract: This issue of Cognitive Linguistics presents a diverse collection of research articles that advance understanding of language structure, processing, and change from a cognitive perspective. The studies featured explore topics including the use of construction grammar to assess developmental language complexity, the influence of event outcome inferences on memory, cross-linguistic conceptualization of event roles among Japanese learners of English, probabilistic mechanisms underlying the diachronic diffusion and conventionalization of Spanish constructions, and historical changes in causative alternation patterns in Chinese change-of-state verbs. Together, these contributions highlight the dynamic interplay between linguistic form, meaning, and cognition across languages and contexts, offering new insights into the mechanisms driving language acquisition, usage, and evolution.
venue: The Oxford Handbook of Cognitive Sociology

title: Community Structure and Crime: Testing Social-Disorganization Theory
abstract: Shaw and McKay's influential theory of community social disorganization has never been directly tested. To address this, a community-level theory that builds on Shaw and McKay's original model is formulated and tested. The general hypothesis is that low economic status, ethnic heterogeneity, residential mobility, and family disruption lead to community social disorganization, which, in turn, increases crime and delinquency rates. A community's level of social organization is measured in terms of local friendship networks, control of street-corner teenage peer groups, and prevalence of organizational participation. The model is first tested by analyzing data for 238 localities in Great Britain constructed from a 1982 national survey of 10,905 residents. The model is then replicated on an independent national sample of 11,030 residents of 300 British localities in 1984. Results from both surveys support the theory and show that between-community variations in social disorganization transmit much of the effect of community structural characteristics on rates of both criminal victimization and criminal offending.

title: Community Structure and Crime: Testing Social-Disorganization Theory
abstract: This study empirically tests social-disorganization theory by examining the relationship between community structural characteristics and crime rates using survey data from 238 British localities. The authors analyze four key dimensions of community organization—socioeconomic status, residential mobility, ethnic heterogeneity, and family disruption—and assess their impact on local friendship networks, organizational participation, and informal social control. Results indicate that structural factors significantly predict variations in community organization, which in turn mediate the effects of structure on crime. The findings support the central tenets of social-disorganization theory, demonstrating that weakened community organization is a critical mechanism linking structural disadvantage to higher crime rates. Implications for criminological theory and policy are discussed.

title: Consequences of Realism for Sociological Theory‐Building
abstract: It is argued that the Achilles heel of contemporary sociology – and great parts of social science – is a) weak theory development, and b) absence of a meta-theory providing a common platform and a shared goal for its practitioners, fostering cumulativity. A meta-theory called causal realism (a variant of critical realism) is suggested for these purposes. The main tenets and key concepts of realism, such as causality and explanation, mechanism, stratified reality, are presented. Thereafter, via an analogy to the physical sciences, it is argued that a natural implication of realism and the search for causal mechanisms is a division of society into levels. The micro-macro issue is approached by a level-ontology for the development of sociological theory. Five levels are suggested, discussed and briefly exemplified. In the concluding remarks, some further positive implications of realism to sociology are touched upon. (Less)

title: Consequences of Realism for Sociological Theory‐Building
abstract: This paper examines the implications of adopting a realist philosophy of science—specifically, causal realism—for sociological theory-building in response to the discipline’s current fragmentation and theoretical stagnation. Arguing that both positivism and epistemological relativism have led to degenerative effects on sociology by constraining methodological innovation and undermining explanatory ambitions, the author contends that a new meta-theoretical foundation is needed. Causal realism is proposed as an alternative that emphasizes the delineation and definition of sociology’s object of study, enabling the development of robust, explanatory theories grounded in a shared understanding of social reality. The paper outlines how this approach can provide a common platform for sociological inquiry, reinvigorate theoretical progress, and restore coherence to the discipline by moving beyond externally derived philosophies and focusing on sociology’s own epistemic needs.

title: Corporate Social and Financial Performance: An Extended Stakeholder Theory, and Empirical Test with Accounting Measures
abstract: Although agreement on the positive sign of the relationship between corporate social and financial performance is observed in the literature, the mechanisms that constitute this relationship are not yet well-known. We address this issue by extending management’s stakeholder theory by adding insights from psychology’s prospect decision theory and sociology’s resource dependence theory. Empirically, we analyze an extensive panel dataset, including information on disaggregated measures of social performance for the S&P 500 in the 1997–2002 period. In so doing, we enrich the extant literature by focusing on stakeholder heterogeneity, perceptional framing, and disaggregated measures of corporate social performance.

title: Corporate Social and Financial Performance: An Extended Stakeholder Theory, and Empirical Test with Accounting Measures
abstract: This study extends stakeholder theory by integrating prospect decision theory and resource dependence theory to examine the mechanisms underlying the relationship between corporate social performance (CSP) and corporate financial performance (CFP). Utilizing a panel dataset of S&P 500 firms from 1997 to 2002 with disaggregated CSP measures, we analyze the effects of stakeholder heterogeneity and perceptual framing on the CSP–CFP nexus. Our findings indicate that secondary stakeholders, who rely more on corporate reputation, exhibit a stronger association between CSP and CFP than primary stakeholders. Additionally, consistent with prospect theory, negative CSP events have a greater impact on CFP than positive ones, particularly for primary stakeholders. These results highlight the importance of nuanced CSP measurement and the asymmetric influence of stakeholder perceptions, offering new insights into how social responsibility translates into financial outcomes.

title: Decision-Making Processes in Social Contexts.
abstract: Over the past half-century, scholars in the interdisciplinary field of Judgment and Decision Making have amassed a trove of findings, theories, and prescriptions regarding the processes ordinary people enact when making choices. But this body of knowledge has had little influence on sociology. Sociological research on choice emphasizes how features of the social environment shape individual behavior, not people's underlying decision processes. Our aim in this article is to provide an overview of selected ideas, models, and data sources from decision research that can fuel new lines of inquiry on how socially situated actors navigate both everyday and major life choices. We also highlight opportunities and challenges for cross-fertilization between sociology and decision research that can allow the methods, findings, and contexts of each field to expand their joint range of inquiry.

title: Decision-Making Processes in Social Contexts.
abstract: This article examines the limited integration of judgment and decision-making (JDM) research into sociology, despite decades of advances in understanding how individuals make choices. While JDM has focused on cognitive processes and deviations from rationality, often in de-socialized settings, sociological research emphasizes the influence of social environments on behavior but pays less attention to underlying decision mechanisms. We argue that bridging these traditions can enrich both fields, particularly for understanding choices characterized by ambiguity and obscurity rather than clear optimal solutions. The article reviews key theories, models, and data sources from decision research relevant to sociological inquiry, discusses methodological challenges and opportunities for observing decision processes in real-world social contexts, and highlights the potential for cross-fertilization between sociology and decision science. By integrating insights from cognitive science with sociological perspectives on context, researchers can better understand how individuals navigate complex social choices and how context shapes decision strategies and outcomes.

title: Developing Difference: Social Organization and the Rise of the Auto Industries of South Korea, Taiwan, Spain, and Argentina
abstract: Theories of economic development as diverse as modernization, dependency, world-system, and market reform take a “critical factor” view. Proponents of each theory argue that countries fail to develop because of an obstacle to economic growth. We argue instead that neither a critical factor nor a single path leads to economic development; viable paths vary. Economic growth depends on linking a country's historically developed patterns of social organization to the opportunities of global markets. We formulate a sociological theory of cross-national comparative advantage including not only economic factor endowments but also institutionalized patterns of authority and organization. Such patterns legitimize certain actors and certain relationships among those actors, which facilitate development success in some activities but not in others. We illustrate this approach to understanding development outcomes with a comparative analysis of the difficult rise of the automobile assembly and components industries in South Korea, Taiwan, Spain, and Argentina.

title: Developing Difference: Social Organization and the Rise of the Auto Industries of South Korea, Taiwan, Spain, and Argentina
abstract: This paper examines the divergent development trajectories of the automobile industries in South Korea, Taiwan, Spain, and Argentina through a comparative institutional analysis. By focusing on the role of social organization, the study demonstrates how differences in state intervention, industrial policy, labor relations, and business networks shaped each country's path to industrialization and integration into the global automotive sector. The findings reveal that while all four countries faced similar challenges as late industrializers, their unique configurations of social and institutional arrangements led to distinct outcomes in terms of industry structure, competitiveness, and internationalization. The analysis underscores the importance of understanding local social dynamics and institutional contexts in explaining variations in economic development and highlights the limitations of universal models of industrial growth.

title: Difference Troubles: Queering Social Theory and Sexual Politics
abstract: teven Seidman examines the implications for social theory and sexual politics of taking difference seriously. He explores the troubles difference can make for the social sciences and for the very people--feminists, queer theorists, postmodernists--who champion difference. This is a wide-ranging and sophisticated discussion of contemporary social theory and sexual politics, focusing on difference, knowledge and power. It also argues persuasively for a pragmatic approach to questions of difference in theory and politics.

title: Difference Troubles: Queering Social Theory and Sexual Politics
abstract: This paper critically examines the historical and theoretical treatment of sexuality within sociology, arguing that classical and contemporary sociological traditions have largely assumed the naturalness and universality of Western sexual categories, particularly the hetero/homosexual binary and the normative status of heterosexuality. Drawing on insights from queer studies and Foucault’s theorization of sexuality as a social construct, the analysis reveals how bodies, desires, and sexual acts are imbued with meaning through social, political, and institutional processes. The paper highlights the silence of foundational sociological texts on sexual conflicts and identities, despite their emergence as central sites of public struggle in modernity alongside class, gender, and race. Through a rereading of canonical sociological works and an exploration of early engagements with sexuality in American sociology, the study demonstrates how sociology has both reflected and contributed to the construction of a sexual social system. Ultimately, it calls for a queering of social theory that interrogates the discipline’s implicit politics of sexual identity and rethinks its conceptual foundations to include the social formation of bodies and sexualities.

title: Discipline and Bounding: The History and Sociology of Science as Seen through the Externalism-Internalism Debate
abstract: From the beginning of the Second World War to the ending of the Cold War no problematic so deeply shaped the academic history and sociology of science than that inscribed in talk of 'internalism' and 'externalism'. Insofar as empirical work was deemed relevant to developing an overall appreciation of the nature of science, its dynamics and its relations with social and cultural environments, that relevance was locally achieved by gestures at opposed 'internalist' and 'externalist' theories, orientations, domains, and accompanying historiographic baggage. Students were initiated into the history and sociology of science by being told about these genres and the present state of play. Graduates' early orientation to their fields was achieved through affiliation with one or other genre and camp of practitioners. Reviews of the state of the history and sociology of science were seemingly obligated to use 'internalism' and 'externalism' as expository structures. Nowadays, however, historians of science commonly tell each other and their students that their discipline has transcended, outgrown or resolved those debates, and that it is a sign of the maturity of the field that references to the 'internal' and the 'external' have become less common or at least less unselfconscious. When uttered at all, the terms are likely to be surrounded by quotes, air-quotes or tones of voice. If in the 1960s the central problematic of the academic discipline known as the history of science was pointed to by reference to the 'internal' and the 'external', by the late 1980s such usages increasingly betrayed the amateur, the neophyte, the outsider, or the out of touch. Within a generation the discourse of 'internalism' and 'externalism' seems to have passed from the commonplace to the gauche. I want to suggest that this trajectory never transmitted the appropriate intermediate stages. I do not think that the theories indicated by 'externalism' and 'internalism' were ever properly defined or described. I do not think that the virtues of any defensible and coherent construals of these theories were ever properly considered and assessed.
