title: Discipline and Bounding: The History and Sociology of Science as Seen through the Externalism-Internalism Debate
abstract: This paper critically examines the externalism-internalism debate as a central axis in the history and sociology of science, analyzing how this dichotomy has shaped disciplinary boundaries and methodological approaches. By tracing the evolution of both perspectives, the study reveals how internalist accounts, focused on intellectual and conceptual developments within science, have been challenged by externalist approaches that emphasize social, cultural, and institutional contexts. The analysis demonstrates that the debate not only reflects differing explanatory priorities but also serves as a means of negotiating the identity and legitimacy of the history and sociology of science as disciplines. Ultimately, the paper argues that the persistence of this debate underscores ongoing tensions over what constitutes valid historical and sociological inquiry into science, highlighting the need for more integrative frameworks that transcend rigid disciplinary boundaries.

title: Durkheim and the Internet: On Sociolinguistics and the Sociological Imagination
abstract: In Durkheim and the Internet, Blommaert proposes new theories of social norms, social action, identity, social groups, integration, social structure and power, all of them animated by a deep understanding of language and social interaction. In drawing on Durkheim and other classical sociologists including Simmel and Goffman, this book is relevant to students and researchers working in sociolinguistics as well as offering a wealth of new insights to scholars in the fields of digital and online communications, social media, sociology, and digital anthropology.

title: Durkheim and the Internet: On Sociolinguistics and the Sociological Imagination
abstract: This book critically examines the foundational assumptions of sociolinguistics through the lens of Durkheim’s concept of the social fact, exploring how language operates as a normative collective system that both reflects and shapes social integration, inequality, and identity. By tracing the evolution of sociolinguistic theory from Durkheim’s era to the complexities introduced by digital communication and globalization, the work proposes new theoretical frameworks—including indexical-polynomic, genre, microhegemonic, and polycentric models—to account for the dynamic, fragmented, and polycentric nature of contemporary language practices online. Ultimately, the book argues for a renewed sociological imagination that recognizes theory as an evolving tool grounded in empirical research, capable of addressing the challenges posed by rapidly changing linguistic landscapes in the digital age.

title: Emotion, rationality, and decision-making: how to link affective and social neuroscience with social theory
abstract: In this paper, we argue for a stronger engagement between concepts in affective and social neuroscience on the one hand, and theories from the fields of anthropology, economics, political science, and sociology on the other. Affective and social neuroscience could provide an additional assessment of social theories. We argue that some of the most influential social theories of the last four decades—rational choice theory, behavioral economics, and post-structuralism—contain assumptions that are inconsistent with key findings in affective and social neuroscience. We also show that another approach from the social sciences—plural rationality theory—shows greater compatibility with these findings. We further claim that, in their turn, social theories can strengthen affective and social neuroscience. The former can provide more precise formulations of the social phenomena that neuroscientific models have targeted, can help neuroscientists who build these models become more aware of their social and cultural biases, and can even improve the models themselves. To illustrate, we show how plural rationality theory can be used to further specify and test the somatic marker hypothesis. Thus, we aim to accelerate the much-needed merger of social theories with affective and social neuroscience.

title: Emotion, rationality, and decision-making: how to link affective and social neuroscience with social theory
abstract: This paper advocates for a deeper integration between affective and social neuroscience and social theory, arguing that each field can significantly enhance the other. The authors review key findings from neuroscience that challenge core assumptions in influential social theories such as rational choice theory, behavioral economics, and post-structuralism, highlighting inconsistencies regarding human cognition, emotion, and decision-making. In contrast, plural rationality theory is shown to align more closely with neuroscientific evidence. The paper also demonstrates how social theories can refine neuroscientific models by providing precise definitions of social phenomena, raising awareness of cultural biases, and generating new hypotheses. Using plural rationality theory and the somatic marker hypothesis as an example, the authors illustrate how interdisciplinary collaboration can yield more comprehensive models of social evaluation in the brain. The review concludes by emphasizing the mutual benefits of merging social theory with affective and social neuroscience to advance understanding of emotion, rationality, and decision-making.

title: Handbook of constructionist research
abstract: Constructionism has become one of the most popular research approaches in the social sciences. But until now, little attention has been given to the conceptual and methodological underpinnings of the constructionist stance, and the remarkable diversity within the field. This cutting-edge handbook brings together a dazzling array of scholars to review the foundations of constructionist research, how it is put into practice in multiple disciplines, and where it may be headed in the future. The volume critically examines the analytic frameworks, strategies of inquiry, and methodological choices that together form the mosaic of contemporary constructionism, making it an authoritative reference for anyone interested in conducting research in a constructionist vein.

title: Handbook of constructionist research
abstract: The Handbook of Constructionist Research, edited by James A. Holstein and Jaber F. Gubrium, offers a comprehensive exploration of the diverse and evolving field of constructionist inquiry within sociology and related disciplines. Rather than seeking to rigidly define constructionism, the volume presents a mosaic of theoretical, methodological, and empirical contributions that collectively illustrate the versatility and richness of constructionist approaches. Spanning historical context, multidisciplinary perspectives, epistemological debates, and practical strategies, the handbook addresses key areas such as identity, health, gender, race, ethnicity, and national belonging through a constructionist lens. Notable sections highlight innovative methodologies like autoethnography and examine the social processes underlying medical knowledge and expertise. The final part engages with ongoing challenges and intersections with other research paradigms, stimulating critical reflection on the future directions of constructionist research. While some emerging topics are underrepresented, the handbook remains an essential resource for scholars and doctoral students seeking to deepen their understanding of social construction and to innovate within sociological research methodologies.

title: Mathematical models in the social sciences
abstract: As the need for more substantial mathematical training has increased among social science students, the lack of any adequate textbook between the very elementary and the very advanced levels has become crutial. The authors, long-time experts in this field, have answered the need with this volume, and the MIT Press has repsonded by bringing it into renewed circulation.Mathematical Models in the Social Sciences investigates and teaches the formation and analysis of mathematical models with detailed interpretations of the results. These models are self-contained, with the necessary mathematics included in each chapter. A vast range of topics in the social sciences and a wide variety of mathematical techniques are covered by the models. Ample opportunity is also provided for the students to form their own models. Republication of this book provides social science and mathematics students with a text that is the analogue of mathematical methods textbooks used in the study of the physical sciences and engineering. Prerequisites are kept to a minimum; a course in finite mathematics and a semester of calculus are all that is necessary.The chapters cover these main topics (and employ the mathematical approach parenthetically indicated): methodology; preference rankings (an axiomatic approach); ecology (two dynamic models); market stability (a dynamic model); a Markov chain model in sociology; stabilization of money flow (an application of discrete potential theory); branching processes; organization theory (applications of graph theory); and optimal scheduling (a problem in dynamic programming).

title: Mathematical models in the social sciences
abstract: This paper explores the development and application of mathematical models within the social sciences, emphasizing both methodological foundations and practical implementations across diverse domains. Beginning with a discussion on the methodology of constructing mathematical models, the work proceeds to examine preference rankings through an axiomatic lens and introduces dynamic models for ecological systems. Market stability is analyzed via a dynamic framework, while sociological phenomena are modeled using Markov chains. The stabilization of money flow is addressed through discrete potential theory, and branching processes are investigated for their relevance to social dynamics. Applications of graph theory in organization theory and dynamic programming in optimal scheduling are also presented. Appendices provide essential mathematical tools, including fixed point theorems, utility functions, finite Markov chains, generating functions, combinatorial lemmas, and functions of two variables. Collectively, the paper demonstrates how rigorous mathematical approaches can yield valuable insights into complex social systems.

title: Norbert Elias and Modern Sociology: Knowledge, Interdependence, Power, Process
abstract: This book explores the interplay between the making of Elias as a sociologist and the development of his core ideas relating to figurations, interdependence, and civilising processes. Focusing on the relevance of Elias's work for current debates within sociology, the authors centrally consider his contributions to the sociology of knowledge and methodology. Dunning and Hughes locate the work of Elias within a discussion of the crisis of sociology as a subject, and compare his figurational approach with the approaches of three major figures in modern sociology: Anthony Giddens, Michel Foucault and Pierre Bourdieu. This highly readable and engaging book will be essential reading for students and scholars of sociological theory and methods.

title: Norbert Elias and Modern Sociology: Knowledge, Interdependence, Power, Process
abstract: This book provides a comprehensive and accessible analysis of Norbert Elias’s enduring contribution to modern sociology, focusing on his theories of knowledge, interdependence, power, and process. Through a critical engagement with figurational sociology, Dunning and Hughes elucidate Elias’s central concepts and their relevance for understanding the development of sociological knowledge as a dynamic social process. The authors address methodological and value-related challenges in the discipline, situating Elias’s work within contemporary debates and disciplinary crises. By highlighting the relational and processual dimensions of Elias’s thought, the book demonstrates how his insights can help overcome fragmentation in sociological theory and practice, offering a path toward a more cumulative and coherent science of human social relations.

title: Rational Choice, Deterrence, and Social Learning Theory in Criminology: The Path Not Taken
abstract: 'Rational choice' theory, which is derived mainly from the expected utility model in economics,' has become a 'hot' topic in criminology, sociology, political science, and law. The evidence is compelling: respected journals have published a major collection of papers as well as several recent articles on the theory;2 sociological treatises and articles have been published in the 1980s on both macroand microrational choice models;3 and finally, James S. title: Rational Choice, Deterrence, and Social Learning Theory in Criminology: The Path Not Taken
abstract: This article critically examines the integration of rational choice and deterrence theories into criminology, arguing that their core concepts are not distinct theoretical advances but are instead special cases within the broader framework of social learning theory. While rational choice models, rooted in economic expected utility principles, have stimulated quantitative research and policy analysis in criminology, they have not contributed fundamentally new propositions to the understanding of criminal behavior. The article demonstrates that both deterrence (focused on fear of punishment) and rational choice (centered on cost-benefit calculations) can be subsumed under the differential reinforcement processes central to social learning theory, which accounts for a wider range of behavioral influences including rewards, punishments, and social context. The author contends that the relevance of learning principles to deterrence has been underappreciated and their applicability to rational choice largely ignored in criminological literature. By tracing the intellectual lineage and empirical applications of these theories, the article advocates for a more comprehensive behavioral approach that recognizes rational decision-making as one component within the general principles of social learning, thus charting a path for future theoretical development in criminology.

title: Social Control Theory and Delinquency.
abstract: Hirschi's social control theory proposes that delinquents fail to form or maintain a bond to society consisting of attachment, commitment, involvement, and belief. Using data from the Youth in Transition Study, the present report develops and tests multivariate models of social control theory which simultaneously consider how the four bond elements operate in relation to delinquency. Factor analysis and communality analysis examine the uniqueness of the four bond elements, and revised and additional measures are suggested. Background factors-measures of social class and ability-are added to the model, and a revised formulation of social control is suggested. title: Social Control Theory and Delinquency.
abstract: This dissertation examines the relationship between social control theory and delinquency, with a focus on extending Travis Hirschi’s influential model by incorporating the effects of educational experiences and social class background. Drawing on longitudinal data from the Marion County Youth Study, which followed a panel of male high school juniors from 1964 to 1967, the research replicates and expands upon Hirschi’s findings regarding the formation and stability of the social bond in adolescence. The study finds that while the social bond is initially formed within the family, its elements can change over time in response to school experiences and class position. Contrary to Hirschi’s assertion that social class is unrelated to delinquency or bond strength, this research demonstrates significant associations between social class, changes in the social bond, and rates of delinquent behavior. The results suggest that both primary group socialization and secondary institutional factors such as educational policies play important roles in shaping adolescent delinquency, highlighting the need for a more comprehensive model of social control that accounts for broader structural influences.

title: Social Norms and Economic Theory
abstract: Elster contrasts two distinct and frequently opposing social science traditions. One was fostered by Adam Smith and is carried forward today by neoclassical economists and rational-choice theorists in political science. It views humans as “economic men,” that is, as motivated by egoistic material concerns. The other tradition has its roots in the work of the French sociologist Emile Durkheim, provides the basis for much contemporary sociology and has adherents among political scientists, particularly political culture theorists such as Eckstein (1988). It views humans as social creatures, having duty-based and other obligations to their fellows. “Sociological man’s” activity is thus constrained by shared social (cultural) norms. Elster is skeptical that these cultural norms generally realize individual self-interest as this is understood in the rational-choice tradition. Indeed, elsewhere he distinguishes “economic man” rationality and “nonra-tional” cultural norms even more sharply than he does in this chapter (Elster 1989b). Overall, Elster holds that, for the most part, cultural norms neither arise from rationality, as neoclassical economists understand it, nor do they serve it.

title: Social Norms and Economic Theory
abstract: This paper explores the fundamental distinction between rational, outcome-oriented behavior as modeled in economic theory and norm-guided action as emphasized in sociology. Social norms, unlike rational choices, are not primarily motivated by future rewards or consequences but are sustained by shared expectations, emotional responses such as shame and guilt, and communal approval or disapproval. The analysis distinguishes social norms from related phenomena including moral, legal, and private norms, as well as habits and compulsions, highlighting their unique social and psychological underpinnings. Through diverse examples—ranging from consumption and work norms to reciprocity, retribution, cooperation, and distribution—the paper demonstrates the pervasive influence of norms on economic behavior. It critically examines attempts by economists to reduce norm-driven actions to forms of individual or collective optimization, arguing that while rationality and norms often interact and constrain each other, many social norms cannot be fully explained by self-interest or strategic manipulation. The paper concludes that understanding economic behavior requires integrating both rational choice and the autonomous motivational force of social norms.

title: Social sustainability: a catchword between political pragmatism and social theory
abstract: The sustainability concepts of the 'Brundtland-Report' and the 'Rio documents' call for a combination of ecological, economic, social and institutional aspects of social development. This paper describes briefly, several models of sustainability and discusses social sustainability as conceptualised in selected sustainability indicators. In an attempt to remedy the lack of sociological theory, the paper proposes a sustainability concept, which is based on the concepts of needs and work, as an activity to fulfil these needs and as the principal exchange process between society and nature. Moreover, this paper argues in favour of recognition of social sustainability as both a normative and analytical concept.

title: Social sustainability: a catchword between political pragmatism and social theory
abstract: This paper critically examines the concept of social sustainability, highlighting its evolution from a politically pragmatic catchword to a subject of social theory. By analyzing sustainability models and selected indicator frameworks, the authors reveal that social sustainability is often ambiguously defined and theoretically underdeveloped compared to its ecological and economic counterparts. The paper argues that current operationalizations frequently reflect political agendas rather than robust sociological foundations, resulting in inconsistent priorities and unclear integration among the three pillars of sustainability. To address these gaps, the authors propose a concept of social sustainability grounded in the notions of human needs and work, emphasizing their role as central processes linking society and nature. The paper concludes that social sustainability should be recognized as both an analytical and normative concept, necessitating clearer theoretical articulation to inform policy and practice.

title: The Architecture of Markets: An Economic Sociology of Twenty-First-Century Capitalist Societies
abstract: Market societies have created more wealth and more opportunities for more people, than any other system of social organization in history. Yet we still have a rudimentary understanding of how markets themselves are social constructions that require extensive institutional support. This groundbreaking work seeks to fill this gap, to make sense of modern capitalism by developing a sociological theory of market institutions. Addressing the dynamism that capitalism brings with it, Neil Fligstein argues that the basic drift of any market and its actors is toward stabilization.“The Architecture of Markets” represents a major and timely step beyond recent, largely empirical studies that oppose the neoclassical model of perfect competition but provide sparse theory toward a coherent economic sociology. Fligstein offers this theory. His political-cultural approach explains why governments remain crucial to markets and why so many national variations of capitalism endure. States help make stable markets possible by, for example, establishing the rule of law and adjudicating the class struggle. State-building and market-building go hand in hand.Fligstein shows that market actors depend mightily upon governments and the members of society for the social conditions that produce wealth. He demonstrates that systems favoring more social justice and redis¬tribution can yield stable markets and economic growth as readily as less egalitarian systems. The journal publishes the chapter 9, «Globalisation», excerpt from «The Architecture of Markets» by Neil Fligstein. The author questions why increasing globalisation has not resulted in convergence of organisational forms at national level. In search of an answer to this puzzle, Fligstein uses the analytical tools of a politicalcultural approach. As the main tasks of the chapter the author considers the development of working definitions of globalisation and a review of arguments demonstrating that globalists exaggerate the scope of its impact on the organisation of production, the state’s role in providing for their citizens and social stratification.

title: The Architecture of Markets: An Economic Sociology of Twenty-First-Century Capitalist Societies
abstract: This paper explores the architecture of markets in twenty-first-century capitalist societies through the lens of economic sociology, critically examining prevailing theoretical approaches and proposing a political-cultural framework for understanding market dynamics. Drawing on interdisciplinary perspectives, the study analyzes how social structures, cultural norms, and political institutions shape market organization, competition, and actor behavior. By synthesizing contemporary sociological theories, the research highlights the embeddedness of markets within broader societal contexts and addresses key challenges facing modern capitalism, including power relations, institutional change, and the interplay between economic and social forces. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how markets are constructed and maintained in an era marked by globalization, technological transformation, and evolving forms of governance.

title: The Cosmopolitan Imagination: The Renewal of Critical Social Theory
abstract: Gerard Delanty provides a comprehensive assessment of the idea of cosmopolitanism in social and political thought which links cosmopolitan theory with critical social theory. He argues that cosmopolitanism has a critical dimension which offers a solution to one of the weaknesses in the critical theory tradition: failure to respond to the challenges of globalization and intercultural communication. Critical cosmopolitanism, he proposes, is an approach that is not only relevant to social scientific analysis but also normatively grounded in a critical attitude. Delanty's argument for a critical, sociologically oriented cosmopolitanism aims to avoid, on the one hand, purely normative conceptions of cosmopolitanism and, on the other, approaches that reduce cosmopolitanism to the empirical expression of diversity. He attempts to take cosmopolitan theory beyond the largely Western context with which it has generally been associated, claiming that cosmopolitan analysis must now take into account non-Western expressions of cosmopolitanism.

title: The Cosmopolitan Imagination: The Renewal of Critical Social Theory
abstract: This article explores the renewal of critical social theory through the lens of cosmopolitanism, arguing for a shift from traditional universalist frameworks to a post-universal, critical cosmopolitanism that is both empirically grounded and normatively engaged. The paper situates cosmopolitanism as a dynamic response to the challenges of globalization and Europeanization, emphasizing its role as an alternative to both nationalism and uncritical globalism. It contends that cosmopolitanism should be understood as a process of self-transformation arising from encounters with others in contexts of global significance, rather than as a fixed Western or universalist project. The concept of critical cosmopolitanism is advanced as a methodological approach that bridges normative ideals and empirical realities, enabling the identification and assessment of diverse cosmopolitan projects across different societies, cultures, and political contexts. By highlighting the dialogic and deliberative dimensions of cosmopolitanism, the article demonstrates how it facilitates learning from others and fosters pluralized forms of belonging that transcend the limitations of both nation-state exclusivity and superficial cultural hybridity. Ultimately, the paper argues that critical cosmopolitanism offers a renewed framework for social analysis capable of addressing the complexities of identity, community, and global interdependence in the contemporary world.

title: The Great Transformation of Embeddedness: Karl Polanyi and the New Economic Sociology
abstract: I argue that in its adaptation from Karl Polanyi's The Great Transformation, the concept of embeddedness has itself undergone a great transformation. In the process, significant meanings of the concept have vanished, while others have been added. First I explore the different meanings the concept of embeddedness has achieved in the new economic sociology. Then I argue that it is not the embeddedness of economic action that should constitute the vantage point of economic sociology, but rather three coordination problems that actors face in economic exchange: the valuation of goods, competition and the problem of cooperation deriving from the social risks of exchange. I show that by proceeding from these coordination problems economic sociology, economic anthropology and economic history can find common research questions which allow them to enter into dialogue with each other more systematically. In the next section I focus on the social-reformist inclinations of Polanyi's use of the notion of embeddedness and thereby highlight a challenge posed in The Great Transformation that was largely not taken up by economic sociologists. Finally, I discuss limitations for developing a macro theory of the economy that result from making embeddedness the core concept of economic sociology.

title: The Great Transformation of Embeddedness: Karl Polanyi and the New Economic Sociology
abstract: This paper examines how the concept of embeddedness, originally articulated by Karl Polanyi in The Great Transformation, has itself undergone significant transformation within the new economic sociology. The analysis traces the shifting meanings of embeddedness, highlighting how certain aspects central to Polanyi’s original formulation have been lost while new interpretations have emerged. Rather than focusing solely on the embeddedness of economic action, the paper argues that economic sociology should center on three core coordination problems faced by actors in market exchange: valuation of goods, competition, and cooperation in light of social risks. By foregrounding these issues, the paper demonstrates how economic sociology, economic anthropology, and economic history can develop shared research agendas and foster interdisciplinary dialogue. The discussion also revisits the social-reformist dimension of Polanyi’s work, noting its relative neglect in contemporary scholarship. Finally, the paper addresses the limitations of using embeddedness as the foundational concept for macro-level theories of the economy, suggesting that a broader focus on coordination problems offers a more productive framework for understanding market societies.

title: The Interaction Order: American Sociological Association, 1982 Presidential Address
abstract: A presidential address faces one set of requirements, an article in a scholarly journal quite another. It turns out, then, that ASR's policy of publishing each year's ASA address provides the editor with an annual breather. Once a year the lead space can be allocated to a known name and the editor is quit of responsibility for standards that submissions rarely sustain: originality, logical development, readability, reasonable length. For in theory, a presidential address, whatever its character, must have some significance for the profession, even if only a sad one. More important, readers who were unable or unwilling to make the trip have an opportunity to participate vicariously in what can be read as the culmination of the meeting they missed. Not the best of warrants. My expectation, then, was not to publish this talk but to limit it to the precincts in which it was delivered. But in fact, I wasn't there either. What I offer the reader then is vicarious participation in something that did not itself take place. A podium performance, but only readers in the seats. A dubious offering. But something would have been dubious anyway. After all, like almost all other presidential addresses, this one was drafted and typed well before it was to be delivered (and before I knew it wasn't to be), and the delivery was to be made by reading from typescript not by extemporizing. So although the text was written as if in response to a particular social occasion, little of it could have been generated by what transpired there. And later, any publication that resulted would have employed a text modified in various ways after the actual delivery.

title: The Interaction Order: American Sociological Association, 1982 Presidential Address
abstract: In his 1982 American Sociological Association presidential address, Erving Goffman articulates his central theoretical contribution to sociology: the concept of the interaction order. He argues that face-to-face interactions constitute a distinct, ordered, and foundational domain of social life that cannot be reduced to broader social structures. Goffman examines how this interaction order interfaces with macrostructural dimensions of society, advocating for its analytical autonomy and the value of microanalysis in sociological research. The address also reflects on the ritualistic nature of academic ceremonies and the challenges inherent in sociological inquiry, ultimately underscoring the enduring significance of everyday interactions as a core subject for sociological analysis.

title: The Oxford handbook of sociology, social theory, and organization studies : contemporary currents
abstract: Sociology and social theory has always been a major source of new perspectives for organization studies. Access to a series of authoritative accounts of theorists and research themes in sociology and social theory which have influenced developments in organization studies is essential for those wishing to deepen and extend their knowledge of the intersection of sociology and organization studies. This goal is achieved by drawing on a group of internationally renowned scholars committed in their own work to strengthening these links and asking them to provide critical accounts of particular theorists and research themes which have straddled this divide.  This volume aims to strengthen ties between organization studies and contemporary sociological work at a time when there are increasing institutional barriers to such cooperation, potentially generating a myopia that constricts new developments. Used in conjunction with its companion volume, The Oxford Handbook of Sociology and Organization Studies: Classical Foundations, the reader is provided with a comprehensive account of the productive and critical interaction between sociology and organization studies over many decades.

title: The Oxford handbook of sociology, social theory, and organization studies : contemporary currents
abstract: This chapter examines the evolving relationship between social movement theory and organization studies, tracing their distinct historical origins and the gradual convergence of their analytical frameworks. Initially, social movement research focused on spontaneous, emotional collective action, often viewed as irrational and disruptive, while organization theory centered on rational, bureaucratic structures promoting stability and order. Over time, scholars in both fields began to recognize the interplay between movements and organizations, with social movement theorists incorporating concepts of formal organization, resources, and strategy, and organizational scholars drawing on movement theory to understand contestation and change within institutions. The chapter reviews key theoretical developments, highlights influential contributions that bridge the two traditions, and identifies emerging directions for research at their intersection, emphasizing how activism and grassroots mobilization inform our understanding of organizational dynamics and institutional transformation.

title: The Social Lens: An Invitation to Social and Sociological Theory
abstract: This fully updated Third Edition of Kenneth Allan’s acclaimed The Social Lens emphasizes the diversity of classical and contemporary theory, critical thinking, and the importance of historical context. Chosen for the diversity of their perspectives and their suitability for introducing students to contemporary social thought, a wide variety of theorists appear in the text with their individual voices vividly intact. The author engages students in the historic and contemporary changes that have spawned diverse social theories and invites them to see theory as an element within a broader range of critical thinking skills that can be applied to current social problems.

title: The Social Lens: An Invitation to Social and Sociological Theory
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive introduction to social and sociological theory, tracing the evolution of sociological thought from classical to contemporary perspectives. It examines foundational responses to modernity, the development of key theoretical frameworks such as structural functionalism, conflict theory, exchange theory, and critical theory, and explores the works of influential theorists including George Herbert Mead, Georg Simmel, Charlotte Perkins Gilman, and W. E. B. Du Bois. The analysis addresses core issues such as contradictions in capitalism, the irrationality of rationality, and the complexities of diversity, gender, and race. Attention is given to the construction of self and identity in modern society, the dynamics of power and social exchange, and the implications of globalizing systems and network societies. By integrating classical insights with contemporary critiques and new theoretical visions, the paper invites readers to engage with the ongoing challenges and possibilities inherent in understanding social structures, inequalities, and transformations in an increasingly complex world.

title: The Social Roots of Suicide: Theorizing How the External Social World Matters to Suicide and Suicide Prevention
abstract: The past 20 years have seen dramatic rises in suicide rates in the United States and other countries around the world. These trends have been identified as a public health crisis in urgent need of new solutions and have spurred significant research efforts to improve our understanding of suicide and strategies to prevent it. Unfortunately, despite making significant contributions to the founding of suicidology – through Emile Durkheim’s classic Suicide (1897/1951) – sociology’s role has been less prominent in contemporary efforts to address these tragic trends, though as we will show, sociological theories offer great promise for advancing our understanding of suicide and improving the efficacy of suicide prevention. Here, we review sociological theory and empirical research on suicide. We begin where all sociologists must: with Durkheim. However, we offer a more comprehensive understanding of Durkheim’s insights into suicide than the prior reviews provided by those in other disciplines. In so doing, we reveal the nuance and richness of Durkheim’s insights that have been largely lost in modern suicidology, despite being foundational to all sociological theories of suicide – even those that have moved beyond his model. We proceed to discuss broadly acknowledged limitations to Durkheim’s theory of suicide and review how more recent theoretical efforts have not only addressed those concerns, but have done so by bringing a larger swatch of sociology’s theoretical and empirical toolkit to bare on suicide. Specifically, we review how recent sociological theories of suicide have incorporated insights from social network theories, cultural sociology, sociology of emotions, and sociological social psychology to better theorize how the external social world matters to individual psychological pain and suffering. We conclude by making explicit bridges between sociological and psychological theories of suicide; by noting important limitations in knowledge about suicide – particularly regarding the roles of organizations, inequality, and intersectionality in suicide – that sociology is well situated to help address.

title: The Social Roots of Suicide: Theorizing How the External Social World Matters to Suicide and Suicide Prevention
abstract: This paper reviews and advances sociological theories of suicide, emphasizing the critical role of the external social world in shaping suicide risk and informing prevention strategies. Drawing on Durkheim’s foundational work, the authors provide a nuanced account of his concepts of social integration and regulation, highlighting their enduring relevance and the ways in which their complexity has been overlooked in contemporary suicidology. The review addresses limitations of Durkheim’s model and explores how recent sociological approaches—incorporating social network theories, cultural sociology, sociology of emotions, and social psychology—offer deeper insight into how collective structures and relationships influence individual psychological distress. The authors advocate for bridging sociological and psychological perspectives to enhance understanding and prevention of suicide, and identify key gaps in current knowledge, particularly regarding organizations, inequality, and intersectionality, that sociology is well positioned to address. This synthesis underscores the necessity of integrating sociological insights into public health responses to the ongoing suicide crisis.

title: The sociology of childhood
abstract: The Sociology of Childhood is the Second Edition of a text that has been universally acclaimed as the best book on the subject available today. It is the only text that thoroughly covers children and childhood from a sociological perspective. The Second Edition retains the same quality coverage of social theories of childhood, the consideration of children and childhood in historical and cultural perspective, children′s peer cultures from preschool through preadolescence, and the social problems of children. The book has been updated to include new research, information, and discussions on the latest social indicators regarding children in the United States and around the world.

title: The sociology of childhood
abstract: This report presents comprehensive state-level data on teenage pregnancy, birth, and abortion rates in the United States for 2008, with trends analyzed from 1988 to 2008 and birth data extended to 2010. Utilizing revised population estimates following the 2010 census, the study examines demographic variations by age, race, and ethnicity among women aged 15–19. Findings indicate substantial variation across states, with New Mexico reporting the highest and New Hampshire the lowest teen pregnancy rates in 2008. While overall teenage pregnancy rates declined in all states between 1988 and 2005, shifts from 2005 to 2008 were more variable, with some states experiencing increases. Racial and ethnic disparities are pronounced, with higher pregnancy rates among black and Hispanic teens in several states compared to non-Hispanic whites. The report underscores ongoing declines in teen pregnancy and abortion rates nationally but highlights persistent state-level and demographic disparities. Methodological considerations regarding population estimates and data limitations by race and ethnicity are discussed, emphasizing the importance of accurate demographic data for monitoring trends in adolescent reproductive health.

title: The Sutherland-Glueck Debate: On the Sociology of Criminological Knowledge
abstract: During the 1930, Edwin Sutherland established the sociological model of crime as the dominant paradigm in criminology and as a result became the most influential criminologist of the 20th century. This article examines Sutherland's debate with Sheldon Glueck and Eleanor Glueck about the causes of crime and the proper focus of social science research. Previously unavailable correspondence and unpublished papers are examined along with published works from the period (1925-45) when Sutherland was developing the theory of differential association and the Gluecks were launching research on criminal careers. The competing paradigms of the Gluecks and Sutherland are also placed in the socio-intellectual and institutional context in which they worked. It is shown that Sutherland's attack on the Gluecks' interdisciplinary research program was driven by: (a) a substantive version of sociological positivism that attempted to establish criminology as the proper domain of sociology, (b) a commitment to the method of analytic induction, and (c) Sutherland's rise to prominence in sociology. In addition, key aspects of the Gluecks' perspective reflecting their own professional interests in law and psychiatry further contributed to sociologists' hostile reaction. Nevertheless, the article presents evidence that the Gluecks' research on such fundamental issues as age and crime, criminal careers, and social control is more correct than commonly believed and, in fact, occupies center stage in contemporary research.

title: The Sutherland-Glueck Debate: On the Sociology of Criminological Knowledge
abstract: This article analyzes the intellectual and institutional dynamics underlying the influential debate between Edwin Sutherland and Sheldon and Eleanor Glueck regarding the causes of crime and the direction of criminological research. Drawing on previously unpublished correspondence, archival materials, and published works from 1925 to 1945, the authors situate the Sutherland-Glueck exchange within its broader socio-intellectual context, highlighting how Sutherland’s commitment to sociological positivism and analytic induction led him to challenge the Gluecks’ interdisciplinary, multiple-factor approach to crime. The paper argues that Sutherland’s efforts to establish criminology as a domain of sociology contributed to the marginalization of the Gluecks’ work, despite its foundational contributions to contemporary issues such as age-crime relationships, criminal careers, longitudinal research, and social control theory. By reassessing the debate and the enduring relevance of the Gluecks’ findings, the article demonstrates that disciplinary boundaries and professional interests shaped not only the trajectory of criminological knowledge but also perceptions of scientific legitimacy within the field.

title: Towards a general theory of implementation
abstract: Understanding and evaluating the implementation of complex interventions in practice is an important problem for healthcare managers and policy makers, and for patients and others who must operationalize them beyond formal clinical settings. It has been argued that this work should be founded on theory that provides a foundation for understanding, designing, predicting, and evaluating dynamic implementation processes. This paper sets out core constituents of a general theory of implementation, building on Normalization Process Theory and linking it to key constructs from recent work in sociology and psychology. These are informed by ideas about agency and its expression within social systems and fields, social and cognitive mechanisms, and collective action. This approach unites a number of contending perspectives in a way that makes possible a more comprehensive explanation of the implementation and embedding of new ways of thinking, enacting and organizing practice.

title: Towards a general theory of implementation
abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of understanding and evaluating the implementation of complex interventions in healthcare by proposing a general theory of implementation. Building on Normalization Process Theory and integrating constructs from sociology and psychology, the paper develops a theoretical framework that explains implementation as a dynamic process shaped by the interplay between emergent expressions of agency and contextual resources. Four core constructs—capability, contribution, capacity, and potential—are defined to capture agentic actions and contextual elements influencing implementation. The framework is illustrated through its application to clinical practice guideline implementation in nursing, demonstrating its utility for generating context-specific theories of practice. The paper concludes by discussing the limits of the proposed theory and emphasizing its relevance for advancing comprehensive, interdisciplinary approaches to implementation science.

title: Women Directors on Corporate Boards: A Review and Research Agenda
abstract: This review examines how gender diversity on corporate boards influences corporate governance outcomes that in turn impact performance. We describe extant research on theoretical perspectives, characteristics and impact of women directors on corporate boards (WOCB) at micro, meso and macro levels: individual, board, firm and industry/environment. Research Finding/Insights: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive review of WOCBs, incorporating and integrating research from over 400 publications in psychology, sociology, leadership, gender, finance, management, law, corporate governance and entrepreneurship domains. In addition, we organized our findings to provide a new lens enabling the field to be readily examined by level and by theoretical perspective. The review indicates that WOCB research is about improving corporate governance through better use of the whole talent pool’s capital, as well as about building more inclusive and fairer business institutions that better reflect their present generation stakeholders. Theoretical/Academic Implications: With only one in ten papers addressing theoretical development, the predominant perspectives are human and social capital theories and gender schema at individual level; social identity, token and social networks theories at board level; resource dependency, institution and agency theories at firm level, and institutional, critical and political theories at environmental level. We provide a short synopsis of findings at each level, and conclude with an outline of fruitful directions for future research. Practitioner/Policy Implications: There are increasing pressures for WOCBs, from diverse stakeholders such as the European Commission, national governments, politicians, employer lobby groups, shareholders, Fortune and FTSE rankings, best places for women to work lists as well as expectations from highly qualified women who are likely to leave if they see no women board members. Rationales generally draw on the business case, however the moral justice case is also used by those who seek a fairer gender balance in all aspects of society. From our review, the ‘Impact’ section charts the effect of WOCB at all four levels of analysis.

title: Women Directors on Corporate Boards: A Review and Research Agenda
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive review of over 400 publications examining the presence and impact of women directors on corporate boards (WOCB) across individual, board, firm, and industry/environmental levels. Synthesizing interdisciplinary research from psychology, sociology, leadership, gender studies, finance, management, law, and entrepreneurship, the review identifies key theoretical perspectives including human and social capital, gender schema, social identity, tokenism, resource dependency, institutional and agency theories. Findings reveal that while much of the literature is descriptive and lacks strong theoretical grounding, WOCB research is increasingly framed as both a business imperative for effective corporate governance and a matter of social justice for more inclusive institutions. The review highlights growing stakeholder pressures for gender-diverse boards and notes that women directors bring distinct qualifications and experiences to boardrooms. The paper concludes by outlining gaps in current research and proposing a future agenda emphasizing theory development and multi-level analysis to better understand the mechanisms and outcomes associated with women’s board participation.
